Sections 51 to 66 deal with working hours of adults. 
1. Weekly hours (S. 51) 
No adult worker shall be required or allowed to work in a factory for more than forty-eight hours in a week. 
2. Weekly holidays (S. 52) 
An adult worker shall not be required or allowed to work on the first day of the week unless— 
(a) he has or will have a holiday for a whole day on one of the three days im- Mediately before or after the said day; and 
(b) the manager has, before the said day or the substituted day, whichever is earlier (i) delivered a notice at the Inspector’s Office of working on that day and the day to substituted, and (ii) displayed such notice in the fac- tory. This notice may be cancelled in the same manner. 
The provisions of clause (b) above will operate on a notice being delivered by the employer at the office of the Inspector of his intention to require the worker to work on the said day, i.e. Sunday, and of the day which is to be substituted. Where a worker was required to work in a factory without giving notice to the Inspector and without fixing notice in the manner prescribed by the Act it was held that there was only one offence. 
No substitution can be made which will result in any worker working for more than 10 consecutive days without a holiday for a whole day. Where any worker works on the said day and has had a holiday on one of the three days immediately before it, that said day shall be included in the preceding week for calculating his weekly hours of work. 
200 


236 Part II—The Factories Act, 1948 
This provision, which is designed to enable the more important religious festivals 
to be substituted for Sundays appear to give general satisfaction, and in a few centres 
there are more holidays on substituted days than on Sundays. (Report of the Royal 
Commission on Labour.) 
The intendment of the section is not that the employers will at their sweet will con- 
vert successive on all the Sundays primarily intended to be holidays as working days 
and make any other working day of the week a holiday instead of Sunday. 
3. Compensatory Holidays (S. 53) 
Where, as a result of the passing of an order or the making of a rule under the pro- 
visions of the Act exempting a factory or the workers from the provisions of section 
52, a worker is deprived of any of the weekly holidays for which provision is made 
in S. 52(1), he shall be allowed, within the month in which the holidays were due to 
him or within the two months immediately following that month, compensatory holi- 
days of equal number to the holidays so lost. [Sub-s. (1)]. 
The State Government may prescribe the manner in which the holidays for which 
provision is made in sub-section (1) shall be allowed. [Sub-s. (2)]. 
4, Daily Hours (S. 54) 
According to S. 54, subject to the provisions of S. 51, no adult worker shall be re- 
quired or allowed to work in a factory for more than nine hours in any day. 
Subject, however, to the previous approval of the Chief Inspector, the daily maxi- 
mum specified hours in this section may be exceeded in order to facilitate the change 
of shifts. 
5. Intervals for rest (S. 55) 
The periods of work of adult workers in a factory each day has to be so fixed that 
no period shall exceed five hours and that no worker shall work for more than five 
hours before he has had an interval for rest of at least half an hour. [Sub-s. (1)]. 
The State Government or, subject to the control of the State Government, the Chief 
Inspector, may, by written order and for specified reasons, exempt any factory from 
the provisions of sub-section (1). But the total number of hours worked by a worker 
without an interval should not exceed six. 
“Merely because a factory enjoyed an exception as regards the section, it cannot be 
presumed that it was not required to observe the provision of Section 61.” There is 
no longer nay distinction between seasonal and non-seasonal factories. “As the 
hours of daily work have been reduced to nine, the period of work before rest has 
been reduced to five, the State Government has been empowered to prescribe a 
higher limit of rest up to one hour in case where they consider a longer rest interval is 
necessary.” 
Mere presence of workers during rest intervals is not violation of law, unless it is 
proved that they were required or allowed to work, there is no offence. 
Absence of mens rea is good defence to contravention of section 555

6. Spread over (S. 56) 
The periods of work of an adult worker in a factory shall be so arranged that inclu- 
sive of his intervals for rest under section 55, they shall not be spreadover to more 
than ten and a half hours in any day. 
The Chief Inspector may, for reasons to be specified in writing increase the spread 
over up to twelve hours. 
7. Night shifts (S. 57) 
Where a worker in a factory works on a shift which extends beyond midnight,— 
(a) for the purposes of sections 52 and 53, a holiday for a whole day shall 
mean in his case a period of twenty-four consecutive hours beginning when 
his shift ends; | 
(b) the following day for him shall be deemed to be the period of twenty-four 
hours beginning when such shift ends, and the hours he has worked after 
midnight shall be counted in the previous day. 
8. Prohibition of overlapping shifts (S. 58) 
According to s. 58, no work shall be carried on by means of a system of shifts in 
such a way that more than one relay of workers is engaged in work of the same kind 
at the same time. The State Government may exempt any factory or class of factories 
or any category of workers, from this provision. In exercise of this power printing 
press attached to the newspaper offices have been exempted subject to certain condi- 
tions. 
9, Extra wages or overtime (S. 59) 
A worker working in excess of 9 hours in any day or 48 hours in any week shall be 
entitled to wages at the rate of twice his ordinary rate of wages for overtime work. 
[Sub-s. (1)]. : 
For the purposes of sub-section (1), ordinary rate of wages means the basic wages plus 
such allowances inciuding the cash equivalent of the advantage accruing through the 
concessional sale to workers of foodgrains and other articles, as the worker is for the time 
being entitled to, but does not include a bonus and wages for overtime work. [Sub-s. (2)]. 
The claim for inclusion of house rent allowance notionally is not sustainable.” 
Where any workers in a factory are paid on a piece rate basis the time rate shall 
be deemed to be equivalent to the daily average of their full-time earnings for the 
days on which they actually worked on the same or identical job during the month 
immediately preceding the calendar month during which the overtime work was 
done, and such time rates shall be deemed to be the ordinary rates of wages of 
those workers. 
In the case of a worker who has not worked in the immediately preceding calen- 
dar month on the same or identical job, the time rate shall be deemed to be equiva- 
lent to the daily average of the earning of the worker for the days on which he ac- 
tually worked in the week in which the overtime work was done. 
5. Union of India v. Suresh C. Baskey, 1996-1 LLJ 1094: AIR 1996 SC 849. 


238 Part II—The Factories Act, 1948 
The Explanation to the section says that for the purposes of this sub-section in 
computing the earnings for the days on which the worker actually worked, such 
allowances including the cash equivalent of the advantage accruing through the 
concessional sale to workers of foodgrains and other articles, as the worker is for 
the time being entitled to shall be included but any bonus or wages for overtime 
work payable in relation to the period with reference to which the earnings are be- 
ing computed shali be excluded. | 
The cash equivalent of the concessional sale of foodgrains and other articles shall 
be computed as often as prescribed on the basis of the maximum quantity of food- 
grains and other articles admissible to a “standard family”. 
“Standard family” means a family consisting of the worker, his or her spouse and 2 
children below the age of 14 years requiring in all 3 adult consumption units. 
“Adult consumption unit” means the consumption unit of a male above the age of 
14 years. The consumption units of a female above 14 years and a child below 14 
years shall be calculated at the rate of 0.8 and 0.6 respectively of one adult consump- 
tion unit. 
The State Government may frame rules for computation in cash of concessional 
sale of foodgrains and other articles to workers and for maintenance of registers in 
connection with it. 
In the case of Mahalaxmi Mills, Beawar v. Labour Court, Jaipur® it has been 
held that section 59 creates an obligation on the employer to pay extra wages for 
overtime if a worker works for more than 9 hours in any day or for more than 48 
hours in any week. In another case, it was held by the Supreme Court that S. 59 
of the Factories Act, 1948 defines “ordinary rate of wages” (in order to calculate 
overtime allowance) as basic wages plus allowance including the cash equivalent 
of food grains and other articles but not bonus and wages for overtime work. 
Since the legislature has not included the cash equivalent of house accommoda- 
tion, it would be fallacious to include an allowance “notionally” which has been 
excluded, specifically. 
In a case of piece-rated workers, the Supreme Court held that S. 59 of the Factories 
Act, 1948 in a strict sense applies to cases of overtime work beyond 9 hours a day or 
48 hours a week. The grant of overtime wages for the period in excess of the normal 
working hours of 44-3/4 per week and up to 48 hours is governed by the relevant 
Departmental Rules. Section 59(1) comes into play only if the piece-rated worker has 
worked beyond 9 hours in.a day or 48 hours in a week and not otherwise. The deci- 
sion in Union of India v. V.G.H. Kokil,® is not applicable to the facts of this particular 
case. 
10. Restriction on Double Employment (S. 60) 
Section 60 says that no adult worker shall be required or allowed to work in any 
factory on any day on which he has already been working in any other factory, save 
in such circumstances as may be prescribed.

11. Notice of periods of work for adults (S. 61) 
In section 61, there are 10 sub-sections which deal with details of notice of periods of work for adults. According to sub-section (1) a factory has to display a correctly maintained in accordance with the provisions of S. 108(2) a notice of periods of work for adults, showing clearly for every day the periods during which adult workers may be required to work. [Sub-s. (1)]. 
The periods shown in the notice required by sub-section (1) shall be fixed before- hand in accordance with the provisions of this section, and shall be such that workers working for those periods would not be working in contravention of any of the provi- sions of sections 51, 52, 54, 55, 56 and 58. [Sub-s. (2)].'° 
Where all the adult workers in a factory are required to work during the same peri- ods, the manager of the factory has to fix those periods for such workers generally. [Sub-s. (3)]. 
Where all the adult workers in a factory are not required to work during the same periods, the manager of the factory has to classify them into groups ac- cording to the nature of their work indicating the number of workers in each group. [Sub-s. (4)]. 
For each group which is not required to work on a system of shifts, the manager of the factory has to fix the periods during which the group may be required to work. [Sub-s. (5)]. 
Where any group is required to work on a system of shifts and the relays are not to be subject to predetermined periodical changes of shifts, the manager of the factory has to fix the periods during which each relay of the group may be required to work. 
[Sub-s. (6)]. 
Where any group is to work on a system of shifts and the relays are to be subject to predetermined periodical changes of shifts, the manager of the factory has to draw up a scheme of shifts where under the periods during which any relay of the group may be required to work and the relay which will be working at any time of the day can 
be known for any day. [Sub-s. (7)]. 
The State Government may prescribe forms of the notice required by sub-section 
(1) and the manner in which it has to be maintained. [Sub-s. (8)]. A 
In the case of a factory beginning work after the commencement of this Act, a copy of the notice referred to in sub-section (1) has to be sent in duplicate to the Inspector 
before the day on which work is begun in the factory. [Sub-s. (9)]. | 
Any proposed change in the system of work in any factory which will necessitate a change in the notice referred to in sub-section (1) has to be notified to the Inspector 
in duplicate before the change is made, and except with the previous sanction of the Inspector, no such change shall be made until one week has elapsed since the last 
change. [Sub-s. (10)]. 
12. Register of adult workers (S. 62) 
Section 62 of the Factories Act, 1948 says that the manager of every factory has to 
maintain a register of adult workers, to be available to the Inspector at all times dur- 
ing working hours, or when any work is being carried on in the fa¢tory, showing— 
10. S.M. Datta v. State of Gujarat, (2001) 7 SCC 659 : AIR 2001 SC 3253 : (2002) 1 LLJ 3, entries are required to be made “before hand”’. 


240 Part II—The Factories Act, 1948 
(a) the name of each adult worker in the factory. 
(b) the nature of his work. 
(c) the group, if any, in which he is included. 
(d) where his group works on shifts, the relay to which he is allotted. 
(e) such other particulars as may be prescribed. 
If the Inspector is of opinion that any muster roll or register maintained as part of 
the routine of a factory gives in respect of any or all the workers in the factory the 
particulars required under this section, he may, by order in writing, direct that such 
muster roll or register shall to the corresponding extent be maintained in place of, 
and be treated as, the register of adult workers in that factory. 
It is further provided in sub-section (1A) that no adult worker shall be required or 
allowed to work in any factory unless his name and other particulars have been en- 
tered in the register of adult workers. 
The State Government may prescribe the form of the register of adult workers, the 
manner in which it is to be maintained and the period for which it shall be preserved. 
These provisions have to be liberally construed and the register should be honestly 
maintained. Good faith or bona fide practices or absence of mens rea are not good 
defences as there is absolute and statutory liability. 
It has been held that a separate and distinct offence is not committed in respect of 
each particular which is omitted to be shown in the register of adult workers but it is 
the failure to maintain a register of adult workers showing the various particulars that 
constitute the offence, whether it be one or two or many.’ 
13. Hours of work to correspond with notice under S. 61 and register under 
S. 62 (S. 63) 
Section 63 says that no adult worker shall be required or allowed to work in any 
factory otherwise than in accordance with the notice of periods of work for adults 
displayed in the factory and the entries made beforehand against his name in the reg- 
ister of adult workers of the factory. 
14. Power to make exempting rules (S. 64) 
Section 64 defines the power of the State Government to make exempting rules re-

dential positions. |

son, other than a person defined by such rules, as a person holding position of super- 
vision or management or employed in a confidential position in a factory if, in the 
opinion of the Chief Inspector, such person holds such position or is so employed, 
and the provisions of this Chapter, other than the provisions of clause (b) of sub-

(1) the total number of hours of work in any day shall not exceed ten. 
(1i) the spread-over inclusive of intervals for rest shall not exceed 12 hours in 
any day. 
It may, however, be prescribed that subject to conditions specified, these twin re- 
strictions shall not apply to workers engaged in work which for technical reasons 
must be carried on continuously, to enable a shift worker to work the whole or part of 
a subsequent shift in the place of an absentee worker. 
(iii) The total number of hours of overtime shall not exceed sixty for any one 
quarter. ‘Quarter’ means a period of three consecutive months beginning on 
the Ist of January, April, July and October. (Explanation) 
Reference my be made to Rule 102 and its Schedule for exemptions relating to 
adult workers. 
Sub-section (5) provides that rules made under this section shall remain in force for 
not more than five years. 
15. Power to make exempting orders (S. 65) 
Section 65 which provides for the power of the State Government to make ex- 
empting orders says that the State Government can relax or modify the provisions 
relating to the notice of periods of work for adults in case of factories where owing to 
the nature of work it is unreasonable to fix such periods beforehand. It may also ex- 
empt adult workers from provisions relating to weekly hours, weekly holidays and 
daily hours, to enable the factory or factories to deal with an exceptional pressure of 
work subject to the limitation in respect of working hours for adult workers set out 
above. 
Any exemption granted under sub-section (2) of sec. 65 shall be subject to the fol- 
lowing conditions, namely:— 
(1) the total number of hours of work in any day shall not exceed twelve: 
(ii) the spreadover, inclusive of intervals for rest shall not exceed thirteen hours 
in any one day; 
(ili) the total number of hours of work in any week, including overtime, shall 
not exceed sixty; 
(iv) no worker shall be allowed to work overtime for more than seven days at a 
stretch and the total number of hours of overtime work in any quarter shall 
not exceed seventy-five. 


242 Part II—The Factories Act, 1948 
The Explanation attached to the section says that in this sub-section “quarter” has 
the same meaning as in S. 64(4) i.e., “Quarter” means a period of three consecutive 
months beginning on the Ist of January, the Ist of April, the Ist of July or the Ist of 
October. 
16. Further restrictions on employment of women (S. 66) 
Section 66 of the Factories Act, 1948 provides that the provisions of this Chapter 
shall, in their application to women in factories, be supplemented by the following 
further restrictions, namely:— 
(a) no exemption from the provisions of section 54 may be granted in respect 
of any woman; 
(b) no woman shall be required or allowed to work in any factory except be- 
tween the hours of 6 A.M. and 7 P.M. 
The State Government may, however, by notification in the Official Ga- 
zette, in respect of any factory or group or class or description of factories, 
vary the limits laid down in clause (b), but so that no such variation shall 
authorize the employment of any woman between the hours of 10 P.M. and 
3AM. 
(c) there shall be no change of shifts except after a weekly holiday or any other 
holiday. [Sub-s. (1)]. 
The State Government may make rules providing for exemption from the restric- 
tions set out in sub-section (1), to such extent and subject to such conditions as it 
may prescribe, of women working in fish-curing or fish-canning factories, where the 
employment of women beyond the hours specified in the said restrictions is neces- 
sary to prevent damage to, or deterioration in, any raw material. [Sub-s. (2)]. 
The rules made under sub-section (2) shall remain in force for not more than three 
years at a time. [Sub-s. (3)].

Sections 67 to 77 deal with employment of young persons in factories. 
1. Prohibition of employment of young children (S. 67) 
Any child who has not completed his fourteenth year shall not be required or per- 
mitted to work in a factory. In an important case of M.C. Mehta v. State of Tamil 
Nadu,’ the Supreme Court held that the employment of children within match facto- 
ries directly connected with the manufacturing process up to final production of 
match sticks or fireworks should not at all be permitted. 
2. Working hours for children (S. 71) 
Another section which deals with employment of children in factories is section 71 
which provides for working hours for children. It says that no child shall be em- 
ployed or permitted to work, in any factory— 
(a) for more than four and a half hours in any day; 
(b) during the night. 
The Explanation to the section says that for the purpose of this sub-section “night” 
shall mean a period of at least twelve consecutive hours which shall include the in- 
terval between 10 P.M. and 6 A.M. [Sub-s. (1)]. 
The period of work of all children employed in a factory has to be limited to two 
shifts which shall not overlap or spread over more than five hours each; and each 
child shall be employed in only one of the relays which shall not, except with the 
previous permission in writing of the Chief Inspector, be changed more frequently 
than once in a period of thirty days. [Sub-s. (2)]. 
The provisions of section 52 shall apply also to child workers and no exemption 
from the provisions of that section may be granted in respect of any child. 
No child can be required or allowed to work in any factory on any day on which he 
has already been working in another factory. 
1. AIR 1991 SC.417 : (1991) 1 SCC 283. 
243 


244 Part I]—The Factories Act, 1948 
No female child can be required or allowed to work in any factory except between 
8 A.M. and 7 P.M. - 
3. Notice of periods of work for children (S. 72) 
According to section 72, there shall be displayed and correctly maintained in every 
factory in which children are employed, in accordance with the provisions of 
S. 108(2) a notice of periods of work for children, showing clearly for every day the 
periods during which children may be required or allowed to work. [Sub-s. (1)]. 
The periods shown in the notice required by sub-section (1) shall be fixed before- 
hand in accordance with the method laid down for adult workers in section 61, and 
shall be such that children working for those periods would not be working in con- 
travention of any of the provisions of section 71. 
The provisions of S. 61(8), (9) and (10) shall apply also to the notice required by 
sub-section (1) of this section. 
4. Register of child workers (S. 73) 
The manager of every factory in which children are employed has to maintain a 
register of child workers, to be available to the Inspector at all times during working 
hours or when any work is being carried on in a factory, showing— : 
(a) the name of each child worker in the factory, 
(b) the nature of his work, 
(c) the group, if any, in which he is included, 
(d) where his group works on shifts, the relay to which he is allotted, and 
(e) the number of his certificate of fitness granted under section 69. 
No child worker shall be required or allowed to work in any factory unless his 
name and other particulars have been entered in the register of child workers. 
The State Government may prescribe the form of the register of child workers, the 
manner in which it shall be maintained and the period for which it shall be preserved. 
5. Non-adult workers to carry tokens (S. 68) 
‘According to s. 68, a child who has completed his fourteenth year or an adolescent 
shall not be required or allowed to work in any factory unless— 
(a) a certificate of fitness granted with reference to him under section 69 is in 
the custody of the manager of the factory, and 
(b) such child or adolescent carries while he is at work a token giving a refer- 
ence to such certificate. 
6. Certificate of fitness (S. 69) 
Section 69 provides that on the application of any young person or his parent or 
guardian, with the manager’s recommendation, or that of the manager himself, 
such person shall be examined by the Certifying Surgeon who may grant in the 
prescribed form or renew the certificate of fitness if he is satisfied (a) that the child 
is above 14 years; (b) that the young person has completed his fifteenth year and is 
fit for full work. Where the place of work of the child or young person and the 
manufacturing process in which he is likely to be engaged are not known person- 


Chap. VII—Employment of Young Persons 245 
ally to the Certifying Surgeon, he shall not grant or renew a certificate unless he 
has examined such place. 
A certificate of fitness granted or renewed shall be valid only for a period of 12 
months from its date of issue. It may also be subject to conditions regarding the na- 
ture of the work in which the child or the young person may be employed or his re- 
examination before the expiry of 12 months. In such a case, the child or young per- 
son shall not be required or allowed to work without fulfilment of the specified con- 
dition. A certificate may be revoked by the Certifying Surgeon, if in his opinion, the 
holder of it is no longer fit to work in the capacity stated therein. In case of refusal by 
the Certifying Surgeon to grant or renew a certificate or revocation of certificate, the 
Certifying Surgeon must state his reasons in writing for so doing. Any fee for the . 
certificate shall be paid by the occupier and shall not be recoverable from the young 
person, his parent or guardian. 
7. Effect of certificate of fitness granted to adolescent (S. 70) 
Section 70 says that an adolescent with such a certificate of fitness shall be deemed 
to be an adult for the purposes of provisions relating to working hours for adults and 
employment of young persons. However, such adolescent below the age of 17 shall 
not be employed on night duty. ‘Night’ means a period of at least 12 consecutive 
hours which include an interval of at least seven consecutive hours between 10 p.m. 
and 7 a.m. An adolescent without such certificate of fitness shall be deemed to be a 
child, notwithstanding his age. 
8. Hours of work to correspond with notice under S. 72 and register under S. 73 
(S. 74) 
No child shall be employed in any factory otherwise than in accordance with the 
notice of periods of work for children displayed in the factory and the entries made 
beforehand against his name in the register of child workers of the factory. 
9. Power to require medical examination (S. 75) 
According to section 75, an Inspector is empowered to direct the manager or have 
a young persons examined by a Certifying Surgeon, if he is satisfied that he is work- 
ing without a certificate of fitness or he is no longer fit to work in the capacity stated 
in the certificate and not to employ him in the meanwhile. 
10. Power to make rules (S. 76) 
According to S. 76, the State Government may make rules— 
(a) prescribing the forms of certificates of fitness to be granted under S. 69, 
providing for the grant of duplicates in the event of loss of original certifi- 
cates, and fixing the fees which may be charged for such certificates and 
renewals and such duplicates; 
(b) prescribing the physical standards to be attained by children and adoles- 
cents working in factories; 
(c) regulating the procedure of certifying surgeons under this chapter; 
(d) specifying other duties which certifying surgeons may be required to per- 
form in connection with the employment of young persons in factories, and 
fixing the fees which may be charged for such duties and the persons by 
whom they shail be payable. 


246 Part II—The Factories Act, 1948 
11. Certain other provisions of law not barred (S. 77) 
The provisions of this Chapter shall be in addition to and not in derogation of the 
provisions of Employment of Children Act, 1938 (XXVI of 1938).

1. Applicability 
These provisions shall not prejudice any rights of workers under any other law, award, agreement (including settlement) or contract of service. Where such award, 
agreement or settlement or contract of service provides for annual leave longer than that under the provisions herein, the worker shall be entitled only to such longer an- nual leave but in matters not covered or provided for less favourably by them, the provisions of sections 79 to 82 so far as applicable will apply. Workers in railway workshops administered by the Government shall be governed by leave rules applied » by the Central Government and provisions of this Act will not be applicable to them. 
2. Annual leave with wages (S. 79) 
Section 79 of Chapter VIII of the Factories Act, 1948 deals with annual leave with wages. Sub-section (1) says that every worker who has worked for a period of 240 days or more in a factory during a calendar year shall be allowed during the subse- quent calendar year, leave with wages for a number of days calculated at the rate of-— 
(i) if an adult, one day for every twenty days of work performed by him during 
the previous calendar year; . 
(ii) if a child, one day for every fifteen days of work performed by him during 
the previous calendar year. 
The Explanation to the section says that for the purposes of this sub-section— 
(a) any days of lay off, by agreement or contract or as permissible under the 
standing orders; 
(b) in the case of a female worker, maternity leave for any number of days not 
exceeding twelve weeks; and 
(c) the leave earned in the year prior to that in which the leave is enjoyed, 
247 


248 Part II—The Factories Act, 1948 
shall be deemed to be days on which the worker has worked in a factory for the pur- 
pose of computation of the period of 240 days or more, but he shall not earn leave for 
these days. 
The second Explanation says that the leave admissible under this sub-section shall 
be exclusive of all holidays whether occurring during or at the either end of the pe- 
riod of leave. [Sub-s. (1)]. 
A worker whose service commences otherwise than on the first day of January 
shall be entitled to leave with wages at the rate laid down in clause (i) or, clause (11) 
of sub-section (1) if he has worked for two-thirds of the total number of days in the 
remainder of the calendar year. [Sub-s. (2)]. 
If a worker is discharged or dismissed from service or quits his employment or is 
superannuated or dies while in service, during the course of the calendar year, he or 
his heir or nominee shall be entitled to wages in lieu of the quantum of leave to 
which he was entitled immediately before his discharge, dismissal, quitting of em- 
ployment, superannuation or death calculated at the rates specified in sub-section (1) 
even if he had not worked for the entire period specified in that sub-section or sub- 
‘section (2) making him eligible to avail of such leave. Such payment shall be made— 
(i) where the worker is discharged or dismissed or quits employment, before 
the expiry of the second working day from the date of such discharge, dis- 
missal or quitting; and 
(ii) where the worker is superannuated or dies while in service, before the ex- 
piry of two months from the date of such superannuation or death. [Sub-s. 
(3)]. 
In calculating leave under this section, fraction of leave of half a day or more shall 
be treated as one full day’s leave, and fraction of less than half a day shall be omit- 
ted. {Sub-s. (4)]. 
If a worker does not in any one calendar year take the whole of the leave allowed 
to him under sub-section (1) or sub-section (2), as the case may be, any leave not 
taken by him shall be added to the leave to be allowed to him in the succeeding cal- 
endar year. | 
The total number of days of leave that may be carried forward to a succeeding year 
shall not exceed thirty in the case of an adult or forty in the case of a child. 
_ A worker, who has applied for leave with wages but has not been given such leave 
in accordance with any scheme laid down in sub-sections (8) and (9) or in contra- 
vention of sub-section (10) shall be entitled to carry forward the leave refused with- 
out any limit. [Sub-s. (5)]. 
_A worker may at any time apply in writing to the manager of a factory not less than 
fifteen days before the date on which he wishes his leave to begin, to take all the 
leave or any portion of it allowable to him during the calendar year. 
The application shall be made not less than thirty days before the date on which the 
worker wishes his leave to begin, if he is employed in a public utility service as de- 
fined in clause (n) of section 2 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.’ The number of 
times in which leave may be taken during any year shall not exceed three. [Sub-s. 
(6)]. 
1. Act No. 14 of 1947. 


Chap. VIII—Annual Leave with Wages 249 
If a worker wants to avail himself of the leave with wages due to him to cover a pe- 
riod of illness, he shall be granted such leave even if the application for leave is not 
made within the time specified in sub-section (6); and in such a case wages as admis- 
sible under section 81 shall be paid not later than fifteen days, or in the case of a 
public utility service not later than thirty days from the date of the application for 
leave. [Sub-s. (7)]. | 
For the purpose of ensuring the continuity of work, the occupier or manager of the 
factory, in agreement with the Works Committee of the factory constituted under 
section 3 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, or a similar Committee constituted 
under any other Act or if there is no such Works Committee or a similar Committee 
in the factory, in agreement with the representatives of the workers chosen in the pre- 
scribed manner, may lodge with the Chief Inspector a scheme in writing according to 
which the grant of leave allowable under this section may be regulated. [Sub-s. (2)]. 
A scheme lodged under sub-section (8) shall be displayed at some conspicuous and 
convenient places in the factory and shall be in force for a period of twelve months 
from the date on which it comes into force, and may be renewed with or without 
modification for a further period of twelve months at a time, by the manager in 
agreement with the Works Committee or a similar Committee, or in agreement with 
the representatives of the workers as specified in sub-section (8). A notice of renewal 
has to be sent to the Chief Inspector before the scheme is renewed. [Sub-s. (9)]. 
An application for leave which does not contravene the provisions of sub-section 
(6) shall not be refused, unless refusal is in accordance with the scheme for the time 
being in operation under sub-sections (8) and (9). [Sub-s. (10). 
If the employment of a worker who is entitled to leave under sub-section (1) or 
sub-section (2), is terminated by the occupier before he has taken the entire leave to 
which he is entitled, or if having applied for and having not been granted such leave, 
the worker quits his employment, before he has taken the leave, the occupier of the 
factory shall pay him the amount payable under section 80 in respect of the leave not 
taken, and such payment shall be made, where the employment of the worker is ter- 
minated by the occupier, before the expiry of the second working day after such ter- 
mination, and where a worker who quits his employment, on or before the next pay 
day. [Sub-s. (11)]. 
The unavailed leave of a worker is not be taken into consideration in computing 
the period of any notice required to be given before discharge or dismissal. [Sub-s. 
(12)]. 
3. Wages during leave period (S. 80) 
Section 80 provides for wages during the leave period as following:— 
For the leave allowed as above, a worker shall be paid at a rate equal to the daily 
average of his total full time earnings for the days of which he actually worked dur- 
ing the month immediately preceding his leave, exclusive of any overtime and bonus, 
but inclusive of dearness allowance and cash equivalent of the advantage accruing 
through the concessional sales to the worker, or foodgrains and other articles. Such 
cash grain concession shall be computed as often as may be prescribed on the basis 
of the maximum quantity of foodgrains and other articles admissible to a standard 
family. 
“Standard family” means a family consisting of a worker, his or her spouse and 
two children below the age of 14 years requiring in all three consumption units. 


250 Part Il—The Factories Act, 1948 
“Adult consumption unit” means the consumption unit of a male above the age of 
14 years; and the consumption unit for a female above the age of 14 years and that a 
child below the age of 14 years has to be calculated at the rates of 0.8 and 0.6 re- 
spectively of one adult consumption unit. 
4. Payment in advance in certain cases (S. 81) 
According to section 81, a worker who has been allowed leave for not less than 
four days, in the case of an adult, and five days, in the case of a child, shall before his 
leave begins, be paid the wages due for the period of the leave allowed. 
It has been held that standing orders of a company have merely statutory flavour 
whereas section 81 of the Act is a provision of a statute, therefore, the provisions of 
section 81 must prevail over the standing orders of the company. 
5. Mode of recovery of unpaid wages (S. 82) 
Any sum payable by the employer under these provisions shall be recoverable as 
delayed wages under the Payment of Wages Act, 1936. 
6. Payment of wages, if worker dies 
If a worker dies before resumption of work, the balance of his pay, if any, for the 
period of leave, shall be paid to his nominees within one week of the receipt of inti- 
mation of such death. 
7. Power to make rules (S. 83) 
The State Government may make rules directing managers of factories to keep 
registers containing such particulars as may be prescribed and requiring the registers 
to be made available for examination by Inspectors. 
8. Power to exempt factories (S. 84) 
Section 84 provides power to the State Governments to exempt factories. It says that 
where the State Government is satisfied that the leave rules applicable to workers in a 
factory provided benefits which in its opinion are not less favourable than those for 
which this Chapter makes provision, it may, by written order; exempt the factory from 
all or any of the provisions of this Chapter subject to such conditions as may be speci- 
fied in the order. 
By the Amendment of 1976, an explanation was added to this section. The Explana- 
tion says that the purposes of this section, in deciding whether the benefits which are 
provided for by any leave rules are less favourable than those for which this Chapter 
makes provision, the totality of the benefits shall be taken into account. 
9, Leave with wages register 
Under the Rules, the manager is required to keep a Leave with Wages Register in 
Form 20. If any muster roll or register or return in respect of the factory gives the 
information, the Chief Inspector may order in writing that such muster roll or register 
or return shall, to the corresponding extent, be treated as such register. The leave 
with Wages Register shall be preserved for three years from the last entry in it and 
shall be available to the Inspector on demand. 
2. Maharashtra General Kamgar Union vy. Bharat Petroleum Corpn. Ltd., 1996 LLR 899. 


Chap. VIIi—Annual Leave with Wages 251 
10. Leave book 
It is also the duty of the manager to provide each worker with a Leave Book in 
Form 21 not later than the 28th February of the year. The Leave Book shall be the 
workers’ property and the manager or agent shall demand it only for entering dates of 
holidays or interruptions in service and not keep it for more than a week at a time. A 
worker who has lost his Leave Book shall be provided with another copy on payment 
of ten paise within 15 days which shall be completed from his record. 
11. Medical certificate 
In case of absence due to sickness, a worker shall submit a medical certificate 
signed by a registered medical practitioner or a registered or recognised vaid or ha- 
kim, if so notified by the Manager in writing. It shall state the cause of the absence, 
the period for which the worker is, in the opinion of such medical practitioner, vaid 
or hakim, unable to attend his work. If in any village there is no such medical practi- 
tioner, vaid or hakim, a certificate of the President of the Village Panchayat or 
Headman of the village shall suffice. 
12. Notice to Inspector of involuntary unemployment 
All cases of involuntary unemployment shall be notified by the manager to the In- 
spector with reasons and recorded in the Leave with Wages Register and the leave 
book of workers concerned. 
13. Register to be maintained by exempted factory 
The manager of a factory providing benefit not less favourable than that described 
in the Act and so exempted therefrom, shall maintain a Register showing the leave 
due, leave taken, and wages granted in respect of each worker. A full and detailed 
notice of the system for leave with wages in the factory shall be displayed at the main 
entrance of the factory and a copy thereof sent to the Inspector. No change is to be 
made in the scheme as approved by the State Government while granting exemption, 
without its previous sanction.

Chapter IX of the Factories Act, 1948 containing sections 85 to 91A deals with 
special provisions regarding working in factories. 
1. Power to apply the Act to certain premises (S. 85) 
According to s. 85, the State Government may, by notification in the Official Ga- 
zette, declare that all or any of the provisions of the Act shall apply to any place in 
which a manufacturing process is carried on with or without the aid of power or is so 
ordinarily carried on. Such notification can be made even if— 
The number of persons employed is less than ten, if working with the aid of power 
and less than twenty if working without the aid of power, or the persons working 
there are not employed by the owner but are working with the permission of, or un- 
der agreement with, the owner. 
It is however, necessary that the manufacturing process should not be such as is 
being carried on by the owner only with the aid of his family. [S. 85(1)]. 
Sub-section (2) says that after a place is so declared, it shall be deemed to be a 
factory for the purposes of the Act and the owner shall be deemed to be the occupier. 
And any person working in it would be deemed to be a worker. 
An Explanation attached to the section says that for the purposes of the section, 
“owner” shall include a lessee or mortgagee with possession of the premises. 
The power exercisable under section 85 of the Act is neither a judicial nor a quasi- 
judicial power. It is a legislative activity to make the legislative instrument exten- 
sively operative by making it applicable to places where the manufacturing process is 
carried on. 
2. Power to exempt public institutions (S. 86) 
The State Government may exempt any workshop or workplace where a manu- 
facturing process is carried on and which is attached to a public institution main- 
1. Panneerselvam Match Industries v. Govt. of T.N., (1998) 92 IFJ 762. 
23 


2 D4 Part II—The Factories Act, 1948 
tained for the purposes of education, training, research or reformation, from all or 
any of the provisions of the Act. The exemption may be subject to such conditions as 
the State Government may like to impose. 
No exemption can be granted from the provisions relating to hours of work and 
holidays, unless the persons having the control of the institution submit, for the ap- 
proval of the State Government, a scheme for the regulation of the hours of employ- 
ment, intervals for meals, and holidays of the persons employed in or attending the 
institution or who are inmates of the institution, and the State Government is satisfied 
that the provisions of the scheme are not less favourable than the corresponding pro- 
visions of the Act. 
3. Dangerous operations (S. 87) 
Section 87 provides about dangerous operations. It says that where the State Gov- 
ernment is of opinion that any manufacturing process or operation carried on in a 
factory exposes any persons employed in it to a serious risk of bodily injury, poi- 
soning or disease, if may make rules applicable to any factory or class or description 
of factories in which the manufacturing process or operation is carried on. Such rules 
may be made for the purpose of— 
(a) specifying the manufacturing process or operation and declaring it to be 
dangerous; 
(b) prohibiting or restricting the employment of women, adolescents or chil- 
dren in the manufacturing process or operation; 
(c) providing for the periodical medical examination of persons employed, or 
seeking to be employed, in the manufacturing process or operation, and 
prohibiting the employment of persons not certified as fit for such employ- 
ment and requiring the payment by the occupier of the factory of fees for 
such medical examination; 
(d) providing for the protection of all persons employed in the manufacturing 
process or operation or in the vicinity of the places where it is carried on; 
(e) prohibiting, restricting or controlling the use of any specified materials or 
processes in connection with the manufacturing process or operation; 
(f) requiring the provision of additional welfare amenities and sanitary facili- 
ties and the supply of protective equipment and clothing, and laying down 
its the standards, having regard to the dangerous nature of the manufactur- 
ing process or operation. 
4, Power to prohibit employment on account of serious hazard (S. 87-A) 
Under this section, where it appears to the Inspector that conditions in a factory or in any part of it are such that they may cause serious hazard by way of injury or death 
to the persons employed in it or to the general public in the vicinity, he may, by order 
in writing to the occupier of the factory, state the particulars in respect of which he considers the factory or any part of it to be the cause of such serious hazard. He may 
prohibit such occupier from employing any person in the factory or any part of it other than the minimum number of persons necessary to attend to the minimum tasks 
till the hazard is removed. 
Any order issued by the Inspector under sub-section (1) has effect for a period of 
three days until extended by the Chief Inspector by a subsequent order. [S. 87A (2)]. 


Chap. 1X—Special Provisions Ze), 
Any person aggrieved by an order of the Inspector under sub-section (1) and the 
Chief Inspector under sub-section (2), has the right to appeal to the High Court. [S. 
87A (3)]. 
Any person whose employment has been affected by an order issued under-sub- 
section (1), becomes entitled to wages and other benefits and it is the duty of the oc- 
cupier to provide alternative employment to him wherever possible and in the man- 
ner prescribed. [S. 87A(4)]. 
The provisions of sub-section (4) are not prejudice the rights of the parties under 
the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. 
5. Notice of certain accidents (S. 88) 
In addition to the notices required to be displayed under the Act, a notice contain- 
ing (i) the abstract of the Act and the Rules in Form 26, and (ii) the names and ad- 
dresses of the Inspector and the Certifying Surgeon has to be displayed in every fac- 
tory. : 
All notices under the Act have to be displayed in English and in a language under- 
stood by the majority of the workers in the factory, at some conspicuous and con- 
venient place at or near the main entrance and have to be maintained in a clean and 
legible condition. The Chief Inspector may order in writing the manager to arrange 
for display in the factory another notice or poster regarding health, safety or welfare 
of the workers in the factory. 
Where a notice given under sub-section (1) or s. 88 relates to an accident causing 
death, the authority to whom the notice is sent has to make an inquiry into the occur- 
rence within one month of the receipt of the notice or, if such authority is not the In- 
spector, cause the Inspector to make an inquiry within the that period. 
The State Government may make rules for regulating the procedure at inquiries 
under the section. ; 
6. Notice of certain dangerous occurrences (S. 88-A) 
Where in a factory any dangerous occurrence of such nature as may be prescribed 
occurs, whether causing any bodily injury or disability or not, the manager of the 
factory shall send notice of it to such authorities, and in such form and within such 
time, as may be prescribed under s. 88-A. 
The despatch or any notice or order by post under registered cover is deemed to be 
sufficient service on the occupier, owner or manager of such notice or order. 
7. Notice of certain diseases (S. 89) 
According to s. 89, where any worker in a factory contacts any disease specified in 
the Third Schedule, the manager of the factory shall send notice of it to such authori- 
ties and in such form and within such time, as may be prescribed. 
Sub-section (2) says that if any medical practitioner attends on a person who is or 
has been employed in a factory, and who is, or is believed to by the medical practi- 
tioner to be, suffering from any disease specified in the Third Schedule, the medical 
practitioner has without delay to send a report in writing to the office of the Chief 
Inspector stating— 
(a) the name and full postal address of the patient. 


256 Part II—The Factories Act, 1948 
(b) the disease from which he believes the patient to be suffering, and 
(c) the name and address of the factory in which the patient is, or was last em- 
ployed. 
Sub-section (3) provides that where the report under sub-section (2) is confirmed to 
the satisfaction of the Chief Inspector, by the certificate of a certifying surgeon or 
otherwise, that the person is suffering from a disease specified in the Third Schedule, 
he has to pay to the medical practitioner such fee as may be prescribed. The fee so 
paid is recoverable as an arrear of land-revenue from the occupier of the factory in 
which the person contacted the disease. 
Any medical practitioner who fails to comply with the provisions of sub-section 
(2) is punishable with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees. 
It has been provided by the amendment of 1987 that the Central Government may 
by notification in the Official Gazette, add to or alter the Third Schedule, and any 
such addition or alteration shall have effect as if it had been made by the Act. 
8. Power to direct enquiry into cases of accident or disease (S. 90) 
Where the State Government considers it expedient to do so, it may appoint a 
competent person to inquire into the causes of any accident occurring in a factory or 
into any case where any disease specified in Third Schedule has occurred or is sus- 
pected to have been contacted in a factory. It may also appoint one or more persons 
possessing legal or special knowledge to act as assessors in such inquiry. [S. 90(1)]. 
Such person appointed under sub-section (1) shall have all the power of a Civil 
Court under Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, for the purposes of enforcing the atten- 
dance of witnesses and compelling the production of documents and material objects. 
He may also exercise any of the powers of an inspector under the Act. Every person 
required by such person making the inquiry to furnish any information is legally 
bound to do so within the meaning of section 176 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. 
[S. 90(2)]. 
The person making the inquiry shall send a report to the State Government stating 
the causes of the accident or the disease, as the case may be, and any attended cir- 
cumstances and any other observation which he or any of the assessors may think fit 
to make. [S. 90(3)]. 
The State Government may publish any report made under this section or any ex- 
tract of it, if it thinks fit. [S. 90(4)]. 
The State Government may make rules for regulating the procedure of inquiries 
under the section [s. 90(5)]. 
9. Power to take samples (S. 91) 
_ An Inspector may at any time during the normal working hours of a factory, after 
informing the occupier or manager of the factory or other person for the time being 
purporting to be in charge of the factory, take in the manner provided in this section 
a sufficient sample of any substances used or intended to be used in the factory. The 
purpose of such use being— 
(a) in the belief of the Inspector in contravention of any of the provisions of 
this Act or the rules made thereunder, or 


Chap. [IX—Special Provisions Zoi 
(b) in the opinion of the Inspector likely to cause bodily injury to, or injury to 
the health of, workers in the factory. 
Where the Inspector takes such sample, he shall, in the presence of the person who 
was informed under the sub-section, unless such person wilfully absents himself, 
divide the sample into three portions and effectively seal and suitably mark them, and 
shall permit such person to add his own seal and mark on it. 
The person informed shall, if the Inspector so requires, provide the appliances for 
dividing, sealing and marking the sample taken under this section. 
The Inspector shall— 
(a) forthwith give one portion of the sample to the person informed; 
(b) forthwith send the second portion to a Government Analyst for analysis and 
report; 
(c) retain the third portion for production to the Court before which proceed- 
ings, if any, are instituted in respect of the substance. 
Any document purporting to be a report under the hand of any Government Ana- 
lyst upon any substance submitted to him for analysis and report, may be used as 
evidence in any proceedings instituted in respect of the substance. 
10. Safety and occupational health surveys (S. 91A) 
According to sub-section (1), the Chief Inspector, or the Director General of Fac- 
tory Advice Service and Labour Institutes, or the Director General of Health Serv- 
ices, to the Government of India, or such other officer as may be authorised in this 
behalf by the State Government or the Chief Inspector or the Director General of 
Factory Advice Service and Labour Institutes or the Director General of Health 
Services may, at any time during the normal working hours of a factory, or at any 
other time as is found by him to be necessary, may give notice in writing to the occu- 
pier or manager of the factory or any other person who for the time being purports to 
be in charge of the factory, and may then undertake safety and occupational health 
surveys. The occupier or manager or other person has to afford all facilities for such 
survey, including facilities for the examination and testing of plant and machinery 
and collection of samples and other data relevant to the survey. 
For the purpose of facilitating surveys under sub-section (1) every worker shall, if 
so required by the person conducting the survey, present himself to undergo such 
medical examination as may be considered necessary by such person and furnish all 
information in his possession and relevant to the survey. 
The time spent by a worker for undergoing medical examination or furnishing in- 
formation under sub-section (2) is, for the purpose of calculating wages and extra 
wages for overtime work, to be deemed to be time during which such worker worked 
in the factory. 
The Explanation appended to the section says that for the purposes of the section, 
the report, if any, submitted to the State Government by the person conducting the 
survey under sub-section (1) shall be deemed to be a report submitted by an Inspector 
under this Act.

Chapter X i.e., sections 92 to 106A, of the Factories Act, 1948 deals with penalties 
and procedures. 
1. General penalty for offences (S. 92) 
Save as is otherwise expressly provided in this Act and subject to the provisions of 
section 93, if in, or in respect of, any factory there is any contravention of any of the 
provisions of the Act or of any rules made it or of any order in writing given under it, 
the occupier and manager of the factory shall each be guilty of an offence and pun- 
ishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years or with fine 
which may extend to one lakh rupees or with both. Where the contravention is con- 
tinued even after conviction, there will be a further punishment which may extend to 
one thousand rupees for each day for which the contravention is so continued. 
Where the contravention of any of the provisions of Chapter IV or any rule made 
under it or under section 87 has resulted in an accident causing death or serious bod- 
ily injury, the fine shall not be less than twenty-five thousand rupees in the case of an 
accident causing death, and five thousand rupees in the case of an accident causing 
serious bodily injury. 
The Explanation appended to the section says that in this section and in section 94 
“serious bodily injury” means an injury which involves, or in all probability will in- 
volve, the permanent loss of the use of, or permanent injury to, any limb or the per- 
manent loss of, or injury to, sight or hearing, or the fracture of any bone, but shall not 
include, the fracture of bone or joint (not being fracture of more than one bone or 
joint) of any phalanges of the hand or foot. 
Under this section, the “occupier” cannot escape liability by showing that he had 
left it to the manager of the factory to do everything necessary for compliance with 
the Act. The section makes both the occupier and the manager of a factory punish- 
able with imprisonment. 
Zo9 


260 Part II—The Factories Act, 1948 
The words of the section “save as is otherwise expressly provided in this Act” do 
not make any difference to the law laid down earlier. Under this section, even the 
occupier will be guilty of an offence. Thus, for the offence of contravention of sec- 
tion 88 of the Act, both the occupier and manager were held liable to be prosecuted 
and cognizance could be taken against them. 
2. Liability of owner of premises in certain circumstances (S. 93) 
The owner of any premises, in which separate buildings are leased to different oc- 
cupiers for use as separate factories, shall be responsible for the provisions and 
maintenance of common facilities and services such as approach roads, drainage, 
water supply, lighting and sanitation. Subject to the control of the State Government, 
the Chief Inspector shall have the power to issue orders to the owner of the premises 
in respect of carrying out such obligations. 
Where in any premises independent or self-contained floors or flats are leased to 
different occupiers for use as separate factories, the owner of the premises shall be 
liable as if he were the occupier or manager of a factory, for any violation of the pro- 
visions of the Act in the following respects— 
(1) latrines, urinals and washing facilities in so far as the maintenance of the 
common supply of water for these purposes is concerned; 
(ii) fencing of machinery and plant belonging to the owner and not specifically 
entrusted to the custody or use of any occupier; 
(111) safe means of access to the floors or flats and maintenance and cleanliness 
of stair-cases and common passages; 
(iv) precautions in case of fire; 
(v) maintenance of hoists and lifts; and 
(vi) maintenance of any other common facilities provided in the premises. 
Subject to the control of the State Government, the Chief Inspector shall have the 
power to issue orders to the owners of the premises in connection with carrying out 
of the above mentioned provisions. 
Such owner shall also be liable where in any premises independent rooms with 
common latrines, urinals and washing facilities are leased to different occupiers for 
use as separate factories. The responsibility for compliance with the requirements 
regarding provision and maintenance of latrines, urinals and washing facilities shall 
be that of the owner. The Chief Inspector shall, subject to the control of the State 
Government, have the power to issue orders to the owner of such premises in respect 
of carrying out of the provisions relating to canteens and creches. 
Where in any premises, portions of a room or a shed are leased to different occupi- 
ers for use as separate factories, the owner of the premises shall be liable for breaches 
of the provisions relating to health (except provisions regarding dust and fumes and 
artificial humidification), safety (except provisions as regards work on or near ma- chinery in motion, employment of young persons on dangerous cotton openers, ex- 
1. R.N. Mehta & A.K. Das Gupta v. Kalyan K. Sengupta, 1987 CrLR 193 at p. 195 (Cal). Where the manager was acquitted, it was no use prosecuting a director for the same offence, State of U.P. vy. Cawnpore Sugar Works Ltd., (1998) 3 Lab LJ (Supp) 802 : (1993) Suppi (1) SCC 488. Constitu- 
tionality of s. 92 upheld in /.K. Industries Ltd. y. Chief Inspector of Factories, (1997) | Lab LJ 
722: (1996) 6 SCC 665. 


Chap. X—Penalties and Procedure 261 
cessive weights, protection of eyes and precautions against dangerous fumes), and 
washing facilities. In respect of the provisions relating to fencing of machinery, 
striking gear and devices for cutting off power, and floors, stairs and means of ac- 
cess, the owner’s liability shall be restricted to things under his control. The occupier 
shall, however be responsible for compliance with provisions relating to safety in 
respect of plant and machinery belonging to or supplied by him. Subject to the con- 
trol of the State Government, the Chief Inspector is authorised to issue orders to the 
owner of the premises for carrying out these provisions. 
In computing the total number of workers for the purposes of any of the foregoing 
provisions, the whole of the premises shall be deemed to be a single factory. . 
In the case of a factory belonging to the Central Government or any State Govern- 
ment or any local authority the person or persons appointed to manage the affairs of 
the factory shall be deemed to be the occupier of the factory for the purposes of this 
Chapter. 
3. Enhanced penalty after previous conviction (S. 94) 
If any person who has been convicted of any offence punishable under s. 92 is 
again guilty of an offence involving a contravention of the same provision, he shall 
be punishable on a subsequent conviction with imprisonment for a term which may 
extend to three years or with fine which shall not be less than ten thousand rupees but 
which may extend to two lakh rupees or with both. The court may, for any adequate 
and special reasons to be mentioned in the judgement, impose a fine of less than ten 
thousand rupees. Where the contravention of any of the provisions of Chapter IV or 
any rule made under it or under section 87 has resulted in an accident causing death 
or serious bodily injury, the fine shall not be less than thirty-five thousand rupees in 
the case of an accident causing death and ten thousand rupees in the case of an acci- 
dent causing serious bodily injury. 
For the purposes of sub-section (1) no cognizance can be taken of any conviction 
made more than two years before the commission of the offence for which the person 
is subsequently being convicted. 
4, Penalty for obstructing Inspector (S. 95) 
Section 95 provides that whoever wilfully obstructs an Inspector in the exercise of 
any power conferred on him by or under the Act, or fails to produce on demand by an _ 
Inspector any registers or other documents in his custody kept in pursuance of this 
Act or of any rules made under it, or conceals or prevents any worker in a factory 
from appearing before, or being examined by, an Inspector, shall be punishable with 
imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months or with fine which may 
extend to ten thousand rupees or with both. 
5. Penalty for wrongfully disclosing results of analysis under section 91 (S. 96) 
Section 96 provides that whoever, except in so far as it may be necessary for the 
purposes of a prosecution for any offence punishable under this Act, publishes or 
discloses to any person the results of an analysis made under section 91, shall be 
punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months or with 
fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees or with both. 


262 Part II—The Factories Act, 1948 
6. Penalty for contravention of provisions of Ss. 41B, 41C and 41H (S. 96-A) 
According to s. 96-A, whoever fails to comply with or contravenes any of the pro- 
visions of sections 41-B, 41-C or 41-H or the rules made under it, shall in respects of 
such failure or contravention, be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may 
extend to 7 years and with fine which may extend to two lakh rupees, and in case the 
failure or contravention continues, with additional fine which may extend to five 
thousand rupees for every day during which such failure or contravention continues 
after the conviction for the first such failure or contravention. 
Sub-section (2) says that if the failure or contravention referred in sub-section (1) 
continues beyond the period of one year after the date of conviction, the offender 
shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may be extend to ten years. 
7. Offences by workers (S. 97) 
Subject to the provisions relating to obligations of workers, if any worker in a fac- 
tory violates any provisions of the Act or Rules or Order made under it, imposing any 
duty or liability on workers, he shall be punishable with fine imposing any duty or 
liability on workers, he shall be punishable with fine extending to five hundred ru- 
pees. Where a worker is thus convicted of an offence, the occupier or manager, shall 
not be deemed to be guilty of an offence in respect of that breach, unless it is proved 
that he failed to take all reasonable measures for its prevention. 
8. Penalty for using false certificate of fitness (S. 98) 
Any person, knowingly using or attempting to use, a certificate granted to another 
person as a certificate of fitness to himself, or who having procured such a certificate 
knowingly allows it to be used or an attempt to use it is made by another person, 
shall be punished with imprisonment which may extend to two months or with fine 
extending to one thousand rupees or with both. 
9. Penalty for permitting double employment of child (S. 99) 
If a child works in a factory on a day on which he has already been working in an- 
other factory, the parent or guardian of the child or the person having custody of or 
control over him or obtaining any direct benefit from his wages shall, unless it ap- 
pears to the Court that the child so worked without the consent or connivance of such 
parent, guardian or person, be punishable with fine extending to one thousand rupees. 
10. Deletion of S. 100 
This section was omitted by the Amendment Act of 1987 with effect from 1-12-1987. 
11. Exemption of occupier or manager from liability in certain cases (S. 101) 
Section 101 says that where the occupier or manager of a factory is charged with an offence punishable under this Act, he shall be entitled, upon complaint duly made by him and on giving to the prosecutor not less than three clear days’ notice in writ- ing of his intention so to do, to have any other person whom he charges as the actual offender brought before the Court at the time appointed for hearing the charge; and if, after the commission of the offence has been proved, the occupier or manager of the factory, as the case may be, proves to the satisfaction of the Court— 
(a) that he has used due diligence to enforce the execution of the Act, and 


Chap. X—Penalties and Procedure 263 
(b) that the said other person committed the offence in question without his 
knowledge, consent or connivance, 
that other person shall be convicted of the offence and shall be liable to the like pun- 
ishment as if he was the occupier or manager of the factory, and the occupier or 
manager, as the case may be, shall be discharged from any liability under the Act in 
respect of such offence. 
In seeking to prove such a position, the occupier or manager of the factory, as the 
case may be, may be examined on oath, and his evidence and that of any witness 
whom he calls in his support shall be subject to cross-examination on behalf of the 
person he charges as the actual offender and by the prosecutor. 
If the person charged as the actual offender by the occupier or manager cannot be 
brought before the Court at the time appointed for hearing the charge, the Court shall 
adjourn the hearing from time to time for a period not exceeding three months and if 
by the end of that period the person charged as the actual offender cannot still be 
brought before the Court, the Court shall proceed to hear the charge against the oc- 
cupier or manager and shall, if the offence be proved, convict the occupier or man- 
ager. 
12. Power of Court to make orders (S. 102) 
According to section 102, where the occupier or manager of a factory is convicted 
of an offence punishable under this Act the Court may, in addition to awarding any 
punishment, by order in writing require him, within a period specified in the order 
(which the court may, if it thinks fit and on application in such behalf, from time to 
time extend) to take such measures as may be so specified for remedying the matters 
in respect of which the offence was committed. 
Where an order is made under sub-section (1) the occupier or manager of the fac- 
tory, as the case may be, shall not be liable under this Act in respect of the continua- 
tion of the offence during the period or extended period, if any, allowed by the Court, 
but if, on the expiry of such period or extended period, as the case may be, the order 
of the Court has not been fully complied with, the occupier or manager, as the case 
may be, shall be deemed to have committed a further offence, and may be sentenced 
therefor by the Court to undergo imprisonment for a term which may extend to six 
months or to pay a fine which may extend to one hundred rupees for every day after 
such expiry on which the order has not been complied with, or both to undergo such 
imprisonment and to pay such fine, as aforesaid. 
13. Presumption as to employment (S. 103) 
Section 103 provides that if a person 1s found in a factory at any time, except dur- 
ing intervals for meals or rest, when work is going on or the machinery is in motion, 
he shall, until the contrary is proved, be deemed for the purposes of the Act and the 
rules made under it to have been at that time employed in the factory. 
The Supreme Court has observed that it is a rebuttable presumption. It is restricted 
only to the purposes of the Act. Its application to the proceedings under s. 10 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 was held to be improper. 
2. Factory Manager, Cimmco Wagon Factory v. Virendra Kumar Sharma, AIR 2000 SC 2524 : (2000) 
6 SCC 554 : (2000) Lab IC 2659. 


264 Part II—The Factories Act, 1948 
14. Onus as to age (S. 104) 
According to s. 104, where it is necessary to decide whether a person is under a 
certain age for the purpose of an act or omission which constitutes an offence pun- 
ishable under the Act, the burden of proof shall be on the accused. A declaration in 
writing by a certifying surgeon that he has personally examined the worker and be- 
lieves him to be under the age stated in such declaration shall be admissible as evi- 
dence of the age of that worker for the purposes of the Act. 
15. Onus of proving limits of what is practicable, etc. (S. 104-A) 
Section 104-A deals with onus of proving limits of what is practicable, etc. It says 
that in any proceeding for an offence for the contravention of any provision of this 
Act or rules made under it consisting of a failure to comply with a duty or require- 
ment to do something, it shall be for the person who ts alleged to have failed to com- 
ply with such duty or requirement, to prove that it was not reasonably practicable, or 
as the case may be, all practicable measures were taken to satisfy the duty or the re- 
quirement. 
16. Cognizance of offences (S. 105) 
According to section 105, no Court shall take cognizance of any offence under this 
Act except on complaint by or with the previous sanction in writing of, an Inspector. 
No Court below that of a Presidency Magistrate or of a Magistrate of the First Class 
shall try any offence punishable under this Acct. 
17. Limitation of prosecution (S. 106) 
No Court will take cognizance of any offence punishable under the Act unless a 
complaint is made within three months of the date on which the alleged offence came 
to the knowledge of the Inspector. 
Where the offence consists of disobeying a written order made by an Inspector, a 
complaint may be made within six months of the date on which the offence is alleged 
to have been committed. 
An £xplanation attached to this section provides that for the purposes of the sec- 
tion. 
(a) in the case of a continuing offence, the period of limitation shall be com- 
puted with reference to every point of time during which the offence con- 
tinues; 
(b) Where for the performance of any act, time is granted or extended on an 
application, made by the occupier or manager of a factory, the period of 
limitation shall be computed from the date on which the time so granted or 
extended expired.
