contract or agreement shall be null and void. The workman can enforce the right or 
privilege in question. 
46. Exemptions and exceptions (S. 26) 
Sub-section (1) says that the appropriate Government may, subject to such condi- 
tions, if any, as it may think fit to impose, direct that the provisions of the Act shall 
not apply in relation to the wages payable to disabled employees. 
The appropriate Government may, if for special reasons it thinks so fit, by notifi- 
cation in the Official Gazette, direct that subject to such conditions and for such pe- 
riod as it may specify, the provisions of the Act or any of them shall not apply to all 
or any class of employees employed in any scheduled employment or to any locality 
where there is carried on a scheduled employment. 
The appropriate Government may, if it is of opinion that having regard to the terms 
and conditions of service applicable to any class of employees in a scheduled em- 
ployment generally or in a scheduled employment in a local area or to any establish- 
ment or a part of any establishment in a scheduled employment, it is not necessary to 
fix minimum wages in respect of such employees of that class or in respect of em- 
ployees in such establishment or such part of any establishment as are in receipt of 
wages exceeding such limit as may be prescribed in this behalf, direct, by notifica- 
tion in the Official Gazette and subject to such conditions, if any, as it may think fit 
to impose, that the provisions of the Act or any of them shall not apply in relation to 
such employees. 
Nothing in this Act shall apply to the wages payable by an employer to a member 
of his family who is living with him and is dependant on him. 
The Explanation appended to the section says that in this sub-section a member of 
the employer’s family shall be deemed to include his or her spouse or child or parent 
or brother or sister. 
47. Power of State Government to add to Schedule (S. 27) 
The appropriate Government, after giving by notification in the Official Gazette,

the Schedule any employment in respect of which it is of opinion that minimum 
rates of wages should be fixed under the Act. Upon such notification the schedule 
shall in its application to the State be deemed to be amended accordingly.

any person with any punishment or penalty whatsoever by reason of the payment by 
him by way of wages to any of his employees during any period specified in the sec- 
tion of an amount which is less than the minimum rates of wages referred to in the 
section or by reason of non-compliance during the period aforesaid with any order or 
rule issued under section 13.

. PART IV 
THE PAYMENT OF WAGES ACT, 1936. 
[4 OF 1936]

HISTORY 
SYNOPSIS

In an economy where even minimum wages are not paid to the workers, the need 
to protect the wages earned by them has the greatest significance. The first sugges- 
tion for legislation in regard to payment of wages was made in 1925 in a private 
member’s Bill called the “Weekly Payment Bill” which was brought before the Leg- 
islative Assembly. The Bill was withdrawn on the assurance that the question was 
under consideration by the Government. 
Imposition of fines was a fairly general practice in perennial factories and railways. 
A common practice in the cotton mills was the handing over to the weaver of cloth 
from his own loom the cloth spoilt in the course of manufacture and the deduction 
from his wages of the wholesale selling price. Another practice followed in some 
mills was the deduction of two days’ pay for one day’s absence. In 1926 the Gov- 
ernment raised the question of the desirability of legislation regulating the extent to 
which fines and other deductions from wages might be made by employers. 
1. Recommendations of Royal Commission 
The question was again considered by the Royal Commission on Labour in India. 
The Commission recommended that legislation regarding deductions from wages and 
fines was necessary and desirable. The recommendations of the Commission formed 
the basis of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936. 
2. Preamble of the Act 
The Payment of Wages Act, 1936 is “an Act to regulate the payment of wages of 
certain classes of employed persons.” The preamble says: 
“Whereas it is expedient to regulate the payment of wages to certain classes 
of persons employed in industry.” 
3. Object of the Act 
As is stated in the preamble to the Act, the object of the Act is to regulate the pay- 
ment of wages to certain classes of persons engaged in industry. The regulations 
contemplated by the Act are of two kinds, namely, (1) about the date of the payment 
6 his. 


316 Part IV—The Payment of Wages Act, 1936 
of wages, and (2) about deductions from wages whether as fine or otherwise. The 
words “certain persons” are important because the Act does not apply to persons 
drawing on an average sixteen hundred rupees a month or more. 
In R.V. Shah v. V.R. Savarkar,' it was observed about the object of the Act that the 
Payment of Wages Act was enacted for the purpose of safeguarding the wages of 
employees under certain conditions laid down under that Act and payment to them 
without unauthorized deductions. 
4, Short title, extent, commencement and application 
(1) This Act may be called the Payment of Wages Act, 1936. 
“Ka It extends to the whole of India.” Ee as 
(3) It shall come into force on such date* as the Central Government may by notifi- 
cation in the Official Gazette, appoint. [enforced w.e.f. March 28, 1937] 
(4) It applies in the first instance to the payment of wages to persons employed in 
any “[factory, to persons] employed (otherwise than in a factory) upon any railway 
by a railway administration or, either directly or through a sub-contractor, by a per- 
son fulfilling a contract with a railway administration, [and to persons employed in 
an industrial or other establishments specified in sub-clauses (a) to (g) of clause (ii) 
of section 2.] 
(5) The State Government may, after giving three months’ notice of its intention of 
so doing, by notification in the Official Gazette, extend the provisions of Ithis Act] 
or any of them to the payment of wages to any class of persons employed in ‘[any 
establishment or class of establishments specified by the Central Government or a 
State Government under sub-clause (h) of clause (ii) of section 2:] 
*( Provided that in relation to any such establishment owned by the Central Gov- 
ernment no such notification shall be issued except with the concurrence of that 
Government. | 
(6) Nothing in this Act shall apply to wages payable in respect a wage-period 
which, over such wage-period, average [Six thousand five hundred rupees] “a month 
or more. | 
5. Amendment Act 41 of 2005 
According to statement of objects and reasons of Amendment Act 41 of 2005, the 
Payment of Wages Act, 1936 was enacted with a view to ensuring that wage payable 
to employed persons covered by the Act were disbursed by the employers within the 
prescribed time limit and no deductions other than those authorised by law were

made to them. The least amendment was made in 1982 and several provisions of the 
Act have become obsolete over the years. In order to bring this law in uniformity 
with other labour laws and also to make it more effective and practicable, it is pro- 
posed to make the following— 
(i) Enhancing the wage ceiling of Rs. 1600 per month to Rs. 6500 per month. 
(ii) To substitute the expressions “The Central Government” or a “State Gov- 
ernment” by the expression “‘appropriate Government”. 
(iii) Removing the ambiguities/weaknesses from the extant provision of the Act 
and prescribing more effective grievance redressesal. For this, appropriate 
changes are made in sections 3, 7, 8 and 15 of the Act which respectively 
deal with responsibility for payment of wages, deductions from wages, 
fines and claims in certain cases. 
(iv) Strengthening compensation and penal provisions of the Act. It is proposed 
to make the penal provisions more stringent by enhancing the question of 
penalties by amending section 20 of the Act.

1. Employed Person [s. 2(i)] 
S. 2 (1) of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 says that “employed person” includes 
the legal representative of a deceased person. 
2. Employer [s. 2(ia)] 
According to s. 2(ia), “employer” includes the legal representative of a deceased 
employer. 
3. Factory [s. 2(ib)] 
According to s. 2(ib), “factory” means a factory as defined in clause (m) of section 
2 of the Factories Act, 1948 and includes any place to which the provisions of that Act have been applied under section 85(1). wit 
4. Industrial or other establishment [s. 2(ii)] 
According to s. 2(1i), “industrial or other establishment” means any— 
(a) tramway service, or motor transport service engaged in carrying passenger 
or goods or both by road for hire or reward; 
(aa) air transport service other than such service belonging to, or exclusively 
employed in the military, naval or airforces of the Union or the Civil Avia- 
tion Department of the Government of India; 
(b) dock, wharf or jetty; 
(c) inland vessel, mechanically propelled; 
(d) mine, quarry on oil-field; 
(e) plantation; 
(f) workshop or other establishment in which articles are produced, adapted or 
manufactured, with a view to their use, transport or sale; 
(g) establishment in which any work relating to the construction, development 
or maintenance of buildings, road bridges or canals, or relating to operation 
connected with navigation, irrigation, development or maintenance of 
319 


320 Part IV—The Payment of Wages Act, 1936 
building roads, bridges or mission and distribution of electricity or any 
other form of power is being carried on. 
(h) any other establishment or class of establishment which the Central Gov- 
ernment or a State Government may, having regard to its nature, the need 
for protection of persons employed in it and other relevant circumstances, 
specify, by notification in the Official Gazette. 
5. Mine [s. 2(iia)] 
S. 2(iia) provides that “mine” has the meaning assigned to it in clause (j) of sub- 
section (1) of section 2 of the Mines Act, 1952. 
6. Plantation [s. 2(iii)] 
“Plantations” has the meaning assigned to it in clause (f) of section 2 of the Planta- 
tions Labour Act, 1951. 
7. Prescribed [s. 2(iv)] 
“Prescribed” means prescribed by rules made under the Act. 
8. Railway administration [s. 2(v)] 
“Railway Administration” has the meaning assigned to it in clause (6) of section 3 
of the Indian Railways Act, 1890. 
9. Wages [s. 2(vi)] 
“Wages” means all remuneration (whether by way of salary, allowances, or other- 
wise) expressed in terms of money or capable of being so expressed which would, if 
the terms of employment, express or implied, were fulfilled, be payable to a person 
employed in respect of his employment or of work done in such employment. It in- 
cludes— 
(a) any remuneration payable under any award or settlement between the par- 
ties or order of a Court; 
(b) any remuneration to which the person employed is entitled in respect of 
overtime work or holidays or any leave period; 
(c) any additional remuneration payable under the terms of employment 
(whether called a bonus or by any other name); 
(d) any sum which by reason of the termination of employment of the person 
employed is payable under any law, contract or instrument which provides 
for the payment of such sum, whether with or without deductions, but does 
not provide for the time within which the payment is to be made; 
(e) any sum to which the person employed is entitled under any scheme framed 
under any law for the time being in force. 
The term “wages” does not include— 
(1) any bonus (whether under a scheme of profit-sharing or otherwise) which 
does not form part of the remuneration payable under the terms of employment or 
which is not payable under any award or settlement between the parties or order of 
a court; 


Chap. I]—Definitions a1 
(2) the value of any house-accommodation, or of the supply of light, water, medi- 
cal attendance or other amenity or of any service excluded from the computation of 
wages by a general or special order of the State Government: 
(3) any contribution paid by the employer to any pension or provident fund, and 
the interest which may have accrued on it; 
(4) any travelling allowance or the value of any travelling concession; 
(5) any sum paid to the employed person to defray special expenses entailed on 
him by the nature of his employment; or 
(6) any gratuity payable on the termination of employment in cases other than 
those specified in sub-clause (d). 
Wide definition of the term “wages” in section 2(vi) would include bonus as well, 
since it is remuneration whether by way of salary, allowance or otherwise expressed 
in terms of money. Therefore, the employee can claim for bonus which has not been 
paid. 
In a case before the Supreme Court, a licence was issued to contractor providing 
conditions in Rule 25(v)(a) of Andhra Pradesh Contract Labour (Regulations and 
Abolition) Rules, 1971. Under these rules, the contractor should have paid to the 
workman employed by it some wages as those paid by the principal employer to its 
workmen, performing same or similar kind of work. But he did not comply with the 
conditions of licence. Principal employer argued that it was not liable to pay the ad- 
ditional amount which constituted the difference between wages payable to workmen 
by contractor and wages paid by principal employer to its own employees doing the 
same and similar works. It was held that the definition of wages under Payment of 
Wages Act as well as under Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act does 
not cover additional amount found payable under Rule 25(v)(a). Principal employer 
was held liable to pay to contract workers difference between wages paid by the 
contractor and wages contracted to be paid by the principal employer to contractor in 
respect of contract labourers and recover such amount from the contractor.

to time if the wages are less than that payable from the date of award.

Responsibility for payment of wages (s. 3) 
Every employer shall be responsible for the payment of all wages required to be paid under this Act to persons employed by him and in case of persons employed — 
623 


324 Part IV—The Payment of Wages Act, 1936 
(a) in factories, if a person has been named as the manager of the factory under 
s. 7(1)(f) of the Factories Act, 1948; 
(b) in industrial establishments, if there is a person responsible to the employer 
for the supervision and control of the industrial establishment; 
(c) upon railways (otherwise than in factories), if the employer is the railway 
administration and the railway administration has nominated a person in 
this behalf for the local area concerned; 
(d) in the case of contractor, a person designated by such contractor who is 
directly under his charge; and 
(e) in any other case, a person designated by the employer as a person respon- 
sible for complying with the provisions of the Act; 
the person so named, the person responsible to the employer, the person so nomi- 
nated or the person so designated, as the case may be, shall be responsible for such 
payment. 
It shall be the responsibility of the employer to make payment of all wages re- 
quired to be made under this Act in case the contractor or the person designated by 
the employer fails to make such payment. 
2. Persons responsible for payment 
This section provides for the liability of employer or any other person who is 
named as manager. It is distinctly contemplated that the proceedings in the first in- 
stance should be against either the employer or against the manager but not against 
both. The legislature contemplated that before fixing the employer with any liability, 
it must be found that the whole or part of the amount could not be recovered from the 
manager. 
The responsibility is to be fixed with reference to the date of accrual of wages and 
the person responsible for the payment of wages on that date. The expression “em- 
dloyer” has not been defined in the Act, but the word must be given the widest 
ineaning. If there is no named manager of the factory at the date when application is 
rade then the occupier would be deemed to be the manager of the factory. 
3. Payment of Wages Act 
In a case, Jiyajirao Cotton Mills, which was declared a sick company, owed wages 
to its workers for certain periods. Inspector for the Payment of Wages initiated pro- 
ceedings under section 15 of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936, against the directors 
of the company. The Authorities under the Act found the directors to be personally 
liable to pay the wages. The decision was affirmed by the High Court. Against this 
decision the directors went in appeal. Their appeal was allowed and the appeals filed by the functionaries under the Act were dismissed. 
The Supreme Court referred the provisions of the Act as amended by the Madhya 
Pradesh Act, 1964 and observed that the High Court held the appellant directors li- able by introducing the expression “occupier” used in the Factories Act, 1948 and not in the Payment of Wages Act, 1936. On a plain reading of the provisions of the Pay- ment of Wages Act, 1936, it could not be held that director had any personal liability. The liability can be cast on a person named as Manager of the factory and the em- ployer jointly under s¢ction 3 of the Payment of Wages Act (as amended by the 
1. P.M. Dixit v. Senior Inspector of Factories, AIR 1940 Bom 87 : 41 Bom LR 183: ILR (1940) Bom 396. 


Chap. II]—Provisions 325 
Madhya Pradesh Act, 1964). In order to find out whether the director of a company 
had any responsibility, two things need to be established: 
(1) he was the employer, or 
(ii) he was a person who had been named as Manager of the factory. 
In the recent case there was no such evidence, thus, the directors were not held per- 
sonally liable. 
4. Responsibility of contractors for payment of wages 
A mine-owner is not liable under this Act for wages of labourers employed by the 
contractor. 
5. Responsibility of principal employer for payment 
Under section 21 of the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 the 
liability for payment of wages to each employee engaged by a contractor as contract 
labour is of the contractor. But under sec. 21(4), in case the contractor fails to make 
payment of wages, then the principal employer shall be liable to make payment of 
wages in full or the unpaid balance due to the workers. The principal employer is, 
however, entitled to recover the amount from the contractor. Thus it is clear that un- 
der section 21 also the responsibility for payment of wages of contract labourers is on 
the contractor who employs them. In case of any default by the contractor, the prin- 
cipal employer is required to make good the default, but at the cost of the contractor 
from whom the principal employer can recover the amount. 
Looking at the definition of wages in section 2(1)(h) of the Contract Labour 
(Regulation and Abolition) Act read with the definition of wages in clause (vi) of 
section 2 of the Payment of Wages Act, it is clear that section 21 of the Contract 
Labour Act only deals with the payment of contractual wages. Section 21(4) will not 
apply to such obligations of the contractor which may be the subject-matter of dis- 
pute between the contractor and his workers at the time of disbursement of wages 
and which do not fall within the definition of “wages” under the Contract Labour 
(Regulation and Abolition) Act.’ The principal employer is liable to pay to contract 
workers the difference between the wages paid by the contractor and the wages con- 
tracted to be paid by the principal employer to the contractor in respect of contract 
labourers and recover such amount from the contractor. 
Workmen working in a canteen of the establishment under a contractor appointed 
by the management do not become the employees of the management. All claims of 
such workmen should be met only by the contractor and not by the management. No 
doubt even in case where the canteen is run by a contractor, the management is liable 
to pay wages as recognised in sec. 24(1) of the Contract Labour (Regulation and 
Abolition) Act, 1970, but wages under ID Act, 1947 and Payment of Wages Act, 
1936, specifically exclude Bonus and Gratuity from its purview.” 
6. Responsibility of manager 
The responsibility for payment of wages is primarily that of the employer. Under 
the original Act in the case of factories, the liability is thrown on the person named as

a manager under section 7(1)(f) of the Factories Act, 1948, and in the case of an in- 
dustrial establishment on the person who is responsible to the employer for supervi- 
sion and control of the establishment. In the case of railways, if the administration 
has nominated a person in respect of payment of wages for the local area concerned, 
such person would be liable for the payment of wages. The Bombay State Legislature 
has, however, amended the Act by making these persons jointly and severally liable 
along with the employer. Under the Central Act also, all the persons, named or nominated 
are responsible for payment of wages are jointly and severally responsible. 
7. Fixation of wage-periods (s. 4) 
Every person responsible for payment of wages under section 3 shall fix periods (re- 
ferred to as wage-periods) in respect of which such wages shall be payable. It is also pro- 
vided that no wage period shall exceed one month. : 
8. Time of payment of wages (s. 5) 
(a) Payment according to wage-period 
The wages of every person employed upon or in-— 
(a) any railway, factory or industrial or other establishment upon or in which 
less than one thousand persons are employed are to be paid before the ex- 
piry of the seventh day, 
(b) any other railway, factory or industrial or other establishment are to be paid 
before the expiry of the tenth day, 
after the last day of the wage-period in respect of which the wages are payable. 
In the case of persons employed on a dock, wharf or jetty or in a mine, the balance 
of wages found due on completion of final tonnage account of ship or wages loaded or unloaded, as the case may be, shall be paid before the expiry of the seventh day 
from the day of such completion. [s. 5(1)] 
9. Payment in case of termination of employment 
Where the employment of any person is terminated by or on behalf of the em- ployer, the wages earned by him shall be paid before the expiry of the second working day from the day on which his employment is terminated: provided that where the employment of any person in an establishment is terminated due to the closure of the establishment for any reason other than a weekly or recognized holi- day, the wages earned by him shall be paid before the expiry of the second day from the day on which his employment is so terminated.° Sate 
10. Exemption by State Government 
The State Government may, by general or special order, exempt to such extent and subject to such conditions as may be specified in the order, the person responsible for the payment of wages to persons employed upon any railway (otherwise than in a factory) or to persons employed as daily-rated workers in the public works depart-

11. Saving Provision 
Sub-section (4) lastly says that save as otherwise provided in sub-section (2), all 
payment of wages shall be made on a working day. 
12. Wages to be paid in current coin or currency notes (s. 6) 
According to section 6, all wages shall be paid in current coin or currency notes or 
in both. However, it is provided that the employer may, after obtaining written 
authorization of the employed person, pay him the wages either by cheque or by 
crediting the wages in his bank account. 
13. Deduction which may be made from wages (s. 7a¥ 
Notwithstanding the provisions of the Railways Act, 1989 (24 of 1989), the wages 
of an employed person shall be paid to him without deductions of any kind except 
those authorised by or under this Act. 
The first Explanation to the section provides that every payment made by the em- 
ployed person to the employer or his agent shall, for the purposes of the Act, be 
deemed to be a deduction from wages. 
The second Explanation says that any loss of wages resulting from the imposition 
for good and sufficient cause, upon a person employed of any of the following pen- 
alties, namely: 
(i) withholding of increment or promotion (including the stoppage of incre- 
ment at an efficiency bar); ; 
(ii) reduction to a lower post or time scale or to a lower stage in a time scale; or 
(111) suspension; 
shall not be deemed to be a deduction from wages in any case where the rules framed 
by the employer for the imposition of any such penalty are in conformity with the 
requirements, if any, which may be specified in this behalf by the appropriate Gov- 
ernment by notification in the Official Gazette. 
Deductions from the wages of an employed person shall be made only in accor- 
dance with the provisions of the Act, and may be of the following kinds only, 
namely: 
(a) fines; 
(b) deductions for absence from duty;

Sub-section (3) provides that notwithstanding anything contained in the Act, the 
total amount of deductions which may be made under sub-section (2) in any wage- 
period from the wages of any employed person should not exceed— 
(i) in cases where such deductions are wholly or partly made for payments to 
co-operative societies under clause (j) of sub-section (2), seventy-five per- 
cent of such wages; and 
(ii) in any other case, fifty percent of such wages; 
Where the total deductions authorised under sub-section (2) exceed seventy 
five percent, or, as the case may be, fifty percent, the excess may be recoy-

The provisions of the section are not to be construed as precluding the employer 
from recovering from the wages of the employed person or otherwise any amount 
payable by such person under any law for the time being in force other than the 
Railways Act, 1989 (24 of 1989). 
The following types of deduction require some detailed discussion: 
14. Fines (s. 8) 
Fines can be imposed only for acts or omissions which have been approved by the 
appropriate Government and have been notified at or near the main entrance of the 
factory or industrial establishment. The Chief Inspector of Factories has been recog- 
nised as the authority to approve the list of acts or omissions for which fines can be 
imposed. Fines can be imposed only by the employer or a person whose appointment 
in that respect has been communicated to the Chief Inspector of Factories. No fine 
can be imposed unless the person concerned has been given an opportunity of show- 
ing cause why a fine should not be imposed. The procedure to be followed is laid 


330 Part IV—The Payment of Wages Act, 1936 
down in Rule 14 of the Bombay Payment of Wages Rules, 1937. The total amount of the fine to be imposed on an employee in any wage period shall not exceed half an anna in the rupee in the wages payable for that wage period. No fine can be imposed on an employee who is under 15 years of age. A fine imposed on an employed per- son cannot be recovered from him either in instalments or after the expiry of ninety days from the day of the act or omission for which the fine is being imposed. 
All the amounts realised have to be applied only to such purposes beneficial to the workmen employed in the factory or establishment as are approved by the prescribed authority (the Chief Inspector of Factories). Under section 3 of the Bombay Labour Welfare Fund Act, 1953, all fines realised from employees have to be paid into the Bombay Labour Welfare Fund. 
15. Deductions for absence from duty (s. 9) 
Deductions for absence from duty can be made only on account of the absence of an employed person from the place or places, where according to the terms of em- ployment he is required to work. An employed person shall be deemed to be absent from his place of work, if he, though present in person, refused to carry out his work in pursuance of a stay-in-strike or any other cause which is not reasonable in the cir- cumstances. No such deduction for breach of contract can be made from the wages of a person who is under 15 years or is a woman. The absence which can form the basis of such deduction may be for the whole ‘or any part of the period during which he is required to work. The amount of such deductions must bear to his wages the same proportion as his absence bears to the total period within the wage period during which he was ordinarily required to work. Where workers absented for a part of the day, deduction of salary for full day was not unjustified or illegal.* Deduction for the absence from the place of work is not a deduction at all, but it is a failure on the part of the employee to earn wages by fulfilling the conditions of employment and performing his work. The deduction for absence is normal deduction and not penal deduction. Deduction for absence is not at all a deduction but failure on the part of the employees to earn wages. Therefore, there is no question of employee being taken by surprise or showing any defence. 
The provisions of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936, have been cleverly and clearly worded. The definition of wages itself is as follows: 
“Wages means all remuneration (whether by way of salary, allowances or other- wise) expressed in terms of money or capable of being so expressed which would, if the terms of employment express or implied, were fulfilled, be payable to a per- son employed in respect of his employment or work done in such employment.” Section 2(vi) 
Therefore, employee is eligible to get wages only when he fulfils the terms of em- ployment by doing the work. 
According to section 9(1) of the Act if the employee is absent from the work for a period during which he is required to work, deductions can be made. It is a failure on the part of the employee to earn wages by fulfilling the terms of employment by per- forming the work. The deduction for absence is normal deduction and not penal de- duction. Employer is, therefore, justified in deducting the wages for the absence of the employees without notice or leave.

Chap. ITI—Provisions 351 
(a) Deductions in cases of sit-down or stay-in-strikes 
If ten or more workers, acting, in concert, absent themselves without due notice as 
_ contemplated by the terms of their contracts of employment and without reasonable 
cause, the deductions may include such amount not exceeding his or their wages for 
eight days. The appropriate Government is to make rules in this respect. Accordingly 
the Bombay Government has framed Rule 16 on the question of such deductions. 
Under that rule no such deductions for breach of contract can be made unless: (a) 
there is a provision in writing forming part of the contract of employment requiring a 
workman to give notice of termination of service, (b) the provisions of law in this 
respect are displayed at or near the main entrance of the factory in English and in the 
language of the majority of the workers, at least one month before the commence- 
ment of the absence in respect of which deductions are made, and (c) notice giving 
the names of person from whom deductions are proposed to be made, the number of 
days for which wages are to be deducted and the conditions on which deductions 
shall be remitted, is exhibited at or near the main entrance of the factory. If the con- 
tract of employment provides the period of notice and the notice given by the worker 
falls short of that period, deductions to be made cannot exceed the wages for the pe- 
riod by which the notice falls short of the period prescribed in the contract. 
Deduction of wages for the period during which a worker absented himself to par- 
ticipate in a bandh was held to be justified. 
16. Deductions for damage or loss (s. 10) 
Deductions for damage to or loss of goods entrusted to the employed person for 
custody or for loss of money for which he is required to account, where such damage 
or loss is directly attributable to his neglect or defauit cannot exceed the amount of 
loss or damage suffered by the employer, that is to say, the employer cannot make a 
profit out of such deduction. | 
Such deduction can be made only after giving the workman concermed an opportu- 
nity to show cause against the proposed deductions. 
17. Deductions for house accommodation, amenities and services (s. 11) 
Clauses (d) and (e) can be taken together. It must be borne in mind, that, ‘“Sery- 
ices” referred to in clause (e) do not include the supply of tools and raw materials 
required for the purposes of the employment and that no deduction can be made in 
that respect. Deductions under these clauses cannot be made unless the workman has 
accepted the facilities provided for by the employer as a term of his employment. 
The amount of deduction cannot exceed an amount equivalent to the value of the - 
house accommodation amenity or service supplied. In the case of deductions for 
amenities and services, appropriate Government is authorised to frame rules govern- 
ing the deductions. The amenities and services for which deductions can be made 
have to be authorised by the appropriate Government by general or special order’! or 
any officer specified by it in this behalf. 
18. Deductions for recovery of advances (s. 12) 
Advances may have been made either before employment or after employment. 
Advances before employment can be of two kinds, namely, (i) towards travelling

19. Deductions of income-tax payable by employed person [TDS] 
The amount of tax payable by a particular person is governed by the provisions of 
the Income-tax Act and the deductions would be to the extent of the tax payable. As 
it would be a hardship for an employed person if the whole of that amount is recov- 
ered.in one month, the amount can be recovered in twelve instalments. 
20. Deductions for subscriptions to, for payment of advances from provident fund 
For making such deductions certain conditions have to be satisfied, namely: 
(1) the provident fund must be one to which the Provident Funds Act, 1925, 
applies; or 
(2) the provident fund must have been recognised by the Commissioner of In- 
come-tax as contemplated by clause (38) of section 2 of the Income-tax 
Act, 1961 (43 of 1961); or 
(3) the provident fund must have been approved by the appropriate Government. 
In case of condition (3), the deductions can be made only during the continuance of 
such approval by the appropriate Government. 
Under section 10 of the Employees’ Provident Funds Act, 1952, the Provident 
Fund constituted under that Act shall be deemed to be a recognised provident fund 
within the meaning of Chapter IX-A of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, [now 1961 
Act] and deductions towards subscription to or towards repayment of advances taken 
from the said provident fund will be covered by this clause. 
21. Deductions for payment to co-operative societies and insurance schemes (s. 13) 
Deductions under clauses (j) and (k) of sub-section (2) of section 7 shall be subject 
to such conditions as the appropriate Government may impose. 
22. Maintenance of registers and records (s. 13A) 
Every employer shall maintain such registers and records giving such particulars of 
persons employed by him, the work performed by them, the wages paid to them, the 


Chap. III—Provisions a) 
deductions made from their wages, the receipts given. by them and such other par- 
ticulars and in such forms as may be prescribed. [s. 13A(1)] 
Every register and record required to be maintained under this section has, for the 
purposes of the Act, to be preserved for a period of three years after the date of the 
last entry made therein. [s. 13A(2)] 
23. Inspectors (s. 14) 
For the purpose of enforcing compliance with the provisions of the Act, the appro- 
priate Government appoints Inspectors. Inspectors of Factories appointed under the 
Factories Act shall be Inspectors under the Act in respect of factories within their 
respective local limits. Power has been given to the appropriate Government to ap- 
point other Officers also as the Inspectors under this Act. 
24. Powers of Inspectors [s. 14(4)] 
These Inspectors can enter on the premises at all reasonable hours and examine the 
registers and documents relating to calculations and payment of wages. They can 
also take evidence of any person either on the spot or otherwise. 
An Inspector may,— 
(a) make such examination and inquiry as he thinks fit in order to ascertain 
whether the provisions of the Act or rules made under it are being observed; 
(b) with such assistance, if any, as he thinks fit, enter, inspect and search any 
premises of any railway, factory or industrial establishment at any reason- 
able time for the purpose of carrying out the objects of the Act; 
(c) supervise the payment of wages to persons employed upon any railway or 
in any factory or industrial establishment; 
(d) require by a written order the production at such place, as may be pre- 
scribed, of any register or record maintained in pursuance of the Act and 
take on the spot or otherwise statements of any persons which he may con- 
sider necessary for carrying out the purposes of the Act; 
(e) seize or take copies of such register or documents or of any portions of 
them as he may consider relevant in respect of an offence under the Act 
which he has reason to believe has been committed by an employer; 
(f) exercise such other powers as may be prescribed. 
No person shall be compelled under this sub-section to answer any question or 
make any statement tending to incriminate himself. 
The provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 shall, so far as may be, ap- 
ply to any search or seizure made under this sub-section as they apply to any search or 
seizure made under the authority of a warrant issued under section 98 of the Code. 
Every Inspector shall be deemed to be a public servant within the meaning of the 
Indian Penal Code, 1960. 
25. Facilities to be afforded to Inspectors (s. 14A) 
Section 14A says that every employer shall afford an Inspector all reasonable facilities 
for making any entry, inspection, supervision, examination or inquiry under the Act.

28. Single application in respect of claims from unpaid group (s. 16) 
It may be noted here that it is not always necessary for employees to file individu- 
ally separate applications. If there are several employees borne on the same estab- 
lishment and if their wages for the same wage period have remained unpaid after the 
due date, the workers are said to belong to the same unpaid group and a single claims 
application can be filed on behalf of all such employees. ° The ‘same unpaid group’ 
can exit only in the case of delayed payment of wages and not in the case of wrong- 
ful deductions from wages. In such cases every person may be awarded maximum 
compensation to the extent specified in sec. 15(3). 
If several applications are filed by employees belonging to the same unpaid group, 
the authority can deal with them as if it was a single application by”an unpaid 
sroup. 
29. Proceedings before the authority (s. 15) 
After a claim application is filed, the Authority has to issue notice to the employer 
and the person responsible for payment of wages about the claim and call upon them 
to state their objections to the same. The Authority has then to hear the applicant and 
the opponents or to give them an opportunity to be heard. If the claim is established 
the Authority issues directions to the opponents to pay to the employee or employees 
concerned the delayed wages or to refund to him the amount wrongfully deducted. If 
the employee is dead, then the direction is to be in favour of his legal representative 
or heir. The Authority can also direct payment of compensation to the employee or 
his legal representative. The amount of such compensation must not, however, ex- 
ceed ten times the amount deducted in the case of wrongful deductions and not ex- 
ceeding three thousand rupees but not less than one thousand five hundred rupees in 
case of delayed wages. Even if the amount deducted or delayed wages are paid be- 
fore the disposal of the application, authority may direct the payment of such com- 
pensation, as it may think fit, not exceeding two thousand rupees. [s. 15(3)] 
A claim under this Act shall be disposed of as for as practicable within a period of 
three months from the date of registration of the claim by the authority. 
30. Proceeding are of summary nature (s. 15) 
The section provides a summary remedy for wages earned but not paid and it does 
not provide remedy for investigations or inquiries which concern the worker’s office 
or job. In other words, whether the retention of an employee on a pay is proper or not 
is not subject of inquiry. The authority appointed under the Act cannot decide such 
issues.’ In D’Costa v. B.C. Patel,'* the Supreme Court held that the authority has 
jurisdiction not only to make directions contemplated by Section 15(3) to refund to 
the employed person any amount unlawfully deducted but also to find out what the 
terms of the contract were, so as to determine what the wages of the employed person 
were. The Authority under the Act has jurisdiction only to decide propriety of de- 
ductions from wages or delay in payment. The Act does not apply to cases of with-

31. Jurisdiction limited to investigation of existing wages and not potential (s. 15) 
The authority has the jurisdiction to decide what the actual terms of the contract 
between the parties were, that is to say, to determine the actual wages; but the 
authority has no jurisdiction to determine the question of potential wages. If the 
respondent had been on the cadre of monthly wages and if the appellant had with- 
held his rise in wages to which he was automatically entitled, without any orders of 
his superior officers, he might have justly claimed the redress of his grievances 
from the authority under the Act, as it would have amounted to an underpayment. 
On the authority of this Judgment the Bombay High Court has held that the dispute 
regarding the difference of amount due on account of classification of a painter is 
outside the jurisdiction of the Payment of Wages Authority.” 
32. Scope of Authority’s jurisdiction (s. 15) 
The jurisdiction under this section is limited to all claims arising out of deductions 
from wages and delay in payment of wages. This being a special jurisdiction, it must 
be construed strictly. The authority should decide about the quantum of wages pay- 
able and in doing so it is bound to adjudicate upon the terms of the contract under 
which wages were due. The law as to the jurisdiction under the Payment of Wages 
Act is well settled. The leading case on the subject is Sarin v. Patel,” where a Di- 
vision Bench was for the first time called upon to consider the scheme of the Act 
and the jurisdiction of the authority under the Act and in that decision it was laid 
down that the authority had no jurisdiction to decide whether the service of an em- 
ployee was rightly or wrongly terminated or whether the dismissal was lawful or 
unlawful. It was stated that such a question would not come within the purview of 
the special tribunal set up under the Act. Therefore, in order to determine what the 
contract was, what the terms of the contract were and the wages due under the 
contract, it might become necessary for the authority to determine whether in the 
first place there was an employment or not the principle laid down in Sarin’s case 
as followed in Almeda v. Taylor." In D’Costa v. Patel,”” the question that arose for 
the consideration of the learned Judges was entirely different. Mr. Justice SINHA

not only to make directions contemplated by section 15(3) to refund to the em- 
ployed person any amount unlawfully deducted but also to find out what the terms

were. Now that is exactly the proposition to which legal effect is sought to be given

33. Jurisdiction of Authority 
The Authority can decide questions ancillary to main application and germane to 
pleadings too. 
The jurisdiction of the Authority under the Act to deal with the classes of claims as 
mentioned in s. 15 is exclusive and in dealing with claims arising out of deductions 
or delay in making payment of wages, such Authority would have the power to con- 
sider questions incidental to those matters and it is true that while determining such 
incidental questions or issues, proper care must be taken to see that in the name or 
guise of deciding such incidental issues or questions, the limited jurisdiction of the 
Authority is not unduly or unreasonably extended and further care should also be 
taken to see that the scope of the incidental questions is not unduly limited so as to 
affect or impair the limited jurisdiction conferred on the Authority. The Authority 
under s. 15 is given a special jurisdiction and it cannot be disputed that it has the ju- 
risdiction to try matters which are incidental to the claim. Such incidental issues 
should have a bearing to the original claim and not be foreign to the same or contrary 
to the pleadings or should be germane on the pleadings. 
34. Territorial Jurisdiction 
The jurisdiction under the Act is with reference to locality.

and of enforcing the attendance of witnesses and compelling the production of 
documents. Every such authority shall be deemed to be a Civil Court for all the pur- 
poses of section 195 and of Chapter XXXV of the Code of Criminal Procedure,

Section 15(2) clearly lays down that the Payment of Wabee Authority has only ju- 
risdiction to hear and decide the claims arising out of deductions from wages or delay 
in payment of wages which are not permissible under the provisions of the Act of 
1936 and that the Payment of Wages Act does not apply to the cases where the em- 
ployer has withheld the wages on the ground of negligence, misappropriation and 
default, if any, committed by the employee. 
The Authority under the Act is clothed with all the powers of the Civil Court by 
virtue of section 18 of the Act and it is not proper to say that its jurisdiction is limited 
in character in this respect. The Authority under this section has a power to decide all 
claims arising out of deductions from wages or delay in payment of wages and to 
make an order for compensation along with an order for delayed wages or of the 
amount deducted. The proviso to sub-section (3) is restrictive of the power conferred 
on the Authority to make an order for payment of wages. If the circumstances in 
which it is prevented to make an order for compensation required a determination of 
certain matters, obviously it must impliedly be within the competence of the Author- 
ity to determine whether such situation exists or not. If the Authority specifies that 
there was a bona fide dispute as to the amount payable it cannot make an order for 
compensation. For determining whether the dispute was a bona fide one, the Author- 
ity must of necessity have the power of examining the dispute and determining it. It 
is, therefore, implicit in clause “A” of the proviso to section 13(3) that the Authority 
has jurisdiction to decide a dispute as to the amount payable.’ The Authority has 
also jurisdiction to decide the dispute as to whether the employees have worked 
overtime and to determine the wages for over-time payable to them.*° The authority 
has also power to determine whether the employee did or did not continue to be em- 
ployed during the relevant period, whether his employment came to an end or not by 
virtue of certain acts set up by the company which do not amount to acts of dis- 
missal, discharge or termination. 
Where payments are not made inspite of the final orders of the Payment of Wages 
Authority, the very purpose of this social legislation would be defeated. The Author- 
ity, therefore, has the power to recover the amount directed to be paid, as if it were a 
fine imposed by a Magistrate, if the Authority was a Magistrate. It can also apply to a 
Magistrate to make effective recovery of the amount as if it were a fine.

37. Jurisdiction of District Court 
The party aggrieved by the decision of the prescribed authority is allowed to prefer 
an application under sec. 15. Section 17 of the Act permits the aggrieved party to 
prefer an appeal to the District Judge, who has the ordinary appellate jurisdiction 
under the Code of Civil Procedure. The court of District Judge will, therefore, remain 
as ordinary court under the Code of Civil Procedure and the District Judge will exer- 
cise all the powers of the Civil Court provided in the Code of Civil Procedure. The 
orders and decrees issued by the Court of District Judge will, therefore, be governed 
by the rules of Civil Procedure Code. In view of this, it cannot be disputed that a re- 
view is competent against the decision of the District Judge passed in an appeal un- 
der section 17 of the Act. 
It is well settled that while exercising powers under Order XLVII, Rule 1, C.P.C. 
the reviewing court does not sit in appeal on the order of his predecessor and cannot 
reassess the evidence. It is also well settled that the review powers cannot be exer- 
cised on the ground that the earlier decision was erroneous on merit or that a differ- 
ent view was possible than the one taken in the earlier decision. 
38. Powers of High Court 
Article 227 of the Constitution of India confers upon the High Court the power of 
superintendence not only over the subordinate courts but also over the tribunals 
throughout the territories in relation to which High Court exercises jurisdiction. It is, 
therefore, within the power of the High Court to enquire into the order of the Autho- 
rity under section 15 in an appropriate case. 
The authority appointed under this Act is not in fact a Civil Court in the strict sense 
but it has been declared to be Civil Court for limited purpose. 
39. Jurisdiction to order compensation [s. 15(3) proviso] 
It must, be remembered that no order for compensation can be made in the case of 
delayed wages, if the Authority is satisfied that the delay was due to (a) a bona fide 
error or bona fide dispute as to the amount payable to the employee concerned, or (b) 
the occurrence of an emergency or the existence of exceptional circumstances such 
that the person responsible for payment of wages was unable, though exercising rea- 
sonable diligence, to make prompt payment, or (c) the failure of the employee to ap- 
ply for or accept payment. Further, if the Authority hearing the application comes to 
the conclusion that the application was either vexatious or malicious, it can direct the 
person presenting the application to pay to the employer or the person responsible for 
payment of wages a penalty not exceeding three hundred seventy five rupees. If on 
the other hand, the Authority comes to the conclusion that the applicant should not 
have been driven to file a claims application for recovering his dues, the Authority 
can direct the employer or person responsible for payment of wages to pay as penalty 
a sum not exceeding three hundred seventy five rupees. It must be noted that the 
amount of such penalty is to be credited to the appropriate Government by the em- 
ployer or other person responsible for payment of wages.

40. Appeals (s. 17) 
An appeal against an order dismissing either wholly or in part an application under 
section 15(2), or against a direction made under sub-section (3) or sub-section (4) of 
section 15, may be made within 30 days from the date on which the order or direc- 
tion was made. If the order was made in the Presidency Town, an appeal shall be 
preferred before the Court of Small Cause and elsewhere it shall be preferred before 
the District Court.”’ [S. 17(1)] 
An appeal may be preferred by the following persons— 
(a) by the employer or other person responsible for the payment of wages un- 
der section 3, if the total sum directed to be paid by way of wages and 
compensation exceeds three hundred rupees or such direction has the effect 
of imposing on the employee or the other person a financial liability ex- 
ceeding one thousand rupees, or 
(b) by an employed person or any legal practitioner, any official of a registered 
trade union authorized in writing to act on his behalf or any inspector under 
the Act, or any other person permitted by the Authority to make an appli- 
cation under section 15(2), if the total amount of wages claimed to have 
been withheld from the employed person exceeds twenty rupees or from the 
unpaid group to which the employed person belongs or belonged, exceeds 
fifty rupees, or 
(c) by any person directed to pay a penalty under of section 15(4). 
However, no appeal shall lie under sub-s. (1)(a) unless the memorandum of appeal 
is accompanied by a certificate by the Authority to the effect that the appellant has 
deposited the amount payable under the direction appealed against.” [S. 17(1A)] 
A saving provision under sub-section (2) provides that save as provided in sub- 
section (1), any order dismissing either wholly or in part an application made under 
section 15(2), or a direction made under section 15(3) or (4) shall be final.

the appeal has been preferred may and if so directed by the court referred to in sub-

without complying with the requirement of the deposit of the amount payable was held to be not 
maintainable, Mohd. Nasir v. D.J. Rajouri, (2002) 1 Lab LJ 266 (J&K). 
42. The High Court has revisional jurisdiction under sec. 115 CPC, 1908 against orders passed by the 
District Court in appeal under sec. 17 of the PW Act. Bharatpur Central Co-operative Bank vy. 
Ratan Singh, (1995) 3 Lab LJ (Supp) 813 (Raj). Revision can be maintained under sec. 17. Samber- 
nath Bhattacharjee v. Orient Paper Mills, (1995) 1 Lab LJ 159 (Ori); Chhetriya Sahkari Samiti Ltd. 
v. Second Adl. DJ, (1993) 3 Lab LJ (Supp) 857 (All). Ex parte orders were found to be based on co- 
gent and sound reasons, no error of law or of jurisdiction, writ petition dismissed, Prabhu Das v. 
D.J., Pali, (1999) 2 Lab LJ 123 (Raj). Revision petition against order in appeal under sec. 17 has 
been held to be maintainable under sec 115(2) CPC; Chief Manager, Allahabad Bank, Bokaro Steel 
City v. Parsan Kumar, (2002) 1 Lab LJ 264 (Jhar). 


342 Part IV—The Payment of Wages Act, 1936 
section (1) shall, pending the decision of the appeal withhold payment of any sum in 
deposit, with it S. 17(3). 
Sub-section (4) provides for submission of any question of law for the decision of 
the High Court. It says that the court referred to in sub-section (1) may, if it thinks fit, 
submit any question of law for the decision of the High Court and, then the matter is 
to be disposed of in accordance with the High Court decision. 
The Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 and the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 are “‘cor- 
responding law” qua each other particularly as both are part of the same social leg- 
islative canopy made by the Parliament for immediate amelioration of workmen’s 
plight resulting from non-payment, or delayed payment or short payment of their 
wages. The conclusion is irresistible that the “Authority” constituted under section 15 
and the “Appellate Authority” under section 17 of the Payment of Wages Act, fall 
within the exception indicated in section 28 of the Administrative Tribunal Act and 
Payment of Wages Act is positively covered by the connotation “corresponding law” 
used in that section. Consequently, the jurisdiction of the Authority to entertain and 
decide claim cases under section 15 of the Payment of Wages Act is not affected by 
the establishment of the Administrative Tribunals. 
41. Conditional attachment of property of employer or person responsible for 
payment of wages (s. 17A) 
On an application under S. 15 or appeal under S. 17, if the Authority or the Court 
is convinced that the persons responsible for wages may evade payment, their pro- 
perty to the extent of the amount likely to be awarded may be ordered to be attached 
after giving them an opportunity to be heard. 
The provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, relating to attachment before 
judgment under that Code shall, so far as may be, apply to any order for attachment 
under sub-section (1). [S. 17A(2)] 
In the case of Puroshottam Das Goel yv. Prabhakar Pandey,“ it was held that the 
powers of the Authority under section 17A is quasi-judicial in nature. Section 17A 
empowers the prescribed authority to direct the attachment of so much of the prop- 
erty of the employer or other persons responsible for the payment of wages as is, in 
its opinion, sufficient to satisfy the amount which may be payable under the direction 
to be given under section 15 or 17 of the Payment of Wages Act. The satisfaction or 
the opinion contemplated by section 17A_ is objective and has to be founded on le- 
gally cognizable material. The order to be passed on the basis of such satisfaction or 
opinion must disclose and spell out reasons so that it may be discernible to all con- 
cerned that the material which contributed to the satisfaction on formation of the 
opinion of the Authority or Court was adequate to sustain the order. The power of the 
Authority under section 17A is quasi-judicial in nature. The authority is, therefore, 
bound to give reasons for exercise of such power. Non-disclosure of reasons is viola- 
tive of the principles of natural justice rendering the order void. 
42. Powers of authorities appointed under sec. 15 (s. 18) 
Every Authority appointed under section 15(1) shall have all the powers of a Civil 
Court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, for the purpose of taking evidence 
and of enforcing the attendance of witnesses and compelling the production of

documents. Every such authority shall be deemed to be a Civil Court for all the pur- 
poses of section 195 and of Chapter XXVI of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. 
43. Penalty for offences under the Act (s. 20) 
A person responsible for payment of wages to an employed person who contra- 
venes any of the provisions of the following sections, namely: 
(i) section 5 excepting sub-section (4), 
(ii) section 7, 
(ill) section 8 excepting sub-section (8), 
(iv) section 9, 
(v) section 10, excepting sub-section (2), 
(vi) sections 12 to 13, both inclusive, 
is punishable with fine which is not to be less one thousand fine hundred rupees but which may extend to seven thousand five hundred rupees. 
Whoever contravenes the provisions of following sections, namely 
(i) section 4, or (il) section 5, (iii) section 6, (iv) sub-section 8 of section 8 (v) 
sub-section (2) of section 10, or (vi) section 25. 
shall be punishable with fine which may extend to three thousand seven hundred fifty 
rupees. 
Whoever being required to nominate or designate a person under section 3 fails to 
do so, he shall be punishable with fine which may extend to three thousand rupees. 
(sub s. 2A ). 
Whoever being required under the Act to maintain any records or registers or to 
furnish any information or return— 
(a) fails to maintain such register or record; or 
(b) wilfully refuses or without lawful excuse neglects to furnish such informa- 
tion or returns; or 
(c) wilfully furnishes or causes to be furnished any information or return which 
he knows to be false; or 
(d) refuses to answer or wilfully gives a false answer to any question neces- 
sary for obtaining any information required to be furnished under the Act; 
shall for each such offence, be punishable with fine which shall not be less than one 
thousand five hundred rupees but which may extend to seven thousand five hundred 
rupees. 
Sub-section (4) provides that whoever 
(a) wilfully obstructs an inspector in the discharge of his duties under this Act; or 
(b) refuses or wilfully neglects to afford an inspector any reasonable facility for 
making any entry, inspection, examination, supervision, or inquiry author- 
ized by or under the Act in relation to any railway factory or industrial or 
other establishment; or 
(c) wilfully refuses to preclude on the demand of an inspector and register or 
other document kept in pursuance of the Act; or 


344 Part 1V-—The Payment of Wages Act, 1936 
(d) prevents or attempts to prevent or does anything which he has any reason to 
believe is likely to prevent any person from appearing before or being ex- 
amined by an inspector acting in pursuance of his duties under the Act; 
shall be punishable with fine which shall not be less than one,thousand five hundred 
rupees but which may extend to seven thousand five hundred rupees. 
If any person who has been convicted of any offence punishable under the Act is 
again guilty of an offence involving contravention of the same provision, he shall be 
punishable on a subsequent conviction with imprisonment for a term which shall not 
be less than one month but which may extend to six months and with fine which 
shall not be less than three thousand seven hundred fifty rupees but which may ex- 
tend to twenty-two thousand five hundred rupees, provided that for the purpose of 
this sub-section, no cognizance shall be taken of any conviction made more than two 
years before the date on which the commission of the offence which is being pun- 
ished came to the knowledge of the Inspector. [S. 20(5)] 
If any person fails or wilfully neglects to pay the wages of any employed person by 
the date fixed by the authority in this behalf, he shall, without prejudice to any other 
action that may be taken against him, be punishable with an additional fine which 
may extend to seven hundred fifty rupees for each day for which such failure or ne- 
glect continues. 
44, Procedure in trial of offences (s. 21) 
A court shall not take cognizance of a complaint against any person for an offence 
under section 20(1) unless an application in respect of the facts constituting the of- 
fence has been presented under section 15 and has been granted wholly or in part and 
the authority empowered under the latter section or the appellate court granting such 
application has sanctioned the making of the complaint. 
In cases of complaints arising out of non-compliance with the provisions of the Act 
relating to delay in payment of wages and wrongful deductions from wages, the 
Court can entertain such a complaint only if a claim application had been filed and 
the Authority or the Appellate Court had granted it wholly or in part and the State 
Government or any officer authorised by it in that behalf had sanctioned the making 
of a complaint. [S. 21(1)] 
Before granting such sanction to make a complaint, the State Government or the 
Officer authorised by it in that behalf shall give to the person against whom the 
sanction is to be granted an opportunity to show cause why such sanction should not 
be granted. Sanction shall not be granted if the State Government or the Officer 
authorised is satisfied that the default was due to (a) bona fide error or bona fide dis- 
pute as to the amount payable to the employee concerned or his legal representative, 
or (b) the occurrence of an emergency or the existence of exceptional circumstances 
which prevented him from complying with the provisions of the Act, or (Cc) the fail- 
ure of the employee or his legal representative to apply for and accept payment. 
Complaints in respect of offences under section 20(3) or (4) must be made by the 
Inspector alone. [S. 21(2)] : 
It may be noted that these grounds are the same as the grounds on which the 
Authority can refuse to direct payment of compensation. 
45. Bar of suits (s. 22) 
A suit for recovery of wages or any wrongful deductions from wages shall not be 
entertained by a Civil Court under the following circumstances: 


Chap. I1II—Provisions 345 
(a) The amount claimed formed the subject matter of a claims application 
which had been filed and is pending in the Court or the Authority or in re- 
spect of which an appeal is pending before the Appellate Court; or 
(b) The amount claimed had formed the subject of a direction given in favour 
of the plaintiff on a claims application; or 
(c) The amount claimed had been found in a claim application not to be due to 
the plaintiff; or 
(d) The amount claimed could have been recovered by a claims application. 
46. Protection of action taken in good faith (s. 22A) 
No suit, prosecution or other legal proceeding shall lie against the Government or 
any officer of the Government for anything which is in good faith done or intended 
to be done under the Acct. 
47. Contracting out (s. 23) 
Any contract or agreement, whether made before or after the commencement of 
Act, whereby an employed person relinquishes any right conferred by the Act shall 
be null and void in so far as it purports to deprive him of such right. 
48. Delegation.of powers (s. 24) 
The appropriate Government may by notification in the Official Gazette direct that any 
power exercisable by it under this Act, in relation to matters and subject to conditions, if 
any, as may be specified in the direction, shall also be exercisable by the following: 
(a) where the appropriate Government is the Central Government, by such of- 
ficer or authority subordinate to the Central Government or by the State 
Government or by such officer or authority subordinate to the State Gov- 
ernment, as may be specified in the notification; 
(b) Where the appropriate Government is a State Government, by such officer 
or authority subordinate to the State Government as may be specified in the 
notification. 
49. Display by notice of abstracts of the Act (s. 25) 
The person responsible for payment of wages to persons employed in a factory or an 
industrial or other establishment shall cause to be displayed in such factory or indus- 
trial or other establishment a notice containing such abstracts of the Act and of the rules 
made thereunder in English and in the language of the majority of the persons em- 
ployed in the factory, or industrial or other establishment as may be prescribed. 
50. Payment of undisturbed wages in cases of death of employed person (s. 25A) 
Subject to the other provisions of the Act, all amounts payable to an employed per- 
son as wages shall, if such amounts could not or cannot be paid on account of his 
death before payment or on account of his whereabouts not being know,— 
(a) be paid to the person nominated by him in this behalf in accordance with 
the rules made under the Act; or 
(b) where no such nomination has been made or where for any reasons such 
amounts cannot be paid to the person so nominated, be deposited with the

prescribed authority who shall deal with the amounts so deposited in such 
manner as may be prescribed. [S. 25A(1)] 
Where, in accordance with the provisions of sub-section (1), all amounts payable to 
an employed person as wages— 
(a) are paid by the employer to the person nominated by the employed person, 
or 
(b) are deposited by the employer with the prescribed authority, the employer 
shall be discharged of his liability to pay those wages. [S. 25A(2)]

PART V 
THE PAYMENT OF BONUS ACT, 1965 
CHAPTER I 
INTERPRETATION 
SYNOPSIS 
1. Available surplus formula of bonus..... 350 3. Available surplus formula and statu- 
2. Statement of objects and reasons......... 350 tory formula ........scesereseseesetstetetereees 350 
4. Short title, extent and application........ 350 
The Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 is an Act to provide for the payment of bonus to 
persons employed in certain establishments on the basis of profits or on the basis of 
production or productivity and for other connected matters. 
The term “Bonus” means an ex gratia payment or bounty or payment by way of 
gift. 
The origin of payment of bonus ‘n India can be traced to “War Bonus” given in 
Bombay to the workers in textile industry in July 1917, in the form of an increase of 
10% in wages. In 1924 the Government of Bombay appointed the Bonus Disputes 
Committee presided over by Sir Noman Mcleod, the then Chief Justice of the Bom- 
bay High Court. The Committee held that the workers had no enforceable claim, 
customary, legal or equitable to the payment of bonus. Thus, the payment of bonus in 
the earlier years was an ex gratia payment. Bonus used to be paid on ad hoc basis at 
that time by a few industrial undertakings. 
During the period of the Second World War, industries reaped large profits and 
started voluntary payments of bonus regularly. Under the Defence of India Act and 
Rules made it, a provision was made for compulsory reference of industrial disputes for 
adjudication. The adjudicators found varying bases to uphold the payment of bonus to 
workers. However, it was recognised that the demand for a bonus being an industrial 
claim could be upheld when wages fell short of living standard and the industries made 
huge profits, part of which were due to the contribution which workers made, in in- 
creasing the production. From the year 1946 onwards, this basis of payment of bonus 
became a settled principle of industrial law. With the advent of the Constitution of In- 
dia, the notions of progressive social philosophy and the need for giving social justice 
to the workers, the concept of bonus established firm roots in industrial adjudication. 
The Supreme Court declared in emphatic terms that as both capital and labour contri- 
bute to the earnings of an industrial concern, it is only fair and just that the labour 
should derive some benefit if there is surplus available after meeting prior and neces- 
ee ee ae ener 
1. Bonus is not deferred wage. Mukund Iron & Steel Works Ltd. y. Workmen, (1950) 1 LLJ 587 (Bom); 
Lever Bros (India) Ltd. y. Employees, (1950) 2 LLJ 1314 (T—Mad). 
349 


350 Part V—The Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 
sary charges. Thus a bonus formula was evolved based on considerations of social jus- 
tice intending to satisfy legitimate claims of both labour and capital. 
1. Available surplus formula of bonus 
The Bonus formula is also known as Full Bench Formula or Available Surplus 
Formula. It was first evolved in the case of Mill Owners’ Association, Bombay vy. 
Rashtriya Mill Mazdoor Sangh, Bombay. 
In this case the Full Bench of the Industrial Tribunal, Bombay, said that the available surplus should be determined after making provision for depreciation, reserves for re- habilitation, return at 6% on paid-up capital and a return on the working capital at a lesser rate than the one paid-up capital. This available surplus should be equitably dis- tributed between capital and labour. The Supreme Court in the Associated Cement Co. Ltds.’ case,” considered the whole formula and in principle affirmed the same. It is noteworthy that under this formula bonus was not payable if there was no available surplus left with the employer. Thus bonus was linked to profits. 
2. Statement of objects and reasons 
In 1961, a Tripartite Commission was set up by the Government of India to con- sider in a comprehensive manner the question of payment of bonus based on profits to employees employed in establishments and to make recommendations to the Gov- ernment. The Commission gave its Report on 24th January, 1964. The Government on 2nd September, 1964, announced acceptance of the Commission’s recommenda- tions subject to a few modifications. In order to given statutory effect to the recom- mendations of the Bonus Commission, as modified by the Government of India, an ordinance known as Payment of Bonus Ordinance, 1965 was promulgated. The re- sulting Act of this Ordinance was Payment of Bonus Act, 1965. 
3. Available surplus formula and statutory formula 
The following are the important and broad distinctions between the two: 
(a) Under the available surplus formula there was no system of payment of minimum and maximum bonus and no device of set-on and set-off existed. Under the statutory formula notwithstanding losses, the employer is bound to pay minimum bonus of 8.33% and is not bound to pay more than 20% whatever may be his profits. 
(b) Unlike the available surplus formula statutory formula does not accept “Re- habilitation’ as a prior charge and the quantum of other prior charges has been fixed and not left for determination by the Tribunal. 
(c) The employee’s share in the available surplus, i.e., allocable surplus is also fixed under the statutory formula but it was not so under the earlier for- mula. 
(d) The method and manner of payment and recovery of bonus has been sim- plified and regulated by statutory rules now but it was not so earlier. 
4. Short title, extent and application 
The Payment of Bonus Act, 1965, extends to the whole of India and save as other- wise provided in this Act, it shall apply to every factory and every other establish- pi EN A RA 
2. The Associated Cement Co. Ltd. y. Their Workers, AIR 1959 SC 967 : 1959 SCR 925. 3. (1950) 2 LLJ 1247. 


Chap. [—Interpretation 351 
ment in which twenty or more persons are employed on any day during an account- 
ing year. 
It is also provided that the appropriate Government may, after giving not less than 
two months’ notice of its intention so to do, by notification in the Official Gazette, 
apply the provisions of the Act with effect from such accounting year as may be 
specified in the notification, to any establishments or class of establishment (includ- 
ing an establishment being a factory within the meaning of section 2(m)(ii) of the 
Factories Act, 1948, employing such number of persons less than twenty as may be 
specified in the notification; so however, that the number of persons so specified 
shall in no case be less than ten. 
The provisions of the Act in relation to a factory or other establishment to which 
the Act applies, same as otherwise provided in the Act, shall have effect in respect of 
the accounting year commencing on any day in the year 1964 and in respect of every 
subsequent accounting year. 
In relation to the State of Jammu and Kashmir, the reference to the accounting year 
commencing on any day in the year 1964 and every subsequent accounting year shall 
be construed as reference to the accounting year commencing on any day in the year 
1968 and every subsequent accounting year. 
When the provisions of the Act have been made applicable to any establishment or 
class of establishments by the issue of a notification under the proviso to sub-section 
(3), the reference to the accounting year commencing on any day in the year 1964 
and every subsequent accounting year or, as the case may be, the reference of the 
accounting year commencing on any day in the year 1968 and every subsequent ac- 
counting year shall in relation to such establishment or class of establishments be 
construed as a reference to the accounting year specified in such notification and 
every subsequent accounting year. 
An establishment to which the Act applies shall continue to be governed by the Act 
notwithstanding that the number of persons employed in it falls below twenty or, as 
the case may be, the number specified in the notification issued under the provision 
to sub-section (3). 
The Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 does not bar claims to customary bonus or those 
claims based on conditions of service. It is not necessary that right to receive bonus 
including customary bonus should be dealt with only by the Payment of Bonus Act 
and not by any other Parliamentary Legislation. Payment of bonus in regard to em- 
ployees of State Bank of India can also be dealt with by the State Bank of India Act, 
1955. Similarly, any amendment introduced to State Bank of India Act with regard to 
right of employees to receive customary bonus can be governed by the State Bank of 
India Act, 1955.°

1. Accounting year [s. 2(1)] 
(1) “Accounting year” means — 
(i) in relation to a corporation, the year ending on the day on which the 
books and all accounts of the corporation are to be closed and balanced; 
(ii) in relation to a company, the period in respect of which any profit and 
loss account of the company laid before it in annual general meeting 1s 
made up, whether that period is a year or not, 
(iii) in any other case— 
(a) the year commencing on the Ist day of April; or 
(b) if the accounts of an establishment maintained by the employer are 
closed and balanced on any day other than the 31st day of March, 
then, at the option of the employer, the year ending on the day on 
which its accounts are so closed and balanced. 
An option once exercised by the employer under paragraph (b) of 
this sub-clause shall not again be exercised except with the previous 
permission in writing of the prescribed authority and upon such con- 
ditions as that authority may think fit. 
2. Agricultural income [s. 2(2)] 
“A oricultural income” has the same meaning as in the Income-tax Act. 
3. Agricultural Income-tax Law [s. 2(3)] 
“A oricultural income-tax law” means any law for the time being in force relating 
to the levy of tax on agricultural income.

4. Allocable surplus [s. 2(4)] 
‘““Allocable surplus’? means— 
(a) in relation to an employer, being a company which has not made the ar- 
rangements prescribed under the Income-tax Act for the declaration and 
payment within India of the dividends payable out of its profits in accor- 
dance with the provisions of section 194 of that Act, sixty-seven per cent of 
the available surplus in an accounting year; 
(b) in any other case, sixty per cent of such available surplus. 
5. Appropriate Government [s. 2(5)] 
“Appropriate Government” means— 
(i) in relation to an establishment in respect of which the appropriate Govern- 
ment under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, is the Central Government. 
The National Dairy Development Board is an establishment engaged in the 
industry carried on by or under the authority of the Central Government, as 
required by sec. 32(IV) of the Act.’ 
(ii) in relation to any other establishment, the Government of the State in which 
establishment is situate. 
6. Available surplus [s. 2(6)] 
“Available surplus” means the available surplus computed under section 5S. 
7. Award [s. 2(7)] 
“Award” means an interim or a final determination of any industrial dispute or of 
any question relating to it by any Labour Court, Industrial Tribunal or National Tri- 
bunal constituted under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, or by any other authority 
constituted under any corresponding law relating to investigation and settlement of industrial disputes in force in a State and includes an arbitration award made under Section 10A of that Act or under that other law. 
8. Banking company [s. 2(8)] 
“Banking company” means a banking company as defined in section 5 of the Banking Companies Act, 1949, and includes the State Bank of India, any subsidiary bank as defined in the State Bank of India (Subsidiary Banks), Act, 1959, “any corre- sponding new Bank specified in the First Schedule to the Banking Companies (Ac- quisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970, any corresponding new Bank constituted under sec. 3 of the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Un- dertakings) Act, 1980, any cooperative bank as defined in clause (bii) of sec. 2 of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934’, and any other banking institution which may: be notified in this behalf by the Central Government. 
9. Company [s. 2(9)] 
“Company” means any company as defined in section 3 of the Companies Act, 1956, and includes a foreign company within the meaning of section 591 of that Act.
