10. Co-operative society [s. 2(10)] 
“Co-operative society” means a society registered or deemed to be registered under

11. Corporation [s. 2(11)] 
“Corporation” means any body corporate established by or under any Central, Pro-

“Direct tax’’ means—

(iv) the agricultural income-tax law; and

clared by the Central Government, by notification in the Official Gazette, to 
be a direct tax for the purposes of the Act. 
13. Employee [s. 2(13)] 
“Employee” means any person (other than an apprentice) employed on a salary or 
wage not exceeding three thousand and five hundred rupees per mensem in any in- 
dustry to do any skilled or unskilled manual, supervisory, managerial, administrative, 
technical or clerical work for hire or reward, whether the terms of employment be 
express or implied. 
14. Employer [s. 2(14)]

(i) in relation to an establishment which is a factory, the owner or occupier of

(ii) in relation to any other establishment, the person who, or the authority 
which, has the ultimate control over the affairs of the establishment and 
where the said affairs are entrusted to a manager, managing director, such 
manager, managing director.

1. Establishments to include departments, undertakings and branches (s. 3) 
Where an establishment consists of different departments or undertakings or has 
branches, whether situated in the same place or in different places, all such depart- 
ments or undertakings or branches are to be treated as parts of the same establish- 
ment for the purpose of computation of bonus under this Act. 
Where for any accounting year a separate balance-sheet and profit and loss account 
are prepared and maintained in respect of any such department or undertaking or 
branch, then, such department or undertaking or branch is not to be treated as a sepa- 
rate establishment for the purpose of computation of bonus, under the Act for that 
year, unless such department or undertaking or branch was, immediately before the 
commencement of that accounting year treated as part of the establishment for the 
purpose of computation of bonus. 
Where a subsidiary company, wholly owned by the principal company, is amalga- 
mated with the principal company, the workmen of the principal company are enti- 
tled to bonus by including the income of the subsidiary company along with the gross 
profits of the principal company.

In case of amalgamation of undertaking of six companies with Binny Ltd., the 
scheme provided that employees of amalgamating companies will become employ- 
ees of new company and separate profit and loss account would be prepared for each 
of the amalgamated company for the financial year 1969, the new company did not 
prepare balance sheet though separate P/L account was prepared for each of the 
amalgamating company for the same year, it was held that omission to prepare sepa- 
rate balance sheet cannot deny a demand of bonus to the employees of erstwhile 
Binny Co. Ltd. and the tribunal can direct the employer to prepare balance sheet. 
2. Computation of gross profits (s. 4) 
According to section 4, the gross profits derived by an employer from an estab- 
lishment in respect of the accounting year has: 
(a) in the case of a banking company, be calculated in the manner specified in 
the First Schedule; 
(b) in any other case, to be calculated in the manner specified in the Second 
Schedule.° 
3. Working of bonus formula under the Act 
Working of the bonus formula under the Act involves four steps— 
(1) Net profit—Step I 
(11) Gross profits—Step II 
(iii) Available surplus—Step III 
(iv) Allocable surplus—Step IV 
Each of these steps has been taken up below one by one. 
4. Net Profits—Step I 
The bonus formula provided under the Act presumes about the accuracy of bal- 
ance-sheet and profit and loss account of companies and corporations. It, therefore, 
starts with the presumption that the net profit shown in the profit and loss account 
and balance-sheet should be taken as the first step for determination of the bonus. 
5. Presumption about accuracy of balance-sheet and profit and loss account of 
corporations and companies (s. 23) 
Where, during the course of proceedings before any arbitrator or Tribunal under the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, or under any corresponding law relating to investigation 
_ and settlement of industrial disputes in force in a State to which any dispute of the na- 
ture specified in section 22 has been referred, the balance-sheet and the profit and loss account of an employer, being a corporation or a company (other than a banking com- 
pany), duly audited by the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India or by auditors

Sec. 4 and Second Schedule, surplus brought forward to revenue account wrongly men- tioned by the Tribunal as net profit, direction was issued to decide afresh to ascertain net profit as per second schedule. Workmen of principal company are entitled to bonus by including dividend re- ceived by subsidiary company with gross profits of the principal company when the subsidiary company, which was doing no other business, earning no other income except from the shares trans- ferred to it by the principal company, was amalgamated with the principal company, Workmen vy. duly qualified to act as auditors of companies under sub-section (1) of section 226 of

statements and particulars contained in the balance-sheet and profit and loss account to 
be accurate. It would not be necessary for the corporation or the company to prove the 
accuracy of such statements and particulars by the filing of an affidavit or by any other 
mode. 
Where the authority is satisfied that the statements and particulars contained in the 
balance-sheet or the profit and loss account of the corporation or the company are not 
accurate, it may take such steps as it thinks necessary to find out the accuracy of such 
statements and particulars. [S. 23(1)] 
When an application is made to the authority by any trade union being a party to 
the dispute or where there is no trade union, by the employees being a party to the 
dispute, requiring any clarification relating to any item in the balance-sheet or the 
profit and loss account, it may, after satisfying itself that such clarification is neces- 
sary, by order, direct the corporation or, the company to furnish to the trade union or 
the employees such clarification within such time as may be specified in the direction 
and the corporation or, the company, has to comply with such direction. [S. 23(2)] 
6. Powers of Tribunal 
An Industrial Tribunal cannot overlook the presumption and hold that the company 
derived profits, without any material, simply on the contention raised by the work- 
men that the depreciation allowed was excessive and interest for losses was debited 
from the total profits of the company. 
Section 23 cannot prevent the corporation from deducting from total income an 
item which was shown as income in the profit and loss account. 
Interest paid by one office of company to its other office for advances received 
from that office has to be disallowed in calculating gross profit of the office even if 
such expenditure is accepted as proper by auditors. Presumption under section 23 is 
not available to justify such deduction. 
Section 23 does not give any authenticity to the method of accounting of the clos- 
ing stock adopted by a particular company. It is designed to authorise the drawing up 
of a presumption of the accuracy of the particulars given in the profit and loss ac- 
count. 
The section does not limit the power of the Tribunal to give such directions though 
it can do so only after a hearing or after evidence is adduced. 
In a claim for depreciation the burden of proof is on the company who must prove 
by legal evidence the amount claimed, Presumption of accuracy attaching to balance 
sheet and Profit & Loss account is not applicable to auditor’s certificate. Mere pro- 
duction of auditor’s certificate is not conclusive. Employees should be given ade- 
quate opportunity to verify figures in certificate but not by cross-examination of em- ‘ : 8 
ployer and his witnesses.” [S. 23(3)]

Employees claimed three months bonus, alleging full production and available sur- 
plus, but the management agreed only for minimum bonus of 8.33% only. The Union 
entered into a settlement for the minimum bonus. It subsequently walked out of it 
and raised industrial dispute. The Labour Court awarded the maximum bonus of 20% 
because the management failed to produce the necessary documents like profits and 
loss account. The Court refused to interfere in the award. 
In a case involving calculation of available surplus, the claim of the company for 
deducting the annual estimated liability of gratuity under the gratuity scheme for its 
employees estimated on an actuarial valuation from the gross receipts of the year in 
question for the purpose of determine its net profit was held justified and proper. It 
was held that provision of an accrued liability though not actually paid could be 
made against the profit of the year in question when such liability is properly ascer- 
tainable and is possible to arrive at a proper discounted present value. It was also held 
that contingent receipts, if capable of valuation could be taken into account as trading 
receipts where, it is necessary to ascertain the true profits. The claim of the company 
was challenged on the ground that the Bonus Act permits the deduction of amount ac- 
tually paid during the accounting year and not for provision of any estimated liabilities 
to be paid in future. The employer was held entitled to ask for deduction of the esti- 
mated liability of gratuity as made in the profit and loss account of the year in question 
for arriving at the net profits for calculating the available surplus. 
7. Audited accounts of banking companies not to be questioned (s. 24) 
Where any dispute of the nature specified in section 22 between an employer, be- 
ing a banking company, and its employees has been referred to the authority under 
section and during the course of proceedings the accounts of the banking company 
duly audited are produced before it, the authority is not to permit any trade union or 
employees to question the correctness of such accounts. But the trade union or em- 
ployees may be permitted to obtain from the banking company such information as is 
necessary for verifying the amount of bonus due under the Act. 
Sub-section (1) does not enable the trade union or the employees to obtain any in- formation which the banking company is not bound to give. 
8. Presumptions 
If audited balance-sheets and profit and loss account of any corporation or com- pany are produced in the course of proceedings before any authority to whom a dis- pute has been referred, that authority may presume the statements and particulars contained in such balance-sheet and profit and loss account to be accurate. However, where that authority is satisfied that the particulars are not correct, it may take neces- sary steps to find out the accuracy of such statements or particulars. 
The authority may also, if it thinks necessary, require the corporation or the com- pany to furnish to the union or employees any clarification required by the balance- sheet or the profit and loss account. 
9. Prohibitions questioning correctness under section 23 
Section 23 contains two prohibitions. Sub-section (1) prohibits the employees or trade unions from questioning the correctness of the accounts produced before the 
9. Management of Tamil Nadu Gears & Shafts Corpn. v. Presiding Officer, Addl. Labour Court, (2001) 2 Lab LJ 1689 (Mad). 
19. Metal Box Co. of India Ltd. v. Workmen, (1969) 1 LL) 785; AIR 1969 SC 612.

authorities while sub-section (2) prohibits the obtaining of information which the 
banking company is not competent to furnish under sec. 34A of the Banking Compa-

10. Audit of accounts of employers, not being corporation or companies (s. 25) 
Where any dispute or difference of the nature specified in section 22 between an 
individual employer, and his employees has been referred to the authority under that 
section and the accounts of such employer audited by any qualified“ auditor, are 
produced before the authority, the provisions of section 23, so far as may be, apply 
to the account so audited. [S. 25(1)] | 
When the authority finds that the accounts of the employer have not been audited by 
any such auditor and its is of opinion that an audit of the accounts of such employer is 
necessary for deciding the question referred to it, it may, direct the employer to get his 
accounts audited within such time as may be specified in the direction or within such 
further time as it may allow by such auditor or auditors as it thinks fit. The employer is 
bound to comply with such direction. [S. 25(2)] 
Where an employer fails to get the accounts audited under sub-section (2) the 
authority may, without prejudice to the provisions of section 28, get the accounts 
audited by such auditor or auditors as it thinks fit. [S. 25(3)] 
When the accounts are audited under sub-section (2) or sub-section (3) the provi- 
sions of section 23, apply to the accounts so audited. [S. 25(4)] 
The expenses of, and incidental to, any audit under sub-section (3) (including the 
remuneration of the auditor or auditors) shall be determined by the authority (which 
determination shall be final) and paid by the employer. In default of such payment 
the same shall be recoverable from the employer in the manner provided in section 
21. [S. 25(5)] 
11. Gross Profits—Step II 
The second step is to determine the gross profits for the purpose of bonus formula. 
It has been seen under section 4 as to how the gross profits are to be calculated. 
This gross profit would be a notional gross profit because it would be arrived at by 
the process provided in the Act. Hence, it would be different from the gross profit 
which might be shown as gross profit in the profit and loss account. In order to de- 
termine the gross profit, the Act provides that for banking company the calculations 
must be made in the manner specified in the First Schedule of the Act, and in other 
cases, be calculated according to the manner specified in the Second Schedule i.e., to 
the net profit as shown in the profit and loss account, after making usual and neces- 
sary provisions, the following amounts must be added: 
1. Bonus to employees 
2. Depreciation 
3. Direct taxes, including provisions for previous years 
11. A foreign company charged interest for advance made by the head office in London to the branch

held that such amount of interest could not be debited as an expenditure for the purpose of calcula- 
tion of available surplus, Workmen v. William Jack & Co. Ltd, (1971) 1 LLJ 503 : AIR 1971 SC 
1821.

4. Development rebate/development allowance/investment allowance 
5. Any other reserves provided in the year 
6. Bonus paid to employees in respect of previous accounting years. 
To this aggregate should be added back items at 3 and 4 of Second Schedule and 
from the total of all these deductions stated in item 6 should be made. The result 
would be the gross profit. 
12. Available Surplus—Step III 
13. Computation of available surplus (s. 5) 
Section 5 deals with the computation of available surplus. It provides that the 
available surplus in respect of any accounting year is the gross profits for that year 
after deducting the sums referred to in section 6. 
There is, however, this proviso that the available surplus in respect of the account- 
ing year commencing on any day in the year 1968 and in respect of every subsequent 
accounting year shall be the aggregate of— 
(a) the gross profits for that accounting year after deducting therefrom the 
sums referred to in section 6; and 
(b) an amount equal to the difference between— 
(i) the direct tax, calculated in accordance with the provisions of section 
7, in respect of an amount equal to the gross profits of the employer 
for such immediately preceding accounting year; and 
(ii) the direct tax, calculated in accordance with the provisions of section 
7, in respect of an amount equal to the gross profits of the employer 
for such preceding accounting year after deducting therefrom the 
amount of bonus which the employer has paid or is liable to pay to 
his employees in accordance with the provisions of the Act for that 
year. 
In the Supreme Court decision in Workmen v. Associated Rubber Industries Ltd.,"* 
a company created a subsidiary and transferred its investment holdings to it in a bid 
to reduce its liability to pay bonus to its workers, the Supreme Court brushed aside 
the separate existence of the subsidiary company. It is the duty of the court, in every 
case where ingenuity is expended to avoid taxing and welfare legislation, to get be- 
hind the smoke-screen and discover the true state of affairs. The following statement 
in the judgment of CHINNAPPA REDDY J. shows how the court guessed that evasion 
was the only purpose: 
A new company is created, wholly owned by the principal company, with no 
assets of its own except those transferred to it by the principal company, with 
no business or income of its own except receiving dividends from shares trans- 
ferred to it by the principal company and serving no purpose whatsoever except 
to reduce the gross profits of the principal company. These facts speak for 
themselves. There cannot be direct evidence that the second company was 
formed as a device to reduce the gross profits of the principal company for 
13. See Management of Kota Central Co-operative Bank Ltd. v. Industrial Tribunal, (2000) 2 Lab LJ 1075; mercantile system of accounting, accrued income by way of interest to be added back. 
14. (1986) 1 Lab LJ 142 (SC).

whatever purpose. An obvious purpose that it served and which shares one in 
the face is to reduce the amount to be paid by way of bonus to workmen. 
This finding was further supported by the fact that the subsidiary was subsequently 
wound-up and amalgamated into the holding company. The workmen of the principal 
company were held entitled to be paid bonus by including the dividend received by 
the subsidiary with the gross profit of the principal company.

15. Depreciation 
Depreciation is the first prior charge on gross profits. The real profit of the ac- 
counting year is ascertained only after deducting depreciation. Depreciation is an 
estimated sum representing the loss incurred by wear and tear of an asset and must be 
written off to keep the capital intact. 
Under the Income-tax Act depreciation is allowed on the “written down value” 
system /.é., at the prescribed rates of depreciation applied to the full cost of the assets 
in the first year and to their reducing values in subsequent years. This is the “normal” 
depreciation. However, under the Labour Appellate Tribunal formula it is the “no- 
tional normal” depreciation that is to be allowed as a deduction for purposes of bo- 
nus. The Bonus Commission observed: “We are in favour of allowing as prior charge 
only the normal depreciation admissible under the Income-tax Act (including multi- 
ple shift allowance). 
Regarding cases in which bonus has been determined and paid in the past after de- 
ducting from profits the “notional normal” depreciation, the Commission” has rec- 
ommended that in such agreements or awards, the depreciation to be deducted from 
the profits for the purpose of bonus formula should at the option of such company, 
continue to be the “notional normal” depreciation. [proviso under clause (a)] 
16. Development rebate or allowance 
Where an assessee is entitled to both development rebate and development allow- 
ance and the profits are not sufficient to absorb both of them, then, development re- 
bate under section 33 (whether it be in respect of new ships or machinery or plant or 
in respect of second-hand ships or machinery or plant) has to be allowed first. Nei- 
ther development rebate nor development allowance is deductible in ascertaining the 
limit prescribed by section 37(2) for the allowance of entertainment expenditure. In 
the event of a conflict between development rebate (whether the same relates to a 
past year or to the current assessment year) and depreciation of any type (current or 
carried-forward), depreciation has to be allowed first. In the event of a conflict be- 
tween unabsorbed depreciation (i.e., the “carry-forward” under this head) and car- 
ried-forward loss the latter claims priority. If the conflict is between current depre- 
ciation and carried-forward loss, then, of course, the former has priority. Develop- 
ment rebate not set apart as reserve cannot be added back to net profit to compute 
gross profit under section 4(b) read with Item 2(d) of Sch. ik 
Development rebate deduction under section 6 out of gross profits. Amount actu- 
ally allowable as development rebate under section 33. Income-tax Act, 1961 should 
be allowed as deduction.

Return on capital is a prior charge as provided in section 6(d) which says that such

(a) In respect of a company 
(i) The dividends payable on its preference share capital for the accounting 
year calculated at actual rate at which such dividends are payable; 
(ii) 8.5 per cent of its paid up equity share capital as at the commencement of the 
accounting year; 
(111) 6 per cent of its reserves shown in its balance-sheet as at the commence- 
ment of the accounting year, including any profits carried forward from the 
previous accounting year. 
Where the employer is a foreign company within the meaning of section 591 of the 
Companies Act, 1956, the total amount to be deducted under this item shall be 8.5 per 
cent, on the aggregate of the value of the net fixed assets and the current assets of the 
company in India after deducting the amount of current liabilities in India. 
(b) In respect of a corporation | 
(i) 8.5 per cent of its paid-up capital as at the commencement of the account- 
ing year; 
(ii) 6 per cent of its reserve, if any, shown in its balance-sheet as at the com- 
mencement of the accounting year, including any profits carried forward 
from the previous accounting year. 
(c) In respect of a Co-operative Society 
(1) 8.5 per cent of the capital invested by such society in its establishment as evidenced from its books of accounts at the commencement of the ac- counting year; 
(ii) such sum as has been carried forward in respect of the accounting year to a reserve fund under any law relating to co-operative societies for the time being in force.

Allocable surplus has been defined in section 2(4) as a sum:

Under sections 10, 11 and 15 of the Act, the liability of the employer is only to pay 
minimum bonus of 4 per cent of wages, maximum bonus of 20 per cent of wages in 
one accounting year. Under section 15, the employer may make a provision to meet 
further liability which may arise in a future year when the allocable surplus in such 
year may prove to be inadequate. Such a provision does not become the liability of 
the year in which it is made. While determining the allocable surplus, such provision 
should not be included as an expenditure of the year in which it is made. 
20. Payment of minimum bonus (s. 10) 
Subject to the other provisions of the Act, every employer is bound to pay to every 
employee in respect of accounting year, a minimum bonus which is to be 8.33 per cent 
of the salary or wage earned by the employee during the accounting year or one hun- 
dred rupees, whichever is higher, whether or not the employer has any allocable sur- 
plus in the accounting year. 
Where an employee has not completed fifteen years of age at the beginning of 
the accounting year, the above provisions will have effect in relation to such em- 
ployee as if for the words “one hundred rupees,” the words “sixty rupees” were 
substituted.” 
21. Payment of maximum bonus (s. 11) 
Where in respect of any accounting year, the allocable surplus exceeds the amount 
of minimum bonus payable to the employees, the employer, in lieu of such minimum 
bonus, is bound to pay to every employee in respect of that accounting year has to 
pay an amount in proportion to the salary or wage earned by the employee during the accounting year subject to a maximum of twenty per cent of such salary or wage 
[sub-section (1)]. 
In computing the allocable surplus under this section, the amount set on or the amount set-off under the provisions of section 15 has to be taken into account in ac- cordance with the provisions of that section. [sub-section (2)]

Section 13 provides for proportionate reduction in bonus in such cases where an 
employee has not worked for all the working days in any accounting year. The bonus

24. Rule of set-on and set-off of allocable surplus (s. 15) 
The scheme for providing minimum and maximum bonus is based on the device of 
set-on and set-off of the allocable surplus of a particular year. This device was first 
applied in the Bonus Pact of an Ahmedabad Textile Industry. It is pertinent to note 
that the amount of set-on or set-off has to be taken into account for the payment of 
bonus with the allocable surplus. The available allocable surplus for the relevant ac- 
counting year has to be arrived at after taking into account the figures of set-on and 
set-off in the previous year. This provision comes into operation only when, in a 
given accounting year, the allocable surplus exceeds the maximum bonus under the 
Act so that after payment of maximum bonus, there is surplus left which can be car- 
ried forward and set on, subject to the limit of 20% of total salary or wages. 
The method for setting-off the allocable surplus is as under: 
(1) Where for any accounting year the allocable surplus exceeds the amount of 
bonus payable to the employees in the establishment under section 11, then, 
the excess has to be, subject to a limit of twenty per cent of the total salary 
or wage of the employees employed in the establishment in that accounting 
year, carried forward for being set on in the succeeding accounting year and 
so on. This is to be utilised for the purpose of payment of bonus, in the 
manner illustrated in the Fourth Schedule. 
(2) Where for any accounting year there is no available surplus or the allocable 
surplus in respect of that year falls short of the amount of bonus payable to 
the employees in the establishment under section 10, and there is no suffi- 
cient amount carried forward and set on which could be utilised for the 
purpose of payment of minimum bonus, then, so much minimum amount or 
the deficiency as the case may be, as is necessary for the payment of mini- 
mum bonus under the Act has to be carried forward for being set off in the 
succeeding accounting year and so on. This has to be done in the manner 
illustrated in the Fourth Schedule. 
(3) The principle of set-on and set-off as illustrated in the Fourth Schedule ap- 
plies to all other cases not covered by section 15(1) or (2) for the purpose of 
payment of bonus.

2. Disqualification for bonus (s. 9) 
Section 9 contains a non obstante clause which says that notwithstanding anything 
contained in the Act, an employee shall be disqualified from receiving bonus under 
the Act, if he is dismissed from service for— 
(a) fraud’, or 
(b) riotous or violent behaviour while on the premises of the establishment, 
or 
(c) theft, misappropriation or sabotage of any property of the establishment. 
Provisions of section 9 cannot be given a restricted meaning and the words “‘an 
employee shall be disqualified from receiving bonus under the Act” cannot be 
read so as to mean that the employee shall be disqualified from receiving the bo- 
nus of the accounting year only in which he is dismissed because such disqualifi- 
cation is dependent only upon the order of dismissal from service. No such re- 
striction in section 9 of the Act has been put by the legislature and the words 
“employee shall be disqualified from receiving bonus” under the Act are wide in 
their import and must be construed as receiving any bonus the the Act. If the 
legislature intended to put such restriction in section 9 of the Act then it would 
have used the word “in accounting year.” Therefore, on proper construction of 
section 9 it must be held that if an employee is dismissed from service, he stands 
disqualified from receiving any bonus under the Act and not the bonus only of 
the accounting year. 
If the workman is dismissed from service for riotous or violent behaviour while on 
the premises of the establishment, he is not entitled to bonus. In view of the finding 
of the labour court that the workmen concerned were involved in violent behaviour, 
the workmen were disqualified from any bonus by virtue of section 9(b).’ The Kar- 
nataka High Court has held that the right to forfeit bonus has to be confined only to 
the accounting year in which the act of misconduct was committed and cannot be used for earlier or succeeding accounting years. 
3. Adjustment of customary or interim bonus against bonus payable (s. 17) 
Whether in any accounting year— 
(a) an employer has paid any puja bonus or other customary bonus to an em- ployee; or 
(b) an employer has paid a part of the bonus payable under this Act to an em- ployee before the date on which such bonus becomes payable, 
then, the employer is entitled to deduct the amount of bonus so paid from the amount of bonus payable by him to the employee under the Act in respect of that accounting year and the employee is entitled to receive only the balance. 
The provision for deduction of the amount of customary bonus paid from the amount of bonus payable under the Act indicates the independent existence of cus-

Chap. IV—Eligibility for Bonus “yi 
tomary bonus, although to some extent, its quantum is adjustable towards statutory 
bonus. 
The statutory bonus and customary bonus operate in two fields and do not clash 
with each other. 
A bank had been paying since 1941 two months substantive pay as bonus. Such 
bonus was not hit by the introduction of the Act. It would remain payable as a part of 
the terms of employment. The Court said that the payment was not related with the 
profit sharing bonus. It was rather either a customary bonus, or implied condition of 
ate or deferred wages. The management was bound to pay the same irrespective 
of the Act. 
In a case, the workmen and management entered into settlement for payment of bo- 
nus since 1959 to 1970 on the pattern that for the accounting years 1959 to 1963 bonus 
was paid at 344 months basic pay, for 1964 bonus paid at 4% and for subsequent ac- 
counting years from 1965 to 1973 bonus was paid at 10.5% of salary or wages. It was 
held that as payment of bonus has been made at a uniform rate during the years 1965 to 
1973 has ripened into a claim for customary or traditional bonus on the occasion of 
Pooja festival. The Bonus Act is confined to profit bonus and not other kinds of bonus. 
It was held that the management could be entitled to deduct customary bonus from bo- 
nus under Payment of Bonus Act in respect of accounting year. 
4. Deduction of certain amounts from bonus payable under the Act (s. 18) 
Where in any accounting year, an employee is found guilty of misconduct causing 
financial loss to the employer, then, it is lawful for the employer to deduct the 
amount of loss from the amount of bonus payable to the employee under the Act in 
respect of that accounting year. If any balance is left, the employee is entitled to re- 
ceive that balance.

Like sections 9, 31-A also contains a non obstante clause. It says that notwith- 
standing anything contained in the Act— 
(i) where an agreement or a settlement has been entered into by the employees 
with their employer before the commencement of the Payment of Bonus 
(Amendment) Act, 1976, or 
(ii) where the employees enter into any agreement or settlement with their em- 
ployer after such commencement, for payment of an annual bonus linked 
with production or productivity in lieu of bonus based on profits, then, such

employees are entitled to receive bonus due to them under such agreement 
or settlement. 
But any such agreement or settlement under which employees relinquish 
their right to receive the minimum bonus under section 10 is null and void 
in so far as it purports to deprive them of the right to minimum bonus. 
It is also provided that such employees are not be entitled to be paid such bonus in 
excess of twenty percent of the salary or wage earned by them during the relevant 
accounting year. 
Keeping the scheme of the Act in view, it has been held that section 9 provides that 
if an employee is dismissed for acts of misconduct mentioned in the section, he will 
be disqualified from claiming bonus. If a dispute regarding bonus for three consecu- 
tive accounting years is pending under section 22 of the Act and the workman is 
dismissed for misconduct during the third accounting year, it is not proper to extend 
the scope of section 9 in that case to the earlier accounting years, in which the work- 
men had a clean record of service and during which period he did not incur any dis- 
qualification as provided under section 9 of the Act...... Hence the omission of the 
words “accounting year” in section 9 does not mean that the legislature had the in- 
tention of disqualifying the workmen from claiming bonus for all the previous years 
preceeding the accounting year in question or year/years succeeding the accounting 
year. 
Full effect has to be given to non-obstante clause in sections 9 and 31-A of the Act 
and they have to be interpreted with reference to the object and purpose of the Act un- 
der consideration, since these two non-obstante clauses operate in the same field over- 
riding anything contained in the Act. The object and purpose of the Act are to confer a 
statutory right on the employees for minimum and maximum bonus under the Act and, 
therefore, non-obstante clause in section 9 should not be given full effect so as to over- 
ride the non-obstante clause in section 31-A of the Act which will result in an interpre- 
tation that is contrary to the object and purpose of the Act. The object of section 31-A 
is to enable the parties to enter into a collective bargaining settlement as contemplated, 
under sections 12(3) and 18(1) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. If the object of 
collective bargaining is kept in view, the fact that an individual workman commits mis- 
conduct or a small group of men commit misconduct in an accounting year is not rele- 
vant and of no consequence to their claim of bonus linked with production or produc- 
tivity under a settlement between the parties for payment of annual bonus. When sec- 
tion 31-A was inserted by the amendment of 1976, with effect from 25th September 
1975, the legislature must be deemed to have in view the non-obstante clause in section 
9 and, therefore, the later non-obstante, clause overrides the earlier clause in section 9. 
Hence the might of the management to forfeit bonus on the ground the workman was 
dismissed from the service for misconduct, more particularly mentioned in section 9 of 
the Act, would be only with reference to the accounting year in which the act of mis- 
conduct was committed and not with reference to any year or years preceding or suc- 
ceeding the accounting year in question.’ 
In a case it has been held that a reading of sections 9 and 18 of the Act, would re- 
veal the differing scopes of operations of the two sections: 
(1) section 9 contains a total disqualification for bonus whereas section 18 en- 
ables the employer to deduct the amount of loss from the amount of bonus 
payable. 
13. Himalaya Drug Co. v. II Addl Labour Court, (1986) 2 Lab LJ 45 (Kant). 


Chap. IV—Eligibility for Bonus 9 a 
(2) section 9 can be invoked only if an employee is dismissed on the grounds 
specified in the section, whereas section 18 deals with an employee found 
guilty of misconduct causing financial loss to the employer and the pun- 
ishment can be by any penalty short of dismissal. 
(3) section 9 specifies misconduct’ whereas section 18 does not specify mis- 
conduct but at the same time the conduct must result in causing financial 
loss to the employer. 
(4) section 9 opens with non-obstante clause “notwithstanding anything con- 
tained in this Act.” Thereby it has overriding effect on all the provisions of 
the Act including section 18, whereas it is not so in the case of section 18. 
Provisions of sections 9 and 18 have to be harmoniously construed keeping in view 
the objects sought to be served by these provisions and without doing any violence to 
them. Therefore, where the employee who is dismissed from service on the grounds 
enumerated in section 9 will be disqualified to receive bonus in respect of the ac- 
counting year in which the dismissal takes place, or even in respect of the accounting 
years prior to the accounting year, if the bonuses for the prior accounting years have 
not been paid. 
Part V 
6. Computation of working days (s. 13) 
For the purposes of section 13, an employee shall be deemed to have worked in an 
establishment in any accounting year also on the days on which— 
(a) he has been laid-off under an agreement or is permitted by standing orders 
under the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946, or under the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 or under any other law applicable to the es- 
tablishment; 
(b) he has been on leave with salary or wage; 
(c) he has been absent due to temporary disablement caused by accident arising 
out of and in the course of employment; and 
(d) the employee has been on maternity leave with salary or wage during the 
accounting year. 
It has been held that in the case of a factory which works seasonally during an ac- 
counting year, “working days in any accounting year” can only mean those days of 
the year during which the employee concerned was actually allowed to work. The 
question in this case was whether the company could refuse to pay bonus to seasonal 
employees on the ground that they were not employed throughout the year. 
7. Time limit for payment of bonus (s. 19) 
All amounts payable to an employee by way of bonus under the Act have be paid 
in cash by the employer— 
(a) where there is a dispute regarding payment of bonus pending before any 
authority under section 22, within a month from the date on which the 
award becomes enforceable or the settkement comes into operation in re- 
spect of such dispute;

The proviso to the section says that the appropriate Government or such authority

8. Special provisions with respect to certain establishments (s. 16) 
The Act makes certain special provisions with regard to new establishments and 
establishments in the public sector. 
(1) Where an establishment is newly set-up, whether before or after the com- 
mencement of the Act, the employees of such establishment shall be entitled to be 
paid bonus under the Act in accordance with the following provisions of the section. 
(1A) In the first five accounting years following the accounting year in which the 
employer sells the goods produced or manufactured by him or renders services, from 
such establishment, bonus is payable only in respect of the accounting year in which 
the employer derives profit from such establishment. Such bonus is to be calculated 
in accordance with the provisions of the Act in relation to that year, but without ap- 
plying the provisions of section 15. 
(1B) For the sixth and seventh accounting years following the accounting year in 
which the employer sells the goods produced or manufactured by him or renders 
services, from such establishment, the provisions of section 15 shall be subject to the 
following modifications, namely: 
(1) for the sixth accounting year — 
set-on or set-off, shall be made in the manner illustrated in the Fourth 
Schedule taking into account the excess or deficiency, if any, of the al- 
locable surplus set on or set off in respect of the fifth and sixth ac- 
counting years; 
(ii) for the seventh accounting year — 
set-on or set-off, shall be made in the manner illustrated in the Fourth 
Schedule taking into account the excess or deficiency, if any, of the al- 
locable surplus set-on or set-off in respect of the fifth, sixth and seventh 
accounting years. 
(1C) From the eighth accounting year following the accounting year in which 
the employer sells the goods produced or manufactured by him or renders serv- 
ices, from the establishment, the provisions of section 15 are to apply in relation 
to such establishment as they apply in relation to any other establishment. 
The first explanation to the section says that for the purpose of sub-section (1), an 
establishment is not to be deemed to be newly set up merely by reason of a change in 
its location, management, name or ownership. 
The second explanation says that for the purpose of sub-section (1A), an employer 
shall not be deemed to have derived profit in any accounting year unless— 
(a) he has made provision for that year’s depreciation to which he is entitled 
under the Income-tax Act or, under the agriculture income-tax law; and 


Chap. IV—Eligibility for Bonus 379 
(b) the arrears of such depreciation and losses incurred by him in respect of the 
establishment for the previous accounting years have been fully set-off 
against his profits. 
The third explanation provides that for the purposes of sub-sections (1A), (1B) and 
(1C), sale of goods produced or manufactured during the course of the trial running 
of any factory or of the prospecting stage of any mine or an oil-field is not to be 
taken into consideration. Where any question arises with regard to such production or 
manufacture, the decision of the appropriate Government, made after giving the par- 
ties a reasonable opportunity of representing the case, is to be final and is not to be 
called in question by any court or other authority. 
The provisions of sub-sections (1A), (1B) and (1C), apply to new departments or 
undertakings or branches set-up by existing establishments to the extent to which 
they are so applicable. 
The proviso to the section says that if an employer in relation to an existing estab- 
lishment consisting of different departments or undertakings or branches (whether or 
not in the same industry) set-up at different periods has, before the 29th May 1965, 
been paying bonus to the employees on the date on which such departments or un- 
dertakings or branches were set-up, on the basis of the consolidated profits computed 
in respect of all such departments or undertakings or branches, then, such employer 
shall be liable to pay bonus in accordance with the provisions of the Act to the em- 
ployees of all such departments or undertakings or branches (whether set-up before 
or after that date) on the basis of the consolidated profits computed as aforesaid. 
In a case, M/s Alloy Steel Project, an undertaking owned, controlled and managed by 
M/s. Hindustan Steel Ltd. went into production in 1964-65 and no profits were earned 
right upto the year 1967-68, the workers claimed for bonus at the minimum rate for the 
year 1965-66 on the ground that the Alloy Steel Project was not a new establishment, 
the tribunal directed the payment of bonus at the minimum rate holding all units of 
Hindustan Steel Ltd. as one establishment. On appeal by special leave, the Supreme 
Court held that the Alloy Steel Project should have been treated as a separate estab- 
lishment newly set-up which went into production in 1964-65 but did not earn profit at 
all fill 1967-68, therefore, no bonus was payable for the year 1965-66.'° 
9. Application of Act to establishments in public sector (s. 20) 
If in any accounting year an establishment in public sector sells any goods pro- 
duced or manufactured by it or renders any services, in competition with an estab- 
lishment in private sector, and the income from such sale or services or both is not 
less than 20 per cent of the gross income of the establishment in public sector for that 
year, then, the provisions of the Act will apply in relation to such establishment as 
they apply in relation to a like establishment in private sector. [Sub-section (1)] 
Save as otherwise provided in sub-section (1), the Act is not to apply to the em- 
ployees of any establishment in public sector. [Sub-section (2)] 
10. Recovery of bonus due from an employer 
It is the duty of the employer to pay the amount of bonus which becomes due in 
accordance with the provisions of the Act, to the employees within the time limit 
prescribed for the purpose. If the employer fails to fulfil his obligation in respect of 
the payment of bonus or if any dispute arises between the employer and employees

on the question of bonus payable under the Act, then two remedies are provided for 
the employees for the recovery of bonus. 
The first remedy is provided by section 21 of the Act. This section says that when 
any money is due to an employee by way of bonus from his employer under a settle- 
ment or an award or agreement, the employee himself or any other person authorised 
by him in writing, or in the case of the death of the employee, his assignee or heirs 
may, without prejudice to any other mode of recovery, make an application to the 
appropriate Government for the recovery of the money due to him. If the appropriate 
Government, or such authority as the appropriate Government may specify, is satis- 
fied that any money is due, it has to issue a certificate for that amount to the Collec- 
tor who shall proceed to recover the same in the same manner as arrears of land 
revenue. 
Such application has to be made within one year from the date on which the money became due to the employee from the employer. Any such application may be enter- 
tained after the expiry of the period of one year, if the appropriate Government is Satisfied that the applicant had sufficient cause for not making the application within 
time. 
In this section and sections 22,23, 24 and 25 “employee” includes a person who is entitled to payment of bonus under the Act but who is no longer in employment. 
This remedy is of the same nature as the one provided by section 33C of the In- dustrial Disputes Act, 1947 and it is a remedy of summary nature. This remedy is only available in case where the amount of bonus is due under a settlement or an award or an agreement. 
11. Reference of disputes under the Act (s. 22) 
According to section 22, where any dispute arises between an employer and his employees with respect to the bonus payable under the Act or with respect to the ap- plication of the Act to an establishment in public sector, then, such dispute is deemed to be an industrial dispute within the meaning of Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, or of any corresponding law relating to investigation and settlement of industrial disputes in force in a State. The provisions of that Act or, as the case may be, such law, shall, save as otherwise expressly provided, apply accordingly.

12. Maintenance of registers, records etc. (s. 26) 
Every employer has to prepare and maintain such registers, records and other documents in such form and in such manner as may be prescribed. Following records are to be maintained: 
(a) a register showing the computation of the allocable surplus referred to in section 2(4), in form ‘A’, ; 
(b) a register showing the set-on and set-off of the allocable surplus, under section 15, in form ‘B’, 
(c) a register showing the details of the amount of bonus due to each of the employees, the deduction under sections 17 and 18 and the amounts actu- ally disbursed, in form ‘C’.

13. Inspectors (s. 27) 
The appropriate Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, appoint

An Inspector appointed under sub-section (1) may, for the purpose of ascertaining

(a) require an employer to furnish such information as he may consider neces- 
sary;

(c) examine with respect to any matter relevant to any of the above-stated pur- 
poses, the employer, his agent or servant or any other person found in 
charge of the establishment or any premises connected with it or any person 
whom the Inspector has reasonable cause to believe to be or to have been 
an employee in the establishment; 
(d) make copies of, or take extracts from any book, register or other documents 
maintained in relation to the establishment; 
(e) exercise such other powers as may be prescribed. [Sub-section (2)] 
An Inspector shall be deemed to be a public servant within the meaning of the In 
dian Penal Code. [Sub-section (3)] | 
Any person required to produce any accounts, book, register or other documents or 
to give information by an Inspector under sub-section (1) is legally bound to do so. 
[Sub-section (4)] 
This section will not enable an Inspector to require a banking company to furnish

compelled to furnish, disclose, produce or give inspection of, under the provisions 
of section 34A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. [Sub-section (5)] 
14. Penalty (s. 28) 
If any person—(a) contravenes any of the provisions of the Act or any rule made 
under it; or (b) to whom a direction is given or a requisition is made under the Act, 
fails to comply with the direction or requisition, he is punishable with imprisonment 
for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to one 
thousand rupees, or with both. [Sub-section (3)] 
15. Offences by companies (s. 29) 
If the person committing an offence under the Act is a company, every person who, 
at the time the offence was committed, was in charge of, and was responsible to, the 
company for the conduct of business of the company, as well as the company, are 
deemed to be guilty of the offence and liable to be proceeded against and punished 
accordingly. 
The proviso to the section says that nothing contained in the sub-section shall ren- 
der any such person liable to any punishment if he proves that the offence was com- 


382 Part V—The Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 
mitted without his knowledge or that he exercised all due diligence to prevent the 
commission of the offence. [Sub-section (1)] 
Where an offence has been committed by a company and it is proved that the of- 
fence has been committed with the consent or connivance of, or is attributable to any 
neglect on the part of, any director, manager, secretary or other officer of the com- 
pany, such person is deemed to be guilty of that offence and liable to be proceeded 
against and punished accordingly. 
The explanation to the section says that for the purposes of this section,—(a) 
“company” means any body corporate and includes a firm or other association of 
individuals; and (b) “director” in relation to a firm, means a partner in the firm. 
16. Cognizance of offences (s. 30) 
No court can take cognizance of any offence punishable under the Act, save on 
complaint made by or under the authority of the appropriate Government. 
No court inferior to that of a presidency magistrate of a magistrate of the first 
class can try any offence punishable under the Act.

This section made the Act applicable to ail pending disputes regarding payment of bonus wherein bonus was claimed for any year whose any day falls in the year 1962 or 1963 or 1964 or 1965 but not prior to 1962. (d) Constitutionality of the Remaining Act.—In view of the radical departures

challenged in Jalan Trading Co. Pvt. Ltd. v. Mill Mazdoor Union's case before the

The question whether a claim relating to bonus is an Industrial Dispute and re-

1947, becomes a needless question. Section 10 of the Bonus Act is intended to re-

the I.D. Act, 1947 is intended to consider quantum of money claimed pursuant to that 
right already accrued. 
20. Effect of laws and agreements inconsistent with the Act (s. 34) 
Subject to the provisions of section 31A, the provisions of the Act shall have effect 
notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in any other law for the time 
being in force or in the terms of any award, agreement, settlement or contract of service. 
The Bonus Act as amended in 1975 declared in section 34 that the Act would have 
overriding effect over any award, agreement, settlement etc. Under an agreement 
between workmen and employers made in August, 1975 bonus at the rate of 8.33% 
was payable and paid to 329 workers. By then the amended Act came into force. The 
question raised in the appeal before the Supreme Court was whether section 31A of 
the Bonus Act vis-a-vis. Article 14 of the Constitution was discriminatory in so far as 
payment of bonus at the rate of 8.33% was made to certain workmen and after the 
amending Act came into force payment at the lesser rate of 4% was made to others. It 
was held that the group which has been paid earlier to the introduction of these pro- 
visions obviously is a class apart than the remaining one who are to be governed and 
have to be paid under the newly introduced provisions. On the face of things the pro- 
visions do not distinguish between one class and another similarly situated. ? 
Where the bonus at the same rate was allowed to staff of Primary Agricultural Co- 
operative Banks (Primary Banks) as allowed to employees of Apex Bank, the Su-

no scope for disputing the liability.

Central Legislation, Basti Sugar Mills Co. Ltd. v. State of U.P., (1978) 2 LLJ 412: AIR 1979 SC 262.

preme Court held that Primary Co-operative Banks are distinct entities having their 
Own registration or incorporation maintaining separate balance-sheet and profit and

Provisions of section 34 do not mean that there can not be contractual bonus or 
other species of bonus, the provision only emphasises the importance of the obliga- 
tion of the employer, in every case to pay the statutory bonus. 
21. Saving (s. 35) 
Nothing contained in the Act is deemed to affect the provisions of the Coal Mines 
Provident Fund and Bonus Schemes Act, 1948, or of any scheme made under it. 
22. Power of exemption (s. 36). 
If the appropriate Government, having regard to the financial position and other relevant circumstances of any establishment or class of establishment, is of opinion that it will not be in public interest to apply all or any of the provisions of the Act thereto, it may, by notification in the Official Gazette, exempt for such period as may be specified therein and subject to such conditions as it may think fit to impose, such establishment or class of establishment from all or any of the provisions of the Act. 
23. Power to make rules (s. 38) 
The Central Government may make Rules for the purpose of Carrying into effect the provisions of the Act. [Sec. 38(1)] 
In particular, and without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing power, such 
rules may provide for— 
(a) the authority for granting permission under the proviso to sub-clause (iii) of 
clause (1) of section 2; 
(b) the preparation of registers, recorcs and other documents and the form and manner in which such registers, records and documents may be maintained under section 26; 
(c) the powers which may be exercised by an Inspector under clause (e) of sub- section (2) of section 27; 
(d) any other matter which is to be, or may be, prescribed. [Sec. 38(2)] 
Every rule made under this section shall be laid as soon as may be after it is made, before each House of Parliament while it is in session for a total period of thirty days, which may be comprised in one session or in two or more successive sessions, and if before the expiry of the session immediately following the session or the successive

24. Application of certain laws not barred (s. 39) 
Save as otherwise expressly provided, the provisions of this Act shall be in addi- 
tion to and not in derogation of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, or any corre- 
sponding law relating to investigation and settlement of industrial disputes in force in 
a State. 
Section 39 makes the machinery under Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 and similar 
Acts in States available for disputes, under the Bonus Act, other than those covered 
by Section 20.8 
25. Repeal and Saving (s. 40) 
The Payment of Bonus Ordinance, 1965 (3 of 1965), was repealed by the Act. 
Notwithstanding such repeal, anything done or any action taken under the Ordinance 
was deemed to have been done or taken under this Act as if this Act had commenced 
on the 29th May, 1965.

29. Case-law on Schedule III 
Calculation of the gross profit for purposes of bonus.—Interest paid by one office 
of the company to its other office on advances received from that office has to be disallowed in calculating gross profit of the office even if such expenditure is ac- 
cepted as a proper expenditure by auditors. 
The words “working funds”, when used in relation to a banking company, are not 
to be construed in their ordinary popular sense by reference to a dictionary. They 
have a history of their own and they have acquired a definite meaning. So far as 
banking companies are concerned, the words ‘working funds’ have always been un- 
derstood in the sense and that is the sense in which they must be deemed to have 
been used by the legislature when it enacted Clauses (ii) and (iii) of the proviso to 
Item 2 of the Third Schedule.” 
Rebate to consumers as provided in Electricity Act, 1948 is not ‘reserve’ for pur- pose of deduction from gross profits and authorised in Section 6 (d) read with Item 6 
of Sch. III. 
If the entire sum advanced to each unit is loan from the Head Office, the interest 
paid on that sum can be claimed as interest paid on moneys borrowed for the busi- ness in which event the figure of net profit in the Profit and Loss Account itself would get reduced. Then there would probably be no need to deduct under section 
6(d) read with the Third Schedule.* 
Interest on capital reserve: Allowance was provided for transfer of increased value 
of assets on revaluation to capital reserve accounts. Interest on it was allowed to be 
deducted from gross profits.” 
Company accounts were kept on mercantile basis. Provision for contingent liability 
under gratuity scheme and estimated liability on an actuarial valuation was preferred. Claim for deduction in profit and loss account for ascertainment of net profits was

The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 is an Act to provide for a scheme for the pay- 
ment of gratuity to employees engaged in factories, mines, oilfields, plantations, 
ports, railway companies, shops or other establishments and for matters connected 
with or incidental to them. 
1. Statement of Objects and Reasons 
The Act attempts to provide for a uniform scheme for payment of gratuity to em- 
ployees throughout the country. The statement of objects appended to the Bill, as 
introduced in Lok Sabha, stated as follows: 
“There is at present no Central Act to regulate the payment of gratuity to in- 
dustrial workers, except the Working Journalists (Conditions of Services) and 
Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1955. The Government of Kerala enacted a legis- 
lation last year for payment of gratuity to workers employed in factories, planta- 
tions, shops and establishments. The West Bengal Governor promulgated an Or- 
dinance which has since been replaced by the West Bengal Employees’ Payment 
of Compulsory Gratuity Act, 1971, enacted by the President on 28th August, 
(1971. Gratuity is also being paid by some employers to their workers under 
Awards and Agreements. 
Since the enactment of the Kerala and the West Bengal Acts, some other State 
Governments have also voiced their intention of enacting similar measures in their 
respective States. It has become necessary, therefore, to have a Central law on the 
subject so as to ensure a uniform pattern of payment of gratuity to employees 
throughout the country. The enactment of a Central law would also avoid different 
treatment to employees of establishments having branches in more than one State 
when, under the conditions of their service, the employees are liable to transfer from 
one State to another. 
The proposal for Central legislation on gratuity was discussed in the Labour 
Ministers’ Conference held at New Delhi on the 24th and 25th August, 1971 and 
also in the Indian Labour Conference at its Session held on the 22nd and 23rd Oc- 
tober, 1971. There was general agreement at the Labour Ministers’ Conference and 
the Indian Labour Conference that Central legislation on payment of gratuity might 
be undertaken as early as possible. It is accordingly proposed to undertake such 
legislation. 
_ In enacting the President’s Act for West Bengal in August, 1971, care has been 
taken to so design its provisions that they could serve as far as possible as norms for 
the Central law. The Bill has, therefore, been drafted on the lines of the West Bengal 
Employees’ Payment of Compulsory Gratuity Act, 1971 with some modifications 
which have been made in the light of the views expressed at the Indian Labour Con- 
ference relating to forfeiture of gratuity in cases of dismissal for gross misconduct. 
The Bill provides for gratuity to employees drawing wages up to Rs. 270 per 
month in factories, plantations, shops, establishments and mines, in the event of su- 


Chap. [—Interpretation 401 
perannuation, retirement, resignation and death or total disablement due to accident 
or disease. The quantum of gratuity payable will be 15 days’ wages based on the rate 
of wages last drawn by employees concerned for every completed year of service or 
part thereof in excess of six months subject to a maximum of 15 months’ wages. The 
term “wages” will mean “basic wage plus dearness allowance.” 
It is proposed that the appropriate Government for administering the Act in relation 
to establishments belonging to or under the control of the Central Government or a 
railway company, or mine, a major port and oilfield or in relation to establishments - 
having departments or branches in more than one State, will be the Central Govern- 
ment, and, in relation to other establishments, the State Government. 
The Bill seeks to give effect to the above proposals. 
2. Salient Features of the Act 
Salient features of the Central Act i.e. the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 are as 
under: 
(1) The Act is a self-contained and an exhaustive Act and the provisions of the 
Act and rules made under it have an over-riding effect on all other Acts or 
instruments or contracts so far as they are inconsistent with the Act. 
(2) The Act is fairly sweeping in coverage, as it applies to all factories, mines, 
oil fields, plantations, ports and railways irrespective of the number of 
workmen employed by them. It also covers shops and establishments em- 
ploying 10 or more persons. 
(3) The Act gives a statutory right of gratuity to all employees, who have ren- 
dered five years’ continuous service and whose services stand terminated 
after coming into force of the Act on account of superannuation, or retire- 
ment, or resignation, or death, or disablement. 
(4) The Act provides both executive as well as quasi-judicial machinery for 
matters pertaining to nomination, determination and recovery of gratuity. 
(5) The executive machinery pertains to maintenance of records regarding 
opening, change, or closure or establishments, display of notices, and 
maintenance of records by the controlling authority. The quasi-judicial 
functions have been divided between the employees and the Controlling 
Authority in as much as for payment of gratuity, for the first forum pro- 
vided is an application to the employer. When the employer has declined or 
avoided payment of gratuity, then applications are required to be made to 
the Controlling Authority. 
(6) The machinery provided for recovery rests with the Controlling Authority. 
(7) The orders of the Controlling Authority for payment or determination of 
gratuity are appealable before the appropriate Government or the appellate 
authority. 
3. Short title, extent, application and commencement (s. 1) 
(1) The Act is called the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972. 
(2) It extends to the whole of India: provided that in so far as it relates to 
plantations or ports, it shall not extend to the State of Jammu and Kashmir. 


402 Part VI—The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 
(3) The Act applies to— 
(a) every factory, mine, oilfield, plantation, port and railway company; 
(b) every shop or establishment within the meaning of any law for the 
time being in force in relation to shops and establishments in a State, 
in which ten or more persons are employed, or were employed, on 
any day of the preceding twelve months; 
(c) such other establishments or class of establishments, in which ten or 
more employees are employed, or were employed on any day of the 
preceding twelve months, as the Central Government may, be notifi- 
cation, specify. 
(3A) A shop or establishment to which the Act has become applicable shall con- 
tinue to be governed by the Act notwithstanding that the number of persons 
employed at any time after it has become so applicable falls below ten. 
(4) It shall come into force on such date as the Central Government may, be 
notification, appoint. 
The Act received the assent of the President of India on 21st August, 1972 and 
came into force w.e.f. 16th September, 1972 as notified in the Gazette of India dated 
16th September, 1972. 
4. Gratuity law is comprehensive and exhaustive on the subject 
Like the provisions of the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 similar provisions are to 
be found in the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 making it applicable to certain catego- 
ries of establishments and industries. A question, therefore, arises whether those who 
are excluded are governed by the adjudicational process or not. 
Unless the law expressly excludes application of a statute to any person or class of 
persons, beneficent construction of a labour law should operate in favour of benefici- 
ary classes. What has not been expressly excluded cannot be impliedly excluded. 
Sec. 4(5) of the Act itself should suggest that the Parliament has conceived of pay- 
ment of gratuity other than one under this law and thus saved the gratuity schemes 
operating under awards or contracts or agreements. 
The provisions of Sec. 4 notwithstanding, it would be against the spirit of the Act if 
an employee is denied his right to claim gratuity for the period during which his wages can be enhanced beyond the ceiling. 
5. Meaning and Scope of “Shop” under Gratuity Act 
A shop under the Act carries the same import as it has under the State shops and establishments law. 
The definition of “shop” in the Bombay Shops and Establishments Act, consists of three parts: 
(1) Shop means any premises where goods are sold, either by retail or whole- sale, or where services are rendered to customers: 
1. Gujarat Agricultural University y. Laxmiben Chhibabhai Talaviya, (2001) 2 Lab LJ 448 (Guj), a Notification issued by the Central Government declared that educational institutions employing 10 or more persons are to be covered by the Act. It was held that an Agricultural University could not contend that it was not covered by the Act. 
2. Steel Authority of India Ltd. vy. Labour Commr., (1995) 1 LLJ 1007 (Ori). 


Chap. I—Interpretation 403 
(2) and the expression includes office and godown whether in the same premises 
or otherwise, mainly used in connection with such trade or business; 
(3) but the expression does not include a factory, etc. 
It is clear that the legislature has devised a special definition of “Shop” of wide 
import for the purpose of the Act. 
It has also been held that movable stalls of hawkers are not shops. If there is a de- 
fined premises where the articles are received for and on behalf of the customers and 
are returned to them after executing the required work, that is a premises where 
services are rendered to the customers irrespective of whether the customers them- 
selves have brought the articles to the premises or have sent them with their agents or 
~ servants. The fact that in such a case the articles sent by the customers are received 
outside the premises and are delivered back to the customers after executing the 
work, could not make any difference. 
6. Premises not amounting to factories under Factories Act may come under 
Shops Act 
If such an establishment is neither a factory under Sec. 2(m) of the Factories Act 
nor one which could be deemed a factory under Sec. 85 of the Factories Act by the 
Central Government, it could not be contended that it is excluded from the operation 
of the Bombay Shops and Establishments Act as manufacturing process is carried on 
in such establishment. 
7. Establishment: Meaning and Scope 
An ‘establishment’ under the Bombay Law has been defined in sec. 2(8) as under.” 
‘““Fctablishment’ means a shop, commercial establishment, residential hotel, res- 
taurant, eating house, theater or other place of public amusement or other entertain- 
ment to which this Act applies, and includes such other establishment as the State 
Government may by notification in the official gazette declare.” 
The term ‘commercial establishment’ has also been defined in sec. 2(4) of the 
Bombay Shops and Establishments Act, 1948. It would appear that ‘establishment’ is 
a general term while ‘Commercial establishment, is a specific term. The former is 
genus while the latter is species. The second point of distinction is that while ‘com- 
mercial establishments’.are establishments whose economic activities concern busi- 
ness, trade or profession, the ‘establishment’ may be wider than it. The definition of 
‘establishments’ under S. 7 of the Delhi Act, is in pari matiria with the Bombay 
definition. But the definition of ‘commercial establishment’ under the Delhi Act is 
different from the definition under the Bombay Act. 
- The establishment of a new trade or industry is a different thing altogether from the 
entry of a particular person into an existing trade or industry. _

An educational institution, such as a university, carrying on a systematic activity 
by employing more than 10 persons, was held to be an establishment within the 
meaning of the Payment of Gratuity Act.

9. Sales Organisation 
A sales organisation with a regional officer at the head of a region and having 
salesmen in different parts of the State, the organisation having no specific office of 
its own, would nonetheless be a commercial establishment if the organisation carries 
on any business, trade or profession etc. Where the company carries on business in 
cigarettes manufactured by it at Calcutta by appointing salesmen and an incharge 
regional officer and by appointing stockists in this State, such organisation would be 
a commercial establishment within the meaning of the Act. 
Commercial establishment is not only an establishment which carries on trade but 
also business, whether for the purpose of gain or not. The profit or intention to make 
profit is not an essential part of the legal definition of trade or business. Business 
includes trade. 
In the matter of construing the language of Sec. 2(4) of the Bombay Shops and 
Establishments Act. 1948, the principle of noscitur a sociis must be adopted. This 
rule means that, when two or more words which are susceptible of analogous mean- 
ing are coupled together, they are understood to be used in their cognate sense. 
The words take, as it were, their colour from each other, that is, the more general is 
restricted to a sense analogous to a less general. Associated words take their meaning 
from one another under the doctrine of noscitur a sociis, the philosophy of which is 
that the meaning of a doubtful word may be ascertained by reference to the meaning 
of words associated with it. Such doctrine is broader that the maxim ejusdem generis. 
10. Professions are not commercial activities 
(a) Profession of a Chartered Accountant : There is undoubtedly some co- 
operation between the articled clerk and the chartered accountant. But the articled 
clerk is not a salaried employee. He is there to learn methods of accountancy. There- 
fore, his co-operation with the Chartered accountant in checking receipts and pay- 
ments is not the sort of co-operation which will reduce what is essentially a profes- 
sion, into a commercial establishment. 
(b) Professional activities: It is clear that a professional activity must be an activity 
carried on by an individual by his personal skill and intelligence. There is a funda- 
mental distinction, therefore, between a professional activity and an activity of a 
commercial character and unless the profession carried on partakes of the character 
i a ee any vile activity, the dispensary cannot fal! within the ambit of Sec. 2(4) of 
the Act. 
(c) Profession of a Lawyer : A lawyer who carries on his profession as an advocate 
cannot possibly answer the definition of an employer in Sec. 2(7) of the Act. An em- 
ployer is one who owns or has ultimate control over the employees of the establish- 
ment. In a sense this postulates some activity other than his own. He can be an owner 
or he may be a person who may be controlling the activity of his employees. So far 
as a lawyer is concerned it is he who himself carries on the activity and there is no 
question of either bringing in or controlling the activities of any other person who

11. Mine 
‘Mine’ has the same meaning as given to it under the Mines Act, 1952. 
The definition of “mine” as given in cl. (f) of Sec. 2 of the Mines Act, 1952 reads 
as follows : 
“(j) ‘Mine’ means any excavation where any operation for the purpose of searching 
for or obtaining minerals has been or is being carried on, and includes — 
(i) all borings, bore holes and oil wells; 
(ii) all shafts, in or adjacent to and belonging to a mine, whether in the course 
of being sunk or not; 
(iii) all levels and inclined planes in the course of being driven; 
(iv) all open cast workings; 
(v) all conveyors or aerial ropeways provided for the bringing into or removal 
from a mine of minerals or other articles of for the removal of refuse there 
from; 
(vi) all adits, levels, planes, machinery, works, railways, tramways and sidings, 
in or adjacent to and belonging to a mine; 
(vii) all workshops situated within the precincts of a mine and under the same 
management and used solely for purposes connected with that mine or a 
number of mines under the same management; 
(viii) all power stations for supplying electricity solely for the purpose of work- 
ing the mine or a number of mines under the same management; _ 
(ix) any premises for the time being used for depositing refuse from a mine, or 
in which any operation in connection with such refuse is being carried on, 
being premises exclusively occupied by the owner of the mine; 7 
(x) unless exempted by the Central Government by notification in the Official 
Gazette, any premises or part thereof, in or adjacent to and belonging to a 
mine, on which any process ancillary to the getting, dressing or preparation 
for sale of minerals or of coke is being carried on.” 
12. Plantation 
The definition of “plantation” as given in cl. (f) of Sec. 2 of the Plantation Labour 
Act, 1951 reads as follows : 
“(f) ‘Plantation’ means any plantation to which this Act, whether wholly or in 
part, applies and includes offices, hospitals, dispensaries, schools, and any 
other premises used for any purpose connected with such plantation, but 
does not include any factory or the premises to which the provisions of the 
Factories Act, 1948 (63 of 1948) apply.”
