13. Definitions (S. 2) 
14. Appropriate Government [s. 2(a)] 
“Appropriate Government” means,— 
(i) in relation to an establishment— 
(a) belonging to, or under the control of, the Central Government, 
(b) having branches in more than one State, 
(c) of a factory belonging to, or under the control of, the Central Gov- 
ernment, 
(d) of a major port, mine oilfield or railway company, the Central Gov- 
ernment 
(ii) in any other case, the State Government.” 
15. Completed year of service [s. 2(b)] 
“Completed year of service” means continuous service for one year. 
16. Continuous service [s. 2(c)] 
“Continuous service” means continuous service as defined in section 2A [See notes 
under the section 7]. 
17. Controlling Authority [s. 2(d)] 
“Controlling authority” means an authority appointed by the appropriate Govern- 
ment under section 3. 
18. Employee [s. 2(e)] 
“Employee” means any person (other than an apprentice) employed on wages, in 
any establishment, factory, mine, oilfield, plantation, port, railway company or shop, 
to do any skilled, semi-skilled, or unskilled, manual, supervisory, technical or clerical 
work, whether the terms of such employment are express or implied, and whether or 
not such person is employed in a managerial or administrative capacity, but does not 
include any such person who holds a post under the Central Government or a State 
Government and is governed by any other Act, or by any rules providing for payment 
of gratuity. 
A teacher in an educational institution not doing skilled or unskilled manual work or supervisory, technical or clerical work and imparting education as a main function 
was held to be not an employee within the meaning of the Payment of Gratuity Act. 
Apprentice, trainee.—Certain persons were employed as trainees. But they were assigned duties equivalent to those of the other staff and treated as full members of 
13. Narra Koteswara Rao v. Deputy Commr. of Labour, (2001) 1 Lab LJ 685, the State Government has jurisdiction to go into disputes, the employer company had branches in more than one State. 14. H.E. Society v. Appellate Authority under PG Act, (2001) 1 Lab LJ 691 (MP); Ahmedabad (P) Pri- mary Teachers Association vy. Administrative Officer, (2004) 1 LLJ 596 : AIR 2004 SC 1426, 


Chap. I—Interpretation 407 
the Department. They were held to be not apprentice but as full employees, and, 
therefore, entitled to gratuity.  MURUGESAN, J. said: 
“A plain reading of the Act shows that it excludes an apprentice from the applica- 
tion of the provisions of “the Act’. In order to find out whether the word “‘appren- 
tice” includes the trainee also, and in the absence of any definition of an apprentice 
under ‘‘the Act” this Court has to consider the same with reference to the dictionary 
meaning as well as the interpretation of the section with reference to the object of the 
Act coupled with the definition of apprentice or training in any other statute.” 
“In the CONCISE OXFORD DICTIONARY the word ‘apprentice’ means, a person 
learning a trade from a skilled employer’. In BLACK’s LAW DICTIONARY the word 
‘apprentice’ means, a person bound by an indenture to work for an employer for a 
specific period to learn a craft, trade or profession and a learner in any field of em- 
ployment or business. As per P. RAMANATHA AIYAR’S LAW LEXICON the word ‘ap- 
prentice’ means, “‘a learner is one who is taken to learn a trade, a person under a con- 
tract of apprenticeship, to a master to learn from him his trade or business and to 
serve him during his time of the apprenticeship”. Correspondingly as per CONCISE 
OXFORD DICTIONARY the word ‘trainee’ means, “‘a person undergoing training for a 
particular job or profession”. As per P. RAMANATHA AIYAR’S LAW LEXICON, the 
word ‘training’ means ‘systematic instruction’, From the above expressions from 
various dictionaries, it is seen that both the words ‘apprentice’ and ‘trainee’ are not 
either similar, identical or same as both the words have been distinctly defined with 
reference to the nature of the job. As referred to in BLACK’S LAW DICTIONARY to be 
an ‘apprentice’ means, ‘“‘a person must be either a learner in any field of employment 
or business or a person was bound by indenture to work for an employer for specific 
period to learn a craft, trade or profession”. With the above definitions in the back- 
ground, it is to be now considered as to the nature of the duties that were performed 
by the petitioner. According to the petitioner, the petitioner was treated as a full 
member of the department and he was allotted duties equivalent to other staff of per- 
sonnel department. 
“In fact, the Bombay High Court in the judgment reported in Khanderan P. Ra- 
jopadhye v. United Western Bank Ltd.,'° considered that mere nomenclature of a post 
is not of much consequence and what is to be seen is the nature of the duties per- 
formed by the employee concerned so as to arrive at a conclusion as to whether he is 
an employee within the meaning of Section 2(e) of the Act. On the above facts, it is 
seen that the petitioner was appointed not for learing a trade from a skilled employer, 
but was appointed trainee not to learn any designated trade and therefore cannot be 
considered as apprentice. 
Further, when the provisions of any Act are interpreted, the Court has to read the 
provisions literally in its ordinary, natural and grammatical meaning as used by the 
legislature. The Supreme Court in Jugalkishore Saraf v. Rao Cotton Co. Ltd.,\" held 
that when any of the provisions of Statute is interpreted, the provisions has to be read 
in its ordinary, natural and grammatical meaning. While interpreting a Statute, the 
object of the Act also has to be kept in mind. The object of Payment of Gratuity Act 
is to provide a scheme for payment of gratuity to the employees engaged in factory, 
mine, oilfield, port, railway company or shop, or other establishments. The Act is

33. Continuous service (s. 2A) | 
Section 2A provides for the concept of continuous service. For the purpose of this 
Act— 
(1) an employee shall be said to be in continuous service for a period if he has, for 
that period, been in uninterrupted service, including service which may be inter- 
rupted on account of sickness, accident, leave, absence form duty without leave (not 
being absence in respect of which an order imposing a punishment or penalty or treating the absence as break in service has been passed in accordance with the standing orders, rules or regulations governing the employees of the establishment), 
lay-off, strike or a lock-out or cessation of work not due to any fault of the employee, — whether such uninterrupted or interrupted service was rendered before or after the 
commencement of this Act; 
(2) where an employee (not being an employee employed in a seasonal establish- ment) is not in continuous service within the meaning of Clause (1), for any period of one year or six months, he shall be deemed to be in continuous service under the em- ployer— 
(a) for the said period in one year, if the employee during the period of twelve calendar months preceding the date with reference to which calculation is to be made, has actually worked under the employer for not less than— 
(i) one hundred and ninety days, in the case of an employee employed below the ground in a mine or in an establishment which works for less than six days in a week; and 
(ii) two hundred and forty days, in any other case; 
(b) for the said period of six months, if the employee during the period of six calendar months preceding the date with reference to which the calculation 1s to be made, has actually worked under the employer for less than— 
(1) ninety-five days, in the case of an employee employed below the ground in a mine or in an establishment which works for less than six days in a week; and 
(ii) one hundred and twenty days, in any other case;

(3) where an employee, employed in a seasonal establishment, is not in continuous 
service within the meaning of Clause (1), for any period of one year or six months, 
he shall be deemed to be in continuous service under the employer for such period if 
he has actually worked for not less than seventy-five per cent of the number of days 
on which the establishment was in operation during such period. 
34, Appropriate Government [s. 2(a)] 
The definition given in this Act is different from the one given in other Acts. ehe 
Central Government is the appropriate Government for the following categories of 
establishments : 
(1) establishment where ownership vests with the Central Government. 
(2) establishments which are controlled by the Central Government. 
(3) establishments which have branches in more than one State. 
(4) establishments or factories i.e. manufacturing establishments which are 
owned by or which are under the control of the Central Government. 
establishments of major ports, mines, oil-fields or railway companies. 
The word ‘establishment’ which has been used in this part of the definition has a 
wider coverage and meaning as distinguished from a commercial establishment. 
Sometimes it is canvassed that all the above establishments in relation to which 
Central Government is the appropriate Government should be commercial estab- 
lishment but the provisions of Sec. 2(a) sub-section (c) which cover establishments 
in relation to factories belonging to or under the control of the Central Government 
cut at this argument because even an establishment in relation to a factory would be 
an establishment in relation to which Central Government is the appropriate Gov- 
ernment. Where a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act has an 
administrative office at one place, its registered office at another place and a fac- 
tory at yet another place, the question arises as to whether the employees working 
in the administrative office or the registered office would come under the purview 
of State Government or the Central Government. It would be canvassed further that 
the establishment of administrative or head office may be concerned only with the 
affairs of the factory. It is submitted that such an establishment would not be an 
establishment in relation to which Central Government would be the appropriate 
government. In this very case if the company would have branches in more than 
one State, the establishment would be one in relation to which Central Government 
would be the appropriate Government. 
The State Government has jurisdiction as appropriate Government in all residuary 
cases. It would, therefore, seem that a company having more branches in one State 
only, would fail under this category. Here again, a case arose where a company had 
branches in one State and some branches in Union territories of Goa, Daman and 
Diu. Would such a company fall under the residuary jurisdiction of the State Gov- 
ernment or Central Government? This takes us to the interpretation of the term 
‘State’ in Sec. 2(a)(i)(b). Under the Constitution of our country the Union territories 
are not ‘States’ as such. It would , however, appear that the word ‘State’ has not been 
used in this provision in a narrow sense.

The term ‘major port’ has been defined in Sec. 2(la) and the definition is as fol-

In a case, the employer retrenched some of the employees in the departments of 
clearing and shipping and godown treating them as distinct and different industrial 
establishments. However, this contention was negatived by the Bombay High Court 
which held that the activities carried on in the two departments could be said to con- 
cerning a major port and as the dispute related to retrenchment in these two depart- 
ments, the Central Government would be the appropriate Government for making the 
reference. 
36. Continuous Service 
The definition is not exhaustive but illustrative. ‘Continuous service’ means serv- 
ice without interruption or break. Some classes of interruptions have been artificially 
made as non-interruptions for the purposes of ‘continuous services’. Breaks or inter- 
ruptions caused by sickness, accident, leave, lay-off, strike or lock-out or cessation of 
work not due to any fault of employee concerned are treated mostly as non- 
interruptions. If the service of an employee, therefore, meets with any such breaks 
then nevertheless it will be treated as ‘continuous services’. The logical corollary of 
this artificial designation of breaks as non-interruptions is that, all other types of in- 
terruptions will be taken as breaks in service which will destroy the continuity of 
service. 
Continuity of Service is an issue of fact.—In absence of any other material to show 
that there was any interruption in service, it was futile to contend that workmen 
worked less than 240 days in a year.

38. Payment of Gratuity (s. 4) 
Gratuity is payable to an employee at the end point of his employment after he has 
rendered continuous service for not less than five years,— 
(a) on his superannuation, or 
(b) on his retirement or resignation, or 
(c) on his death or disablement due to accident or disease. 
The completion of continuous service of five years is not necessary where the ter- 
minations of the employment of any employee is due to death or disablement. 
In the case of death of the employee, gratuity payable to him shall be paid to his 
nominee or as the case may be, the guardian of such nominee or if no nomination has 
been made, to his heirs. 
The Explanation to the sub-section provides that for the purposes of the section, 
disablement means such disablement as incapacitates an employee for the work 
which he was capable of performing before the accident or disease resulting in such 
disablement [Sub-s. (1)]. 
(a) Gratuity 
Gratuity is a reward for good, efficient and faithful service rendered for a consider- 
able period. A workman becomes experienced during the tenure of his employment. 
This enables him to move out for better job avenues. Other employers can throw 
temptations to him. To lose him may be a loss to the employer. But if stays on, that is 
his loyality to the employer. 
(b) Governing Act, whether Central or State 
Where employees were getting wages in excess of the maximum limit prescribed

39. Rate of gratuity 
For every completed year of service or part thereof in excess of six months, the 
employer shall pay gratuity to an employee at the rate of fifteen day’s wages based 
on the rate of wages last drawn by the employee concerned. In the case of a piece- 
rated employee, daily wages are to be computed on the average of the total wages 
received by him for a period of three months immediately preceding the termination 
of his employment. For this purpose, the wages paid for any overtime work shall not 
be taken into account. In the case of an employee who is employed in a seasonal es- 
tablishment and who is not so employed throughout the year the employer has to pay 
the gratuity at the rate of seven days’ wages for each season [Sub-s. (2)]. 
The term ‘last drawn wage’ in section 4(2) of Act should receive its full meaning 
and not a fractured interpretation, ‘wages’ must include not only what was paid but 
also what was payable to workman. 
The claim of employees for gratuity on basis of settlement requiring calculation of 
39 paise per point over 100 points of. Madras Cost of Living Index was upheld as 
proper by the Supreme Court’ 
The Supreme Court has held in a case that as per the settlement providing rates of 
DA, which was to be on par with the rates sanctioned by the Government, an em- 
ployee was entitled to gratuity based on the revised wages in terms of the Govern- 
ment order implementing the settlement. 
Incentive wages paid in respect of extra work, although worked out on the basis of 
pieces was held to be not includible in wages for the purposes of computing wages 
under the first proviso to s. 4(2) of the Act. The court also pointed out that there is 
not basic difference between the expression “basic wages” as defined in the Act and 
as defined in the Employees’ Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 
WZ, 
Two conditions are necessary for attracting this proviso. The establishment in 
question must be seasonal and the employee should not have been employed 
throughout the year. The employer company could not, in this case, prove that it was a seasonal establishment. The company was carrying on the coffee curing work. 
The amount of gratuity payable to an employee shall not exceed twenty months’ wages. The maximum amount of gratuity payable to an employee shall not exceed three lakhs and fifty thousand rupees [Sub-s. (3)].

41. Agreement for better terms 
Nothing in the section shall affect the right of an employee to receive better terms 
of gratuity under any award or agreement or contract with the employer [Sub-s. (5)]. 
This sub-section permits a settlement, but on better terms.” If the employee gives a 
full satisfaction certificate for a lesser sum than what was due, the balance would 
remain recoverable. The Madras High Court held in a case like this that a full quit 
receipt by an employee is valid and protected under s. 4(5) of the Act. 
42. Forfeiture of gratuity 
N otwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1),— 
(a) the gratuity of an employee, whose services have been terminated for any 
act wilful omission or negligence causing any damage or loss to, or de- 
struction of, property belonging to the employer, shall be forfeited to the 
extent of the damage or loss so caused; 
(b) the gratuity payable to an employee may be wholly or partially forfeited— 
(i) if the services of such employee have been terminated for his riotous 
or disorderly conduct or any other act of violence on his part, or 
(ii) if the services of such employee have been terminated for any act 
which constitutes an offence involving moral turpitude, provided that 
such offence is committed by him in the course of his employment 
[Sub-s. (6)].

have been regular in the employment. However, if an employee is re-employed with- 
out any break in service he will also be eligible for gratuity. According to section 
4(2), every employee is entitled to gratuity at the rate of 15 days’ wages for every 
completed year of service. An employee who resigns from the service is entitled to 
gratuity. The nominee of an employee can make an application for gratuity without 
producing a succession certificate. 2

tent of loss or damage caused if termination is effected for any act, wilful omission or 
negligence. However, the employer has to prove the extent of damage or loss caused 
by the employee’s misconduct. In the absence of any proof the right to forfeit the 
gratuity under section 4(6)(a) is not available to the employer.” The right to recover

In a Supreme Court case, it was held that provision of a period of 5 years service as 
qualifying period in section 4(1){b) is one of minimum service conditions made 
available to employees notwithstanding financial capacity of employer to bear its 
burden and it is reasonable restriction on the right of the employer to carry on busi- 
ness and its constitutionally valid. Even assuming that the presumption that a longer 
period of service for entitlement to gratuity on voluntary retirement or resignation is 
necessary to prevent labour from changing employment frequently, that considera- 
tion has no bearing on the question whether a short period of qualifying service is 
violative of Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. That Article comes into picture only 
if, among others— 
(a) it is shown that the short qualifying period of service throws on any par- 
ticular employer such financial burden as would force him to close his es- 
tablishment and 
(b) the provision is not one of the minimum service conditions, which must be 
made available to the employees. 
Hence the provision for a short qualifying period per se is not invalid and cannot 
be struck down generally as being violative of Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution as 
is done by the High Court in present case. The High Court’s reliance on the decision 
referred to by it for the purpose of holding that the provision of a period of service of 
5 years is violative of Article 19(1)(g) is misplaced, for, the court has failed to notice 
that the view taken by this court was in a different factual context. In the first in- 
stance, at that time, gratuity had not come to be accepted as one of the minimum 
service conditions, much less any particular scheme of gratuity. Secondly, the courts 
in those cases were concerned with establishments of differing financial capacity in a 
particular industry and with evolving uniform service conditions for the industry as a 
whole for the maintenance of industrial peace. 
The provisions of the Act were meant for laying down gratuity as one of the mini- mum service conditions available to all employees covered by the Act. There is no provision in the Act for exempting any factory, shop etc. from the purview of the Act 
covered by it except those where, the employees are in receipt of gratuity or pensionary benefits which are no less favourable than the benefit conferred under the Act. The payment of gratuity under the Act is thus obligatory being one of the minimum condi- ee

tions of service. The establishments which have no capacity to give to their workmen 
the minimum conditions of service prescribed by the statute have no right to exist. 
Payment of Gratuity Act is on the genre of statutes like the Minimum Wages Act, 
ESI, etc. which lay down the relevant minimum benefits which must be made avail- 
able to the employees. 
Payment of Gratuity Act is a welfare measure introduced in the interest of the gen- 
eral public to secure social and economic justice to workmen to assist them in old 
age and to ensure them a decent standard of life on their retirement. Therefore the 
Act imposed a reasonable restriction on the employer in respect of the fundamental 
right under Article 19(1)(g). 
The provision for payment of gratuity contained in section 4(1)(b) of the Act is one 
of the minimum service conditions which must be made available to the employees 
notwithstanding the financial capacity of the employer to bear its burden and the said 
provisions are a reasonable restriction on the right of the employer to carry on his 
business within the meaning of Article 19 of the Constitution. Hence, section 4(1)(b) 
of the Act is legal and valid. | 
44. Employee not to be deprived of this right 
The Supreme Court has observed that gratuity is the right of an employee. This 
right cannot be taken away indirectly.” The Court said: ‘Gratuity under the Payment 
of Gratuity Act, 1972 is no longer in the realm of charity but a statutory right given 
to the employee. The mandate of the statute is that gratuity is to be paid to the em- 
ployee on his retirement or to his dependants on his death. Introduction of the family 
benefit scheme by which the employee is compelled to deposit gratuity amount runs 
counter to the mandate of the Act. Though no final opinion is being expressed in this 
regard but it is clear that statutory obligations under the Act cannot be left high and 
dry on the whims of the employer. 
The Supreme Court has also held that conferment of an absolute discretion by the- 
gratuity Rules to give or deny the benefit of gratuity cannot be upheld and such dis- 
cretion on the part of the employer must be rejected as unenforceable. 
An office order provided for payment of a retirement allowance. It was held that the 
employee’s right to such allowance was not lost on the enactment of the Gratuity Act. 
45. Act not retrospective 
It is clear that both the determination of the amount and the event leading to the 
claim for gratuity have to arise-after the coming into force of the Act. In view of 
these factors, the Act cannot become retrospective. It is only the reason for deter- 
mining the quantum or the quantum of entitlement that is embedded in the past. Had 
this Act permitted payment of gratuity in those cases where the event leading to enti- 
tlement of gratuity would have had occurred prior to the coming into force of the 
Act, then it could have been said that the Act was retrospective in operation. This not 
being the position under law, it is fallacy to say that Act is retrospective, because it 
takes into consideration the past service for computation of gratuity.

Employees drawing more than Rs. 1000 per month and who did not fall within the

46. Entitlement 
The following points may be stated regarding entitlement— 
(i) the Act is not retrospective in operation. 
(ii) the provision regarding consideration of past service for computation of 
gratuity do not make the Act retrospective. 
(iii) All employees, whose services were terminated on or after 16th September 
1972, and who are eligible for gratuity by having a five years’ continuous 
service to their credit would be entitled to gratuity. 
(iv) All those employees, who have resigned from service or whose services 
have been terminated prior to the coming into force of the Act, would not 
be entitled to gratuity under the Act, even though they may have rendered 
continuous service of five or more years. 
(v) All those employees, whose services became terminated on or after 16th 
September 1972 or afterwards and who would otherwise fulfil the condi- 
tions of grant of gratuity, would be entitled to gratuity under the Act. 
47. The payment of gratuity is neither substitute nor alternate to any other 
payments or claims like retrenchment compensation, provident funds, etc. 
The distinction between the true character of gratuity and retrenchment compensa- 
tion was considered by the Supreme Court in Indian Hume Pipe Co. Ltd. v. Its Work- 
men, where the court pointed out that gratuity paid to workmen was intended to help 
them after retrenchment on superannuation or physical disability. The general principle 
underlying a claim for gratuity is that by reason of length of service workmen should 
be entitled to claim a certain amount as retirement benefit. On the other hand, re- trenchment compensation is not a retirement benefit at all. Retrenchment compensation 
is intended to give to the workman concerned some relief against retrenchment and to soften the rigour of hardship which retrenchment inevitably causes. This is the concept on which the grant of retrenchment compensation is based. It is essentially different form the concept on which gratuity is founded. In fact the whole object of granting retrenchment compensation is to enable the workman to keep his gratuity safe and un- used so that it may be available to him after his retirement. 
48. Computation of period of service for gratuity 
Where there is a mere change in the partnership, the business remaining the same, there will be no change in the employment and it would be open to the employees to contend that their services should be treated as continuous notwithstanding the change in the partnership. If the firm is dissolved and if the employees of the firm are retained in the same business continued by one or more of the partners of the dis- solved firm, no transfer of ownership is involved and it will be open to the employ- ees to contend that there is no break in service. But, where an employee working un- der an individual considers that his services have come to an end and applies for ap-

pointment to the firm which continues the business, even though the previous em- 
ployer is taken as one of the partners of the firm, the employee is not entitled to claim 
the benefit of the service put in by him under the individual employer before the 
formation of the partnership. Such an employee cannot claim benefit of gratuity on 
the basis of his employment with the individual employer but only from the date on 
which he was appointed by the partnership. 
When the partnership is converted into a private limited company and continues 
employment of some workers, the claim for gratuity by the workers cannot be de-

49. Rate of Gratuity 
As regards the contention that inasmuch as the workman works generally for 26 
days in a month, a month’s salary has to be calculated on that basis and, therefore, in 
law under section 4(2) of the Act what the employee is entitled to get by way of gra- 
tuity will be the wages of 13 days and not 15 days, the tribunal observed that gratuity 
is required to be paid under the provisions of section 4(2) for every completed year 
of service or part thereof in excess of 6 months at the rate of 15 day’s wages. 15 
day’s wage is the rate of wages at which the gratuity is to be calculated. Now so de- 
scribing the rate of wages the legislature could not have intended that something less 
than 15 day’s wages should be paid on the ingenious interpretation sought to be put 
on the provision by the employer. The legislature has further provided how the wages 
are to be calculated, that is, how 15 day’s wages are to be calculated and the provi- 
sion is that 15 days wages are to be calculated on the basis of the rate of wages drawn 
by the employee concerned and a special method is prescribed in the provision of 
section 4(2) in the case of piece rated employees. In the case of time rated employ- 
ees, there should be no difficulty because the method of calculating the daily wage is 
not difficult to deduce. 
Section 4(2) provides for the mode of calculation of the amount of gratuity, 
whereas Section 4(3) imposes a ceiling on the amount of gratuity on 26 days wage 
basis. These two sub-sections complement each other, each one of them is not to be 
interpreted as depending on the other.”” Sub-sections (2) and (3) have been designed 
to achieve a separate and distinct objects at two different stages. One sub-section 
must be understood without reference to the other. Confusion arises only if these two 
sub-sections are sought to be interpreted together as if each one depends upon the 
other for a proper appreciation. 
The intention of the legislature in enacting section 4(2) was not only to achieve 
uniformity and reasonable degree of certainty, but also to create and bring into force 
a self-contained all embracing complete and comprehensive code relating to gratuity 
as a compulsory, retiral benefit. The quantum of gratuity payable under sub-section 
(2) of section 4 has to be fifteen days’ wages based on the rate of wages last drawn 
by the employee concerned for every completed year of service or more in excess of 
six months subject to the maximum of 20 months wages as provided in sub-section 
(3). The whole object is to ensure that the employee concerned must be paid gratuity 
at the rate of 15 days wages for 365 days in a year of service. The total amount of 
gratuity payable to such employee at that rate has to be multiplied by the number of

viz., that the amount shall not exceed 20 months wages. It the determination of the 
amount of gratuity payable under section 4(2) depends on the number of calender 
days in a month in which the services of the employee concerned terminate, the 
quantum of gratuity payable would necessarily vary between one employee and an- 
other belonging to the same class, drawing the same scale of wages, with like service 
for the same number of years. Obviously this could not have been the legislative 
intention. 
Sub-sections (2) and (3) of section 4 are designed to achieve two separate and dis- 
tinct objects and they operate at two different stages. While sub-section (2) provides 
for a mode of calculation of the amount of gratuity, sub-section (3) seeks to impose a 
ceiling as the amount of gratuity payable at 20 months wages. It is meant to provide 
an incentive to employees to serve for the period of 30 years or more. By no rule of 
construction, sub-section (2) be called in aid for construction of the words ‘20 
months wages” appearing in sub-section (3) of section 4 of the Act.

lation, that although under section 4(5) of the Act an employee may be entitled to a 
higher period of gratuity but for enforcing such favourable terms of service for uigher gratuity, he would have to go to a different forum and the authority under the 
Act connot entertain such a claim for higher amount of gratuity. The Payment of Gratuity Act being a beneficial legislation, the provisions of the Act should be con- 
Scrued liberally.”

422 Part VI—The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 
An employee may, in his nomination, distribute the amount of gratuity payable to him under this Act amongst more than one nominee [Sub-s. (2)]. 
If an employee has a family at the time of making a nomination, the nomination shall be made in favour of one or more members of his family, and any nomination made by such employee in favour of a person who is not a member of his family shall be void [Sub-s. (3)]. 
If at the time of making a nomination the employee has no family, the nomination may be made in favour of any person or persons but if the employee subsequently acquires a family, such nomination shall forthwith become invalid and the employee shall make, within such time as may be prescribed, a fresh nomination in favour of one or more members of his family [Sub-s. (4)].

If a nominee predeceases the employee, the interest of the nominee shall revert to the employee who shall make a fresh nomination, in the prescribed form, in respect of such interest. [Sub-s. (6)]. 
Every nomination, fresh nomination or alteration of nomination, as the case may be, shall be sent by the employee to his employer, who shall keep the samé in his safe custody.

57, Recovery cannot be withheld for other dues 
Payment of gratuity cannot be withheld in the event of the employee’s failure to 
vacate the quarter provided to him during service. There is no provision in the Act 
permitting the withholding of payment on this ground.

59. Reopening case because of enhancement 
A claim for gratuity can be made only on the date of retirement on the basis of the 
salary drawn on the date of retirement and being already paid on that footing, the 
transaction was completed and closed. It could then not be reopened as a result of the 
enhancement made at a later date for persons retiring subsequently. The concept of 
gratuity is different from pension.

61. Remedies under other statutes 
Unlike many other procedural Acts which make provisions for barring remedies or actions under other laws, for example, sec. 22 of the Payment of Wages Act which bars remedy of suits for recovery of wages, no such provision has been made in the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972. From the provisions of the Act it also cannot be gathered that the intention of the Parliament was to bar the remedies which might be available to the employees under any other Act. It would, therefore, be logical to conclude that in so far as the remedies provided under any other Acts are not incon- sistent with the remedies provided under the Act are concerned the employees can pursue remedies under other laws. 
Such remedies may be discerned under the following statutes : | 
(1) Remedy of a civil suit under the provisions of Code of Civil Procedure.” 
(2) An application under s. 15 of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936. 
(3) Application under s. 33C of the Industrial Disputes Act for recovery of money due by way of gratuity. 
A gratuity payable under a law which does not provide for time within which the gratuity is to be paid amounts to “wages” under the Payment of Wages Act, 1936. All other cases of gratuity are not wages under the Act. Where gratuity falls within the scope of ‘“wages” under the Act only then it is recoverable under section 15 of the Act, otherwise it is not. 
Specific remedy is provided under the Payment of Gratuity Act, for recovery of gra- tuity and special authority has been created for settlement and adjudication of gratuity claims. The remedy under the Payment of Gratuity Act, should, therefore, be preferred to the one under the Payment of Wages Act, 1936. Moreover gratuity payable under the Payment of Gratuity Act, is not “wages” as defined under the Payment of Wages Act, as time for payment is provided under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972. 
The labour court under section 33C(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act can determine gratuity payable under this Act. In Railway Employees’ Co-operative Bank Ltd. Ma- dras v. Labour Court, Madras," the Madras High Court held that the jurisdiction of a tribunal or of the labour court under sec. 33C (1) (2) extends to the computation in terms of money not merely of all benefits which workmen are entitled to receive from the employer under a settlement or award under the Industrial Dispute Act but also benefits to which they might be entitled in their character as workmen under contract or by virtue of any other enactment. 
62. Powers of Controlling Authority 
_ The Controlling Authority has no jurisdiction to adjudicate upon the right of gratu- ity under this section but it can issue certificate for recovery if the amount is already ascertained.

due has been ascertained. Under this sub-section the Controlling Authority has no 
jurisdiction to ascertain or to fix the amount of money due. Its jurisdiction is con- 
fined only to looking into pleas such as discharge or payment. It has no power of 
adjudication. 
In Bengal Nagpur Cotton Mills Ltd. v. State of Madhya Pradesh,"' while inter- 
preting analogous provisions it was held that Sec. 33C(1) dealt with the recovery of 
an amount which had already been ascertained and not with the ascertainment of the 
amount. 
The Controlling Authority, however, has no power to grant interest while quanti- 
fying gratuity at the stage for recovery of gratuity from the employer. The_Control- 
ling Authority is not a court for the purpose of the Code of Civil Procedure. 
63. Administration of the Act 
64. Inspectors (s. 7-A) 
The appropriate Government may, by notification, appoint as many inspectors, as 
it deems fit, for the purposes of this Act [Sub-s. (1)]. 
The appropriate Government may, by general or special order, define the area to 
which the authority of an inspector so appointed shall extend and where two or 
more inspectors are appointed for the same area, also provide, by such order, for 
the distribution or allocation of work to be performed by them under the Act [Sub- 
4B 
Every Inspector shall be deemed to be a public servant within the meaning of sec- 
tion 21 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. 
65. Powers of Inspector (s.7-B) 
Subject to any rules made by the appropriate Government in this behalf, an In- 
spector may for the purpose of ascertaining whether any of the provisions of the Act 
or the conditions, if any, of any exemption granted under it, have been complied with 
exercise all or any of the following powers, namely :— 
(a) require an employer to furnish such information as he may consider neces- 
sary; 
(b) enter and inspect, at all reasonable hours, with such assistants (if any), be- 
ing persons in the service of the Government or local or any public author- 
ity, as he thinks fit, any premises of or place in any factory, mine oilfield, 
plantation, port, railway company, shop or other establishment to which the 
Act applies, for the purpose of examining any register, record or notice or 
other document required to be kept or exhibited under the Act or the rules 
made under it, or otherwise kept or exhibited in relation to the employment 
of any person or the payment of gratuity to the employees, and require their 
production for inspection; 
(c) examine with respect to any matter relevant to any of the purposes afore- 
said, the employer or any person whom he finds in such premises or place

72. Charan Singh v. Birla Textiles, (1989) 1 LLJ 250: AIR 1988 SC 2022.

and who, he has reasonable cause to believe, is an employee employed 
there; 
(d) make copies of, or take extracts from, any register, record, notice or other 
document, as he may consider relevant, and where he has reason to believe

and seize with such assistance as he may think fit, such register, record no- 
tice or other document as he may consider relevant in respect of that of-

Any person required to produce any register, record, notice or other document or to 
give any information by an Inspector under sub-section (1) shall be deemed to be 
legally bound to do so within the meaning of Section 175 and 176 of the Indian Penal 
Code [Sub-s. (2)]. 
The provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 shall so far as may apply 
to any search or seizure under this section as they apply to any search or seizure 
made under the authority of a warrant issued under Section 94 of that Code. 
66. Penalties (s. 9) 
Whoever, for the purpose of avoiding any payment to be made by himself under 
the Act or of enabling any other person to avoid such payment knowingly makes or 
causes to be made any false statement or false representation is punishable with im- 
prisonment for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may ex- 
tend to one thousand rupees, or with both [Sub-s. (1)]. 
An employer who contravenes, or makes default in complying with, any of the 
provisions of the Act or any rule or order made under it is punishable with impris- 
onment for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine which may extend to 
one thousand rupees, or with both [Sub-s. (2)]. 
Where the offence relates to non-payment of any gratuity payable under this 
Act, this employer is punishable with imprisonment for a term which shall not be 
less than three months unless the court trying the offence for reasons to be re- 
corded by it in writing is of opinion that a lesser term of imprisonment or the im- 
position of a fine would meet the ends of justice. Pension and gratuity are no 
longer any bounty to be distributed to employees on their retirement. They are 
valuable rights and properties in their hands. The Supreme Court has fixed a pe- 
riod of 2 months for payment of gratuity to an employee after retirement. Non- 
payment within the period so fixed would make the employer liable to pay penal 
interest to the employee at the rate of 24% per annum till the date of payment. 
[Sub-s. (2), proviso]. 
67. Exemption of employer from liability in certain cases (S. 10) 
Where an employer is charged with an offence punishable under the Act, he will be 
entitled, upon complaint duly made by him and on giving to the complainant not less 
than three clear days’ notice in writing of his intention to do so, to have any other 
person whom he charges as the actual offender brought before the court at the time 
appointed for hearing the charge; and if, after the commission of the offence is 
proved, the employer proves to the satisfaction of the court— 
73. Balakrishnan Nambiar v. State, (1997) 1 LLJ 1244 (Ker). 


Chap. I—Interpretation 429 
(a) that he has used due diligence to enforce the execution of the Act, and 
(b) that the said other person committed the offence in question without his 
knowledge, consent or connivance, 
that other person shall be convicted of the offence and shall be liable to the like pun- 
ishment as if he were the employer and the employer shall be discharged from any 
liability under the Act in respect of such offence. 
In seeking to prove as aforesaid, the employer may be examined on oath. His evi- 
dence and that of any witness whom he calls in his support shall be subject to cross- 
examination on behalf of the person he charges as the actual offender and by the 
prosecutor. 
If the person charged as the actual offender by the employer cannot be brought 
before the court at the time appointed for hearing the charge, the court shall ad- 
journ the hearing from time to time for a period not exceeding three months and if: 
by the end of the said period the person charged as the actual offender cannot still 
be brought before the court, the court shall proceed to hear the charge against the 
employer and shall, if the offence be proved, convict the employer. 
68. Cognizance of offences (s.11) 
No court shall take cognizance of any offence punishable under the Act save on a 
complaint made by or under the authority of the appropriate Government. [Sub-s. (1)] 
Where the amount of gratuity has not been paid, or recovered, within six months 
from the expiry of the prescribed time, the appropriate Government shall authorise the 
controlling authority to make a complaint against the employer, and then the control- 
ling authority shall, within fifteen days from the date of such authorisation, make such 
complaint to a magistrate having jurisdiction to try the offence [Sub-s. (1) proviso]. 
No court inferior to that of a Presidency Magistrate or a Magistrate of the first class 
shall try any offence punishable under the Act [Sub-s. (2)]. 
69. Protection of action taken in good faith (s. 12) 
No suit or other legal proceeding shall lie against the controlling authority or any 
other person in respect of anything which is in good faith done or intended to be done 
under the Act or any rule or order made under it. 
70. Due care and attention 
The phrase “due care and attention” implies genuine effort to reach the truth. When 
a question arises as to whether a person acted in good faith, then it devolves upon 
him to say not merely that he had a good intention but that he exercised such care 
and skill as the duty reasonably demanded for its due discharge. 
71. Protection of Gratuity (s. 13) 
No gratuity payable under the Act and no gratuity payable to an employee em- 
ployed in any establishment, factory, mine, oilfield, plantation, port, railway com-

72. Act to override other enactments etc. (s. 14) 
The provisions of the Act or any rule made under it shall have effect notwith- 
standing anything inconsistent with it contained in any enactment other than the Act 
or in any instrument or contract having effect by virtue of any enactment other than 
the Act. The importance of the overriding effect was stressed in Rajamani v. Deputy 
Commissioner of Labour and Appellate Authority under PG Act.’® The Court added 
that there is no scope of paying a lesser amount than that provided under the Act. 
Any receipt or voucher signed by the employee will not bar the employee from 
claiming the full amount due under the Act. 
An employer is not permitted to withhold the gratuity payable to an employee for 
the reason that the employee is in occupation of the land belonging to the employer. 
This section provides statutory protection to the employee that no gratuity payable 
under the Act is liable to be attached in execution of any decree or order of any civil, 
revenue or criminal court. Amount of gratuity due to an employee can be withheld 
only on any of the grounds mentioned in the Act and not otherwise. 
73. Rule making power (s. 15) 
The appropriate Government may, by notification, make rules for the purpose of 
carrying out the provisions of the Act. [Sub-s. (1)] 
Every rule made by the Central Government under the Act shall be laid, as soon as 
may be after it is made, before each House of Parliament while it is in session, for a 
total period of thirty days which may be comprised in one session or in two or 
more successive sessions, and if before the expiry of the session immediately fol- 
lowing the session or the successive sessions aforesaid, both Houses agree in 
making any modification in the rule, or both Houses agree that the rule should not 
be made, the rule shall, thereafter, have effect only in such modified form or be of 
no effect, as the case may be; so however, that any such modification or annulment 
shall be without prejudice to the validity of anything previously done under that 
rule.

In State of Bombay vy. United Motors India Ltd.,*' sub-rule (2)(i) of Rule 5 framed 
under the Bombay Sales Tax Act was held by the Supreme Court to be ultra vires the 
rule-making authority for violating Art. 286(2) of the Constitution. 
In Anant Sadashiv v. Ratnagiri Jila District Local Board,” the Bombay High 
Court observed that the rules framed by the District Local Board could not go beyond 
the scope of the Act itself, nor could they be inconsistent with the Act. 
In Borough Municipality of Amalner v. Pratap Spinning, Weaving and Manufac- 
turing Co. Ltd.,~ the Bombay High Court held that if the rules were ultra vires, the 
fact that they had not been challenged at the preliminary stage, or even that they had 
not been challenged during all the time that they have been in force, was immaterial, 
although in dealing with the argument that the rule was arbitrary or capricious that 
fact would not be wholly irrelevant. 
In Pramod C. Bhat v. Kanwar Raj Nath,™ the Bombay High Court held that it did 
not necessarily follow that because the rule-making authority took a particular view 
of the law that it was necessarily the right view. Many rules have been framed which 
Courts of law have declared to be ultra vires. If the rules went beyond the scope of 
the authority conferred by the statute, then, the rule would obviously be bad. But, in 
cases where there is ambiguity in the language used by the Legislature, or where 
more than one construction is possible, then the rules framed may help the Court in - 
coming to the right conclusion as to the construction to be placed upon a particular 
provision in the law. 
In Ganendra Kumar v. Narayan C "handra,” and in Huzrat Syed Shah Mustarshid 
Ali Al Quadari v. Commissioner of Wakfs,® the Calcutta High Court held: “In some 
statutes, power is given to frame rules and when so framed, they are made part of the 
statute. That is quite a different matter. In such a case, it may be permissible to sup- 
plement the provisions of the statute itself, within limits. But where rules are to be 
framed for ‘carrying out the purposes of the Act’, such rules cannot travel beyond the 
four corners of the Act itself.”

17.4 Trade Union Structure ici. ausciteees bu 446 
Trade Union is a complete institution which has many aspects—economic, psy- 
chological, sociological and political.’ All these characteristics differ from country to 
country. A classical definition of trade union was given by Sidney and Beatrice 
Webbs. According to this definition, “a trade union is a continuous association of 
wage earners for the purpose of maintaining and improving the conditions of their 
1. V.V. Giri, Labour Problems in Indian Industry, (1972). 
433 


434 Part VII— The Trade Unions Act, 1926 
working lives”. * Thus, trade union is a voluntary and continuous association, the ob- 
jective of which is to maintain and improve the working conditions of its members. 
According to S.D. Punekar:’ “a trade union is a monopolistic combination of 
wage-earners who as individual producers are complementary to one-another but 
who stand to employers in relation of dependence for the sale of their labour and 
production, and that the general purpose of association is in view of that dependence 
to strengthen their power to bargain with the employers or bargaining collectively.” 
The English Trade Unions Act says that “a trade union is a combination with the 
main objective of regulating the relation between workmen and masters or between 
workmen and workmen or between masters and masters for imposing of restrictive 
conditions on the conduct of any trade or business and also provision of benefits to 
members”’. 
The Indian Trade Union Act, 1926" defines a trade union as “Trade Union means 
any combination, whether temporary or permanent, formed primarily for the purpose 
of regulating the relations between workmen and employers, or between workmen 
and workmen, between employers and employers, or for imposing restrictive condi- 
tions on the conduct of any trade or business, and includes any federation of two or 
more trade unions.” 
The definition given by the Trade Unions Act, 1926 is wider in perspective be- 
cause it has used the term ‘combination’ instead of the term ‘association’ and it in- 
cludes association of employees as well as employers to protect their respective in- 
terests. But it does not include voluntary organisations formed for the purpose of 
giving benefits to their members in sickness, infirmity, old age etc. 
However, some writers like Sydney and Beatrice Webbs and Cunnison have re- 
fused to recognise employers’ associations and the professional bodies as trade un- 
ions because they-are not the workers’ organisations. J. Cunnison defines trade union 
as “a monopolistic association of wage earners, who as individual producers are 
complementary to one another but who stand to the employers in relation of depend- 
ence for the sale of their labour and even for its production and that the general pur- 
pose of the association is in view of that dependence to sk their power to 
bargain with their employers.” 
1. Birth of modern trade unionism 
_ Modern trade unionism is product of conditions created by the Industrial revolu- 
tion. The possible consequences of revolution are following: 
(i) Too much emphasis on individualism resulting in free enterprise. 
(ii) The attitude of non-interference by the State which regarded industry as a 
private competitive effort and on that ground granted it universal freedom, 
resulting in formulation of the doctrine of laissez-faire i.e., non-interference 
by the Government or State. 
(iii) Freedom of contract which proclaimed that free contract is the perfect con- 
dition. 
2. Sidney and Beatrice, History of Trade Unionism, (1920). 
3. §.D. Punekar, Trade Unionism in India, 1948, p. 23. 
4. S. 2(b), Trade Unions Act, 1926 (16 of 1926). 
5. J. Cunnison, Labour Organisation, (1930). 


Chap. I—Development of Trade Union Law etc. 435 
These conceptions about the individual, the State and the sources of wealth led to the 
theory of natural rights and the concept of a free and an open market which formed the 
basis of early labour law in all the countries of the world. However, the conception of a 
free and open market as it is considered today is far different from the one as it was 
understood in the beginning of the labour movement. 
With the decline of mercantilism, the entrepreneur’s right to a free and open market 
soon became an undisputed right at common law and anything done in constraint of it 
was considered as a wrong. The fallacy of applying to this right free and open market 
vis-a-vis combinations of labour lay in the fact that while harm caused by one employer 
to another employer in business competition was ‘damnum abs que injuria’, i e. loss or 
damage without injury. 
But the same harm when inflicted or caused by labour combinations was considered 
illegal. It was because of this partial application of the theory that labour combinations 
were considered unlawful. 
2. Common law theories proved biggest-hurdle in jural sanction of trade un- 
ions 
The analysis of the common law cases dealing with combinations and collective 
action discloses that a number of principles of law were used in illegalising and un- 
justifying the union activities and labour combinations. The following are the main 
theories in this respect: 
(i) Doctrine of Conspiracy—Doctrine of conspiracy deals with those acts which 
are privileged if done by individuals but may be actionable if done in combination. 
The trade unions were looked upon from the very beginning as prima facie illegal 
bodies or combinations which were meant for causing restraints of trade. This was 
the reason of general feeling of hostility towards trade unions during the nineteenth 
century. The earlier theory was that the labour combinations are organised for com- 
mitting the crime of conspiracy. On the basis of this theory the earlier strike cases 
were held as criminal conspiracies. 
The doctrine of criminal conspiracy seems to be based on the ideas that combina- 
tion by itself is sufficient to render an act criminal which is not criminal if done by a 
number of persons singly and that the resulting injury from a combination is suffi- 
cient to constitute combination as a criminal conspiracy even though the injury may 
not be a crime or a tort, Later on, the trade unions were given statutory immunity 
from criminal conspiracy under trade union laws in different countries. 
Combinations were also attacked on the basis of civil conspiracy. 
(ii) Doctrine of restraint of trade—Combinations in restraint of trade are consid- 
ered illegal. This doctrine was another legal obstacle which came in the way of 
growth of trade unionism during the nineteenth century. The general belief of the 
courts in the nineteenth century was that ‘unions of whatever sort are by the very 
nature contrary to public interest and this object in itself will vitiate every association 
and every transaction into which they enter.’ Thus, any transaction entered into by 
any association was considered to be contrary to public interest and in restraint of 
trade. 
In Hornby v. Clokes,° the court held that the purposes of a trade union, if no longer 
a criminal conspiracy, were in restraint of trade thereby rendering it for civil pur- 
6. (1867) LR 2 QB 153 


436 Part VII— The Trade Unions Act, 1926 
poses an illegal association. However, in the subsequent cases the courts held the 
view that a trade union by itself does not import illegality and thus, depending on the 
objects of the trade unions, some trade unions could be lawful, while others could be 
unlawful combinations. It was open to the courts to examine the objects and rules of 
a trade union to evaluate the degree of interference imposed by it on the individual’s 
freedom and as a result of such examination if the union survived then it could be 
said to a lawful union. : 
(iii) Protection of legitimate interests.—Economic injuries inflicted for the purpose 
of promoting some legitimate interest are privileged but they are actionable, if in- 
flicted: 
(a) without justification, or 
(b) maliciously, or 
(c) in bad faith, or 
(d) where the direct or primary object is to harm others and not to benefit the 
actors. 
(iv) Action for interference in business relations —An action will lie for a non- privileged interference in business and contractual relations. 
(v) Concerted action—Concerted action subjects the actors to liability for injuries inflicted if either the object sought or means used is improper. 
3. Development of Trade Union Movement and Laws in India 
‘Development of trade union movement in India can be discussed under three broad phases which are as follows: 
Phase I-1850 to 1900 
Phase IT-1900 to 1947 
Phase III-After independence in 1947 
Phase I-1850 to 1900.—From 1850 onwards the process of industrialisation began in India. In 1881, the Factories Act was enacted to safeguard the interests of the workers which prohibited child labour and brought the concept of factory inspectors. Growth of trade union movement was slow during this period. There were many strikes in all industrial centres like Bombay, Ahmedabad, Calcutta and Madras due to low wages, poor working conditions, long hours of work. But at that time there ex- isted no trade union in the real sense of the term. In 1885, the Indian National Con- gress came into existence as political party against British colonialism. Workers united under its flag. During this time-period, small association of workers in the form of welfare bodies were established. aa 
In 1890, the first trade union, the Bombay Millhands Association was formed by N.M. Lokhande, who himself was a factory worker. However, this Association could not be regarded as a trade union in the real sense of the term because it acted merely as a clearing house for the grievances of Bombay Mill Workers. In 1897, the Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants of India and Burma was also established. 
Phase II-(1900 to 1947).—During Phase II, the Printers Union (1904), the Bom- bay Postal Union (1907), the Kamgar Hitwardhak Sabha (1909), the Social Service League (1910) and the Press Employees Union were established. Although these organisations were not trade unions in the real sense of the term but they germinated 


Chap. I—Development of Trade Union Law etc. 437 
the seed of consciousness among the Indian workers to fight for their legitimate 
rights. These organisations were guided by a number of educated philanthropists and 
social workers. In 1914, the First World War occurred and during the time-period of 
four years (1914-1918) the Indian independence struggle intensified tremendously 
and this helped the trade union movement during this period. After the First World 
War, there was intense industrial unrest in the country because of high cost of living. 
This economic discontent was accelerated by the political agitation in the country 
which ultimately resulted in strikes. However, these strikes gave rise to labour con- 
sciousness and the establishment of International Labour Organisation (ILO) in 1919. 
This influenced the growth of trade union movement in India. 
In 1918, India’s first Trade Union, the Madras Labour Union was founded by PP 
Wadia who had sympathy for the working class. This was the first systematic attempt 
at Trade Union Organisation with regular membership dues and relief fund. How- 
ever, the movement was confined only to three cities of Bombay, Ahmedabad and 
Madras, where the textile industry was established. After 1919, the trade unionism 
spread to other cities and other industries like Railways and Iron and Steel Industry 
also joined the unionism. 
By the year 1920, the trade unions had established their roots in almost all the 
sectors for protecting working class. There were 125 unions with a total membership 
of approximately 2,50,000 workers. In 1920 itself, the All India Trade Union Con- 
gress (AITUC) was formed to co-ordinate the activities of different labour organisa- 
tions and protect the interest of Indian labour. Since the establishment of AITUC, the 
Indian labour movement remained very close to the notional movement led by Indian 
National Congress. 
Until 1920, there was no law in India for registration and protection of trade un- 
ions. In 1920, the High Court of Madras granted an injunction in a case restraining 
the union officials from influencing the workers to break their contracts with the em- 
ployers by striking. This led to an agitation and it finally resulted in 1926 as the In- 
dian Trade Unions Act, 1926. This Act was enacted on the pattern of English law. 
Despite the enactment of Trade Unions Act, labour unrest increased in the late twen- 
ties. From 1928 onwards trade union movement came under the influence of com- 
munists. AITUC affiliated with communist frontal organisation (Pan Pacific Trade 
Union Secretariat) resulting in breaking up of AITUC into All India Trade Union 
Federation (AITUF) and RTUC (Red Trade Union Congress) and National Trade 
Union (NTU) (1933). In 1929, the Government enacted Trade Disputes Act, 1929 for 
preventing strikes and improving labour conditions. 
In 1929, a Royal Commission on Labour in India was appointed to study and re- 
port on the India Labour conditions. The Commission recommended that employers 
should adopt a more liberal policy towards recognition of Trade Unions. The Royal 
Commission examined the working of the Trade Unions Act and found that the Act 
had ‘helped to give trade unions stability and enhanced sense of responsibility’. It 
recommended, inter alia, that the Act should be re-examined in not more than three 
years’ time, that all the limitations imposed on the activities of the registered unions 
and their officers and members should be reconsidered. However, no significant ac- 
tion was taken in this matter. 
During the thirtees, political rivalries dominated the labour movement and indus- | 
trial unrest was very acute due to wage cuts and retrenchments imposed by employ- 
ers—particularly in Bombay. The Bombay Government enacted the Bombay Trade 
7. Report of the Royal Commission on Labour, p. 331. 


438 Part VII— The Trade Unions Act, 1926 
Dispute Conciliation Act which provided for compulsory conciliation and the ap- 
pointment of Government labour officer with a statutory power to enquire into labour 
conditions prevailing in factories. 
During the period of 1935 to 1947, the India National Congress came in power in 7 
provinces on the basis of elections held under the Government of India Act, 1935. 
Effect of political parties became prominent and trade unions were formed in line 
with political parties. At this time, Second World War (1939-1945) intervened and 
this period marked polarisation of political parties in India favouring and non- 
favouring India’s participation in War. The Congress ministries resigned in the 
provinces as a protest against the unilateral decision taken by the Governor-General 
in declaring War on behalf of India without consulting them. The effect of this pro- 
test was that the national leaders were arrested and the leadership of AITUC passed 
into the hands of communists. 
During Phase II, the progress of trade unionism was not coherent and systematised. 
The Royal Commission on Labour’ observed: “Trade Unionism to be fully effective, 
demands two things, a democratic spirit and education. The democratic ideal still has 
to be developed in the Indian workers and the lack of education is the most serious 
obstacle of all. The latter difficulty does not arise merely or even mainly from illiter- 
acy. Few trade unions can afford to conduct benevolent work, and the majority find it 
hard to convince the worker that subscription is worth while except when a dispute is 
eminent or in progress.” 
Phase III-1947 onwards.—This Phase is the golden era of trade unionism in In- 
dia. India became independent in 1947 and Indian National Congress formed the 
Central Government. However, the industrial unrest continued and the three factors 
which were responsible for industrial unrest included the following: 
(i) in relation to cost of living the wages of the workers were low, workers 
demanded greater participation in war profits; 
(ii) the renewal of the political activity in the labour field; and 
(ili) the changed political context on India’s independence which resulted in a 
new psychology of workers. 
To control the labour unrest, the Government enacted the Industrial Disputes Act, 
1947 which embodied restrictive features of the war time Defence of India Rule 
81(A). However, this Act proved inadequate in arresting strikes and falling produc- 
tion. To improve the relations between employers and employees, an Industrial Con- 
ference was convened in 1947 in New Delhi consisting of representatives of Gov- 
ernment, employers and employees. At this conference the following Truce Resolu- 
tion’ was adopted: 
“The increase in industrial production which is so vital to the economy of the 
country cannot be achieved without the fullest co-operation between labour and 
management and stable and friendly relations between them ....... mutual dis- 
cussion of all problems common to both and a determination to settle all dis- 
putes without recourse to interruption in or slowing down of production should 
be the common aim of employer and labour. The system of remuneration to capital as well as labour must be so devised that while in interests of consumers 
and the primary producers excessive profits should be presented by suitable 
8. Ibid. 
9. Proceedings of the Standing Committee, (10th Session). 


Chap. I—Development of Trade Union Law etc. 439 
measures of taxation and otherwise, both will share the product of their com- 
mon effort after making provision for payment of fair wages to labour, a fair 
return on capital employed in the industry and the reasonable reserve for the 
maintenance and expansion of the undertaking.” 
Many labour legislations were passed like Employees’ State Insurance Act (1948), 
Employees Provident Fund and Miscellaneous Provision Act (1952), Payment of 
Gratuity Act (1972) and Equal Remuneration Act (1976) etc. 
After independence, trade unions formed in line with political parties, for example, 
Hind Mazdoor Sabha (HMS) as a trade union wing of Socialist Party in 1948, Indian 
National Trade Union Congress (INTUC) as part of Congress Party in 1947, Centre 
of Indian Trade Union (CITU) as a part of Communist Party (Marxists) in 1970 dur- 
ing the split of Communist Party as CPM and CPI. 
4. Difference between Labour Movement and Trade Union Movement 
Although both the terms ‘labour movement’ and ‘trade union movement’ are used 
interchangeably but they are distinct. The labour movement is ‘for the workers’ 
whereas the trade union movement is ‘by the workers’. In the industrial scenario la- 
bour movement came first. The social reformers made efforts to improve the working 
and living conditions of the workers/labours which can be traced back to 1875. These 
efforts were the part of labour movement. The trade union movement came when the 
workers organised themselves into trade unions. The labour movement conveys a 
higher degree of consciousness of rights amongst workers then by mere trade union 
movement. A large member of measures were taken by the social workers, enlight- 
ened employers and the Government during labour movement. The trade union 
movement started after 1918 when the workers formed their association for improv- 
ing their conditions. 
In the recent years, there has been a marked increase in the registered unions in our 
country. At present there are about 56,000 registered workers’ unions and 10 Central 
Labour Organisations in our country. Not only the member of trade unions has in- 
creased, their base has also widened. For example, the Hind Mazdoor Sabha believes 
and propagates the philosophy of economic development and the establishment of a 
democratic, socialist society in India, where the labour should be given the equal 
status. According to AITUC: “‘the ultimate aim of the trade union movement is to 
abolish capitalism and wage slavery and establish socialism in which not only the 
working class but all layers of society is freed from exploitation”. In the view of 
INTUC, besides the traditional role of trade unions, a trade union should serve their 
membership and cater to the requirements of workers as responsible citizens in all 
spheres, plan for sustaining the interests of their members during industrial peace by 
organising social, intellectual, cultural and recreational activities and educate their 
workers so that the traditional agitational role can be transformed gradually into one 
of understanding. 
The trade union movement continues to be dominated by political influences and 
thus the ideologies of trade unions differ according to the political influence over 
them. These political and ideological differences of trade unions hampered the cause 
of labour classes in India. According to National Commission on Labour: “after in- 
dependence, unions rivalries based on political considerations have become sharper. 
The splitting up of unions and formation of new unions having sympathies with po- 
litical parties have permeated unions operating at different ends.” 
10. Report of National Commission on Labour, 1969. 


440 | Part VII— The Trade Unions Act, 1926 
The union consciousness has grown amongst the working class in almost every 
profession. The All India Railway Men Federation, the National Federation of Posts 
and Telegraph Employees, the All India Defence Employees Federation and the Con- 
federation of Central Government Employees covering almost all the sections of 
Government departments have been very active in fighting for causes of working 
class. They have compelled the Government to appoint Pay Commissions in order to 
review the pay structure from time to time to neutralise the rise in cost of living. 
Following this pattern, employees of banking industry, electricity, dock workers, 
insurance, airline employees and teachers have formed unions to fight for their de- 
mands collectively. Besides these, we also have unions of taxi-drivers and rickshaw 
pullers etc. 
For the settlement of industrial disputes, the country has adopted the system of 
compulsory adjudication. The State has been given the responsibility of forming a 
welfare State under the Directive Principles of State Policy by our Constitution. The 
Government has changed its labour policy and has encouraged tripartite and bipartite 
consultations and collective bargaining. The industrial workers were given the status 
of co-partners in the industrial development by the First and Second Five Year Plans. 
The First Five Year Plan stated: “the trade unions can play a positive and important 
role in the execution of plans ...... for the successful implementation of the plans in 
India, co-operation from trade unions and employers is absolutely essential...... The 
representatives of employers and trade unions should be associated at every step in 
the implementation of the plan.” 
5. Amendments to Trade Unions Act, 1926 
The Trade Unions Act, 1926 was enacted on the pattern of English law. In 1929, 
the Act was amended by the Act XV of 1928 to facilitate the procedure of appeal 
against decisions of the Registrar to register a trade union or withdrawing a certifi- 
cate of registration. 
Though, the 1926 Act provided for the registration of trade unions complying with 
various specified requirements, it imposed no obligation on employers to recognise 
and deal with such registered unions. The Royal Commission on Labour in India, had 
also pleaded for the recognition of unions by employers in spirit as well as in letter. 
The matter figured prominently on the agenda of successive Labour Minister’ Con- 
ferences held 1940 and 1941 and of the meetings of the Standing Labour Committee 
(1944) and the Indian Labour Conference (1945). The result was the adoption of the 
Indian Trade Union (Amendment) Act of 1947, which provided for compulsory rec- 
ognition by employers of representative trade union by order of a labour court. The 
Act confers on the executive of a recognised trade unions by order of a labour court. 
The Act confers on the executive of a recognised trade union the right to negotiate 
with employers in respect of matters connected with the employment or non- 
employment terms of employment and the conditions of work of all or any of its 
members. The Amendment Act has not, however, come into force at all. Similarly 
the Trade Union Bill 1950 providing for administrative controls on trade unions also 
lapsed. 
The Trade Union (Amendment) Act, 2001 amended sections 4, 5, 6, 9, 11 and 29 
and section 22 was substituted by a new section. 
6. Recommendations by the National Labour Commission, 1969 
The Commission has made following recommendations: 


Chap. I—Development of Trade Union Law etc. 441 
(1) trade union registration should be made compulsory; 
(2) the Registrar should be time bound to decide the issue of registration; 
(3) effective measures should be taken for cancellation if unions do not comply 
with conditions regarding filing of returns or membership; 
(4) trade union recognition by employers be made compulsory by Central 
Legislation; 
(5) such recognised unions should be given statutorily exclusive rights and 
facilities like right of sole representation, entering into collective bar- 
gaining agreements, holding discussions and negotiations, inspection, 
check-off etc. 
(6) the minority unions should also be allowed to represent workers in redres- 
sal of individual grievances like dismissal, discharge, etc. 
The suggested measures are likely to promote growth of healthy and strong trade 
unionism and eliminate inter-union rivalry to some extent. Compulsory recognition 
of one union for one undertaking will make the unions effective instruments of col- 
lective action and give them requisite bargaining equality. 
TRADE UNION REGULATION IN INDIA 
7. Trade union rights in India 
The trade union rights in our country are found scattered in various laws, voluntary 
measures like the Code of Discipline and the Constitutional provisions under Article 
19 of the Constitution of India. These trade union rights may be divided into the fol- 
lowing categories: 
1. Rights of freedom of speech and expression which includes rights of pick- 
eting’ and demonstrations. | 
. Rights regarding formation and registration of the trade unions. 
. Rights regarding recognition of the trade unions by the employers. 
. Rights regarding collective bargaining and collective actions. 
nA fb W WN . Rights regarding conduct and functioning of the trade unions. 
6. Miscellaneous rights. 
8. Right to form a trade union 
The right to form and continue a trade union is a fundamental right guaranteed under 
Art. 19(1)(c) of the Constitution of our country, which can only be subjected to reason- 
able restrictions in public interest as provided by Art. 19(1)(6) of the Constitution of 
India.'° Provision is also made in the Indian Trade Unions Act, 1926 for providing 
immunities to trade unions from criminal prosecution in certain circumstances which 
further ensure the safe conduct of trade unions. Under various laws, trade unions are 
required to get themselves registered for certain purposes. Every trade union is required 
to register itself under the Trade Unions Act in order to operate as a trade union. —
