9. Trade Union not necessary for industrial disputes/demands 
As a matter of fact, under the Industrial Disputes Act even a group of employees 
who have not formed a trade union can raise an industrial dispute in respect of their 
demands and the whole machinery under the Act would be available for settlement of 
the disputes without making it obligatory at any stage for the employees to get them- 
selves organised in a trade union. Thus, the law does not compel employees to form 
themselves into a trade union and as such any employee who does not want to join 
any trade union cannot be treated with any disfavour under the law. 
10. Recognition of trade unions by employers 
After the registration of a trade union, the question of its recognition by the em- 
ployer comes to the forefront inasmuch as if it is recognised by the employer for the 
purpose of collective bargaining, then it will have certain privileges and an opportu- 
nity to fulfil its role. There is no provision in the Indian Trade Unions Act or Indus- 
trial Disputes Act, 1947, the only two Central enactments in this respect in the coun- 
try, regarding recognition of a trade union by the employers. 
No union, registered or otherwise, can lay claim to recognition by the management 
for participation in negotiations as a matter of a legal right. However, it cannot be 
denied that fair play requires the management to consider grant of recognition when 
a body of persons legitimately expects to be affected." 
The right of recognition has to be secured by trade unions by raising an industrial 
dispute. 
The Gajendragadkar Commission in 1969 made historic recommendations on the 
need for recognition of unions. The Commission observed: “It would be desirable to 
make union recognition compulsory under a Central law, in all undertakings em- 
ploying 100 or more workers or where capital invested is above a stipulated size. A 
trade union, seeking recognition as a bargaining agent, from an individual employer, 
should have a membership of at least 15% of the workers in the establishment. It is 
for an industry in a local area, the minimum membership should be 25% where more 
unions than one contend for recognition, the union having the larger following 
should be recognised.” 
The Union Government’s effort to give effect to the recommendations of the First 
National Commission did not bear fruits as the unions were divided on the issue. 
In 1978, Industrial Relations Bill came which hoped that the provisions relating to 
recognition of unions and other measures would provide the much needed stability in 
the employer-employee relationship in industrial establishments. Chapter IV of the 
Bill provided for selection of the sole bargaining agent (representing 65% of the 
workers in a unit), Chief Negotiating Agent (more then 50% and less than 65%), As- 
sociate Unions (representing not less than 20% of the workers), a Local Union (in 
industries) and a Negotiating Committee (where there are more unions). However, 
this Bill lapsed due to certain reasons. 
In 1999, the Second High Powered National Commission on Labour (with Sri 
Ravindra Verma as Chairman) was appointed. The terms of reference were two in 
number, rationalisation of labour laws and suggestions on an umbrella legislation for 
14. Indian Airlines Technical Assistants Union v. Indian Airlines, (1995) 1 LLJ 578 (AP). 
15. Report of the First National Commission on Labour, p. 329. 
16. Trade Union Recognition — The Crucial Issue in the Industrial Relations Agenda, C.P. Chandra Das, LLJ, Feb. 2003. 


Chap. I—Development of Trade Union Law etc. 443 
unrecognised labour in the back drop of certain important factors including globa- 
lisation, privatization and liberalisation of trade and industry. The Commission in its 
report felt that there was a need for new work culture. The Commission also referred 
to the International Labour Organisation (ILO) declaration of 1998 and felt that Gov- 
ernment of India was committed to guarantee in the labour policy, to all the workers, 
“the right to organise and form trade unions and right to collective bargaining”. For 
realising this, the issue regarding the recognition of the bargaining agent was para- 
mount to create a climate of harmonious industrial relations. Several views were put 
forward by the Commission and after analysing in depth the Commission held that 
the selection of the negotiating agent should be on the basis of check-off system and 
the unions with 66% backing can be accepted as the single negotiating agent and if 
such a union was not there, unions with more than 25% of the support of the workers 
will be given proportionate representation in the negotiating college of unions. The 
Commission felt that the check-off system should be compulsory in establishments, 
employing 300 or more number of employees. The Commission also felt that in the 
case of establishments employing less than 100 workers, the mode of selection of the 
negotiating agent will be decided by the Labour Relations Commission appointed by 
the government. The recognised union will continue to enjoy the privileges for four 
years. The Commission further held that bipartism will promote harmonious relations 
and the awareness of mutual defence can create an active realization on the “Com- 
monality of stakes”. This commonality will promote not only trade union and em- 
ployee growth but also the industrial as well as the country’s growth. 
According to the National Commission on Labour, 2002,'’ a settlement entered 
into with a recognised negotiating agent must be binding on all workers and for this, 
the provision must be made in the law for determining negotiating agents, particu- 
larly on behalf of workers. Negotiating agent should be selected for recognition on 
the basis of check-off system, with 667% entitling the union to be accepted as the sin- 
gle negotiating agent, and if no union has 66% support, then the unions that have the 
support of more than 25% should be given proportionate representation on the col- 
lege. The Commission felt that any formula which militates against increasing un- 
ionisation should be ab initio avoided. The Commission further held that the check- 
off system has the advantage of ascertaining the relative strengths of trade unions 
based on continuing loyalty reflected by the regular payment of union subscription. 
The check-off system in an establishment employing 300 or more workers must be 
made compulsory for members of all registered trade unions. Though the check-off 
system will be preferred in the case of establishments employing less than 300 per- 
sons too, the mode of identifying the negotiating agent in these establishments may 
be determined by the Labour Relations Commissions. Any union in such smaller 
enterprises may approach the Labour Relation Commissions for conducting a secret 
ballot. The Commission recommended a slightly different dispensation for units em- 
ploying less than 300 workers as the Commission felt that it is in such units that the 
possibility of victimisation has to be provided against. Recognition once granted 
should be valid for a period of four years to be coterminous with the period of set- 
tlement. No claim by any other trade union/federation/centre for recognition should 
be entertained till at least four years have elapsed from the date of earlier recognition. 
The individual workers’ authorisation for check-off should also be co-terminus with 
the tenure of recognition of the negotiating agent or college.

11. Code of discipline and trade union recognition 
With the evolution of the voluntary measures in the nature of the Code of Disci- 
pline in the industry, an attempt has been made to make a provision for recognition 
of unions by the employers. Thus, under the Code of Discipline the management has 
agreed to recognise the union in accordance with the criteria evolved at the Sixteenth 
Session of Indian Labour Conference held in May 1958. The criteria for recognition 
of a union have been that the membership of_the union should cover at least 15% of 
the workers in the establishment and for this purpose the membership has to be 
counted only of those persons who have paid their subscription for at least three 
months during the period of six months immediately preceding the reckoning. When 
there are more than one unions, a union claiming recognition should have been func- 
tioning for at least one year after registration. The recognition is generally given for a 
period of two years. If there are more than one union in an industry or establishment, 
the one with the largest membership should be recognised. It is a condition of recog- 
nition that the unions should observe the provisions of the Code of Discipline. These criteria for recognition of unions have created many problems and in the absence of 
any statutory sanction underlying the Code of Discipline, in actual practice, the rec- ognition of a union by employers has lost much of its significance. 
12. Rights of recognised unions under the Code 
Under the Code of Discipline, the recognised unions have been given certain rights in preference to unrecognised unions. These rights are: 
(i) to raise, issue and enter into collective agreements with employers on gen- 
eral questions concerning the terms of employment and conditions of serv- 
ice of workers in an establishment; 
(ii) to collect membership fees/subscriptions payable by members to the union within the premises of the undertaking; 
(iii) to put up or cause to put up a notice board on the premises of the undertaking 
in which its members are employed and affix or cause to be affixed thereon notices relating to meetings, statements of accounts of its income and expen- diture and other announcements which are not abusive, indecent or inflama- tory or subversive of discipline or otherwise contrary to the Code; 
(iv) to take steps for the purpose of prevention or settlement of an industrial dispute: 
(a) to hold discussions with the employees who are members of the un- ion at a suitable place or places within the premises of office/factory/ establishment as mutually agreed upon; 
(b) to meet and discuss with an employer or any person appointed by him for the purpose, the grievances of its members employed in the undertaking; 
(c) to inspect by prior arrangement, in an undertaking, any place where any member of the union is employed.

13. Rights of unrecognised unions 
Though under the Code of Discipline an unrecognised union or a de-recognised 
union may not get the rights available to the recognised unions, but still under the 
law it would be entitled to exercise one of the most important functions and rights. 
i.e., representing the employees and sponsoring and taking up the cause of the work- 
ers on certain demands. 
14. Registration of Trade Unions 
Any seven or more members of a trade union may apply for registration of a trade 
union under the Trade Unions Act, 1926 (sec. 4). For registration, the members, e1- 
ther have to subscribe their names to the rules of the trade union or have to comply 
with the provisions of the Act regarding registration. The Registrar, on registering a 
trade union, issues a certificate of registration in the prescribed form which is a con- 
clusive evidence that the trade union has been duly registered under the Act (sec. 8). 
This assures the mind of the employer that the trade union is an authenticated body. 
(For details regarding registration refer Chapter II). 
15. Registration not entitles recognition of trade union 
A registered trade union does not automatically get a right to be recognised by the 
management of industrial establishment. There is no statutory right vested in any 
union to compel the management to recognise it. Generally, there is a misconception 
not only amongst the union leaders but also among the employers that as and when 
the union is formed and registered or when there are more than one union, the one or 
the union representing majority of workers should be recognised. Due to this mis- 
taken view some of the employers have even recognised the unions. 
In employer and employee relations, the existence of union is necessary as a vital 
vehicle of workers’ protection and progress. For effective management, the unions 
are inevitable. Several managements of large progressive organisations prefer their 
workers organised in the union and even encourage them to join the union because in 
that way workers can be reached and handled and are more responsive to arguments 
and reasons while in chaotic, unorganised mass of forces of responsibility, emotion- 
alism comes to the fore more easily. They plead that if the unions do not exist, they 
would have to be invented. In bigger organisations employing thousands of work- 
men, there is no possibility of managing the workers individually but recognition of 
trade union is nowhere provided under the Central Acts. 
Therefore, there is a distinction between registration of a trade union and its recog- 
nition. Registration is an act of the members of the union by which through a proce- 
dure set up by the government the union attains legal identity and status. If the union 
provides the information required by the Trade Union Acct, 1926, the Registrar of 
Trade Union gives it a registration number under that Act. On the other hand, recog- 
nition is an act of the employer whereby he agrees to treat a certain union as the le- 
gitimate representative of all the workmen of the establishment. There is no Central 


446 Part VII— The Trade Unions Act, 1926 
legislation obliging the employer to recognise a union. Even in Maharashtra, Gujarat, 
Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan, there are no uniform legislations either for recogni- 
tion of unions or representative unions. | 
16. Outside Trade Union Leader 
In a number of organisations, the managements are not keen to transact and negoti- 
ate matters pertaining to their workmen with a trade union representative who is an 
ex-employee or an outsider. Therefore, the question is whether an organisation can 
legitimately have a policy to the effect that it would not take to any ex-employee or 
outside leader who is not a workman of the organisation. The Trade Unions Act, 
1926 (as amended in 2001) stipulates that barring one-third of the total number of 
office bearer or five, whichever is less, shall be persons actually engaged or em- 
ployed in the establishment or industry with which the trade union is concerned ex- 
cept in case of a trade union in “unorganised sector’. The Act also clarifies that an 
employee who has retired or has been retrenched shall not be construed as an out- 
sider for the purpose of holding an office in a trade union. Therefore, the Act permits 
the participation of outsiders in the activities of a trade union as one-thirds of the of- 
fice bearers can be drawn from outsiders. 
While the Trade Unions Act specifies the conditions under which a trade union can 
be registered and administered, it nowhere provides for the recognition of such a 
trade union by an employer. Barring the State of Maharashtra where statutes such as 
Maharashtra Recognition of Trade Unions and Prevention of Unfair Labour Practices 
Act and Bombay Industrial Relations Act which govern the recognition of trade un- 
ions, no other states in India have enacted such laws. Therefore, the recognition of 
trade unions in India is largely governed by the code of discipline. 
It is clear that the union has every right to have its own type of leadership, whether 
inside or outside. However, when the union and management decide to have transac- 
tion, both can lay down standards, norms and conditions for such transactions or re- 
lationship. While the right of association is fundamental, the right of transaction can 
be conditional and is based on mutual satisfaction. Merely because a union is regis- 
tered under law to get a legal personality, this registration does not confer a right for 
automatic recognition by the employer. Therefore, an organisation cannot be legally 
compelled to discuss or negotiate with an outsider even if he is duly elected repre- 
sentative of the workmen and is an office bearer of the trade union. 
17. Trade Union Structure 
There may be following types of labour organisations: 
(1) Craft Union.—A craft union is the simplest form of union. It is built around a 
certain specialized skill, which has necessitated a special type of training. Thus, it is 
formed usually of workers belonging to the same craft or occupation. These unions 
are open to members of a certain trade or skill. Craft unions generally secure more 
concessions from the employers because these unions consist of cohesive group of 
people belonging to the same craft or profession which cannot be easily replaced if 
the unions resort to strike for their demands. If a craft union resorts to strikes it may 
paralyse the entire working of any establishment. Thus, the employers generally tend 
to give them better conditions of work. The Indian Pilot’s Guild and the International 
Wood Carvers’ Association are examples of craft union. 
19. “Registration not entitles recognition of Trade Union,” H.L. Kumar, LLJ, Sept 2003. 
20. “Does the management enjoy a right to refuse to deal with an outside trade union leader?” P. Naresh 
Kumar, LLJ, Nov. 2002. 


Chap. I—Development of Trade Union Law etc. 447 © 
(2) General Union.—A general union is open to all the members irrespective of 
. their skills cutting across all the trades/skills. It may include skilled, semiskilled and 
even unskilled workers. The Jamshedpur Labour Union is an example of general 
union. 
(3) Industrial Union.—In an industrial union, workers are organised on the basis of 
industry rather than a craft. The entire labour force of a single factory irrespective of 
their different crafts may constitute together an industrial union. Such unions in- 
crease workers’ solidarity which makes negotiations easy. Industrial unions are the 
need of today because the craft distinctions are becoming obliterated day by day. 
Examples may be taken of the Rashtriya Mill Mazdoor Sangh and the Girni Kamgar 
Union at Bombay. 
(4) White-Collar Unions.—A\i the clerical or office staff, which do not work on the 
shop-floor are termed as white-collar workers. White-collar workers or non-manual 
workers form a distinct social group characterised by divergent socio-economic 
backgrounds, levels of education, manner of speech, social customs and ideology. 
Such workers are generally better educated and are usually involved in a desk job or 
providing services over the counter. Unionisation among these workers began as 
early as 1897 and the National Union of Railwaymen of India and Burma was 
formed in that year. Since 1947, the growth of unionisation among these workers has 
been due to inflation, effectiveness of collective bargaining etc, Important trade un- 
ions of white-collar employees include the All India Bank Employees Union, the All 
India Defence Employees Federation, the Confederation of Central Government Em- 
ployees and the Indian Federation of Working Journalists etc. Such unions are exist- 
ing independently and are not affiliated to any central union organisation. 
(5) Blue-Collar Workers.—All the shop-floor workers who are part of the produc- 
tion system and operate machines and related systems are known as blue-collar 
workers. | 
(6) Agricultural Labourers.—Where the main source of income of labour is farm 
wage, it is know as agricultural labour. They may be categorised into two, i.e., lan- 
dless agricultural labour and small cultivators. Landless agricultural labour may be 
further sub-divided into permanent labour attached to a cultivating household and 
casual labour. Casual labour consists of share croppers, cultivators and households. 
Main source of income of small cultivators is wage employment. Agricultural labour 
forms the most deprived and unprivileged segments of Indian society. Their wages 
are low, they face irregular employment, they perform difficult tasks, they do not 
have assets of great value, they are illiterate and most of them are exploited by their 
employment and they borrow funds from their employers to support their families 
which lead to their becoming bonded labour.” Agricultural labour has not been per- 
fectly unionised. According to 1971 Census, agricultural labour numbered around 
47.49 million of which only 93, 000 were members of trade unions. Therefore, it was 
proposed that rural labour co-operatives be organised instead of trade unions, whose 
objective could be to bring the agricultural labourer into the fold of some organisa- 
tion similar to trade unions. This would have certain advantages.

18. National Level Federations 
In India, four national level federations are existing, namely, the All India Trade 
Union Congress, Indian National Trade Union Congress, United Trade Union Con- 
gress and Hind Mazdoor Sabha. The United Trade Union, Congress has merged with 
Centre of Indian Trade Union (CITU). 
(i) All India Trade Union Congress (AITUC).—Established in 1991, AITUC is 
linked with communist philosophy. Its main objectives are establishment of a social- 
ist State in India and the nationalisation of the means of production, distribution and 
exchange as far as possible, safeguarding and promoting the workers’ rights to free 
speech, freedom of association, assembly and the right to strike and improving the 
economic and social conditions of the working class by securing better terms and 
conditions of employment. 
Its organisation structure includes the affiliated unions (unit/local level), provincial 
bodies (State level), the general council including office-bearers and the delegates of 
the general or special session. 
(ti) Indian National Trade Union Congress (INTUC).—Established in 1947 to 
bring about a peaceful and non-violent solution to industrial disputes. Organisation- 
ally, it is an industry level federation. Here the units are grouped together for the 
purpose of negotiating the terms and conditions of ernployment. Its main objectives 
include ensuring full employment, securing greater participation of workers in the 
management of enterprises, organisation of workers on an industry-wise basis, im- 
proving the conditions at work and improving social security measures, developing a sense of responsibility in workers towards industry and the community. 
(iii) Hind Mazdoor Sabha (HMS).—Established in 1948, espousing social philoso- 
phy, its main objectives are promotion of economic, political and social interests of the workers and improvement in terms and conditions of employment, promotion of co-operative societies and fostering workers’ education. 
(iv) Centre of Indian Trade Union (CITU).—Established in 1971 as < result of the 
split in AITUC which was a sequel to the split in the CPI, a new centre, the Centre of Indian Trade Union (CITU) emerged owing its allegiance to the CPI(M). Its main objective is to organise workers to further their interests in economic, social and po- . litical matters. In its organisational set-up, it has a Central Committee (national level, general council), a State Committee (State level) and affiliated unions (unit level). 
19. Problems of Trade Unionism in India 
The issue of trade union recognition is still a source of industrial conflict in many industries. It appears that though some progressive industries and employers have taken the trade union movement as a necessity for industrial harmony, there are yet many employers who frown upon the ideas of trade union recognition and it is not infrequent to find cases where the employers make frantic efforts to break trade un- ions in their formative stages. It is obvious that a section of the employers have not been able to adjust themselves with the trade union movement and hence problems of recognition efc. arise. But as experience teaches them, they learn to deal with the trade unions and even find it more convenient and easier to settle their issues with the trade unions than the collective and mob-minded ones. It would, therefore, be neces- sary that the legislation must provide measures for recognition of trade unions and procedure and method for granting, suspending and cancelling their recognition. The provisions in the Code of Discipline in industry, which have been discussed earlier 


Chap. I—Development of Trade Union Law etc. 449 
are no doubt a step in the right direction, but have, however, suffered from the fol- 
lowing two defects: 
(1) They are not exhaustive in themselves and are supplemented by frequent deci- 
sions taken at the different labour committees with the result that these provisions are 
mostly unknown to the industry in general. 
(2) Lack of statutory sanction : Since the provisions of the Code of Discipline in 
industry have come to stay and they have formed an essential part of any integrated 
set-up of trade union organisation, it is necessary that an appropriate statutory recog- 
nition and sanction be provided to these provisions. It wouid, therefore, be necessary 
to incorporate appropriate provisions in the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 or in the 
Trade Unions Act, 1926. © 
For the purpose of introducing these measures by legislation the experience of the 
State laws can be availed of and though the provisions of the Bombay Industrial Re- 
lations Act, 1946 themselves need some amendments, still at the initial stage, adop- 
tion of those provisions in a Central Act, thereby extending them to all the industries 
throughout the country, except as excluded by some of the State laws, would be a 
step in this direction. 
At this stage, the issue of industry-wise union and their recognition would also as- 
sume significance. Though an elaborate machinery and provision will have to be 
made for ascertaining the union entitled to recognition on an industry-wise basis, still 
from industries point of view, it would be proper step to be adopted. There are many 
advantages to be gained from industry-wise bargaining which will essentially result 
in the uniformity of employment condition throughout the industry but also take into 
consideration the peculiarities and a special characteristic of a particular industry and 
such a bargaining would serve as a permanent method of settlement of industrial dis- 
putes in that industry. 
THE TRADE UNIONS ACT, 1926 
The Trade Unions Act, 1926 is an Act to provide for the registration of Trade Un- 
ions and in certain respects to define the law relating to registered Trade Unions. 
20. Short title, extent and commencement (s. 1) 
This Trade Unions Act of 1926 extends to the whole of India and section 1 says 
that it shall come into force on such date as the Central Government may by notifi- 
cation in the Official Gazette, appoint. The Act came into force on 1-6-1927. 
21. Definitions (s. 2) 
Appropriate Government 
According to section 2, for the purposes of the Trade Unions Act, 1926, the “ap- 
propriate Government” means, in relation to Trade Unions whose objects are not 
confined to one State, the Central Government, and in relation to other Trade Unions, 
the State Government. 
Executive [s. 2(a)] 
“Executive” means the body, by whatever name called, to which the management 
of the affairs of a Trade Union is entrusted. 


450 Part VII— The Trade Unions Act, 1926 
Office-Bearer [s. 2(b)] 
“Office-bearer” in the case of a Trade Union, includes any member of the execu- 
tive thereof, but does not include an auditor. i 
Prescribed [s. 2(c)] 
“Prescribed”? means prescribed by regulations made under the Act. 
Registered Office [s. 2(d)] 
“Registered office’’ means that office of a Trade Union which is registered under 
the Act as the head office thereof. 
Registered Trade Union [s. 2(e)] 
“Registered Trade Union” means a Trade Union registered under the Act. 
Registrar [s. 2(f)] 
“Registrar” means 
(i) a Registrar of Trade Unions appointed by the appropriate Government un- 
der section 3, and includes any Additional or Deputy Registrar of Trade 
Unions; and 
(11) in relation to any Trade Union the Registrar appointed for the State in 
which the Head or Registered Office, as the case may be, of the Trade Un- 
ion is situated. 
Trade Dispute [s. 2 (g)] 
“Trade dispute” means any dispute between employers and workmen or between 
workmen and workmen, or between employers and employers which is connected 
with the employment or non-employment, or the terms of employment or the condi- 
tions of labour, of any person and “workmen” means all persons employed in trade 
or industry whether or not in the employment of the employer with whom the trade 
dispute arises. 
Trade Union [s. 2(h)] 
“Trade Union” means any combination, whether temporary or permanent, formed primarily for the purpose of regulating the relations between workmen and employ- ers or between workmen and workmen or between employers and employers or for imposing restrictive conditions on the conduct of any trade or business, and includes any federation of two or more Trade Unions: 
But the Act shall not affect— 
(i) any agreement between partners as to their own business; 
(ii) any agreement between an employer and those employed by him as to such employment; or 
(iii) any agreement in consideration of the sale of the goodwill of a business or of instruction in any profession, trade or handicraft. 
(a) Who can form.—Only the persons engaged in trade or business can form trade unions.” A federation of trade unions but not a registered body under the Act cannot

22. Representative capacity 
This aspect of a trade union was explained by the Supreme Court in Food Corpo- 
ration of India Staff Union v. Food Corporation of India.® The Court said: ““Where 
there are more than one registered trade unions the question as to with whom the em- 
ployer should negotiate or enter into bargaining assumes importance. The question as 
to who should be the sole bargaining agent where more than one unions claim their 
right has been a matter of some discussion and dispute. The check-off system which 
once prevailed has lost its appeal. The method of secret ballot is accepted. This 
method is so adapted and adjusted that it reflects the correct position as regards the 
membership of the different trade unions operating in the same industry, establish- 
ment or undertaking.” The court also laid down the norms and procedure of assessing 
the representative character of a trade union by secret ballot.

1. Appointment of Registrars (s. 3) 
For registration of trade unions, a person is appointed as the Registrar of Trade 
Unions for the State. The appropriate Government may appoint a person to be the 
Registrar of Trade Unions for each State. In addition, if required, the appropriate 
Government may appoint Additional and Deputy Registrars of Trade Unions. Such 
Additional and Deputy Registrars work under the superintendence and direction of 
the Registrar. They exercise and discharge such powers and functions of the Regis- 
trar which are given to them by the appropriate Government. The appropriate Gov- 
ernment also defines the local limits within which they have to work. Where such 
Additional or Deputy Registrar exercises and discharges the powers and functions of 
a Registrar in an area he is deemed to be the Registrar in relation to the trade unions 
which are situated within that area. 
2. Mode of registration (s. 4) 
Any seven or more members of a Trade Union may apply for registration of a trade 
union under the Act. They may apply either by subscribing their names to the rules of 
the Trade Union or by complying provisions of the Act regarding registration. 
No trade union of workman shall be registered unless at least ten per cent or one 
hundred of workmen, whichever is less, engaged or employed in the establishment or 
industry with which it is connected are the members of such trade union on the date 
of making application for registration. 
No trade union of workman shall be registered unless it has on the date of making 
application not less then seven persons as its members, who are workmen engaged or 
employed in the establishment or industry with which it is connected. 
453 


454 _ Part VII—The Trade Unions Act, 1926 
The application will remain valid even if after applying for registration but before 
the grant of registration some of the applicants (not more than half of the total appli- 
cants)— 
(a) have ceased to be members of the Trade Union; or 
(b) have given notice to the Registrar (in writing) dissociating themselves from 
the application. 
3. Application for registration (s. 5) 
Every application for registration of a Trade Union has to be made to the Registrar 
of Trade Unions. It has to be accompanied by a copy of the rules of the Trade Union 
and a statement containing the following particulars: 
(a) the names, occupations and address of the members making application; 
(aa) in the case of a trade union of workmen, the names, occupations and ad- 
dresses of the place of work of the members of the trade union making the 
application; 
(b) the name of the Trade Union and the address of its head office; and 
(c) the titles, names, ages, addresses and occupations of the office-bearers of 
the Trade Union. 
Where a Trade Union has been in existence for more than one year before applying 
for registration, it has to submit a general statement of its assets and liabilities in the 
prescribed form containing prescribed particulars to the Registrar. 
4. Rules of Trade Union (s. 6) 
A Trade Union becomes entitled to registration only when its executive is consti- 
tuted in accordance with the provisions of the Act and its rules contain the following 
matters: 
(a) the name of the Trade Union; 
(b) the whole of the objects for which it is established; 
(c) the whole of the purposes for which the general funds of the Trade Union 
can be applied. These purposes must be permissible under the Act; 
(d) the maintenance of a list of members and adequate facilities for the inspec- 
tion of such list by the officers and members of the Trade Union; 
(e) the rules relating to the admission of ordinary members and honorary or 
temporary members. Any person who has attained the age of 15 years 
can, subject to the rules of the union, become its member. There is no ab- solute right to be admitted as a member of the Trade Union. Such a right can be brought into existence if there is an express provision in the con- stitution of the Union, that no one, baving the requisite qualification can be refused membership. A mere description in the constitution of the class of persons who can become members or the qualifications necessary for membership, does not confer such an absolute right of becoming a member upon any person who may belong to that class or answer that de- scription or possess such qualification. Honorary or temporary members who may be office-bearers of the union need not be persons actually en- 


Chap. II—Registration of Trade Unions 455 
gaged or employed in the industry with which the trade union is con- 
cerned; 
(ee) the payment of a minimum subscription by members of the Trade Union 
which shall not be less then— 
(i) one rupee per annum for rural workers; 
(ii) three rupees per annum for workers in other unorganised sectors; and 
(iii) twelve rupees per annum for workers in any other case. 
(f) the conditions under which any member shall be entitled to any benefit as- 
sured by the rules and under which any fine or forfeiture may be imposed 
on the members; 
(g) the manner in which the rules shall be amended, varied, or rescinded; 
(h) the manner in which the members of the executive and the other office- 
bearers of the trade union shall be elected and removed; 
(hh) the duration of period being not more than three years, for which the mem- 
bers of the executive and other office-bearers of the trade union shall be 
elected; 
(i) the safe custody of the funds of the trade union, the annual audit of the ac- 
counts and adequate facilities for the inspection of the account books by the 
office-bearers and members of the trade union; 
(j) the manner in which the trade union may be dissolved. 
The Registrar under the Trade Unions Act has no power to decide any dispute be- 
cause it is not a quasi-judicial authority.’ Only the Civil Court having Jurisdiction 
can decide the disputes as there is no provision in the Act permitting or empowering 
the Registrar to refer internal disputes relating to office-bearer for adjudication to any 
other forum. 
The rules framed under the constitution of a trade union or its bye-laws or regula- 
tions do not get the force of law by virtue merely of registration. The rules have only 
the effect of a contract between the members and the union. Any breach of such rules 
cannot be remedied under writ jurisdiction. The proper procedure is to file a civil suit. 
5. Rights of minors to be member of Trade Unions (s. 21) 
Any person who has attained the age of fifteen years may become a member of a 
registered Trade Union provided the Trade Union has such provision in its rules. The 
admission is made subject to the rules of the Trade Union. A minor member may 
enjoy all the rights of a member and execute all instruments and give all acquain- 
tance necessary to be executed or given under the rules. 
6. Executive of Trade Union (s. 21A) 
Section 21A contains certain disqualifications regarding executive or office-bearers 
of the Trade Union. It says that a person shall be disqualified to be a member of the 
executive or an office-bearer of the Trade Union if:

(a) he has not attained the age of eighteen years; 
(b) he has been convicted in India of an offence involving moral turpitude and 
sentenced to imprisonment, unless a period of five years has elapsed since 
his release. 
A provision has been made regarding any member of the executive or other office 
bearer of a registered Trade Union who has been convicted of any offence involving 
moral turpitude and sentenced to imprisonment before the commencement of the 
Indian Trade Union (Amendment) Act, 1964. Such a member or office-bearer shall 
cease to be so from the commencement date of the Amendment Act, 1964 unless a 
period of five years has elapsed since his release before that date. 
An amendment was inserted by Act 51 of 1970 that in its application to the State of 
Jammu & Kashmir, reference in sub-section to the commencement of the Indian 
Trade Unions (Amendment) Act, 1964 shall be construed as reference to the com- 
mencement of the Act in that State. 
One-half of the total number of office-bearers of a registered trade union must be 
persons actually engaged or employed in the industry with which the union is con- 
nected.” The Government may, however, by special or general order, declare that 
this provision shall not apply to any trade union or class of trade unions specified in 
the order. 
An office-bearer of a trade union can be removed from the office he is holding 
only under a power clearly conferred by a rule. A power to suspend or expel an of- 
fice-bearer is of a quasi-judicial character and must be exercised in accordance with 
the principles of natural justice. One of the principles of natural justice is that the 
office-bearer is given an opportunity of being heard before any action of the above 
type is taken against him. 
A workman acting as a trade union office-bearer has no right in law to share manage- 
rial powers. He has a right to espouse the cause of the workmen but no right to order a 
workman to stop his work or otherwise obstruct the work of the establishment. 
Provisions of Sections 6 and 22 of the Trade Unions Act indicate that an ordinary 
or temporary member may be an office-bearer but nowhere do they provide that such 
a member shall also have right to negotiate with the management or the management 
would be under an obligation to negotiate with an office-bearer of the union who is 
no longer under employment in the industry to which the trade union is connected. 
A union which represented less than 2% of workmen was held to have no locus 
standi for seeking representation in wage revision negotiations. A union to establish 
that right must represent a substantial section of workmen.

7. Power of Registrar regarding alteration of name and further particulars 
(s.7) 
The Registrar has been given the power to call for further information, if required. For 
the purposes of compliance with registration procedure, he may call for further informa- 
tion and may refuse to register the Trade Union until such information is supplied. 
The Registrar can also ask the persons applying for registration to alter the name of 
the Trade Union when in his opinion: 
(a) proposed name of the Trade Union (to be registered) is identical with al- 
ready existing registered Trade Union; or 
(b) the proposed name so nearly resembles such name that it is likely to de- 
ceive the public or the members of either Trade Union. 
He may refuse to register the Trade Union until such alteration has been made. 
8. Registration (s. 8) 
When the Registrar is satisfied that the Trade Union has complied with all the re- 
quirements of registration, he will register the Trade Union. He enters the name of 
the Trade Union in the register maintained for the purpose along with the particulars 
relating to the Trade Union contained in the statement accompanying the application 
for registration. 
It is the fundamental right of workers to form Trade Unions and any Trade Union 
fulfilling the requirements of the Trade Unions Act, 1926 is entitled to registration.” 
A registered Trade Union does not automatically get a right to be recognised by the 
management. There is no statutory right vested in any union to compel the management 
to recognise it. Before staking its claim for recognition, a union must establish that it 
represents a substantial section of the work force. It may be 15%, less or more, but by no 
reasonable standard can it be said that the union which represents not more than two per 
cent of the work force can be said to have that representative character which will impel 
the Court to direct the management to give recognition to the Union. 
The function of the Registrar is to assure compliance with the Act and not to en- 
gage himself into the inquiry whether the union could be described as an unlawful 
association. Where the requirements of the Act have been complied with, it is in- 
cumbent upon the Registrar to grant registration. The applicants cannot be called 
upon to give notice to the other existing union.’° Nor it is necessary for the Registrar 
to hear existing unions.

9, Returns (s. 28) 
Every registered Trade Union has to send the following returns to the Registrar an- 
nually on or before the prescribed date: 
(i) A general statement of all receipts and expenditure during the year ending 
on the 31st day of December next preceeding such prescribed date. The 
statement has to be audited in the prescribed manner. : 
(ii) A general statement of the assets and liabilities of the Trade Union existing 
on such 31st day of December. The statement has to be prepared in pre- 
scribed form and should contain the prescribed particulars. 
(iii) A statement showing change of office-bearers made by the Trade Union 
during the year to which the general statement refers. Along with this, a 
copy of the rules of the Trade Union corrected upto the date of despatch to 
the Registrar has also to be sent. 
(iv) A copy of every alteration made in the rules of a registered Trade Union 
has to be sent to the Registrar within fifteen days of the making of the al- 
teration. 
For the purpose of examining the abovestated documents, the Registrar or any 
other officer authorised by him may inspect the certificate of registration, account 
books, registers and other documents relating to a Trade Union, at its registered of- 
fice at all reasonable times. He may also require their production at any place at a 
distance, not more than ten miles from the registered office of a Trade Union. 
The Registrar under the Trade Unions Act, 1926 performs administrative functions 
and he can undertake a reasonable enquiry within the scope and ambit of sections 8 
and 28 of the Act to ascertain who are the elected office-bearers and to register their 
names. The scope of enquiry is limited for the purpose of ascertaining the facts. The 
Registrar under section 28 does not discharge any quasi-judicial functions but he 
discharges only administrative functions. No party under the Act is entitled to lead 
any evidence or cross-examine the witnesses. No detailed and elaborate enquiry is 
envisaged under the Act for determining the controversy between two rival factions 
of the Act. He has to perform a summary enquiry to satisfy himself for registration 
of the union and for effecting the changes in the Register. Neither the Act nor the 
Regulations framed under the Act give powers to the Registrar to hold any quasi- 
judicial enquiry to record the evidence and to decide the claims of the claimants of 
the rival Trade Unions. The Registrar, therefore, cannot decide the disputes between 
the rival office-bearers of the Trade Unions under section 28 of the Act. The dispute 
in the nature of rival claims of the office-bearers is a private dispute which can be 
adjudicated upon by the Civil Court only and not by the Registrar under the Act.” 
The Registrar, while exercising power under Regulation 17(3) of the U.P. Trade 
Union Regulations is not required to hold any elaborate inquiry similar to the process

to be a prima facie satisfaction. 
10. Certificate of registration (s. 9) 
After registering a Trade Union, the Registrar issues a certificate of registration in 
the prescribed form. This certificate is conclusive evidence that the Trade Union has 
been duly registered under the Act. The registration gives a stamp of due formation 
of the trade union and assures the mind of the employer that the Trade Union is an 
authenticated body.” 
11. Minimum requirement about membership of a Trade Union (section 9A) 
A registered Trade Union shall at times continue to have not less than ten per cent 
or one hundred of the workmen, whichever is less, subject to a minimum of seven, 
engaged or employed in an establishment or industry with which it is connected, as 
its members. | 
12. Legal status of Registered Union 
A registered trade union is a statutory legal entity.” It can own property and it can 
act as an agent. In some cases trade unions have been described as quasi- 
corporations.” An unregistered trade union is not a juristic person. Such a union 
~ cannot file a writ petition or raise an industrial dispute. 
The registration of a trade union does not bar the courts from enquiry as to whether 
the association styled as a trade union is legal or not.” 
A trade union is distinct legal entity from its members. When it files a suit on be- 
half of its members, such suit does not take the nature of a representative suit and is, 
therefore, not barred under Order 1 Rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 
13. Advantages of registered trade unions 
A registered trade union is a legal entity separate from its members. If becomes a 
corporate body with the name it is registered. It can hold property, enter into con- 
tracts, sue and be sued in its own name. It gets perpetual succession and common 
seal. It gets immunity from civil and criminal liability. It enjoys a number of statu- 
tory rights like creation of a separate fund for political purposes, use of general funds 
for certain specified purposes etc. 
14. Disadvantages of unregistered trade unions 
An unregistered trade union is not a legal entity separate from its members. It is 
only a voluntary association having no corporate existence. Thus, it cannot hold 
property, cannot sue or be sued in its name. It cannot represent its members in a trade

registered trade unions by the Act. 
15. Cancellation of Registration (s. 10) 
The registration of a trade union can be cancelled either by its own application or 
by the Registrar of Trade Unions. The application of cancellation given by the trade 
union itself must be approved by a general meeting of the Trade Union or a majority 
of its members. The Registrar may cancel the registration by a written notice of not 
less then two months” on any of the following grounds: 
(1) that the registration certificate has been obtained by fraud or mistake;” P 
(2) that the trade union has ceased to exist; 
(3) that it has wilfully and after notice from the Registrar contravened any pro- 
vision of the Act;’ 
(4) that it has wilfully and after notice from the Registrar allowed any rule to 
continue in force which is inconsistent with any provision of the Act; 
(5) that it has rescinded any rule providing for any of the compulsory matters 
required under the Act. 
According to clause (c) inserted by the Trade Unions (Amendment) Act, 2001, if 
the Registrar is satisfied that a registered Trade union of workmen ceases to have the 
requisite number of members, he may cancel the registration.

The registration of a trade union can be cancelled only when a wilful contravention 
of the Act is established and not when contravention occurs by mistake. 
A person who ceases to be a member of a registered trade union would not have a 
right to seek cancellation of registration.” 
The Registrar should have before him sufficient material and evidence to infer a 
wilful contravention of the Act justifying cancellation of registration. Until an inten- 
tional violation of the provisions of the Act or the Rules is established, the Registrar 
should not rush to cancel registration. Mere failure to file returns, for example, can- 
not form good ground for cancellation of registration. 
The Registrar acting under the provisions of sec. 10 may validly cancel registration 
of the Union of employees governed by the Army Act and Article 33 of the Consti- 
tution applies to such Union. 
Where one Trade Union has been denied registration, no other Trade Union can 
intervene and implead itself to prefer the appeal under Sec. 11. 
An order of the Registrar cancelling the registration of Trade Union was rescinded by a 
subsequent order. A writ petition was filed against it but it was taken up a de- 
cade after the order the union in question represented several thousand workers for the 
decade and a settlement was arrived at. The court said that if the impugned order was 
examined after such a long period, it would result in serious prejudice and injustice. The 
petitioner was also not able to show that he was prejudiced by the impugned order. 
16. Incorporation of Registered Trade Union (s. 13) 
Every registered Trade Union shall be a body corporate by the name under which 
it is registered. It shall have perpetual succession and a common seal with power to 
acquire and hold both movable and immovable property. It shall have power to con- 
tract, and by the said name it shall be able to sue others and be sued by others. 
17. Registered Office (s. 12) 
All communications and notices to a registered Trade Union may be addressed to 
its registered office. In case of any change in the address of the head office notice of 
such change shall be given to the Registrar within fourteen days of change in writing. 
The changed address has to be recorded in the register of trade unions. 
18. Appeals (s. 11) 
Under the Trade Union Act, 1926, appeals can be made against the following 
orders of the Registrar: 
(i) Refusal to register a trade union.—Where the Registrar refuses to register 
the trade union which has applied for registration.

(ii) The Co-operative Societies Act, 1912 (2 of 1912) 
(iii) The Companies Act, 1956 (1 of 1956).

1. General funds (s. 15) 
An important pre-requisite for effective functioning of a Trade Union is its finance. 
Two funds are contemplated in the Trade Union Act, 1926, namely, general fund and 
political fund. Every registered trade union has been given the right of creation and 
expenditure out of the two funds maintained by it. These two are not to be intermixed 
but kept separately because the members cannot be compelled to contribute to politi- 
cal fund. The members who do not contribute to the political fund cannot be denied 
any benefits which are otherwise available to them under the provisions of the Act.’ 
The Act itself has named the objects on which the general funds may be spent section 
15 says that the general funds of a registered trade union cannot be spent on any ob- 
jects other than the following:— 
(a) payment of salaries, allowances and expenses of office-bearer of the trade 
union; 
(b) payment of expenses of the administration of the trade union, including its 
audit of accounts; 
(c) expenses of legal proceedings for securing or protecting the rights of the 
trade union or its any member with his employer; 
(d) the conduct of trade disputes on behalf of the trade union or any member of 
it. This provision does not impose an obligation upon a trade union to ex- 
pend a portion of its general funds on trade disputes. It merely renders law- 
ful the expenditure of money belonging to the union on the conduct of any 
trade dispute; 
(e) compensation of members for loss arising out of trade disputes; 
1. S; 16(3) 
2. Raja Kulkarni v. State of Bombay, 1953 ICR (Bom) 107 (HC). 
465 


466 Part VII—The Trade Unions Act, 1926 
(f) allowances to members or their dependants on account of death, old age, 
sickness, accidents or unemployment of such members; 
(g) the issue of, or the undertaking of liability under policies of assurance on 
the lives of members, or under policies insuring members against sickness, 
accidents or unemployment; 
(h) the provision of educational, social or religious benefits for members or 
their dependants including the payment of expenses of funeral or religious 
ceremonies for deceased members; 
(i) the upkeep of periodical published mainly for the purpose of discussing 
questions affecting employers or workmen as such; 
(j) the payment of contributions to any cause intended to benefit workmen in general. However, expenditure in respect of contributions in any financial 
year must not exceed one-fourth or the combined total of the gross income accrued to the general funds during in that year and the balance brought forward from the previous year the general funds. 
(k) any other object notified by the appropriate Government in the Official Ga- zette, subject to the conditions laid down in the notification. The following were notified by the Governor-General in Council as objects under this clause: | 
(i) the financing of Industrial and Technical research connected with the 
Industry concerned; 
(ii) the opening out of new markets for any material dealt with by the Industry concerned. 
2. Separate Fund for Political Purposes (s. 16) 
A registered trade union, if it decides to do so, can constitute a separate fund known as political fund. The fund is constituted from contributions separately levied for or made to a fund for political objects or a fund for political purposes. Payment may be made from such fund for the promotion of the civic and political interests of its members in furtherance of the objects specified in the Act. 
The objects for which the payment may be made are following:— 
(a) the payment of any expenses incurred, either directly or indirectly, by a candidate or prospective candidate for election as a member of any legisla- tive body constituted under the Constitution or of any local authority, be- fore, during, or after the election in connection with his candidature or election; or 
(b) the holding of any meeting or the distribution of any literature or docu- ments in support of any such candidate or prospective candidate; or 
(c) the maintenance of any person who is a member of any legislative body constituted under the Constitution or for any local authority; or 
(d) the registration of electors or the selection of a candidate for any legislative body constituted under the Constitution or for any local authority; or ——————— 
3. Mario Raposo v. H.M. Bhandarkar, (1994) 2 Lab LJ 680 (Bom), the office bearers of the trade union purchased in their own names shares in Unit Trust and this being a speculative activity was held to be against the spirit of industrial jurisprudence. It was outside the scope of union activity, 


Chap. III—Rights and Liabilities of Registered Trade Unions 467 
(e) the holding of political meetings of any kind, or the distribution of politica! 
literature or political documents of any kind. 
Trade Unions cannot compel their members to contribute to the political fund. 
However, any member not contributing to the fund cannot be denied any benefits of 
the trade union which are given to other member. Such a member cannot be placed 
under any disability (directly or indirectly) or at any disadvantage as compared with 
other members of the Trade Union. Only the control or management of the fund is 
given to the members contributing for it. The Act has made it clear that contribution 
to the fund cannot be made a condition for admission to the Trade Union. 
3. Immunities against crimina! conspiracy in trade disputes (s. 17) 
An agreement to do an illegal act is a criminal offence under the criminal law. Ac- 
cording to Indian Penal Code, when two or more persons agree to do or cause to be 
done an illegal act or an act which is not illegal by illegal means, such an agreement 
is known as criminal conspiracy. S. 17 gives protection to the office-bearers and 
members of a registered trade union in respect of any agreement made between the 
members for the purposes of furthering any such object of the trade union on which 
its general funds may be spent. In such a case, no criminal proceedings for conspir- 
acy can be initiated against them unless the agreement is an agreement to commit an 
offence. In other words, the office-bearers or members of a registered trade union are 
given immunity against criminal conspiracy in trade disputes where they agree to 
further the objects of the trade union only but when they agree to commit an offence, 
the immunity disappears. Such immunity is given to them under sub-section (2) of 
section 120(b) of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. 
To enforce their demands it may be necessary for the workmen to resort to collec- 
tive action against the employer. Such collective action may take the form of strike, 
or picketing at his shop or factory with a view to see that his customers do not deal 
with him or that some unemployed persons do not take the place of those who have 
joined in the collective action and do not thereby minimise or nullify the effect of the 
said collective action. The nature of such collective action is such as would such as 
would amount to ‘interference with the trade or business of the employer or with the 
employment of other workers’. These acts when done collectively, or in combination 
by a number to workers would be a conspiracy at conspiracy at common law. Provi- 
sion has, therefore, been made to give protection against prosecutions for criminal 
conspiracies. If a registered union resorts to such an action in furtherance of a trade 
dispute, they would be taken out of the scope of Section 120(b)(2) of the Indian Pe- 
nal Code which deals with conspiracy. An agreement to commit an offence, like an 
assault on any of the officers in the employment of the employer would not be saved, 
though it may be in furtherance of a trade dispute. Similarly if threats or violence are 
used, no protection will be afforded by the Act. It should also be noted that the pro- 
tection does not extend against an action for defamation. 
4. Immunity from civil suit in certain cases (s. 18) 
Section 18 gives immunity to a registered Trade Union or office-bearer or member 
of it from civil suit or other legal proceedings i.e., no civil suit can be maintained 
against them in respect of any act done in contemplation or furtherance of a trade 
dispute to which a member of the Trade Union is a party. But such immunity or pro- 
tection is available on the following grounds only: 
4. R.S. Raiker v. Emperor, AIR 1935 Nag 149 : 36 Cri LJ 1153, an agreement to commit an offence 
would make the conspiring members liable for criminal conspiracy. 


468 Part VI]—The Trade Unions Act, 1926 
(i) that such act induces some other person to break a contract of employment; 
or 
(ii) that it is in interference with the trade, business or employment of some 
other person; or 
(iii) that it is in interference with the right of some other person to dispose of his 
capital or his labour at his will. 
Thus, on the basis of the abovestated grounds no suit can be maintained against a 
registered trade union, its office-bearer or member. 
Next immunity is given against any tortious act done by an agent of the registered 
Trade Union in contemplation or furtherance of a trade dispute. Where an agent of 
the registered Trade Union does any tortious act in contemplation or furtherance of a 
trade dispute either without the knowledge of or against the express instructions 
given by, the executive of the trade union, such a trade union will not be liable in any 
suit or other legal proceeding in any civil court. Such immunity is available only 
when the agent does any tortious act either: — 
(i) without the knowledge of the executive of the trade union, or 
(11) contrary to instructions given by the executive of the trade union. 
Any agitation by the workmen must be peaceful and non-violent. Any concerted 
movement by workmen to achieve their objectives is certainly permissible even in- 
side the industrial establishment within the working hours so long as it does not 
prove to be unlawful, tortious or violent.” Demonstrations and dharnas peaceful 
when they are, have now come to be accepted as falling within the permissible 
sphere of agitations by the labour. Such dharnas and demonstrations, when they do 
not turn unlawful, violent and tortious, cannot be curbed by orders of a Civil Court 
and would come within the purview of section 18 of the Act. 
It is well-settled that there is no fundamental right for anyone to hold demonstra- 
tions in the office premises if by holding such meetings or demonstrations it inter- 
feres with the normal functioning of the office. The fact that citizens have freedom of 
speech, freedom to form associations or unions does not mean that they can exercise 
these freedoms in whatever place they please. The exercise of this freedom will come 
to an end the moment the right of someone else to hold his property intervenes. Such 
a limitation is inherent in the exercise of these rights. The validity of these limitations 
is not to be judged by the tests prescribed by Article 19(2) and (3) of the Constitu- 
tion. The freedom guaranteed under clauses (a), (b) and (c) does not include the right 
to exercise them in the properties belonging to others.’

The law recognises the existence of trade unions as well as the scope and ambit of 
legitimate activities. Depending upon the facts and circumstances of each case, such 
a conduct or act will be protected under section 18 of the Trade Unions Act. How- 
ever, for seeking this protective umbrella; the inducement and intereference must be 
by lawful means.” “It is difficult to subscribe to the view that physical interference or 
duress with the free movement of the executives, contractors, staff, suppliers and 
other public or physically obstructing the free movement of cars, vehicles and lorries 
carrying raw materials, intermediaries, end products into and out of the factory 
premises could be justified as q trade union right or a fundamental right under Article 
19 of the Constitution of India. 
The right to picket is a very intangible one and is closely limited by the equal right 
of others to go about their lawful affairs free from obstruction, molestation or intimi- 
dation. The methods of persuation are limited to oral and visual methods, i.e., use of 
voice and exhibition of play cards and should not be extended to the physical ob- 
struction of a vehicle or a person. That would be illegal. It is not correct to say that 
protection under s. 18 to workers gets enlarged or constricted depending upon 
‘strike’ situation or ‘lock-out’ situation. The considerations and principles are the 
same for both the situations. 
5. Enforceablity of agreements (s. 19) 
Any agreement between the members of a registered trade union will not be void 
or voidable merely because any of the objects of the agreement are in restraint of 
trade according to any law for the time being in force. 
A proviso is added to the section which provides that this section does not enable 
any Civil Court to entertain any legal proceeding instituted for the express purpose of 
enforcing or recovering damages for the breach of any agreement. The agreement 
may be related to the conditions on which any member of the Trade Union shall or 
shall not sell their goods, transact business, work, employ or to be employed. 
6. Right to inspect books of Trade Union (s. 20) 
Any office-bearer or member of the registered trade union may inspect the ac- 
count-books and the list of its members at such times as may be provided for in the 
rules of the Trade Union.

However, the appropriate Government may, by special or general order, 
declare that the provisions of this section shall not apply to any Trade Un-

According to the explanation, “unorganised sector’’ means any sector 
which the appropriate Government may, by notification in the Official Ga-

Any legal proceeding which might have been continued or commenced by or against the trade union by its former name, it may be continued or commenced by it

The agreement may be regarding the conditions on which any members of a trade union shall or shall not sell their goods, transact business, work, employ or be employed."'

12. Amalgamation of Trade Unions (Ss. 24 and 25) 
Any two or more registered trade unions may become amalgamated together as one 
trade union with or without dissolution or division of the funds of such trade unions. 
Amalgamation is possible only when the following two conditions are fulfilled:— 
(i) the votes of at least one-half of the each and every such trade union as enti- 
tled to vote are taken; and 
(ii) at least sixty percent (60%) of the votes recorded are in favour of the pro- 
posal of amalgamation. 
Notice of the amalgamation has to be given to the Registrar in writing. It must be 
singed by the secretary and by 7 members of each and every Trade Union, which is a 
party to amalgamation. Where the head office of the amalgamated trade union is 
situated in a different state, notice should be sent to the Registrar of that State. (sec- 
tion 25). 
If the Registrar of the State in which the head office of the amalgamated Trade 
Union is situated is satisfied that the provisions of the Act in respect of amalgamation 
have been complied with and the Trade Union is entitled to registration he will reg- 
ister it. The amalgamation has effect from the date of such registration. 
An amalgamation of two or more registered Trade Union does not prejudice any 
right of any of such Trade Unions or any right of a creditor of any of them. 
13. Effect of amalgamation (s. 26) 
An amalgamation of two or more registered trade unions does not prejudice any 
right of any of such amalgamating trade unions or any right of a creditor of any of 
them. After the amalgamation of the trade unions, the existing rights or claims of 
creditors or trade unions themselves are not disturbed, they remain the same. 
14. Dissolution (s. 27) 
Section 27 provides that when a registered Trade Union is dissolved the notice of 
dissolution should be sent to the Registrar within fourteen days of such dissolution. 
Notice should be signed by seven members and by the Secretary of the Trade Union. 
When the Registrar is satisfied that the dissolution has been effected in accordance 
with the rules of the Trade Union, he will register the dissolution and the dissolution 
shall have effect from the date of such registration. 
Where the dissolution of a registered Trade Union has been registered and the rules 
of the Trade Union do not provide for the distribution of the funds of the Trade Un- 
ion on dissolution, the Registrar shall divide the funds amongst the members in such 
manner as may be prescribed. 
Where the rules of a Trade Union do not provide for dissolution, it can be dis- 
solved in the same manner as a voluntary association is dissolved. It can be dissolved 
only with the consent of all the members or by the order of court. 


CHAPTER IV 
REGULATIONS 
SYNOPSIS 
1. Power to make regulations (s. 29)....... 473 2. Publication of Regulation (s. 30)......... 473 
1. Power to make regulations (s. 29) 
The appropriate Government has been given the power to make regulations for the 
purpose of carrying into effect the provisions of the Act. This is the general power 
given to the appropriate Government by the Act. In particular, the regulations may 
provide for the following matters: 
(i) the manner in which Trade Unions and the rules shall be registered and the 
fees payable on registration; 
(ii) the transfer of registration in the case of any registered Trade Union which 
has changed its head office from one State to another; 
(iii) the manner in which, the accounts of the registered Trade Unions shall be 
audited. The qualifications of the persons for auditing such accounts will 
also be provided. 
(iv) the conditions under which inspection of documents kept by Registrar shall 
be allowed. The fee chargeable in respect of such inspections shall also be 
provided. 
(v) any matter which is to be or may be prescribed. 
Every notification made by the central Government under section 22(1) and every 
‘regulation made by it under sub-section (1), shall be laid, as soon as may be after it 
is made, before each House of Parliament, while it is in session for a total period of 
thirty days which may be comprised in one session or in two or more successions. If, 
before the expiry of the session immediately following the session, or the successive 
successions aforesaid, both Houses agree in making any modification in the notifica- 
tion or regulation, or both Houses agree that the notification or regulation should not 
be made, the notification or regulation shall have effect thereafter only in such modi- 
fied form or be of no effect, as the case may be. However, any such modification or 
annulment shall be without prejudice to the validity of anything previously done un- 
der that notification or regulation. 
Every notification made by the State Government under section 22(1) and every 
regulation made by it under sub-section(1) shall be laid, as soon as may be after it is 
made, before the state legislature. 
2. Publication of Regulations (s. 30) 
All the regulations made by the appropriate Government under the power given by 
section 29 are to be published in the Official Gazette. For their validity previous 
publication is must. The date to be specified in accordance with General Clauses 
473

Act, 1897 [section 23. Clause (3)] as that after which a draft of regulations proposed 
to be made will be taken into consideration shall not be less than three months from 
the date on which the draft of the proposed regulations was published for general 
information. 
All the regulations are published in the official Gazette and after publication have 
effect as if enacted in this Act.

Section 31 to 33 of the Indian Trade Union Act, 1926 deal with penalties and pro- 
cedure provided under the Act. 
1. Penalties (Ss. 31 and 32) 
The following defaults are made punishable by the Act:— 
(a) default (failure) in sending notices by a registered trade union; 
(b) default in sending statements required to be sent by a registered trade un- 
ion; and 
(c) failure in sending documents required to be sent by a registered trade union. 
For the abovestated failures, every office-bearer or other person (who has been 
given the responsibility under the rules of the trade union to send notices, statements 
and documents) or if there is no such office-bearer or person, every member of the 
executive of the trade union is punishable with fine extending to rupees five. If the 
default is continued, there is an additional fine which may extend to five rupees for 
each week after the first-week during which the default continues. However, the ag- 
gregate fine cannot exceed fifty rupees. 
Any person who willfully makes or causes to be made, any false entry in or omis- 
sion from, the general statement (under s. 28) the copy of the rules or of alterations 
sent to the Registrar, is punishable with a fine not exceeding Rs. 500. 
If any person with the intention to deceit gives:— 
(i) any member or prospective member of a registered trade union, 
(ii) any document purporting to be a copy of the rules of the trade union or of 
any alterations, 
(iii) which he knows or has reason to believe, is not a correct copy of such rules 
or alterations in force, for the time being, 
(iv) he is liable to a fine which may extend to Rs. 200. 
Similarly, if any person with the like intent gives to any person a copy of the rules 
of an unregistered trade union on the pretence that such rules are the rules of a regis- 
tered trade union, he is punishable with an equal fine. (s. 32) 
Section 31 is almost at the end of the enactment. Section 10 is in the beginning of 
the Act. The latter provision providing for a special procedure for a particular offence 
475 


476 Part VII—The Trade Unions Act, 1926 
should be taken to exclude the application of s. 10 which also provides punishment for non-compliance of the provisions of the Act. 
2. Mens rea is immaterial in unfair labour practices 
The Act.provides for civil consequences for committing an unfair labour practice and provides for redressal through a civil remedy under sections 28 and 30. Mens rea is immaterial in an unfair labour practice. It is only upon non-compliance of orders of the Labour Court or Industrial Court, as the case may be, that criminal consequences are provided for. 
3. Industrial violence is punishable under Indian Panel Code 
Workers’ violence is a frequent phenomenon and the unions tend to justify it under the umbrella of permissible agitation. While dealing with industrial violence, courts cannot adopt traditional principles leaning towards the worker. Any violence, how- ever justifiable, inevitably results in loss of life or property. Such acts constitute of- fences under the Indian Penal Code. 
It is of little consequence whether a person was a leader or a follower when the violent act was committed. The presence and participation in an unlawful assembly is a sufficient crime for punishment. 
4, Cognizance of offences (s. 33) 
Any court inferior to that of a presidency Magistrate or a Magistrate of the first class cannot try any offence under the Act. 
No court shall take cognizance of any offence unless a complaint of the offence has been made. Complaint may be made by the registrar or by someone else with he pre- vious sanction of the registrar. Where the offence comes under s. 32 the complaint may be made by the person to whom the copy was given. It is necessary that the complaint is made within six months of the date on which the offence is alleged to have been committed. 
The law in its wisdom seeks to punish the guilty who commits the sin, and not his son, who is innocent.
