1. Historical Study of Compensation Laws in India 
Though the question of granting workmen compensation for fatal or serious acci- 
dents was first raised in India in 1884, the question of framing legislation was taken 
up by the Government of India only towards the end of 1920-21 when the question 
was referred to a small committee composed of Legislative Assembly members, em- 
ployers’ and workers’ representatives and medical and insurance experts. The Com- 
mittee’s detailed recommendations for framing legislation were accepted and a 
Workmen’s Compensation Act was passed in 1923. The measure followed the Brit- 
ish Act in its main principles and in some of its details, but it contained a large num- 
ber of provisions designed to meet the special conditions in India. This Act was the 
first step towards social security in India. This was followed by legislation enacted in 
several States for the protection of women in childbirth. Under these enactments the 
responsibility for payment of compensation rested with employers, a system which 
led to certain hardships. 
2. Workmen’s Compensation Act, 1923 
The most striking feature of the Workmen’s Compensation Act, 1923 is its rigidity, 
designed to prevent vexatious litigation. 
The Workmen’s Compensation Act (VIII of 1923), applied, in the first instance 
only to workers employed otherwise than in a clerical capacity and receiving 
477 


478 Part ViIJ]—The Workmen’s Compensation Act, 1923 
monthly wages not exceeding Rs. 300, in factories, mines and ports, to those engaged on the railways, tramways, on loading, unloading, or coaling ships at docks etc. where mechanical power was used in the building trade, construction of bridges, telegraph and telephone lines and posts and overhead electric cables, in connection with sewers and in the brigade services. The Act also applied to specified occupa- tional diseases and the Government of India was empowered to extend the list of such diseases as well as to hazardous occupations. 
The Act prescribed separate scales of compensation for death, permanent total dis- ablement, permanent partial disablement and temporary disablement. In the case of death of an adult, his dependants (defined as a wife, husband, parent, minor son, un- married daughter, married daughter who was a minor, minor brother or unmarried sister, minor children of a deceased son, and, where no parent was alive a paternal grandparent) were to receive a sum equal to thirty months’ wages or Rs. 2,500, whichever was less; in the case of death of a minor (i.e. a person under 15 years of age) the compensation was Rs. 200. For permanent total disablement the compensa- tion was, for an adult, a sum equal to forty-two months’ wages or Rs. 3,500, which- ever was less, and, for a minor; a sum equal to eighty four months’ wages or Rs. 3,500, whichever was less. Compensation for permanent partial disablement was payable according to the percentage of loss of earning capacity. Temporary disable- ment, whether total or partial, was compensated by half monthly payments during the disablement or during a period of five years, whichever period was shorter, of Rs. 15 or a sum equal to one-fourth of his monthly wages, whichever was less, in the case of an adult, and, in the case of a minor, of a sum equal to one-third or, after he reached 15 years of age, to one-half of his monthly wages but not exceeding Rs. 15. 
The claim arising out of Motor Vehicle Act 1988, can also be claimed under the Workmen’s Compensation Act, 1923. While dispensing justice or exercising the ju- risdiction of the Commissioner of Workmen’s Compensation would have power to review even as regards the claim arising out of the 1988 Act. 
3. Aims and objects of the Act 
The Act, as originally passed, aimed at covering only workmen whose occupations were hazardous and who were engaged in industries which were more or less organ- ised. Thus, the Act covered workers in all but the smallest factories, in mines, on the railways and tramways, on certain types of building work and in certain less impor- tant branches of employment. 
The object of the Workmen’s Compensation Act has been best expressed by the Royal Commission on Labour in India in the following words:— 
“Moreover, provision for compensation is not the only benefit flowing from workmen’s compensation legislation; it has important effects in furthering work on the prevention of accidents, in giving workmen greater freedom from anxiety, and in rendering industry more attractive.’” “The growing complexity of industry with the increasing use of machinery and consequent danger to the workmen along with com- parative poverty of the workmen themselves renders it advisable that they should be protected, as far as possible from hardships arising from accidents.” 
nr 
I. United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Workmen’s Compensation Commr., (1996) 2 LLJ 448 (All). 2. Report of the Royal Commission on Labour in India, p. 298. 


Chap. I—Preliminary 479 
The aims and objects of the Act are given in the statement of objects and reasons 
of the Act which ran as follows: 
(i) The general principles of workmen’s compensation command almost uni- 
versal acceptance, and India was then nearly alone amongst the civilised 
countries in being without legislation embodying these principles. For a 
number of years the more generous employers had been in the habit of 
giving compensation voluntarily but this practice was by no means general. 
The growing complexity of industry in this country with the increasing use 
of machinery and consequent danger to workmen, along with the compara- 
tive poverty of the workmen themselves, rendered it advisable that they 
should be protected, as far as possible, from hardship arising from acci- 
dents. 
(ii) An additional advantage of this type of legislation is that, by increasing the 
importance for the employer of adequate safety devices, it reduces the 
number of accidents to workmen in a manner that cannot be achieved by 
official in spection. Further, the encouragement given to employers to pro- 
vide adequate medical treatment for their workmen should mitigate the ef- 
fects of such accidents as do occur. The benefits so conferred on workmen 
added to the increased sense of security which he will enjoy, make indus- 
trial life more attractive and thus increase the available supply of labour. At 
the same time, a correspouc::iz increase in the efficiency of the average 
workmen may be expected. A system of insurance would prevent the bur- 
den from pressing too heavily on any particular employer. 
(iii) After detailed examination of the question by the Government of India, 
Local Governments were addressed in July, 1921, and provisional views of 
the Government of India were published for general information. The ad- 
visability of legislation had been accepted by the great majority of local 
Governments and the employer’s and worker’s associations, and the Gov- 
ernment of India believed that public opinion generally was in favour of 
legislation. 
(iv) In June, 1922, a committee was convened to consider the question. This 
committee was composed for the most part of members of the Imperial 
Legislature. After considering the numerous replies and opinions received 
by the Government of India, the committee was unanimously in favour of 
legislation, and drew up detailed recommendations regarding the lines 
which, in its opinion, such legislation should follow. The Bill presented 
followed these recommendations closely. A number of supplementary pro- 
visions had been added where necessary, but practically no variations of 
importance had been made. 
(v) The Bill contained two distinct proposals. In Chapter II modifications were 
made in the ordinary Civil Law affecting the liability of employers for 
damages in respect of injuries sustained by their workmen; these clauses 
would operate only in actions before the ordinary Civil Courts. The main 
part of the Bill made provision for compensation to workmen and set up 
special machinery to deal with claims falling under this category. 
(vi) Both parts of the Bill, however, were applied to the same classes of work- 
men. If the scope of the employers’, liability clauses was made wider than 
the scope of workmen’s compensation provisions, there would a consider- 
EERE 
3. Statements of Objects and Reasons, vide Gazette of India, 1922, Part V, p. 313. 


480 Part VIII—The Workmen’s Compensation Act, 1923 
able danger of a great increase in litigation. The classes included are those 
whose inclusion was recommended by the committee and were specified in 
Schedule II. Two criteria had been followed in the determination of classes 
to be included— 
(a) that the Bill should be confined to industries which are more or less 
organised. 
(b) that only workmen whose occupation is hazardous should be in- 
cluded. 
(vii) The general principle is that compensation should ordinarily be given to workmen who sustained personal injuries by accidents arising out of and in the course of their employment. Compensation will also be given in certain limited circumstances for disease. The actual rates of compensation payable were based on unanimous recommendations of the committee. They were in every case subject to fixed maximum in accordance with the committee recommendations. It should be remembered, however, that the more highly paid workmen will be enabled, in cases to which the employer’s liability clauses would apply, to obtain damages on a scale considerably in excess of the maximum fixed for workmen’s compensation. 
(viii) A consistent endeavour had been made to give as little opportunity for dis- putes as possible. Throughout the Bill in the definitions adopted, the scales selected and the exceptions permitted, the great aim had been precision, in order that, in as few cases as possible should the validity of a claim for compensation or the amount of that claim be open to doubt. At the same time, on the unanimous recommendation of the committee, a provision had been made for special tribunals to deal cheaply and expeditiously with any disputes that may arise, and generally to assist the parties in a manner which is not possible for the ordinary Civil Courts. 
4. Preamble of the Act 
The Workmen’s Compensation Act, 1923 is an Act to provide for the payment by certain classes of employers to their workmen of compensation for injury by acci- dent. | 
5. Short title, extent and commencement (s. 1) 
Section 1 says that this Act may be called the Workmen’s Compensation Act, it extends to whole of India and it shall come into force on the first day of July, 1924. 
6. Definitions (s. 2) 
Unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or context, the following terms have been defined as under— 
(a) Commissioner [s. 2(b)] 
“Commissioner” means a commissioner for Workmen’s Compensation appointed under section 20. 
(b) Compensation [s. 2(c)] 
“Compensation” means compensation as provided for by this Act.

(c) Dependent [s. 2(d)] 
“Dependent” means any of the following relatives of a deceased workman, 
namely— 
(i) a widow, a minor legitimate son and unmarried legitimate daughter, or a 
widowed mother; and 
(ii) if wholly dependent on workman’s earnings at the time of his death, a son 
or a daughter who has attained the age of 18 years and who is infirm; 
(iii) if wholly or in part dependent on the earnings of the workman at the time of

(d) a minor brother or an unmarried sister or a widowed sister if a minor, 
(ce) a widowed daughter-in-law, 
(f) a minor child of a pre-deceased son, 
(g) a minor child of a pre-deceased daughter where no parent of the child 
is alive, or 
(h) a paternal grand-parent if no parent of the workman is alive; 
(i) adopted son/daughter/child excluding those given in adoption.” 
(d) Employer [s. 2(e)] 
“Employer” includes any body of persons whether incorporated or not and any 
managing agent of an employer and the legal representative of a deceased employer, 
and, when the services of a workman are temporarily lent or let on hire to another 
person by the person with whom the workman has entered into a contract of service 
or apprenticeship, means such other person while the workman is working for him; 
(e) Managing agent [s. 2(f)] 
“managing agent” means any person appointed or acting as the representative of 
another person for the purpose of carrying on such other person’s trade or business, 
but does not include an individual manager subordinate to an employer. 
(f) Minor [s. 2(ff)] 
“Minor” means a person who has not attained the age of eighteen years. 
(g) Partial disablement [s. 2(g)] 
“Partial disablement” means, where the disablement is of a temporary nature, such 
disablement as reduces the earning capacity of a workman in any employment in 
which he was engaged at the time of the accident resulting in the disablement, and,

death from a height while on work. 
8. Extension and application of Act by State Governments 
The State Government, after giving by notification in the Official Gazette, not less 
than three months’ notice of its intention so to do, may, by a like notification, add to 
Schedule II any class of person employed in any occupation, which it is satisfied is a 
hazardous occupation, and the provisions of the Act will then apply within the State 
to such classes of persons.

9. Exposition of definitions 
10. Dependent [s. 2(1)(d)] 
Relations of workmen are divided into three classes. In the first class are included a 
widow, minor legitimate son, and unmarried legitimate daughter or a widowed 
mother. These would be considered to be the dependants of a workman whether in 
fact they are dependant on the earnings of the workman or not. In the second class 
are included a major son or a major daughter who are infirm and who are wholly de- 
pendant on the earnings of the workman at the time of his death. The third class in- 
cludes a widower, a parent other than a widowed mother, a minor illegitimate son, an 
unmarried illegitimate daughter, a daughter whether legitimate or illegitimate, if mar- 
ried and a minor or if widowed and a minor, or a minor brother, an unmarried or wid- 
owed sister, if minor, a widowed daughter-in-law, a minor child of a pre-deceased son, 
a minor child of a pre-deceased daughter where no parent of the child is alive, or where 
no parent of the workman is alive, a paternal grand-parent. The right of the persons in 
the third class to share in the compensation payable under the Act is dependent on their 
having been dependent on the earnings of the deceased workman at the time of his 
death. The question whether widowed mother or parent other than widowed mother 
would include a step-mother had come up for consideration before the Calcutta High 
' Court and it was held that a step-mother was not covered by those expressions.” It has, 
however, been held by the Nagpur High Court that the expression “widowed mother” 
would include an adoptive “widowed mother.” 
In order to claim compensation it is necessary for the claimants to prove that they 
were dependents on the deceased. A legal representative who is not a dependent is not entitled to claim compensation for the death of the deceased under the Work- 
men’s Compensation Acct. 
11. Employer [s 2(1)(e)] 
_ Employer has been defined to include a body of persons which may or may not be incorporated, and also includes any managing agent of an employer. In the case of death of an employer his legal representatives would also be an employer within the definition. If the services of a person employed by an employer or working as an ap- prentice under him are temporarily lent or let on hire to another person, such other person would also be treated as an employer during the period he is working with

Where the Commissioner of Labour had allowed a claim for compensation of an 
injured worker working under a contractor against the principal employer, the Kerala 
High Court observed that it is not possible to spell out an employer-employee rela- 
tionship between the claimant and the appellant (the owner of the land). The term 
‘employer’ is defined in Sec. 2(1)(e) of the Act. There is nothing to indicate that the 
owner of a land is liable, as employer, for any accident that may take place to a 
workman, under a contractor, who is allowed to extract rock (on the above basis). 
Thus it is not possible to uphold the finding of the Commissioner that the claimant 
was an employee under the appellant and find him liable to compensate for the injury 
sustained by the claimant. 3 
12. Partial and total disablement [s. 2(1)(g) and ()] 
Injury caused to a workman by an accident ordinarily results in the loss of the 
earning capacity of the workman concerned and this loss of earning capacity is tech- 
nically called “disablement”. Disablement can be classified as (a) Total, and (b) Par- 
tial. It can further be classified into (i) Permanent, and (ii) Temporary. Disablement, 
whether permanent or temporary is said to be total when it incapacitates a worker for 
all work he was capable of doing at the time of the accident resulting in such. dis- 
ablement. “Total disablement” is considered to be permanent if a workman, as a re- 
sult of an accident, suffers from the injury specified in Part I of Schedule I or suffers 
from such combination of injuries specified in Part II of Schedule I as would bring 
the loss of earning capacity when totalled to one hundred per cent or more. Partial 
disablement is said to be of permanent nature when it is such as to reduce for all 
times, the earning capacity of a workman in every employment which he was capable 
of undertaking at the time of the accident. Every injury specified in Part II of Sched- 
ule I is deemed to result in permanent partial disablement. Where the disablement is 
of a temporary nature and reduces the earning capacity of a workman in the employ- 
ment in which he was engaged at the time of the accident it is “temporary partial dis- 
ablement.” | 
According to the Act, disability is determined with reference to the work that the 
worker was doing immediately before accident took place and in case the resulting 
injury leaves him incapable of performing any work of a similar nature than his dis- 
ability is considered as 100 %. Where an accident left a coolie with a defect in his leg 
and as a result unfit to perform the work of a coolie, the court stated that the incapac-

13. Wages [s. 2(1)(m)] 
In addition to remuneration, the expression “wages” would include any privilege or 
benefit capable of being estimated in terms of money. It would not, however, include 
travelling allowance or the value of travelling concession or a contribution paid by 
the employer towards any pension or provident fund or a sum paid to a workman to 
cover any special expenses entailed by ‘him by the nature of his employment. 
Dearness allowance is covered, by the definition of wages as it is attached continu- 
ously to the wages with a view to enhancing it to meet the rise in the cost of living. 
The amenities of free quarters and water are privileges and benefits enjoyed by a 
workman employed in a factory and as such would be covered by the definition. 
Profit sharing bonus is also covered by the definition . 
Batta paid to the workers are not to be included for calculating monthly wages.” 
Bonus is a right of the workman and a benefit forming part of ‘wages’. Bonus is 
included for purposes of calculation of compensation payable to a workman who has 
suffered permanent disablement, either total or partial. 
14, Workman [s. 2(1)(n)] 
The first thing to be noted in connection with this definition is that a person whose em- 
ployment is of a casual nature is not covered by the definition unless he has been engaged 
for the trade or business of the employer. Thus, a casual worker who has been employed 
for the trade or business of the employer would be covered by the definition. The second point to be noted is that the person to be workman within the definition must be (a) a 
Railway servant or (b) employed in any such capacity as is specified in Schedule II. A Chowkidar (watchman) of a development authority is a workman under Sec. 2(n) of 
Act.” As regards a railway servant, it is not that all railway servants will be covered by the definition. Persons employed in any administrative, district or sub-divisional office of a railway and not included in the categories mentioned in Schedule II are excluded from the scope of the definition. Persons must be employed for work specified in Schedule IL. The law that the wages must not exceed on an average Rs. 1000 a month,”° has been amended and there is now no wage limit. 
A person provided with work for 24 days in a month on daily wages in a workman under the Act. 
The expression ‘workman’ in Section 2(1)(n) extends even to a clerical employee by virtue of Sec. 38A of the Bombay Shops and Establishments Act, 1948.78

The expression “workman” will also include agricultural labourer employed in a 
farm. Where such labourer died of electric shock: from the motor fitted to the lift- 
pump, he became eligible for compensation under the Act? 
However, the definition of workman under the Act cannot be applied to a person 
not coming under one or other clauses set out in Schedule II. The person appointed 
by an Official Liquidator does not become a workman. 
A person to be excluded from the definition of ‘workman’ under Sec. 2(1)(n), must 
not only be the one whose employment is of a casual nature but also one who is em- 
ployed otherwise than for the purpose of employer’s trade or business. These condi- 
tions are both cumulative and conjunctive. 
Mere designation given to a person as supervisor will not change his status a 
workman if he is otherwise qualified for it. : 
Any reference to a workman who has been injured shall, where the workman is 
dead, include a reference to his dependants or any of them. 
Power has been given to the State Government to add more occupations to 
Schedule II if it is satisfied that the particular occupation is a hazardous occupa- 
tion. For this purpose the State Government is required to give three months’ no- 
tice in the official Gazette. In exercise of this power the Government of Maharash- 
tra has added the following two categories of workers to Schedule II :— 
(i) persons employed for the purpose of loading or unloading in any mechani- 
cally propelled vehicle or in handling or transport of goods which have 
been loaded into any mechanically propelled vehicle. 
(ii) persons employed in any occupation ordinarily. involving outdoor work by 
any Municipality or by any District Local Board.” 
When a State Government, in exercise of this power, adds more categories to Schedule 
II, it is open to it to make the Act applicable only in respect of specified injuries. 
Schedule II contains a list of twenty-seven occupations and persons employed in 
any one of those occupations would be covered by the definition of workman. 
For applicability of the Act to a workman, it is not necessary that he should have 
been working in a factory having the requisite number of workmen under s. 2(m) of 
the Factories Act. Where the manufacturing process as defined in S. 2(k) of that Act 
is being carried on in the establishment, a person working in it would be a workman 
within the purview of the Workmen’s Compensation Act. He would be entitled to 
present his claim under the Act." |

The Central Government or the State Government, after giving, by notification in 
the Official Gazette, not less than three months, notice of its intention so to do, may, 
by a like notification, add any description of employment to the employments speci- 
fied in Schedule III. The Government has to specify in the case of employments so 
added the diseases which shall be deemed for the purposes of this section to be occu- 
pational diseases peculiar to those employments respectively. Thereupon the provi- 
sions of sub-section (2) shall apply in the case of a notification by the Central Gov- 
ernment, within the territories to which the Act extends, or, in case of a notification 
by the State Government, within the State as if such diseases had been declared by 
the Act to be occupational diseases peculiar to those employments [Sub-s. (3)]. 
Save as provided by sub-sections (2), (2A) and (3), no compensation is payable to 
a workman in respect of any disease unless the disease is directly attributable to a 
specific injury by an accident arising out of and in the course of his employment 
[Sub-s. (4)]. 
Nothing contained in this section shall be deemed to confer any right to compensa- 
tion on a workman in respect of any injury if he has instituted in a Civil Court a suit 
for damages in respect of the injury against the employer or any other person. No suit 
for damages shall bé maintainable by a workman in any Court of law in respect of 
any injury— 
(a) if he has instituted a claim to compensation in respect of the injury before a 
Commissioner; or | 
(b) if an agreement has been come to between the workman and his employer 
providing for the payment of compensation in respect of the injury in ac- 
cordance with the provisions of the Act. 
It has been held that a claimant for accident compensation choosing forum under 
Workmen’s Compensation Act can not invoke section 149 (2) of the Motor Vehicles 
Act, 1988 to perclude insurance company from taking up defence by virtue of re- 
strictions laid down therein. 
(i) Causal connection between cause of death and nature of duties 
Causal relationship between the cause of death and the nature of duties is sufficient 
to establish a claim for compensation. It is not necessary that there should be a direct 
connection between the cause of death and the nature of duties. Even if a causal con- 
nection between the two can be shown, then the dependants of the deceased would be 
entitled to claim compensation from the employer. In a matter like this, it is not for 
the courts to look into the minute details of the pleadings and the evidence which has 
been produced in the court. But it is to be seen whether on broad analysis of the ma- 
terial before the court, it can be said that the accident which resulted in any injury 
was in the course of employment or arose out of employment. If it is accepted that 
the deceased was suffering from high blood pressure from last one year, his duties as 
a cook in the running room caused strain and this strain had a causal relationship 
with the cause of death. It was hypertension leading to other complication. This 
causal connection will not go away merely because the deceased died after a week 
from the accident. The natural result of the disease is to be considered in a general 
manner and it cannot be expected that the doctor would be able to analyse each step 
in order to show how the deceased developed the disease and succumbed to the 
same. Suddenly becoming unconscious as a result of strain is an unexpected event 
1. National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Mastan, (2006) I LLJ 704 : AIR 2006 SC 577. 


492 Part VIII—The Workmen’s Compensation Act, 1923 
which can be said to be an accident leading to an injury in the course of employment 
and arising out of employment due to the working conditions, namely heated kitchen 
where the cooking was to be done. The strenuous duties and working condition in 
which the deceased was working accelerated his death and as such the dependants 
were entitled to get compensation. 
Where the deceased workman suffered from heart disease and his job was only to 
switch on or off in the thermal station where he was employed, his wife was held not 
entitled to compensation as there was no causal connection between the death and 
employment of workman. 
Where the workman (driver of vehicle) was killed by miscreants while he was 
engaged in discharging his duties, it was held that a causal relationship existed 
between the cause of death and the employment of the deceased workman. The 
court said: | 
“There is no dispute about the principle of law laid down by the Supreme 
Court in the aforesaid cases. The main question to be decided is as to 
whether there is a causal relationship between the accident and the em- 
ployment. As observed by the Supreme Court,’ the expression “arising out 
of employment” is not confined to the mere nature to employment. “The 
expression applies to employment as such to its nature, its conditions, its 
obligations and its incidents. If by reason of any of these factors, the work- 
man is brought within the zone of special danger, the injury would be one 
which arises ‘out of employment’.” In the decision reported in Saurashtra 
Salt Manufacturing Co. v. Bai Valu Raja, it was observed: 
“Tt is well settled that when a workman is on a public road or a public 
place or on a public transport he is there as any other member of the public 
and is not there in the course of his employment unless the very nature of 
his employment makes it necessary for him to be there. (emphasis

If the deceased would have been travelling on his own and would have 
been killed due to some incident, there cannot be any doubt that the acci- 
dent could not have been taken to be one arising out of employment, but in 
the present case, the very nature of the employment of the deceased made it 
necessary for him to drive the vehicle which ultimately resulted in his death 
as the miscreants way-laid him and killed him obviously with a view to fa- 
cilitate removal of the tins of Amul Spray which were being transported. 
Thus, it can be very well concluded that by the nature of his employment, 
he had to undertake the journey which exposed him to the hazards ulti-

in the decision in United India Insurance Company Ltd. v. Philo,’ that the 
accident arose out of the employment. Similarly, a Division Bench of the 
Bombay High Court presided by CHAGLA, C.J., in the decision in Bhagubai 
v. General Manager, Central Railway,® while allowing compensation to the 
claimants, observed: 
“Now it is clear that there must be a causal connection between the acci- 
dent and the employment in order that the Court can say that the accident 
arose out of the employment of the deceased. It is, equally clear that the 
cause contemplated is the prominent cause and not any remote cause. The 
authorities have clearly laid down that if the employee in the course of his 
employment has to be in a particular place and by reason of his being in 
that particular place he has to face a peril and the accident is caused by rea- 
son of that peril which he has to face, then a causal connection is estab- 
lished between the accident and the employment. It is now well settled that 
the fact that the employee shares that peril with other members of the pub- 
lic is an irrelevant consideration. It is true that the peril which he faces must 
not be something personal to him; the peril must be incidental to his em- 
ployment. It is also clear that he must not by his own act add to the peril or 
extend the peril. But if the peril which he faces has nothing to do with his 
own action or his own conduct, but it is a peril which would have been 
faced by any other employee or any other member of the public, then if the 
accident arises out of such peril causal connection is established between 
the employment and the accident.” 
The decision of the Madras High Court in Special Officer. PA Polythene 
Workers Industrial Cooperative Society Ltd. v. Ayyammal,'” was however, 
clearly distinguishable. In that case, the husband had come to the work-site 
where the wife was working and a quarrel ensued between them and the 
husband killed the wife. In such circumstances, it was held that there was 
no causal connection between the death and the employment of the de- 
ceased. It is obvious that the facts in the that case were completely different 
and the ratio of the decision cannot be applied to the present case.” 
(it) Accident arising out of and in the course of employment 
An accident means a mishap or untoward event not expected or designed by a workman. The driver had gone to the village in the jeep with the officers of the bank 
on official duty. Therefore there is no gainsaying of the fact that the accident had taken place during the course of employment. There was a casual connection be- tween the accident in question and the employment of the driver. The assault on the driver may have been perhaps due to tense situation in the village on account of re- 
covery proceedings. The expression “accident arising out of and in the course of em- ployment” rather denotes a point of time than a factual connection with the employ- 
ment and the accident. The driver died while he was on his duty at the hands of some 
other persons. The cause of death and assault is not known and it does not show that 
the driver had expected or designed or invited the assault on him. Therefore, the driver died during the course of his employment. The risk incurred by the for going 
to the bazar after resting his jeep was incidental to his employment of taking the jeep

to the village as against the risk which all members of the public may have been ex-

The accident having taken place without the fault of the driver and while he was on 
duty in the village must be taken to be during the course of his employment and also 
arising out of the employment on account of risk which was incidental to his duty of 
taking the bank officers to the village. But for the driver going to the village by 
driving a jeep on a weekly bazar day, as part of his duty, he would not been exposed 
to the peril of facing a deadly assault. Hence the death was as a result of an accident 
out of and during the course of his employment and as such the bank is held liable to 
pay compensation in accordance with the provisions of the Act. 
It is well settled that the material words occurring in the relevant statutory provi- 
sion, namely, “if personal injury is caused to a workman by accident arising out of 
and in the course of his employment” have to be liberally interpreted. This judicial 
approach has resulted in the theory of extended liability being propounded. If the 
employee’s unexplained or apparently natural death has occurred during the course 
of employment, the adjudicator is not relieved of the responsibility of finding out 
whether there was any causal connection between the nature of employment and the 
death, whether the employment was an attributable cause or whether it accelerated 
the death, whether the death was not only due to the disease from which the work- 
man was suffering but also on account of the factors which have a bearing upon or 
which are coupled with the employment efc. If such or similar factors are present, 
then the employer is liable and it can be said that the death occurred as a conse- 
quence of and in the course of employment. 
A person employed to look after sales was held to be a workman within the mean- 
ing of the Act. He was directed by the employer to attend a sales conference. He was 
injured while travelling by a train on that mission. It was held that the accident arose 
while the employee was working in the course of his employment.” The court cited 
the following passage from the decision in Armstrong Withworth & Co. v. Redford’ 
and Mcculhum v. Northambrian Shipping Co. Ltd: 4 
“A few words in the English language had been subjected to more micro- 
scopic judicial analysis than the words “arising out of and in the course of 
employment”, and in the effort to expound them many criteria had been 
proposed and many paraphrases suggested. But it was manifestly impoOssi- 
ble to exhaust their content by definition, for the circumstances and inci- 
dents of employment were almost of infinite variety. This atleast, however, 
could be said that the accident in order to give rise to a claim for compen- 
sation, must have some causal relation to the workman’s employment and 
must be due to risk incidental to the employment as distinguished from risk 
to which all members of the public were alike exposed.” 
An American court observed in Cardillo v. Liberty Mutual Insurance Co.'° that the 
phrase “arising out of and in the course of employment” as “deceptively simple and 
litigiously prolific phrase.”

The burden to prove that accident occurred not in the course of employment is on 
the employer. 
The respondent, who was a driver of a tempo van duly insured by the appellant 
company, was injured by a dog bite. When he got down from the van for unloading 
the goods he was bitten by a dog and fell down. The appellant denied the liability to

ployment. The High Court held that in the circumstances of the case, the respondent- 
claimant has satisfied all the three tests, viz., notional extension, causal connection 
and reasonably incidental occurrence of the accident to establish his claim. 
(iii) Notional extension of official premises 
The notional extension of office premises means that office premises do not begin 
when the workman enters the gate of the office and do not end when he leaves the 
gate in the evening. There is notional extension of both the entry and exit by time and 
space. When a workman starts his journey from his home towards office or factory 
and when he leaves his office or factory for his home, all that way is included under 
notional extension of the office premises. A security assistant in the Special Protec- 
tion Group attached to the Cabinet Secretariat sustained injuries resulting in perma- 
nent partial disablement in a motor accident when he was travelling from staff quar- 
ters to the South Block for duty in the official SPG vehicle provided for that purpose. 
It was held that since the security assistant was travelling in the official SPG vehicle 
in which he was required to travel from the staff quarters to the South Block, that 
vehicle not being available to anyone other than the SPG personnel, the security as- 
sistant was at a place or a point or an area which came within the theory of notional 
extension of the official premises for the performance of ‘actual VIP security duty’. 
There was a causal relationship between the accident in which the security assistant 
sustained the injuries and his employment in the SPG for ‘actual VIP security duty’ 
and it was an accident of his employment to travel from the staff quarters to the 
South Block in the SPG vehicle according to the official arrangement. The meaning 
of the expression ‘actual VIP security duty’ in the circular must be the same as that 
of the words “‘in the course of employment” in the Workmen’s Compensation Act, 
1923 and, therefore, the test for determining the liability for payment under the cir-

cular should also be the same. The Central Administrative Tribunal took an unduly 
strict and narrow construction of the expression used in the circular. 
The Authorities concerned must adopt a humane approach and construe the circu- 
lar liberally to advance its object instead of taking a rigid and pedantic stand. Unless 
properly implemented the scheme in the circular would be frustrated resulting in fail- 
ure to achieve the avowed purpose.” — 
The question, when does an employment begin and when does it cease, depends 
upon the facts of each case. Decidedly the employment does not necessarily end 
when the ‘down tool’, signal is given or when the workman actually leaves the actual 
workshop where he is working. There is a “notional extension” of both the entry and 
exit by time and space. The scope of such extension must necessarily depend on the 
circumstances of a given case. An employment may begin or may end not only when 
the employee begins to work or leaves his tools but also when he used the means of 
access and accede to and from the place of employment. A contractual duty or obli- 
gation on the part of an employer to use only a particular means of transport extends 
the area or the field of employment to the course of said transport. Though at the ini- 
tial stage, the word “duty” had been strictly construed, the later decisions have liber- 
alised this concept. When an employee uses the means of access and accede to and 
from the place of employment and even also while attending to his usual pursuits, 
leisure hours, recess time, efc. he is in employment.” The Supreme Court observed 
in Regional Director, ESI Corpn. v. Francis Decosta,~ that every accident arising 
while going to or back from the work place cannot be said to be connected with em- 
ployment. The court further said that if employment is taken to begin from the mo- 
ment the employee sets out from his house for the factory then even if the employee 
stumbles and falls down at the door steps of his house, the accident will have to be 
treated as to have taken place in the course of his employment. This interpretation 
would lead to absurdity. The Supreme Court decision General Manager, BEST Un- 
dertaking v. Agnes,’ was distinguished because in that case the notional extension of 
service had been due to the standing rules of BEST Undertaking requiring its drivers 
to attend duty punctually for which the stipulation was to come and go by the buses 
of the undertaking. 
(iv) Burden of proof 
In the case of death caused by employment injury, the burden of proof rests upon 
the workmen to prove that the accident arose out of employment or occurred in the 
course of employment. But this does not mean that the workmen who comes to the 
court for relief must necessarily prove it by direct evidence. It could also be inferred 
when the facts proved justify the inference. It is, of course, impossible to lay down 
any straight-jacket formula or rule as to the extent and degree of proof in such matter, 
which is sufficient to justify an inference being drawn. Strict proof as to the cause of

(v) Negligence of workman cannot exonerate employer from liability 
It has been held that under section 3(1) proviso (b) of the Workmen’s Compensa- 
tion Act, 1923 the employer cannot be exonerated from his liability to compensate 
merely by reason of negligence of the workman in discharging his duties. 
(vi) Wilful disobedience 
Wilful disobedience comprehends deliberate and intended disobedience. If the ac- 
cident occurred and that to while doing the work in the employment of the respon- 
dent, the question of negligence, great or small is irrelevant. No amount of negli- 
gence in doing employment job can change the workman into unemployment job. 
The appellant in this case met with an accident within the premises of the respon- 
dent and that to while working on machine i.e., while doing the job which was en- 
trusted to him. Therefore, considering the facts and circumstances of the case, the 
question of wilful disobedience as laid down in proviso (b)(ii) could not exonerate 
the company from its liability as specified in the substantive part of section 3(1) of 
the Act. Further, within the meaning section 3(1)(b)(ii) of the Act, the fact that the 
workman was in wilful disobedience may not be sufficient. Disobedience may be the 
result of forgetfulness or the result of impulse of the moment. Such would not be 
sufficient as the statute exempts the employer from liability only when the disobedi- 
ence is wilful, that is deliberate and intended. A man does a thing wilfully when he 
does it intentionally because he expects some benefit to himself either in the shape of 
some convenience or an easy way of doing a piece of work and so forth. 
Mere negligence of the worker cannot be regarded as wilful disobedience by the 
workman to an order expressly given. The expression “accident” generally means 
some unexpected event happening without design even though there may be negli- 
gence to decide whether an occurrence is an accident, it must be regarded from the 
point of view of the workman who suffers from it and if it is unexpected and without 
design on his part, it may be an accident. 
The workman in the instant case, met with an accident while performing his duty, 
though not in a diligent manner, but the fact remained that his two fingers were 
crushed. 
(vii) Theory of Acceleration or Aggravation 
Where the deceased was designated as ‘“‘sound recordist” and died of cardiac arrest 
it was held by the Madras High Court that the nature of work assigned to the de- 
ceased would clearly reveal the onerous nature and the amount of mental strain, and 
skill required to be exercised every day from down to dusk to complete the job. It is 
not always necessary that there should be physical injury or external overt acts to 
cause mental strain but over-exertion also creates a tension in the mind of the em- 
ployee and that would also be a contributing factor for any mishappening. As such, 
the acceleration or aggravation of the heart condition of such an employee due to 
such strain mentally or physically may cause the cardiac problem. Such mental or 
physical strain results in death or disability, which contributed to an injury or acci-

The word “accident” generally denotes an event that takes place without one’s 
foresight or expectation, an event which proceeds from an unknown cause, or is an 
unusual effect of a known cause, and, therefore, not expected; chance, casually, con- 
tingency; an event happening without the concurrence of the will of the person by 
whose agency it was caused. It differs from mistakes in that the latter always sup- 
poses the operation of the will of the agent in producing the event although that will 
is caused by an erroneous impression on the mind. 
The meaning for the word ‘accident’ used in section 3 of the Workmen’s Compen- 
sation Act has to be given a very wider meaning and not a narrow meaning. An acci- 
dent by itself implies that it may happen at any point of time with or without the 
knowledge of the person who suffers by it and it cannot be proved always by direct 
evidence. ; 
Hence it was clear that the view of the Commissioner for Workmen’s Compensa- 
tion that he deceased had died due to the accident while he was engaged in the regu- 
lar course of his employment was correct and/therefore the liability of the employer 
to pay the compensation had been correctly decided. 
A workman was a chronic asthma patient. He was working as the driver of a tractor 
in an open atmosphere. It was held that fumes of a tractor exhaust could aggravate 
his condition leading to death. His death was taken to be the result of his employ- 
ment.’ The court cited the following passage from the decision of the Supreme 
Court in Regional Director, ESI Corpn. v. Francis De Costa: 
“The words of limitation in s. 2(8) are “in the course of his employment. 
The dictionary meaning of “in the course of’ is “during, (in the course of 
time, as time goes by) while doing.’”! The dictionary meaning indicates that 
the accident must take place within or during the period of employment.” 
The court found further support in its opinion from the following references: 
“In an article published in the JOURNAL OF AMERICAN MEDICAL

be more of a syndrome rather than a specific disease entity. Numerous fac- 
tors, including viral infections, allergen and irritant exposure and exercise 
among others, complicate both the short and long term management of 
asthma. Therapeutic intervention has focussed on the appreciation that air-

variable degrees of airway inflammation characterised by edema, mucous 
secretion and the influx of a variety of inflammatory cells. Choosing ap- 
propriate medications depends on the disease severity (intermittent, mild 
persistent, moderate persistent, severe persistent) patterns of disease activ-

The report states that patients at any level of severity can suffer from minor to se- 
vere exacerbations. It states that even a patient with mild intermittent asthma may 
experience life threatening exacerbation between long periods of normal lung func- 
tion and absence of symptom. 
We may also advert to the following passage from “cDAVIDSON’S PRINCIPLES AND 
PRACTICE OF MEDICINE’’.”~ It is stated as under: 
“Chronic bronchitis develops in response to the long-continued action of 
various types of irritant on the bronchial mucosa. The most important of 
these is cigarette tobacco smoke but others include dust, smoke and fumes 
occurring as specific occupational hazards or as part of a general atmos- 
pheric pollution in industrial cities and towns. Infection is sometimes a pre- 
cipitating factor in the onset of chronic bronchitis but its main role is in ag- 
gravating the established condition.” 
Again the same Author at page 333 states as under: 
“Chronic bronchitis is usually a progressive disease, punctuated by acute 
exacerbations and remissions and eventually causing respiratory and right 
heart failure. Some patients die within a few years of the onset of symp- 
toms; others survive for many years with gradually diminishing respiratory 
reserve.” 
The Author indicates to abate the cause for such progressive Asthma and to avoid 
dusty and smoke-laden atmospheres, which in the case of the worker in question, 
may involve a change of occupation itself. It can therefore be concluded from the 
above passage that an aggravated form of asthma can lead to a heart attack. 
Admittedly the deceased was employed as a driver of a tractor. It is common 
knowledge that the fumes of a tractor are contaminated by carbon monoxide and 
other irritant mixture of gas produced by the burning of diesel. Constant exposure to 
it can be an irritant causing mild intermittent Asthma. A person who is a chronic 
Asthma patient and works as a driver in an open and exposed atmosphere has every 
chance of aggravating the disease. The natural result could not be a fatal accident. 
Therefore it could be safely concluded that a person suffering from asthma if ex- 
posed to polluted atmosphere could aggravate his disease which would result in 
death. The worker’s situation in the present case as a tractor driver has aggravated his 
illness of asthma causing ultimately his slow death. In other words, the asthma which 
was the by-product of his employment was the cause of his death. No fatal accident 
was caused by the Asthma which illness arose out of and in the course of employ- 
ment and the death arising therefrom is a death arising out of and in the employment 
within the meaning of s. 3. 
The workman was 55 years of age on the date of his death. The factor for working 
out the compensation in the case of the deceased as per the Act is 135.50. His 
monthly wages was Rs. 1,200/- and the ceiling as per unamended Act is Rs. 1,000/-. 
40% thereof would be the wages to be adopted to arrive at the compensation. Thus it 
works out to Rs 54,500/- and if rounded off, the compensation to be awarded to the 
claimant is Rs. 50,000/-. We disallow the interest to the claimant as we are informed 
that the legal heir of the deceased is gainfully employed by the same employer.

500 Part VIII—The Workmen’s Compensation Act, 1923 
(viii) Proof for Claiming Compensation 
The rules culled from mass of case-law may be restated as under: 
(1) The general burden of proving entitlement for a claim rests on the claim- 
ants. 
(2) Compensation is payable for personal injuries. 
(3) Persona! injury must be due to accident, not natural death, circumstances or 
wear and tear of body. 
(4) The accident must have arisen out of employment. 
(5) The accident must have occurred in the course of employment. 
2. Determination of amount of compensation [s. 4] 
The principle on which compensation is to be awarded has to be determined in ac- 
cordance with the provisions of the Act and cannot be departed from on grounds of 
sentiment. Under the provisions of the Act, the amount of compensation depends 
upon age, monthly wages and nature of injury. 
Sections 3 and 5 must be read to mean that liability to pay compensation arises on 
the date of death of the employee. The revision of pay scale by the employer with 
retrospective effect will not set the provisions of the Sections at naught.

3. Compensation to be paid when due and penalty for default (s. 4A) 
(1) Compensation under section 4 shall be paid as soon as it falls due. 
(2) In cases where the employer does not accept the liability for compensation to 
the extent claimed, he shall be bound to make provisional payment based on the ex- 
tent of liability which he accepts, and, such payment shall be deposited with the 
Commissioner or made to the workman, as the case may be, without prejudice to the 
right of the workman to make any further claim. 
This sub-section has made it clear, in the first place, that the employer has to ac- 
cept the extent of his liability for payment of compensation and on that basis he has 
to make payment either to workmen or to deposit with the Commissioner. The re- 
quirement of this sub-section is payment to the workman and not to any other person 
including his heirs and legal representatives.” 
(3) Where any employer is in default in paying the compensation due under this 
Act within one month from the date it fell due, the Commissioner shall— 
(a) direct that the employer shall, in addition to the amount of the arrears, pay 
simple interest thereon at the rate of twelve per cent per annum or at such 
higher rate not exceeding the maximum of the lending rates of any sched-

in the Official Gazette, on the amount due; and

4. Computation as per rates prevailing on the date of accident 
Compensation will be computed as per law on the date of accident and not as at 
application or order. The rates which may be revised during proceedings will not 
apply retrospectively. Even where a workman claims less compensation than what is 
admissible according to Section 4 and the Schedule to the Act, the Commissioner 
may grant the amount as prescribed by the Statute as compensation. 
The only question that required to be considered in the case cited below was as to 
whether the respondent was entitled to compensation under the Act as per enhanced 
rates of compensation found in Sch. IV pursuant to Amending Act 65 of 1976 or 
whether the appellant was liable to pay compensation to respondent on the basis of 
old rates of compensation which held the field prior to application of the aforesaid 
Amending Act. The Court observed that in the light of the facts and circumstances of 
this case, it must be held that amendment to Sch. IV as effected by Amending Act of 
1976 could not be pressed into service by the respondent-workman for computing 
compensation payable to him for the employment injury suffered by him on 11-10- 
1971. He would be entitled to get compensation as per old rates as reflected by the 
then existing Sch. IV. The amount would be Rupees 9,800 and not Rs. 23,520 as 
awarded by the Commissioner.” (Para 31) 
So far as the present Amending Act of 1976 was concerned, it had provided for ret- 
rospective operation of two provisions viz. the amended definition of the term 
‘workman’ under Section 2(n) as well as the amended Sch. IV from 1-10-1975. Con- 
sequently, provision like Section 43 as found in the Amending Act to Employees’ 
State Insurance Act could not have been engrafted in the present Amending Act as

that would have conflicted with the legislative intention to make the aforesaid two

PATRA, J. in Oriental Fire & General Ins. Co. v. Bibi,’ considered the question in 
the light of the facts situation and held:— 
“The normal rule of construction of a Statute is that its operation is prospective 
unless it is made retrospective either expressly or by necessary implication. The 
rights and liabilities under the Workmen’s Compensation Act get crystallised on the 
date of death of the workman. Therefore, the amount admissible under the Schedule 
as in force on the date of death can only be awarded”. This reasoning of PATRA J. is 
well borne from the statutory scheme of the Act and is in consonance with the well 
established rule of interpretation of statutes. 
The rates for calculating the compensation must be the rates of the Schedule IV 
prevalent on the date of “accident”. 
The following consequences would, therefore, follow in the light of the provisions 
of the Workmen’s Compensation Act as amended by Amending Act of 65:— 
1. If accidental employment injuries are suffered by a workman on or after 1- 
10-1975. Sch. IV as amended by Amending Act of 1976 will apply to the 
applications for compensation for such injuries, which might be pending on 
21-5-1976 when the Amending Act was brought in force. Even if such ap- 
plications were disposed of earlier by the concerned Commissioners prior 
to 21-5-1976, employer’s liability would be to pay compensation as per 
amended schedule IV for such injuries and if the concerned claimants chose 
to agitate the question of proper compensation in appeals, the appellate 
Court would be justified in enhancing the compensation amount by apply- 
ing the enhanced rates of compensation as per amended Schedule IV. 
2. Amended provisions of Sch. IV shall also apply to all proceedings for com- 
pensation in connection with injuries suffered by injured workmen on and 
from 1-10-1975 onwards, even if such applications might come to be filed 
after 21-5-1976 within the period of limitation prescribed by S. 10(1) of the 
Act. 7 | 
3. If, however, accidental injuries were suffered by the injured workman prior 
to 1-10-1975 and if any applications are filed for getting compensation in 
connection with those injuries whether such claim applications are filed 
prior to 1-10-1975 or after that date, and whether such applications were 
pending on 21-5-1976 or whether they were not so pending on account of 
the fact that they had got disposed of prior thereto or that they were filed 
after 21-5-1976, they will have to be decided in the light of the old una- 
mended Schedule IV as applicable at the time the accidental injuries were 
actually suffered by the concerned workman.

compensation sum awarded under the Act was held to be wholly unjustified.

5. Method of calculating wages (s. 5) 
For the purposes of the Act the expression “monthly wages” means the amount of 
wages deemed to be payable for a month’s service (whether the wages are payable by 
the month or by whatever other period or at piece rates), and calculated as follows, 
namely— 
(a) where the workman has, during a continuous period of not less than 
twelve months immediately preceding the accident, been in the service of 
the employer who is liable to pay compensation, the monthly wages of the 
workman shall be one-twelfth of the total wages which have fallen due 
for payment to him by the employer in the last twelve months of that pe- 
riod; 
(b) where the whole of the continuous period of service immediately preceding 
the accident during which the workman was in the service of the employer 
who is liable to pay the compensation was less than one month, the 
monthly wages of the workman shall be the average monthly amount 
which, during the twelve months immediately preceding the accident, was 
being earned by a workman employed on the same work by the same em- 
ployer, or, if there was no workman so employed, by a workman employed 
on similar work in the same locality; 
(c) in other cases including cases in which it is not possible for want of neces- 
sary information to calculate the monthly wages under clause (b), the 
monthly wages shall be thirty times the total wages earned in respect of the 
last-continuous period of service immediately preceding the accident from 
the employer who is liable to pay compensation, divided by the number of 
days comprising such period. | 
The Explanation to the provisions says that a period of service shall, for the pur- 
poses of this section, be deemed to be continuous which has not been interrupted by a 
period of absence from work exceeding fourteen days.

and not a penalty. Even where an insurer is not liable for the penalty for default of 
payment of the insured amount, he shall attract levy of penalty for defaulting interest 
payment. Where parties contracted out liability of insurer to pay interest on the 
amount of compensation, the insurer can not be held liable for payment of interest on

7. Right of lump sum compensation 
If the injury from the accident results in the death of the workman concerned, the 
compensation is payable by the employer to the dependants of that workman. The 
coverage of the expression “dependant” has already been explained in notes on s. 2. 
The factor which determines the amount of compensation on the death of a workman 
is whether he was a minor or an adult. For the purposes of the Act a workman is to be 
considered a minor if he is under fifteen years of age.’ A workman would be consid- 
ered to be an adult if he is not under the age of fifteen years. In the case of the death 
of a minor workman, the compensation payable is Rupees Two Hundred only. In the 
case of an adult worker there is an additional factor which determines the amount of 
compensation payable by the employer, namely, the monthly wage drawn by the 
workman concerned. A tabular statement showing factor for working out the com- 
pensation payable for the various wage groups is given in Schedule IV of the Act. 
Under that Schedule trade relevant factors are given for various age groups which 
have to be applied as per Sec. 4 of the Act.” 
8. Permanent Total Disablement 
In the case of injuries not resulting in death, the amount of compensation depends 
on the nature of the disablement, that is, whether the disablement is total or partial 
and permanent or temporary. The amount of compensation payable for permanent 
total disablement in the case of an adult worker depends upon the age group to which 
the workman concerned belongs and Schedule IV of the Act, which specifies the 
factors applicable to different age groups. ' 
In the case of a permanent disability caused to an employee, the employer cannot es- 
cape liability to pay damages for disability, even if he pays the employee the same or 
more salary subsequent to the permanent disability. For, if the management winds up 
its business subsequently, the employee will be left in the lurch because he would not 
be in a position to obtain an employment once again owing to injury suffered. 
Where a permanent total disablement occurs, the workman is not barred from 
claiming compensation more than the percentage specified in the Schedule I to the 
Act for the loss of earning capability. 
9. Permanent partial disablement 
Some of the injuries which result in permanent partial disablement are specified in 
Schedule I of the Act. The Schedule gives the percentage of disablement in the case 
of different injuries and the amount of compensation payable in case of any of those 
injuries would be that portion of the amount of compensation payable under Sched- 
ule IV for permanent total disablement as would correspond to the percentage speci- 
fied in Schedule I. If, however, the injury is not one specified in Schedule I, then the

earning capacity. 
10. Injury must be traceable to accident 
Under Section 4 of the Act, the employer is liable to compensate the workman ac- 
cording to the scale given in the Act, where permanent partial disablement “results 
from the injury.” The wording indicates that the disablement must result from the 
injury. It has been held by the Calcutta High Court that the law does not insist and 
has nowhere indicated that the disablement should be solely and directly attributable 
to the accident.” It laid down that the true test is not whether the disablement is the 
direct or even probable result of the injury or the injury the natural cause thereof, but 
whether the disablement can be traced to the injury even as an unusual but not un- 
connected result thereof. 
Section 4(1)(c) is wide in its application even to cover accidents taking place while 
cleaning machinery in the factory on a holiday. 
11. Half-monthly payments 
For temporary disablements, whether it is total or partial, compensation is payable in 
the form of recurring half-monthly payments. The first such payment becomes due on the 
sixteenth day after the expiry of the waiting period of three days. Thereafter, the pay- 
ments are to be made half-monthly during the period the disablement lasts or during a 
period of five years, whichever is shorter. The amount of half-monthly payment payable 
to a workman is shown in sec. 4(d) of the Act. 
12. Review and its grounds (s. 6) 
Whether or not the subsequent developments be for the better or for the worse, the 
disablement is for the time being of a temporary nature and since it is temporary,

508 Part VIII—The Workmen’s Compensation Act, 1923 
provision for future adjustment is called for. Provision has, therefore, been made in 
the Act for review.” Whether the half-monthly payments are being made under an 
agreement between the parties or under an order of a Commissioner for Workmen’s 
Compensation, either party can make an application to the Commissioner for review. 
Such application is required to be accompanied by a certificate from a qualified 
medical practitioner to the effect that there has been a change in the condition of the 
workman. 
(a) Grounds on which review can be done 
Government can frame rules laying down the cases in which such an application 
for review may not be accompanied by a medical certificate. Government of India 
has accordingly framed rules in that respect™ and under those rules an application for 
review can be made without a medical certificate in the following cases :— 
(a) by the employer, on the ground that since the right to compensation was de- 
termined, the workman’s wages have increased; 
(b) by the workman, on the ground that since the right to compensation was de- 
termined, his wages have diminished; 
(c) by the workman, on the ground that the employer, having commenced to pay 
compensation, has ceased to pay the same, notwithstanding the fact that 
there has been no change in the workmen’s condition such as to warrant 
such cessation; 
(d) either by the employer or by the workman, on the ground that the determi- 
nation of the rate of compensation for the time being in force was obtained 
by fraud or undue influence or other improper means; 
(e) either by the employer or by the workman on the ground that in the determi- 
nation of compensation there is a mistake or error apparent on the face of the 
record. 
On an application for review being filed, the Commissioner may continue, in- 
crease, decrease or end the half-monthly payments. If, however, on such applica- 
tion being filed, it is found that the accident has resulted in permanent disablement, 
the Commissioner can convert the half-monthly payments into a lump sum com- 
pensation. When such conversion is ordered the amount of half-monthly payments 
already received by the workman will be deducted from the lump sum compensa- 
tion ordered to be paid. If on examining a review application filed by an employer for reduction or discontinuance of half-monthly payments, it appears to the Com- missioner that there is reasonable ground for believing that the employer has a right to such reduction or discontinuance, he may, at any time, issue an order withhold- ing the half-monthly payments in whole or in part pending the decision of the ap- 
plication for review. ° 
13. Commutation (s. 7) 
After the half-monthly payments have been made for six months, either the em- ployer or the workman can get the recurring payments commuted at any time to a single payment. This commutation can be affected either by an agreement between

the parties or by an application to the Commissioner. After such commutation, the 
right of the workman to receive half-monthly payments would come to an end. When 
such an application for commutation of half-monthly payments is made to the Com-

the lump sum payable on the basis of half-monthly payments which will have to be

14. Time of payment of compensation (s. 4A) 
Compensation must be paid as soon as it falls due and if the employer accepts the 
liability partially, part amount must be deposited. Not only interest at 6 per cent p.a. 
but penalty upto 50 per cent of compensation amount may also be ordered. 
15. Distribution of compensation (s. 8) 
Section 8 of the Act deals with distribution of compensation. It says that no com- 
pensation in respect of a workman whose injury has resulted in death, and no pay- 
ment of a lump sum as compensation to woman or a person under a legal disability, 
shall be made otherwise than by deposit with the commissioner, and no such pay- 
ment made directly by an employer shall be deemed to be a payment of compensa- 
tion. 
The proviso to the section says that in the case of a deceased workman, an em- 
ployer may make to any dependant advances on account of compensation of an 
amount equal to three months wages of such workman and so much of such amount 
as does not exceed the compensation payable to the dependant shall be deducted by 
the Commissioner from such compensation and repaid to the employer. [Sub-s. (1)]. 
Any other sum amounting to not less than ten rupees which is payable as compen- 
sation may be deposited with the Commissioner on behalf of the person entitled 
thereto [Sub-s. (2)]. 
The receipt of the Commissioner shall be a sufficient discharge in respect of any 
compensation deposited with him. [Sub-s. (3)]. 
On the deposit of any money under sub-section as compensation in respect of a de- 
ceased workman, the Commissioner shall, if he thinks necessary, cause notice to be 
published or to be served on each dependant in such manner as he thinks fit, calling 
upon the dependants to appear before him on such date as he may fix for determining 
the distribution of compensation. If the Commissioner is satisfied after any inquiry 
which he may deem necessary that no dependant exists, he shall repay the balance of 
the money to the employer by whom it was paid. The Commissioner shall, on appli- 
cation by the employer, furnish a statement showing in detail all disbursements 
made. 
Compensation deposited in respect of a deceased workman shall, subject to any 
deduction made under sub-section (4) has to be apportioned among the dependants of 
the deceased workman or any of them in such proportion as the Commissioner thinks 
fit, or may, in the discretion of the Commissioner, be allotted to any one dependant. 
[sub-s (5)]. 
Where any compensation deposited with the Commissioner is payable to any per- 
son the Commissioner shall, if the person to whom the compensation is payable is 
65. Rule 5, /bid. 


510 Part VIII—The Workmen’s Compensation Act, 1923 
not a woman or a person under a legal disability, and may, in other cases, pay the 
money to the person who is entitled to it. [Sub-s. (6)]. 
When any lump sum deposited with the Commissioner is payable to a woman or a 
person under a legal disability, such sum may be invested, applied or otherwise dealt 
with for the benefit of the woman, or of such person during his disability, in such 
manner as the Commissioner may direct; and where a half-monthly payment is pay- 
able to any person under a legal disability, the Commissioner may, of his own motion 
or on an application made to him, order that the payment be made during the disabil- 
ity to any dependant of the workman or to any other person, whom the Commis- 
sioner thinks best fitted to provide for the welfare of the workman. [Sub-S. (7)]. 
Where on an application made to him or otherwise, the Commissioner is satisfied 
that, on account of neglect of children on the part of a parent or on account of the 
variation of the circumstances of any dependant or for any other sufficient cause, an 
order of the Commissioner as to the distribution of any sum paid as compensation or 
as to the manner in which any sum payable to any such dependant is to be invested, 
applied or otherwise dealt with, ought to be varied the Commissioner may make such 
orders for the variation of the former order as he thinks just in the circumstances of 
the case: 
The proviso to the sub-section says that no such order as is prejudicial to any per- 
son shall be made unless such person has been given an opportunity of showing 
cause why the order should not be made, or shall be made in any case in which it 
would involve the repayment by a dependant of any sum already paid to him [Sub-s. 
(8)]. 
Where the Commissioner varies any order under sub-section (8) by reason of the 
fact that payment of compensation to any person has been obtained by fraud, imper- 
sonation or other improper means, any amount so paid to or on behalf of such person 
may be recovered in the manner provided in section 31. [Sub-s. (9)]. 
From the bare perusal of section 8, it becomes clear that no compensation had to be 
paid in respect of a workman whose injury has resulted in death except by deposit 
with the commissioner and no such payment made directly by an employer shall be 
deemed to be a payment of compensation. This statutory provision prohibits an em- 
ployer from making any payment of compensation in respect of the death of a work- 
man directly to his heirs and legal representatives or any one of them. The employer 
has to deposit the amount of compensation with the Commissioner for the purpose 
and it is also provided that any direct payment made contrary to this provision shall 
be no payment. 
The object of section 8 is that an unscrupulous employer should not take advantage of the ignorance of the employee in making payment of a paltry sum. Therefore, the Act safeguards the interest of the workers by providing that any private payment will not discharge the statutory obligation. 
16. Compensation not to be assigned, attached or charged (s. 9) 
Section 9 says that save as provided by the Act, no lump sum or half-monthly 
payment payable under the Act shall in any way be capable of being assigned or charged, or liable to be attached or pass to any person other than the workman by operation of law, nor shall any claim be set off against the same.
