17. Notice of accident by workman or dependants (s. 10) 
The first thing that a workman, who is injured as a result of an accident, must do is 
to give in writing a notice of the accident. This has to be done as soon as practicable 
after the occurrence of the accident. Such a notice must contain, (1) name and ad- 
dress of the workman injured, (2) the date of the accident, and (3) the cause of the 
injury. The notice is to be served on the employer or upon any one of several em- 
ployers or upon any person who is responsible to the employer for the management 
of the branch of trade or business where the injured workman was employed. The 
notice may be delivered to the person concerned by hand or sent by registered post 
addressed to the residence or any office or place of business of the person to whom it 
is addressed. The State Government has been empowered to direct any prescribed 
class of employers to maintain at their premises where workmen are employed a no- 
tice book in the prescribed form. A notice book, when so directed to be kept, should 
be readily accessible at all reasonable times to any injured workman employed on the 
premises or to any person acting bona fide on behalf of the injured workman. An 
entry in such a notice book would be considered to be sufficient notice of the acci- 
dent to the employer. 
18. Notice of claim [s. 10] 
No claim for compensation shall be entertained by a Commissioner unless notice of the 
accident has been given in the prescribed manner as soon as practicable after the hap- 
pening and unless the claim is preferred before him within two years of the occurrence of 
the accident or, in the case of death, within [two years] from the date of death. 
The first proviso says that, where the accident is the contacting of a disease in re- 
spect of which the provisions of Section 3(2) are applicable, the accident shall be 
deemed to have occurred on the first of the days during which the workman was 
continuously absent from work in consequence of the disablement caused by the dis- 
ease. 
The second proviso says that in case of partial disablement due to the contacting of 
any such disease and which does not force the workman to absent himself from 
work, the period of two years shall be counted from the day the workman gives no- 
tice of the disablement to his employer. 
The third proviso says that if a workman who, having been employed in an em- 
ployment for a continuous period, specified under section 3(2) in respect of that em- 
ployment, ceases to be so employed and develops symptoms of an occupational dis- 
ease peculiar to that employment within two years of cessation of employment, the 
accident shall be deemed to have occurred on the day on which the symptoms were 
first detected. 
(a) Effect of want of notice, or any defect or irregularity in it 
The fourth proviso says that the want of or any defect or irregularity in a_ notice 
shall not be a bar to the entertainment of a claim— 
(a) if the claim is preferred in respect of the death of a workman resulting from 
an accident which occurred on the premises of the employer, or at any place 
where the workman at the time of the accident was working under the con- 
trol of the employer or of any person employed by him and the workman 
died on such premises or at such place, or on any premises belonging to the 
employer, or died without having left the vicinity of the premises or place 
were the accident occurred, or 


512 Part VIIJ—The Workmen’s Compensation Act, 1923 
(b) if the employer or any one of several employers or any person responsible 
to the employer for the management of any branch of the trade or business 
in which the injured workman was employed had knowledge of the acci- 
dent from any other source at or about the time when it occurred. 
The fifth proviso says that the Commissioner may entertain and decide any claim 
to compensation in any case notwithstanding that the notice has not been given, or 
the claim has not been preferred, in due time as provided in this sub-section, if he is 
satisfied that the failure so to give the notice or prefer the claim, as the case may be, 
was due to sufficient cause [Sub-s. (1)]. 
(b) Contents of notice and on whom to be served 
Every such notice shall give the name and address of the person injured and shall 
state in ordinary language the cause of the injury and the date on which the accident 
happened, and shall be served on the employer or upon any one of several employers, 
or upon any person responsible to the employer for the management of any branch of 
the trade or business in which the injured workman was employed. [sub-s. (2)]. 
(c) Notice book as to accidents 
The State Government may require that any prescribed class of employers shall 
maintain at their premises at which workmen are employed a notice book, in the pre- 
scribed form, which shall be readily accessible at all reasonable times to any injured 
workman employed on the premises and to any person acting bona fide on his behalf. 
[sub-s. (3)]. 
(d) Mode of service of notice 
A notice under this section may be served by delivering it at, or sending it by reg- 
istered post addressed to, the residence or any office or place of business of the per- 
son on whom it is to be served, or where a notice book is maintained, by entry in the 
notice book. [Sub-s. (4)]. 
(e€) Condonation of delay 
When there was one year delay in filing the claim for compensation and Commis- sioner refused to condone delay because no sufficient cause was shown, it was held that following the observation of the Supreme Court in the case Trustees of Bombay Port v. Premiere Automobiles® and the injunctions contained in the judgement, which were made in a purely commercial cause, would apply with still greater force in the case of compensation claims under the Workmen’s Compensation Act. It is hoped public authorities would desist from raising pleas of delay in future appropri- ate Cases irrespective of the margin of delay. The State and its limbs should try to avoid defending a claim on the technical plea of delay or limitations avoiding an or- der on merits. 
Tribunal and quasi-judicial authorities must bear in mind that while refusal to con- done delay might result in injustice by a meritorious case being thrown out without trial. Condonotion of delay would at the highest result in decision of the case on merits. 
68. AIR 1974 SC 923. 


Chap. II—Workmen’s Compensation 513 
Further no litigant ordinarily stands to benefit by instituting proceeding beyond 
time and there is no presumption that the delay has been occasioned deliberately on 
account of culpable negligence or that there was want of bona fides. 
The presumption, if any, would be the other way round. Pedantic and unpragmatic 
approach should not be made to the matter and the Court need not be overstrict in 
expecting proof of the suggested sufficient cause. The discretion to condone or not to 
condone the delay has to be exercised with circumspection according to justice, 
common sense and sound judgment and for advancing substantial justice. All facts 
including the status and background of the parties, the previous history, if any, of the 
litigation and the conduct of the parties therein up to the date of claim, the period and 
circumstances leading to the delay and the probity of the suggested cause for delay, 
the quality of legal assistance, guidance and advice received by the defaulting liti- 
gant, difficult terrain and weather etc. are all matters which shall enter into consid- 
eration. 
19. Power to require from employers statements regarding fatal accidents (s. 10-A) 
Where a Commissioner receives information from any source that a workman has 
died as a result of an accident arising out of and in the course of his employment, it 
may send by registered post a notice to the workman’s employer requiring him to 
submit, within thirty days of the service of the notice, a statement in the prescribed 
form, giving the circumstances attending the death of the workman, and indicating 
whether, in the opinion of the employer, he is or is not liable to deposit compensation 
on account of the death. [Sec. 10A(1)] 
If the employer is of opinion that he is liable to deposit compensation, he shall 
make the deposit within thirty days of the service of the notice. [Sec. 10A(2))] 
If the employer is of opinion that he is not liable to deposit compensation, he shall 
in his statement-indicate the grounds on which he disclaims liability. [Sec. 10A(3)] 
Where the employer has so disclaimed liability, the Commissioner, after such in- 
quiry as he may think fit, may inform any of the dependants of the deceased work- 
man that it is open to them to prefer a claim for compensation, and may give them 
such other further information as he may think fit. [Sec. lOA(4)] 
20. Reports of fatal accidents and serious bodily injury (s. 10B) 
Where, by any law for the time being in force, notice is required to be given to any 
authority, by or on behalf of an employer, of any accident occurring on his premises 
which results in death [or serious bodily injury], the person required to give the no- 
tice shall, within seven days of the death or serious bodily injury, send a report to the 
Commissioner giving the circumstances attending the death or serious bodily injury. 
The proviso says that where the State Government has so prescribed the person re- 
quired to give the notice may instead of sending such report to the Commissioner 
send it to the authority to whom he is required to give the notice. 
The explanation to the section says that a “serious bodily injury” means an injury 
which involves, or in all probability will involve, the permanent loss of the use of, or

21. Medical examination (s. 11) 
Before the expiry of three days from the date of receipt of the notice of accident, 
the employer may require the injured workman to submit himself to a medical ex- 
amination at the employer’s expense and when so required the workman has to sub- 
mit to such an examination. In respect of such medical examination, the Government 
has framed rules and the employer has to observe those rules and cannot go beyond 
those rules. The rules lay down that if the injured workman is present on the em- 
ployer’s premises and the employer asks him to submit to a medical examination by 
a medical practitioner who is also present on the premises, the workman must imme- 
diately submit himself to the examination. In other cases, the employer has to send 
the medical practitioner to the place where the workman is residing for the time be- 
ing and the workman has to submit to a medical examination when required by the 
medical practitioner. The employer may also inform the workman in writing that the 
medical examination would take place either at the employer’s place or at any other 
place in the vicinity as specified in the intimation. 
22. Provisions for examination of females 
A female workman can be examined by a male medical practitioner only in the 
presence of some other woman unless the female workman consents otherwise. A 
female workman can insist on being examined by a female medical practitioner but 
in that case the workman will have to dep¢sit a sum sufficient to cover the expenses 
of an examination by a female practitioner. 
23. Consequences of non-submission to medical examination 
If a workman refuses to submit himself to a medical examination or in any way ob- 
structs such examination, his right to compensation is suspended during the period of 
such refusal or obstruction. In the case of refusal, however, this result will not follow 
if the workman establishes that he was prevented from submitting himself to medical 
examination on account of sufficient cause.’’ The right of a workman to receive 
compensation is also suspended, if the workman, who has been asked by his em- ployer to submit to medical examination within three days from the receipt of the 
notice of accident, voluntarily leaves the place without having been so examined. In such a case the suspension will continue till the workman concerned returns and 
submits to medical examination." Such medical examination has to take place within seventy-two hours after the workman has offered himself for examination.

24. Contracting (s. 12) 
According to section 12, where any person (principal) in the course of or for the 
purposes of his trade or business contracts with any other person (contractor) for the 
execution by or under the contractor of the whole or any part of any work which is 
ordinarily part of the trade or business of the principal, the principal shall be liable to 
pay to any workman employed in the execution of the work any compensation which 
he would have been liable to pay if that workman had been immediately employed 
by him. Where compensation is claimed from the principal the Act would apply as if 
references to the principal were substituted for references to the employer except that 
the amount of compensation shall be calculated with reference to the wages of the 
workman under the employer by whom he is immediately employed. [Sub-s. (1)]. 
Where the principal is liable to pay compensation under this section, he will be en- 
titled to be indemnified by the contractor, or any other person from whom the work- 
man could have recovered compensation. Where a contractor who is himself a prin- 
cipal is liable to pay compensation or to indemnify a principal under this section, he 
shall be entitled to be indemnified by any person standing to him in the relation of a 
contractor from whom the workman could have recovered compensation. All ques- 
tions as to the right to and the amount of any such indemnity shall, in default of 
agreement, be settled by the Commissioner. [Sub-s. (2)]. 
Nothing in this section shall be construed as preventing a workman from recover- 
ing compensation from the contractor instead of the principal [Sub-s. (3)]. 
This section does not apply in any case where the accident occurred elsewhere that 
on, in or about the premises on which the principal has undertaken or usually under- 
takes, as the case may be, to execute the work or which are otherwise under his con- 
trol or management. 
Section 12 prescribes that a person who is engaging a contractor for the execution 
of a contract work relating to his trade or business, would be the principal and he 
would be equally liable for payment of compensation to a workman for perusal inju- 
ries under section 3 of the Act. A workman who is engaged by a contractor in exe- 
cution of contract work which is a part of the business of another person, who would 
be the principal, he would be liable for payment of compensation in the event of ac- 
cidental injury to the workman. |

516 Part VIII—The Workmen’s Compensation Act, 1923 
For the purposes of the operation of setion12, the following conditions are required 
to be satisfied :— 
(i) That the principal is carrying on trade or business and in the course of or 
for the purpose of that trade or business engages a contractor. 
(ii) That the work in question is ordinarily a part of trade or business of the 
principal. 
(iii) That the accident had occurred in or about the premises on which the prin- 
cipal has undertaken or usually undertakes to execute the work or which is 
in his control or management, and 
(iv) The accident occurred while the workman was in the course of his em- 
ployment in executing that work. 
If all the aforesaid essential conditions are satisfied then the principal can be made 
liable under session 12 of the Act for payment of compensation under section 3 of 
the Act. 
In view of the clear previsions in section 12 of the Act, a right is given to the 
workman to claim compensation either from the contractor, being the employer or 
from the principal or from both. Thus, option is given to the victim of employment 
injuries to claim compensation either from the principal or employer. The very ob- 
ject behind the provisions of section 12 of the Act is to secure compensation to the 
workman who cannot otherwise fight out his battle for compensation by a speedy 
process. A person who employs others to advance his own business and interest is 
expected to provide a surer basis for payment of the injured workman than the inter- 
mediary, who may often turn out to be a man of straw, from whom compensation 
may not be available. 
25. Remedies of employer against stranger [s. 13] 
Where a workman has recovered compensation in respect of any injury caused un- 
der circumstances creating a legal liability of some person other than the person by 
v’hom the compensation was paid to pay damages in respect thereof, the person by 
wom the compensation was paid and any person who has been called on to pay an 
indemnity under Section 12 shall be entitled to indemnity by the person so liable to 
pay damages. 
26. Insolvency of employer (s. 14) 
Where any employer has entered into a contract with any insurers in respect of any 
liability under the Act to any workman, then in the event of the employer becoming 
insolvent or making a composition or scheme of arrangement with his creditors or, if the employer is a company, in the event of the company having commenced to be 
wound up, the rights of the employer against the insurers as respect of that liability shall, notwithstanding anything in any law for the time being in force relating to in- 
solvency or the winding up of companies, be transferred to and vest in the workman, 
and upon any such transfer the insurers shall have the same rights and remedies and be subject to the same liabilities as if they were the employer, so, however, that the insurers shall not be under any greater liability to the workman than they would have 
been to the employer [Sub-s. (1)].

If the liability of the insurer to the workman is less than the liability of the em- 
ployer to the workman, the workman may prove for the balance in the insolvency 
proceedings or liquidation [Sub-s. (2)]. 
Where in any case as is referred to in sub-section (1), the contract of the employer 
with the insurers is void or avoidable by reason of non-compliance on the part of the 
employer with any terms or conditions of the contract (other than a stipulation for the 
payment of premia), the provisions of that sub-section shall apply as if the contract 
were not void or violable, and the insurers shall be entitled to prove in the insolvency 
proceedings or liquidation for the amount paid to the workman. 
The proviso to the sub-section says that the provisions of this sub-section shall not 
apply in any case in which the workman fails to give the notice to the insurers of the 
happening of the accident and of any resulting disablement as soon as practicable 
after he becomes aware of the institution of the insolvency or liquidation proceedings

There shall be deemed to be included among the debts which under section 49 of

Insolvency Act, 1920, or under Section 530 of the Indian Companies Act, 1956, are 
in the distribution of the property of an insolvent or in the distribution of the assets of 
a company being wound up to be paid in priority to all other debts, the amount due in 
respect of any compensation the liability where for accrued before the date of the 
order of adjudication of the insolvent or the date of the commencement of the wind- 
ing up, as the case may be, and those Acts shall have effect accordingly [Sub-s. (4)]. 
Where the compensation is a half-monthly payment, the amount due in respect 
thereof shall, for the purposes of this section, be taken to be the amount of the lump 
sum for which the half-monthly payment could, if redeemable, be redeemed if appli- 
cations were made for that purpose under Section 7, and a certificate of the Commis- 
sioner as to the amount of such sum shall be conclusive proof thereof [Sub-s. (5)]. 
The provisions of sub-section (4) shall apply in the case of any amount for which 
an insurer is entitled to prove under sub-section (3), but otherwise those provisions 
shall not apply where the insolvent or the company being wound up has entered into 
such a contract with insurers as is referred to in sub-section. [Sub-s. (6)]. 
This section shall not apply where a company is wound up voluntarily merely for 
the purposes of reconstruction or of amalgamation with another company [Sub-s. 
(7)]. 
A reading of the provisions of section 14 makes it clear that it makes provision in 
case of an insolvency of an employer by giving worker the right to proceed against 
the insurance company in respect of liability insured by the insurance company. In- 
surance company cannot be made liable unless the employers have become insol- 
vent.

28. Special provisions relating to masters and seamen (s. 15) 
According to section 15, the Act shall apply in the case of workmen who are mas- 
ters of ships or seamen subject to the following modifications, namely— 
(1) The notice of the accident and the claim for compensation may, except where 
the person injured is the master of the ship, be served on the master of the ship as if 
he were employer, but where the accident happened and the disablement commenced 
on board the ship it shall not be necessary for any seamen to give any notice of the 
accident. 
(2) In case of the death of a master or seamen, the claim for compensation shall be 
made within one year after the news of the death has been received by the claimant 
or, where the ship has been or is deemed to have been lost with all hands, within 
eighteen months of the date on which the ship was, or is deemed to have been so lost: 
The proviso to the sub-section says that the Commissioner may entertain any claim 
to compensation in any case notwithstanding that the claim has not been preferred in 
the time as provided in the sub-section, if he is satisfied that the failure so to prefer 
the claim was due to sufficient cause. 
Where an injured master or seamen is discharged or left behind in any part of India 
or in any foreign country any depositions taken by a Judge or Magistrate in that part 
or by any consular officer in the foreign country and transmitted by the person by 
whom they are taken to the Central Government or any State Government shall, in 
auy proceedings for enforcing the claim, be admissible in evidence. 
(a) if the deposition is authenticated by the signature of the Judge, Magistrate 
or Consular Officer before whom it is made; 
(b) if the dependent or the person accused, as the case may be, had an opportu- 
nity by himself or as agent to cross examine the witness, and. 
(c) if the deposition was made in the course of a criminal proceedings on proof 
that the deposition was made in the presence of the person accused. 
It shall not be necessary in any case to prove the signature or official character of the person appearing to have signed any such deposition and a certificate by such person that the defendant or the persons accused had an opportunity to cross examine the witness and that the deposition if made in a criminal proceedings was made in the presence of the person accused shall, unless the contrary is proved, be sufficient evi- dence that he had that opportunity and that it was so made. 
No half-monthly payment shall be payable in respect of the period during which the owner of the ship is, under any law in force for the time being relating to mer- chant shipping, liable to defray the expenses of the maintenance of the injured master or seaman.

Chap. II—Workmen’s Compensation 519 
No compensation shall be payable under the Act in respect of any injury in respect 
of which provision is made for payment of a gratuity, allowance or pension under the 
War Pensions and Detention Allowances (Mercantile Marine, etc.) Scheme, 1939, or 
the War Pensions and Detention Allowances (Indian Seaman etc.) Scheme, 1941, or 
under the Pensions (Navy, Army, Air Force and Mercantile Marine) Act, 1939, or 
under the War Pensions and Detention Allowances (Indian Seaman) Scheme, 1942, 
made by the Central Government. 
Failure to give a notice or make a claim or commence proceedings within the time 
required by the Act shall not be a bar to the maintenance of proceedings under the 
Act in respect of any personal injury if— 
(a) an application has been made for payment in respect of that injury under 
any of the schemes referred to in the proceeding clause, and 
(b) the State Government certifies that the said application was made in the 
reasonable belief that the injury was one in respect of which the scheme 
under which the application was made makes provision for payments, and 
that the application was rejected or that payments made in pursuance of the 
application were discontinued on the ground that the injury was not such an 
injury, and 
(c) the proceedings under the Act are commenced within one month from the 
date on which the certificate of the State Government was furnished to the 
person commencing the proceedings. 
29. Special provisions relating to captains and members of crew of aircrafts (s. 
15A) 
The Act applies in the case of workmen who are captains or other members of the 
crew of aircrafts subject to the following modifications, namely:— 
(1) The notice of the accident and the claim for compensation may, except 
where the person injured is the captain of the aircraft, be served on the 
captain of the aircraft as if he were the employer, but where the accident 
happened and the disablement commenced on board the aircraft it shall not 
be necessary for any member of the crew to give notice of the accident. 
(2) In the case of the death of the captain or other member of the crew, the 
claim for compensation shall be made within one year after the news of the 
death has been received by the claimant or, where the aircraft has been or is 
deemed to have been lost with all hands, within eighteen months of the date 
on which the aircraft was, or is deemed to have been, so lost: 
The proviso attached to the sub-section says that the Commissioner may entertain 
any claim for compensation in any case notwithstanding that the claim has not been 
preferred in due time as provided in this sub-section, if he is satisfied that the failure 
so to prefer the claim was due to sufficient cause. 
(3) Where an injured captain or other member of the crew of the aircraft is dis- 
charged or left behind in any part of India or in any other country any depo- 
sitions taken by any Judge or Magistrate in that part or by any Consular Of- 
ficer in the foreign country and transmitted by the person by whom they are 
taken to the Central Government or any State Government shall in any pro- 
ceedings for enforcing the claims, be admissible in evidence—

30. Special provision relating to workmen abroad of companies and motor ve- 
hicles (s. 15B) 
Section 15B says that the Act shall apply— 
(1) in the case of workmen who are persons recruited by companies registered 
in India and working as such abroad, and 
(ii) persons sent for work along with motor vehicles registered under the Motor 
Vehicles Act, 1988 as drivers, helpers, mechanics, cleaners or other work- 
men, subject to the following modifications, namely:— 
(1) The notice of the accident and the claim for compensation may be 
served on the local agent of the company, or the local agent of the 
owner of the motor vehicle, in the country of accident, as the case 
may be. 
(2) In the case of death of the workman in respect of whom the provi- 
sions of this section shall apply, the claim for compensation shall be 
made within one year after the news of the death has been received 
by the claimant: 
Provided that the Commissioner may entertain any claim for com- 
pensation in any case notwithstanding that the claim has not been 
preferred in due time as provided in this sub-section, if he is satisfied 
that the failure to prefer the claim was due to sufficient cause. 
(3) Where an injured workman is discharged or left behind in any part of 
India or in any other country, any depositions taken by any Judge or 
Magistrate in that part or by any Consular Officer in the foreign 
country and transmitted by the person by whom they are taken to the 
Central Government or any State Government shall, in any proceed- 
ings for enforcing the claims, be admissible in evidence— 
(a) if the deposition is authenticated by the signature of the Judge, 
Magistrate or Consular Officer before whom it is made; 
(b) if the defendant or the person accused, as the case may be, had 
an opportunity by himself or his agent to cross-examine the 
witness;

31. Returns as to compensation (s. 16) 
The State Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, direct that 
every person employing workmen, or that any specified class of such persons, shall 
send at such time and in such from and to such authority, as may be specified in the 
notification, a correct, return specifying the number of injuries in respect of which 
compensation has been paid by the. employer during the previous year and the 
amount of such compensation together with such other particulars as to the compen- 
sation as the State Government may direct. 
32. Contracting out (s. 17) 
Any contract or agreement whether made before or after the commencement of the 
Act, whereby a workman relinquishes any right of compensation from the employer 
for personal injury arising out of or in the course of the employment, shall be null 
and void in so far as it purports to remove or reduce the liability of any person to pay 
compensation under the Act. | 
Any settlement or contract by which the workmen relinquishes the right of com- 
pensation from the employer for personal injury in so far as it purports to remove or 
reduce the liability of any person to pay compensation under the Act is null and 
void. 
33. Penalties (S. 18A) 
If an employer fails to maintain a notice book when so required to maintain it, or 
fails to send a fatal accident report or a statement regarding fatal accidents or fails to 
submit returns as to compensation, he shall be punishable with a fine which may ex- 
tend to five thousand rupees. A prosecution in respect of such cases can be started 
only by the Commissioner or with the previous sanction of the Commissioner. The 
complaint in that respect has further to be filed within six months of the date on 
which the offence is alleged to have been committed.

1. Reference to Commissioners (s. 19) 
Under section 19, if any question as to liability to pay compensation or amount of 
compensation arises, the Commissioner has been empowered to settle the question. 
Section 19 says that if any question in any proceeding under the Act as to the liability 
of any person to pay compensation (including any question as to whether a_ person 
injured is or is not a workman) or as to the amount or duration of compensation (in- 
cluding any question as to the nature of extent of disablement), the question shall, in 
default of agreement be settled by the Commissioner. [Sub-s. (1)] 
Sub-section (2) says that no civil court shall have jurisdiction to settle, decide or, 
deal with any question which is or by the Act required to be settled, dealt with or 
decided by a Commissioner or to enforce any liability incurred under the Act. 
The Commissioner is not a court within the meaning of section115 of the Code of 
Civil Procedure. The order passed by him under section 19 is not revisable by the 
High Court.’ 
2. Appointment of Commissioners (s. 20) 
The State Government may be notification in the Official Gazette, appoint any per- 
son to be a Commissioner for Workmen’s Compensation Act for such area as may be 
specified in the notification. [Sec. 20(1)] 
1. The Act does not exhaust all remedies. A tort action has been held to be maintainable for additional 
compensation, Jasuben v. Gujarat Electricity Board, (1999) 2 Lab LJ 466 (Gu)j). 
2. Y.R. Sharamji v. S. Tukaram, 1978 MPLJ. 853 at p. 856. See New India Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Jo- 
seph, (2000) 1 Lab LJ 1063 (Ker), the Commissioner can direct the insurer to pay compensation 
even in contingencies other than those specified in s. 14 provided there is no policy against it; in- 
surer will come within the scope of “any person” in s. 19 and thus subject to the jurisdiction of the 
Commissioner. Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Satvir Singh, workman losing both eyes, compensa- 
tion awarded against the same, no tenable ground of appeal could be shown. United India Insurance

stated in s. 149(2) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988.

Where more than one Commissioner has been appointed for any area, the State 
Government may by general or special order, regulate the distribution of business 
between them. [Sec. 20(2)] 
Any Commissioner may, for the purpose of deciding any matter referred to him for 
decision under the Act, choose one or more persons possessing special knowledge of 
any matter relevant to the matter under inquiry to assist him in holding the inquiry. 
[Sec. 20(3)] 
Every Commissioner shall be deemed to be a public servant within the meaning of 
the Indian Penal Code, 1860. [Sec. 20(4) 
3. Venue of proceedings (s. 21) 
Where any matter is under the Act to be done by or before a Commissioner, the 
same shall, subject to the provisions of the Act and to any rules made under it, be 
done by or before a Commissioner for the area in which the accident took place 
which resulted in the injury: 
Provided that, where the workman is the master of a ship or a seaman, any such 
matter may be done by or before a Commissioner] for the area in which the owner or 
agent of the ship resided or carries on business. [Sec. 21(1)] 
4. Transfers (s. 21) 
If 2 Commissioner is satisfied that any matter arising out of any proceedings 
pending before him can be more conveniently dealt with by any other Commissioner 
whether in the same State or not, he may, subject to rules made under the Act, order 
such matter to be transferred to such other Commissioner either for report or for dis- 
posal, and if he does so, shall forthwith transmit to such other Commissioner all 
documents relevant for the decision of such matter and, where the matter is trans- 
ferred for disposal, shall also transmit in the prescribed manner any money remaining 
in his hands or invested by him for the benefit of any party to the proceedings : 
Provided that the Commissioner shall not, where any party to the proceedings has 
appeared before him, make any order or transfer relating to the distribution among 
dependants of a lump sum without giving such party an opportunity of being heard: 
Provided further, that no matter other than a matter relating to the actual payment 
to a workman or the distribution among dependants of a lump sum shall be trans- 
ferred for disposal under this sub-section to a Commissioner in the same State save 
with the previous sanction of the State Government or to a Commissioner in another 
State save with the previous sanction of the State Government of that State, unless 
all the parties to the proceedings agree to the transfer. [Sec. 21(2)] 
Where any proceeding pending before the Commissioner is sought to be trans- 
ferred before any other Commissioner, such transfer cannot be ordered by the Com- 
missioner himself but will require previous sanction of the State Government under 
whom he works. If the second Commissioner works for another State, then prior 
sanction of the Government of that State is required to be obtained for transfer. 
The Commissioner to whom any matter is so transferred shall, subject to rules 
made under the Act, inquire into them and, if the matter was transferred for report, 
return his report thereon or if the matter was transferred for disposal, continue the 
proceedings as if they had originally commenced before him. [Sec. 21(3)] 
3. United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Sasikala Sahoo, (1995) 2 LLJ 1235 (Ori).

On receipt of a report from a Commissioner to whom any matter has been trans- 
ferred for report under sub-section (2), the Commissioner by whom it was referred 
shall decide the matter referred in conformity with such report. 
The State Government may transfer any matter from any Commissioner appointed 
by it to any other Commissioner appointed by it. 
5. Power and procedure of Commissioners (s. 23) 
The Commissioner shall have all the powers of a Civil Court under the Code of 
Civil Procedure, 1908, for the purpose of taking evidence on oath (which such 
Commissioner is hereby empowered to impose) and of enforcing the attendance of 
witnesses and compelling the production of documents and material objects. The 
Commissioner shall be deemed to be a Civil Court, for all the purposes of Section 
195 and of Chapter XXXV of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898. [Sec. 23] 
Where the medical practitioner estimated disability at 50%, but also opined that the 
driver (workman) would not be able to drive any vehicle, and taking this into consid- 
eration the Commissioner estimated the disability at 90%, it was held that he was 
right in holding it as a case of total disablement.” Loss of earning power need not 
necessarily coextensive with the loss of physical capability. It is not for the medical 
practitioner to certify as to loss of earning power while certifying percentage of dis- 
ability. It is for the Commissioner to assess and fix the percentage of disability’. The 
Commissioner can fix percentage of disability which is at variance with that of the 
doctor. The Court also added that the doctor’s medical certificate can be admitted 
without examining him. Where an application is filed before the Commissioner not 
having jurisdiction, the principle of Res Judicata does not come into play between 
_ the parties. No culpable negligence or misconduct can be attributed to the workmen 
in such a case. Consequent delay in filing a fresh application before the Commis- 
sioner having jurisdiction shall be condoned. 
6. Form of application (s. 22) 
Where an accident occurs in respect of which liability to pay compensation under 
the Act arises, a claim for such compensation may, subject to the provisions of the 
Act, be made before the Commissioner. [Sub-s. (1)] 
Subject to the provisions of sub-section (1), no application for the settlement of 
any matter by a Commissioner, other than an application by a dependant or depend- 
ants for compensation, shall be made unless and until some question has arisen be- 
tween the parties in connection with it which they have been unable to settle by 
agreement. [Sub-s. (1A)]. 
An application to a Commissioner may be made in such form and shall be accom- 
panied by such fee, if any, as may be prescribed, and shall contain, in addition to any 
particulars which may be prescribed the following particulars namely:— 
(a) a concise statement of the circumstances in which the application is made 
and the relief or order which the applicant claims; 
(b) in the case of a claim for compensation against an employer, the date of 
service of notice of the accident on the employer and, if such notice has not

If the applicant is illiterate or for any other reason is unable to furnish the required

7. Appearance of parties (s. 24) 
Any appearance, application or act required to be made or done by any person be- 
fore or to a Commissioner (other than appearance of a party which is required for the 
purpose of his examination as a witness) may be made or done on behalf of such per- 
son by a legal practitioner or by an official of an insurance company or a registered 
Trade Union or by an Inspector appointed under sub-section (1) of Section 8 of the 
Factories Act, 1948, or under Section 5(1) of the Mines Act, 1952, or by any other 
officer specified by the State Government, authorized in writing by such person, or, 
with the permission of the Commissioner, by any other person so authorised. 
8. Method of recording evidence (s. 25) 
Section 25 provides that the Commissioner shall make a brief memorandum of the 
substance of the evidence of every witness as the examination of the witness pro- 
ceeds, and such memorandum shall be written and signed by the Commissioner with 
his own hand and shall form part of the record: 
Provided that, if the Commissioner is prevented from making such memorandum, 
he shall record the reason of his inability to do so and shall cause such memorandum 
to be made in writing from his dictation and shall sign the same, and such memoran- 
dum shall form part of the record : 
Provided further that the evidence of any medical witness shall be taken down as 
nearly as may be word for word. 
9. Costs (s. 26) 
All costs incidental to any proceedings before a Commissioner shall, subject to 
rules made under the Act, be in the discretion of the Commissioner. 
10. Power to submit cases (s. 27) 
A Commissioner may, if he thinks fit, submit any question of law for the decision 
of the High Court and, if he does so, shall decide the question in conformity with 
such decision.

11. Registration of agreements (s. 28) 
Where the amount of any lump sum payable as compensation has been settled by 
agreement whether by way of redemption of a half-monthly payment or otherwise, or 
where any compensation has been so settled as being payable to a woman, or a per- 
son under a legal disability, a memorandum of it has to be sent by the employer to 
the Commissioner, who shall, on being satisfied as to its genuineness, record the 
memorandum in a register in the prescribed manner. But, 
(a) no such memorandum shall be recorded before seven days after communi- 
cation by the Commissioner of notice to the parties concerned; 
(b) omitted. 
(c) the Commissioner may at any time rectify the register; 
(d) where it appears to the Commissioner that an agreement as to the payment 
of a lump sum whether by way of redemption of a half-monthly payment or 
otherwise, or an agreement as to the amount of compensation payable, to a 
woman or a person under a legal disability, ought not to be registered by 
reason of the inadequacy of the sum or amount, or by reason of the agree- 
ment having been obtained by fraud or undue influence or other improper 
means, he may refuse to record the memorandum of the agreement and may 
make such order, including an order as to any sum already paid under the 
agreement as he thinks just in the circumstances. 
If the Commissioner considers that the amount of compensation is inadequate or 
that the agreement has been obtained by fraud or undue influence or other improper 
means, the Commissioner may refuse to register the agreement. For this purpose the 
Commissioner has to fix a date to hear the parties and give a notice to that effect to 
the parties concerned, which notice shall also state the grounds on which the Com- 
missioner thinks that the agreement should not be registered. If after hearing the par- 
ties the Commissioner comes to the conclusion that the agreement should not be 
registered, he has to inform the parties to that effect in the prescribed form. 
12. Agreement enforceable 
An agreement for the payment of compensation which has been registered under 
sub-section (1) is enforceable under the Act notwithstanding anything con-tined in 
the Indian Contract Act, 1872, or in any other law for the time being in force. 
13. Consequences of failure to register agreement (s-29) 
Where a memorandum of any agreement, the registration of which is required by 
section 28, is not sent to the Commissioner as required by that section, the employer 
shall be liable to pay the full amount of compensation which he is liable to pay under 
the provisions of the Act, and notwithstanding, anything contained in the proviso to 
sub-section (1) of section 4, shall not, unless the Commissioner otherwise directs, be 
entitled to deduct more than half of any amount paid to the workman by way of com- 
pensation whether under the agreement or otherwise. 
When the Commissioner refuses to register an agreement he has to briefly record 
his reasons for such refusal.’ In other cases the Commissioner shall fix a date for 
recording an agreement and send a notice to the parties about the same. If the parties 
are present before the Commissioner he can even give an oral notice of the date fixed 
9. Rules 50, 51, Workmen’s Compensation Rules. 


528 Part VIII—The Workmen's Compensation Act, 1923 
for recording the agreement. On the date so fixed the Commissioner shall register the 
agreement unless he considers, on hearing the parties that it should not be regis- 
tered.'° An agreement for payment of compensation when so registered becomes en- 
forceable under the provision of the Act in the same manner as an award by the 
Commissioner. 
14. Appeals and Reference [s. 30] 
So far as the proceedings under the Act are concerned the High Court of the State 
is the Appellate Court. If any question of law arises in an application before the 
Commissioner, he may, if he thinks fit, refer that question to the High Court for deci- 
sion and has to decide the matter in conformity with such decision. 
The right to appeal to the High Court against the orders of the Commissioner is not 
rendered nugatory by the condition to deposit compensation amount before prefer- 
ring the appeal. 
An appeal lies to the High Court from the following orders of a Commissioner, 
namely: 
(a) an order awarding as compensation a lump sum whether by way of re- 
demption of a half-monthly payment or otherwise or disallowing a claim in 
full or in part for a lump sum; 
(aa) an order awarding interest or penalty under Section 4A; 
(b) an order refusing to allow redemption of a half-monthly payment; 
(c) an order providing for the distribution of compensation among the depend- 
ants of a deceased workman, or disallowing any claim of a person alleging 
himself to be such dependant; 
(d) an order allowing or disallowing any claim for the amount of an indemnity 
under the provisions of Section 12(2); or 
Where a notice is issued by virtue of Sec. 12(2) to a Government Officer ° 
who might happen to be the principal employer, the period of limitation for 
execution of the order passed under the Act, will be 12 years under Sec. 
136 of the Limitation Act, 1963.'4 
(ce) an order refusing to register a memorandum of agreement or registering the 
same or providing for the registration of the same subject to conditions. 
No appeal lies against any order unless a substantial question of law is involved in the 
appeal and, in the case of an order other than an order such as is referred to in clause (b), 
unless the amount in dispute in the appeal is not less than three hundred rupees:

No appeal by an employer under clause (a) lies unless the memorandum of appeal 
is accompanied by a certificate by the Commissioner to the effect that the appellant 
has deposited with him the amount payable under the order appealed against. [Sub-s. 
B2T- 
The period of limitation for an appeal under this section is sixty days [Sub-s. (2)]. 
The provisions of Section 5 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908, shall be applicable 
to appeals under this section. 
The period of limitation for appeal under Sec. 30 will commence from the date of 
pronouncement of the order by the Commissioner and not from the date on which the 
communication of the order was given. 
Deposit of the amount of interest or penalty imposed under Sec. 4A of the Act in 
addition to the compensation awarded is not a condition precedent for preferring an 
appeal under Sec. 30(1). 
It must, however, be remembered that an appeal would lie against any of the above 
orders only if it involves a substantial question of law. It has, however, been held by 
the Calcutta High Court, that if once the condition that the appeal must involve a 
substantial question of law was satisfied, the High Court was entitled to consider the 
whole case and for that purpose to review the evidence on record and to decide ques- 
tions of fact.'® There is a further restriction on the right of appeal, namely, that, ex- 
cept in the case of an order refusing to allow redemption of half monthly payments, 
the amount in dispute in the appeal must exceed Rs. 300. 
When an employer intends to file an appeal against an order of the Commissioner 
awarding lump sum compensation, the memorandum of appeal must be accompanied 
by a certificate from the Commissioner to the effect that the employer has deposited 
with him the amount payable under the order appealed against. The Patna High 
Court, has, however, held that such a certificate was, no doubt, a material document 
which the law enjoins to be filed in order that the appeal may be entertained, but it 
was doubtful whether merely because of the non-production of the certificate within 
the period of limitation the appeal would be barred. 
The limitation for filing an appeal is sixty days from the date of the order of the 
Commissioner. The delay in filing an appeal can be excused by the High Court if it is 
satisfied that there is sufficient cause for not filing the appeal in time. 
Where an appeal lies against the decision of the Commissioner, the Court will not 
disturb the finding of the facts already made by the Commissioner, if they are sup- 
portable otherwise, even though the court can come to a different conclusion. 
The insurer should deposit the claim amount while making an appeal against an 
award of compensation amount. The appeal by the insurer should be treated as 
making a grievance on behalf of the insured (the employer) because it is the latter

15. Withholding of certain payments pending decision of appeal (s. 30) 
Where an employer makes an appeal under section 30(1)(a), the Commissioner 
may, and if so, directed by the High Court, shall, pending the decision of the appeal, 
withhold payment of any sum in deposit with him. 
16. Recovery (s. 31) 
The Commissioner may recover as an arrear of land-revenue any amount payable 
by any person under the Act, whether under an agreement for the payment of com- 
pensation or otherwise, and the Commissioner shall be deemed to be a public officer 
within the meaning of section 5 of the Revenue Recovery Act, 1890.

1. Power of the State Government to make rules (s. 32) 
1. The State Government may make rules to carry out the purposes-of this Act. 
2. In particular and without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing power, such 
rules may provide for all or any of the following matters namely: 
(a) for prescribing the intervals at which and the conditions subject to which an 
application for review may be made under section 6 when not accompanied 
by a medical certificate; 
(b) for prescribing the intervals at which and the conditions subject to which a 
workman may be required to submit himself for medical examination under 
sub-section (1) of section 11; 
(c) for prescribing the procedures to be followed by commissioner in the dis- 
posal of cases under this Act and by the parties in such cases; 
(d) for regulating the transfer of matters and cases from one Commissioner to 
another and the transfer of money in such cases; 
(e) for prescribing the manner in which money in the hands of a Commissioner 
may be invested for the benefit of dependants of a deceased workman and 
for the transfer of money so invested from one Commissioner to another; 
(f) for the representation in proceedings before Commissioners of parties who 
are minors or are unable to make an appearance; 
(g) for prescribing the form and manner in which memoranda of agreements 
shall be presented and registered; 
(h) for the withholding by Commissioners; whether in whole or in part of half- 
monthly payments pending decision on applications for review of the same; 
(i) for regulating the scales of costs which may be allowed in proceedings un- 
der this Act; 
(j) for prescribing and determining the amount of the fees payable in respect of 
any proceedings before a Commissioner under this Act; 
(k) for the maintenance by Commissioner of registers and records of proceed- 
ings before them; 
531 


Joz Part VIII—The Workmen’s Compensation Act, 1923 
(1) for prescribing the classes of employers who shall maintain notice-books 
under sub-section (3) of section 10, and the form of such notice-books; 
(m) for prescribing the form of statement to be submitted by employers under 
section 10 A; 
(n) for prescribing the cases in which the report referred to in section 10B may 
be sent to an authority other than the Commissioner; 
(o) for prescribing abstracts of this Act and requiring the employers to display 
notices containing such abstracts; 
(p) for prescribing the manner in which diseases specified as occupational dis- 
eases may be diagnosed; 
(q) for prescribing the manner in which diseases may be certified for any of the 
purposes of this Act; 
(r) for prescribing the manner in which, and the standards by which, incapacity 
may be assessed. 
3. Every rule made under this section shall be laid, as soon as may be after it is 
made, before the State Legislature. 
2. Publication of Rules (s. 34) 
(1) The power to make rules conferred by section 32 shall be subject to the condi- 
tion of the rules being made after previous publication. 
(2) The date to be specified in accordance with clause (3) of section 23 of the Gen- 
eral Clauses Act, 1897 (10 to 1897) as that after which a draft of rules proposed to be 
made under section 32 will be taken into consideration, shall not be less than three 
months from the date on which the draft of the proposed rules was published for gen- 
eral information. 
(3) Rules so made shall be published in the Official Gazette and on such publica- 
tion, shall have effect as if enacted in this Act.

The Employees’ State Insurance Act, 1948 is an “Act to provide for certain bene- 
fits to employees in case of sickness, maternity and employment injury and to make 
- provision for certain other matters in relation thereto”. 
1. Objectives of social security 
The objectives of social security can be achieved through a self-balancing scheme 
of social insurance or by public assistance (i.e. contributions from general revenue) 
1. Transport Corporation of India v. ESI Corpn., (2000) 1 SCC 332 : AIR 2000 SC 238, the object is 
to provide certain benefit to employees. 
545 


546 Part IX—The Employees’ State Insurance Act, 1948 
or a combination of the two methods. The exact means adopted in any country and 
the scope of the measures of social security will naturally depend on a variety of 
factors like size, population, economic resources, industrial development, living 
standards, and availability of technical personnel. Despite several difficulties, the 
twentieth century has witnessed a rapid march towards the goal of social security in 
various countries in the world. The need for measures of social security is no longer 
in doubt, countries are currently engaged only in determining the timing of the meth- 
ods of social security, their scope and their progressive enlargement with a view to 
shelter in increasing measure larger and larger sections of the population under the 
“umbrella of social security.” : 
2. The object and scheme of the Act 
The object of the Act is summed up in the Preamble which says that it is an Act to 
provide for certain benefits to employees in case of sickness, maternity and employ- 
ment injury and to make provisions for certain other matters in relation thereto. 
1. (a) The Act provides for payment of maternity, sickness, disablement, depend- 
ents, and medical benefits to the employees. (Chap. 5.) 
(b) For giving benefits, an Employees’ State Insurance Fund has been statutorily 
created by (i) statutory contributions from employees and employers (Chap. 4), (ii) 
grants, donations, etc. (Sec. 26). 
(c) The ESI Fund is held and the Scheme of benefits is administered by the Em- 
ployees’ State Insurance Corporation (Sec. 3) through its executive called “Standing Committee” (Sec. 8) with the assistance, advice and expertise of Medical Benefit Council, efc., via Regional and Local Boards and Committees. (Chaps. 2 and 3). 
(d) The Corporation collects and recovers the contributions from the employers 
(Chaps. 4 and 5A) and pays the benefits directly to the employees and/ or dependents in accordance with a Scheme called Employees’ State Insurance Scheme. 
(e) Disputes may occur between the Corporation and the employers (mostly about payments of contributions or claims) and between Corporation and employees about benefits. A special court known as Employee’s State Insurance Court has been cre- ated for adjudication of all such disputes and claims (Chap. 6). 
2. The Employees’ State Insurance Act has to be read and studied along with the Employees’ State Insurance Regulations framed by the Central Government covering the concrete Scheme of the Benefits, the E.S.I. Rules and the E.S 1. Court Rules of the various State Governments. This jural structure of the main Act, Regulations, Rules, Court Rules and Notifications issued from time to time have complicated the provisions. In this chapter, the law has been presented mainly from a realistic and practical stand so that the student understands not only the provisions of the Act but also the actual operation and administration of the Scheme of the Benefits. 
3. Coverage of the Act (s. 1) 
The Act extends to the whole of India [s. 1(2)]. The appropriate Government may, in consultation with the Corporation and where the appropriate Government is a State Government, with the approval of the Central Government, after giving six months’ notice of its intention of so doing by notification in the Official Gazette, extend the provisions of the Act or any of them, to any other establishment or class of estab- lishments, industrial, commercial, agricultural or otherwise. 


Chap. I—Preliminary 547 
An advertising agency selling expert services for product promotion, sales as well 
as shipping not carrying on stevedoring activity would also be covered by the Act. 
A person availing benefit of the Act is debarred from claiming any compensation 
under any other law. | 
Where a Co-operative Society employs its own members for wages in the manu- 
facturing process, it becomes liable to be covered under the Acct. 
The State Government is not obliged to make the Act applicable to all areas to 
which provisions have been extended. The State Government is entitled to choose the 
class of establishments for the application of the Act. 
- Self-certification scheme 
The Employees State Insurance Corporation has decided to introduce the system of 
self-certification to minimise the need to inspect different establishments. It has ex- 
empted establishments that employ upto 40 persons from ‘visits’ by labour inspec- 
tors, provided the employees give certificates issued by chartered accountants. Previ- 
ously the exemption was limited to establishments employing upto 19 persons. 
Amnesty Scheme 
ESIC has decided to give amnesty to about 18,000 establishments facing charges in 
courts for violation of ESIC Act. The amnesty involves out-of-court settlement of 
cases with 7.5% of relief on damages. 
4. Application of the Act (s. 1) 
The Act applies in the first instance, to all factories (including factories belonging 
to Government) other than seasonal factories.’ Power has been given to the appropri- 
ate Government to extend different provisions of the Act to any other establishment 
or class of establishments, industrial, commercial, agricultural or otherwise. 
The managing director of a company may have a dual capacity of an agent as well 
as an employee. Even so, he is not an employee for the purposes of the coverage of 
the Act. 
Any person having ultimate control over the affairs of a factory is its occupier. The 
question as to whether a director of the company has ultimate control over the affairs 
of the factory of the company is always a question of fact. 
Where a person is named as the manager of a factory, such person need not be con- 
sidered to be in ultimate control over the affairs of the company since he is not a di- 
rector. In the event of prosecution of offences under the Act, all the directors as well

It cannot be denied that kitchen in a hotel conducts manufacturing business. How- 
ever, the lodging facility is also an essential component of services rendered by the 
hotel. The activity in the kitchen has a definite connection with the activities carried 
on in the rest of the hotel premises. The Act is therefore applicable to all the employ- 
ees in the hotel irrespective of whether they perform work in the kitchen or in the 
other sections. 
A co-operative society engaged in lending money to its members and recovering it 
with interest constitute a shop and is to be governed by the Acct. 
Where a company is engaged in the business of finance and investment of deposits 
made by customers, and earns profits by such investment, such business will amount to 
sale of services for remuneration. The Act will therefore apply to such an establishment. 
The petrol pump or service station is considered as a work place wherein manu- 
facturing process is carried on. Manufacturing process is not confined only to make a 
new product emerge. It includes bringing out specific result. The Act will equally 
govern such establishments. 
The employees who were drawing monthly salary of Rs. 6,500 (the limit was ear- 
lier Rs. 3,000) were required to make contributions at the enhanced rate of 1.75% in 
place of the earlier figure of 1.5% vide notification dated December 23, 1996 which 
became effective with effect from the date January 1, 1996. The employers’ contri- 
bution was raised from 4% to 4.75%. In view of the Notification the employees 
drawing salary upto Rs. 6,500 were required to secure new insurance cards after fil- 
ing requisite declaration. The concerned employer notified the employees accord- 
ingly but the union challenged the employer’s notice on the ground that in view of 
proviso to section 1(4) of the Act, the amendment as brought in by the Notification 
had no application to the concerned employees. Their stand was that the employer- 
hotel was a Government of India undertaking and is State within the meaning of Ar- 
ticle 12 of the Constitution of India, thus, the applicability of the Act cannot be ex- 
tended to the employees of the said establishment. The High Court gave direction to 
the ESIC to consider ‘waiver’ of realisation of contribution from the concerned em- 
ployees. The Supreme Court held that the direction given by the High Court was not 
a positive direction and that the corporation would pass necessary order in accor- 
dance with law. . 
The word ‘shop’ defined under Sec. 1(5) will include even places where services 
are rendered or performed. ‘Shop’ will not include an establishment where mainly 
intellectual activity is taking place and where things are not sold or purchased. An 
advertising concern is not, therefore, a shop.' 
Race club is held to be an establishment coming within the purview of the Act.'®

The word “shop” has been held to cover premises from where consultancy services 
were being provided to customers in respect of industrial, technical and management 
activities and preparation of project reports by engaging the services of architects, 
engineers and other experts.” The administrative office of a partnership firm con-

to be covered by the word “shop”. 
A State Notification under S. 1(5) covered the head office of the establishment. It 
was held that the Act would automatically apply to a branch office having functional 
integrality with the activities of the main establishment even if such branch is situate 
in a different state. 
The amendment of 1989 provides that a factory or an establishment to which the 
Act applies will remain under the governance of the Act even if the number of per- 
sons employed in it becomes reduced or the manufacturing process has ceased to 
operate.“ [S. 1(6)]. It has been held that this amendment is prospective and not retro- 
spective. No liability would arise in respect of factories where the Act ceased to ap- 
ply before the amendment.” 
5. Exemptions 
(a) Exemption of a Factory or Establishment etc.—-Any factory or estab- 
lishment or class of factories or establishments or person or persons in any 
area may be exempted by the appropriate Government by notification in the 
Official Gazette from the operation of the Act for a period not exceeding 
one year and such exemption may be renewed from time to time,” after 
giving a reasonable opportunity to the Employee's State Insurance Corpo- 
ration to make representation in the matter. ° Power is given to issue notifi- 
cations to take effect either prospectively or retrospectively. 
(b) Exemption of Factories or Establishments belonging to Government 
or any Local Authority—The appropriate Government may after con- 
sultation with the Corporation by notification in the Official Gazette and 
subject to the conditions specified, exempt any factory or establishment 
belonging to the Government or any local authority, from the operation of 
the Act if the employees in aSny such factory or establishment are other- 
wise in receipt of benefits, substantially similar or superior to the benefits 
provided under the Act. 
(c) Exemption from one or more Provisions of the Act.—With the consent 
of the Corporation, the appropriate Government may, by notification in the 
Official Gazette, exempt any employee or class of employees in any factory 
or establishment or class of factories or establishments from one or more of

6. Appropriate Government [s. 2(1)] 
‘Appropriate government” means, in respect of establishments under the control of 
Central Government or a railway administration or a major port or a mine or oilfield, 
the Central Government, and in-all other cases, the State Government.

“Benefit period” means such period, being not exceeding six consecutive months 
corresponding to the contribution period, as may be specified in the regulations: 
In the case of the first benefit period a longer period may be specified by or under 
the regulations; 
8. Confinement [s. 2(3)] 
“Confinement” means labour resulting in the issue of a living child or labour after 
twenty-six weeks of pregnancy resulting in the issue of a child whether alive or dead. 
9. Contribution [s. 2(4)] 
According to s. 2(4), “contribution” means the sum of money payable to the Cor- 
poration by the principal employer in respect of an employee and includes any 
amount payable by or on behalf of the employee in accordance with the provisions of 
the Act.

14. Employment injury [s. 2(8)] 
“Employment injury” means a personal injury to an employee caused by accident 
or an occupational disease arising out of and in the course of his employment, being 
an insurable ermployment, whether the accident occurs or the occupational disease is 
contracted within or outside the territorial limits of India; 
“Employment Injury” means a personal injury to an employee— 
(i) which is caused by accident or an occupational disease, 
(ii) which must arise out of and in the course of employment, 
(iii) the employment must be insurable, 
(iv) whether the accident occurs or the occupational disease is contracted 
within or outside the territorial limits of India. 
The employment is a contract of service between the employer and employee un- 
der which the employee agrees to serve the employer subject to his control and su- 
pervision.”. Employment is not confined to actual work or place of work but it ex- 
tends to all things which the workman is entitled to do by the contract of employment 
either expressly or impliedly. 
During communal rigts, a workman was assaulted by a mob when he was return- 
ing home and he died in the assault. It was held that the place of accident need not 
necessarily be located within the limits of the factory premises so long as the place of 
accident falls within a zone which can notionally, deemed to be the zone of the fac- 
33. Employee’s State Insurance Corpn. Madras v. Balasundaram, (1998) 2 LLJ 689 (Mad). 
34. Chintaman Rao v. State of M.P., AIR 1958 SC 388. 


poe Part IX—The Employees’ State Insurance Act, 1948 
tory for the purpose of the Act by recourse to theory of notional extension. The death 
was held to be employment injury within the meaning of section 2(8) of the Act. 
Where an employee left his house at about 8:30 am to join his duties at 9 a.m and 
he died at the bus stop while waiting for the local bus, it was held that the employee 
died while he was going to his place of work, and therefore, applying the theory of 
notional extension, death occurred in the course of employment. 
In a case, a workman of the appellant was involved in an accident while travelling 
by his cycle to the work spot. The employee had provided bus facility to all his 
workmen but as the deceased workman did not reside on any of the available bus 
routes he used to go by bicycle. While on the way to workshop he met with an acci- 
dent and died. It was held that although travelling by bus was an implied condition of 
service but in view of the fact that the concerned workman was not residing on any 
of the available bus routes, the exigencies of the employment and circumstances 
obliged him and the company allowed him to ride a bicycle to reach the workspot. 
The workman was held to be in the course of employment from the moment he be- 
gan to ride the bicycle for reaching his place of work.°° 
A workman of a textile mill while on duty went to canteen during the short recess 
to take tea, where he died. When the compensation was claimed by his widow and 
son, it was held that the death arose out of and in the course of employment because 
the recess period is not so long as to disrupt the continuity of the employment. 
15. Employee [s. 2(9)] 
“Employee’’ means any person employed for wages in or in connection with the work of a factory or establishment to which the Act applies and— 
(1) who is directly employed by the principal employer on any work of, or 
incidental or preliminary to or connected with the work of, the factory or 
establishment, whether such work is done by the employee in the factory or 
establishment or elsewhere; or 
(ii) who is employed by or through an immediate employer on the premises of the factory or establishment or under the supervision of the principal em- ployer or his agent on work which is ordinarily part of the work of the fac- 
tory or establishment or which is preliminary to the work carried on in or incidental to the purpose of the factory or establishment; or 
(ili) whose services are temporarily lent or let on hire to the principal employer by the person with whom the person whose services are so lent or let on hire has entered into a contract of service; and includes any person em- ployed for wages on any work connected with the administration of the factory or establishment or any part, department or branch thereof or with the purchase of raw materials for, or the distribution or sale of the products of, the factory or establishment: but does not include—

It has been observed by the Supreme Court that it is clear that the Act is a part of 
social security programme and is intended to provide certain benefits to employees in 
given situations. It would, therefore, be incompatible with that programme to hold 
that representatives who were engaged by the firm for marketing its products could 
not be treated as employees for the purposes of the Act.”’ Persons providing loading 
and unloading services under the directions and control of the establishment were 
held to be a part of the workforce of the establishment.” The employer was held li- 
able to pay compensation. 
Casual workers have been held to be employees for the purposes of the Act. But 
where they are not working even on casual basis and engaged only for a specific and 
limited job, they would not be employees for the purposes of the Act.” The court 
followed the decision of the Supreme Court in Employees’ State Insurance Coprn. v. 
Premier Clay Products, > where it was observed: “The respondent had hired some 
casual coolies for loading and unloading of its goods. The work itself was of sporadic 
nature. The coolies were available for work to others and in fact on the very day 
worked for several others who engaged them. In the circumstances, the coolies can- 
not even be called casual workmen. Hence, no contribution is payable by the re- 
spondent to the corporation for their benefit.” 
The decision in Employees’ State Insurance Corpn. v. Oswal Woolen Mills Ltd.,”° 
as to the status of casual construction workers was approved by the Supreme Court in 
Regional Director, Employees’ State Insurance Corpn. v. South India Flour Mills P. 
Ltd. hy where the court said: “In our opinion the work of construction of additional 
buildings required for the expansion of a factory must be held to be ancilliary, inci- 
dental or having some relevance to or link with the object of the factory. It is not cor- 
rect to say that such work must always have some direct connection with the manu- 
39. Employees State Insurance Corpn. v. M.P. Ranganakalu Naidu, (2001) 2 Lab LJ 67 (Kant), for 
entitlement to benefits the claimant must be an employee at the beginning of the contribution pe- 
riod. Merely because he ceased to be an employee under S. 2(9) during the corresponding benefit 
period, does not preclude him from claiming statutory benefit.

facturing process that is carried on in the factory. The expression “work of the fac- 
tory” should also be understood in the sense of any work necessary for the expansion 
of the factory or establishment or for augmenting or increasing the work of the fac- 
tory or establishment. Such work is incidental or preliminary to or connected with the 
work of the factory or establishment.” 
A tea company entrusted the work of packing tea to a contractor. The employees 
engaged in that work belonged to the contractor. The tea company had no manner of 
control or supervision over them. The right of rejection of packings not coming up to 
specifications or for wanting in quality was held to be not an act of supervision. 
Persons engaged for loading or unloading furniture were held not to be the employ- 
ees of the respondent as they were employees of an independent agency and the re- 
spondent exercised no control over the way in which the work was to be performed. 
The Court distinguished the decision in Rajkamal Transport v. ESI Corpn. In this 
case the transporter engaged certain hamalis for loading and unloading purpose. The 
transporter collected the charges for their service from customers and paid the same 
to hamalis. The Supreme Court held that the source from which the payment came is 
not the main test to be considered, but what is important is if the hamalis work in 
connection with the work of the establishment. The hamalis were directly engaged 
by the carrier himself though the payment was collected and paid through the cus- 
tomers. The employer had direct control and supervision over the work of hamalis. 
Apprentices and trainees not receiving wages were held to be not employees.” 
The managing director of a company is an ‘employer’ within the meaning of Sec. 
2(17). He is not, therefore, an ‘employee’ within the meaning of Sec. 2(9).°°> How- 
ever, where an ordinary director of a company is appointed as managing director and 
entrusted with additional duties on a remuneration, such managing director becomes 
an employee and remuneration received by him constitutes wages. : 
Where the employer claimed that he had made payments to professional experts, 
but did not furnish any details, the court upheld the claim of the ESI Corporation for 
Contribution. 
An employee will not cease to be an ‘employee’ covered by the Act if he is placed 
under interim suspension pending domestic enquiry on any alleged misconduct. Sub- 
sistence allowance paid to such employee, therefore, constitutes ‘wages’ and the em- 
ployer is required to make contribution thereon.°” An employee drawing qualifying 
wages at the commencement of the Act and thereby becoming entitled to the benefits of the Act would remain so entitled even if the wage goes down below the limit dur- 
ing the currency of the relevant period.

A person can be both the principle employer and an employee if there exists an 
employment contract between such a person and the establishment. Such employee 
will be counted for determining the number of employees in the establishment for the 
operation of the Act. 
16. Exempted employee [s. 2(10)] 
According to s. 2(10), “exempted employee” means an employee who is not liable 
under the Act to pay the employee’s contribution. 
17. Family [s. 2(11)] 
Section 2(11) provides for the definition of “family”. A “family” means the spouse 
and minor legitimate and adopted children dependent upon the insured person and his 
dependent parents. 
18. Factory [s. 2(12)] 
“Factory” means any premises including the precincts thereof whereon twenty or 
more persons are employed or were employed for wages on any day of the preceding 
twelve months, and in any part of which a manufacturing process is being carried on 
with the aid of power or is ordinarily so carried on but does not include a mine sub- 
ject to the operation of the Mines Act, 1952; or a railway running shed.”” 
19. Immediate employer [s. 2(13)] 
“Immediate employer’, in relation to employees employed by or through him, 
means a person who has undertaken the execution, on the premises of a factory or an 
establishment to which the Act applies or under the supervision of the principal em- 
ployer or his agent, of the whole or any part of any work which is ordinarily part of 
the work of the factory or establishment of the principal employer or is preliminary 
to the work carried on in, or incidental to the purposes of, any such factory or estab- 
lishment, and includes a person by whom the services of an employee who has en- 
tered into a contract of service with him are temporarily lent or let on hire to the 
principal employer and includes a contractor. | 
20. Insurable employment [s. 2(13A)] 
“Insurable employment” means an employment in a factory or establishment to 
which the Act applies. 
21. Insured person [s. 2(14)] 
According to s. 2(14), “insured person” means a person who is or was an employee 
in respect of whom contributions are or were payable under this Act and who is by 
reason thereof, entitled to any of the benefits provided by the Act.

According to s. 2(14AA), “manufacturing process” shall have the meaning as-

The expression “manufacturing process” does not include transport of goods or 
contract basis from one place to another. But this is a commercial activity. The 
premises at which goods are accepted for purposes of transporting them to othe! 
places amounts to a shop within the meaning of item 3 of the Notification issued un-

“Miscarriage means expulsion of the contents of a pregnant uterus at any perioc 
prior to or during the twenty-sixth week of pregnancy but does not include any mis 
carriage, the causing of which is punishable under the Indian Penal Code, 1860. 
25. Occupier [s. 2(15)] 
“Occupier” of the factory shall have the same meaning as is assigned to it in the 
Factories Act, 1948; A person nominated as an occupier under Section 100(2) of the 
Factories Act, 1948, cannot be treated as occupier under Sec. 2(n) of the Act, unles: 
such nominee has ultimate control over the affairs of the factory.”
