(ii) in the service of the Central Government or a State Government or 
the Central Board in a Group ‘A’ or Group ‘B’ post. [Sub-s. (4) and 
proviso]. | 
A State Board may, with the approval of the State Government concerned, appoint 
such staff as it may consider necessary. [Sub-s. (5)]. 
The method of recruitment, salary and allowances, discipline and other conditions of 
service of the Central Provident Fund Commissioner, and the Financial Adviser and 
Chief Accounts Officer shall be such as may be specified by the Central Government and 
such salary and allowances shall be paid out of the Fund. [Sub-s. (6)] 
Sub-section (7) is in two parts: 
(a) The method of recruitment, salary and allowances, discipline and other con- 
ditions of service of the Additional Central Provident Fund Commissioner, 
Deputy Provident Fund Commissioner, Regional Provident Fund Commis- 
sioner, Assistant Provident Fund Commissioner and other officers and em- 
ployees of the Central Board shall be such as may be specified by the Central © 
Board in accordance with the rules and orders applicable to the officers and 
employees of the Central Government drawing corresponding scales of pay. 
But where the Central Board is of opinion that it is necessary to make a 
departure from the said rules or orders in respect of any of the orders afore- 
said, it shall obtain the prior approval of the Central Government. 
In determining the corresponding scales of pay of officers and employees 
under clause (a), the Central Board shall have regard to the educational 
qualifications, method of recruitment, duties and responsibilities of such of- 
ficers and employees under the Central Government and in the case of any 
doubt, the Central Board shall refer the matter to the Central Government 
whose decision thereon shall be final. (b — 
The method of recruitment, salary and allowances, discipline and other conditions of 
service of officers and employees of a State Board, shall be such as may be specified by 
that Board, with the approval of the State Government concerned. 
10. Acts and proceedings of Central Board or its Executive Committee or State 
Board not to be invalidated on certain grounds (s. 5DD) 
According to section 5-DD, where the Central Board or its Executive Committee or the 
State Board does any act or undertakes any proceedings, such act or proceedings are not 
to be questioned on the ground merely of the existence of any vacancy in, or any defect in 
the constitution of the Central Board or the Executive Committee or the State Board, as 
the case may be. 
11. Delegation by Central and State Boards (s. 5E) 
The Central Board may, with the prior approval of the Central Government and a State 
Board may, with the prior approval of the State Government concermed, delegate to its 
chairman or to any of its officers, subject to such conditions and limitations, if any, as it 
may specify, such of its powers and functions under the Act as it may deem necessary for 
the efficient administration of the scheme and the Family Pension Scheme. 
12. Contributions and matters which may be provided for in Schemes (s. 6) 
The contribution which shall be paid by the employer to the Fund in general shall be 
ten per cent of the basic wages, deamess allowances and retaining allowance (if any) for 


644 Part X—The Employees Provident Funds and Miscellaneous, etc. 
the time being payable to each of the employees (whether employed by him directly or 
by or through a contractor), and the employees’ contribution shall be equal to the contri- 
bution payable by the employer in respect of him and may, if any employee so desires be 
an amount exceeding 10% of the basic wages, dearness allowance and retaining allow- 
ance, if any. This is subject to the condition that the employer shall not be under an obli- 
gation to pay any contribution over and above his contribution payable under the section. 
In its application to any establishment or class of establishments which the Central 
Government, after making such enquiry as it deems fit, may by notification in the Official 
Gazette specify, this section shall be subject to the modification that for the words, “ten 
percent’, the words “twelve per cent” shall be substituted. 
A further proviso says that where the amount of any contribution payable under the Act 
involves a fraction of a rupee, the Scheme may provide for the rounding off of such frac- 
tion to the nearest rupee, half of a rupee or quarter of a rupee. 
Explanation 1I,—For the purposes of this section dearness allowance shall be deemed 
to include also the cash value of any food concession allowed to the employee. 
Explanation 2.—For the purposes of this section, “retaining allowance” means an 
allowance payable for the time being to an employee of any factory or other estab- 
lishment during any period in which the establishment is not working, for retaining 
his services. 
13. Employees’ Family Pension Scheme (s. 6A) 
The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, frame a scheme 
to be called the Employees’ Pension Scheme for the purpose of providing pension and 
life assurance benefits to employees of any establishment or class of establishments to 
which the Act applies. [Sub-s. (1)] 
There has to be established, as soon as may be after the framing of the Pension 
Scheme, a Pension Fund into which shall be paid from time to time in respect of every 
such employee— 
(a) such portion, not exceeding 1.16% of wages, of the amount payable under 
section 6 as contribution by the employer as well as the employee, as may 
be specified in the Pension Scheme. 
(b) such sums as are payable by the employer of an exempted establishment 
under section 17(6), and 
(c) such sums, being not less than the amount payable in pursuance of clause 
(a) out of the employer’s contribution under section 6, as the Central Gov- 
ernment may, after due appropriation made by Parliament by law in this 
behalf, specify. [Sub-s. (2)] 
The Pension Fund vests in and is administered by the Central Board. [Sub-s. (3)] 
The Pension Scheme may provide for all or any of the matters specified in Schedule 
HI. [Sub-s. (4)] 
The Pension Scheme may provide that any of its provisions shall take effect either pro- spectively or retrospectively on such date as may be specified in this behalf in that Scheme. [Sub-s. (5)] 
14. Special Grant by Central Government for Scheme (s. 6B) 
The Central Government can, after due appropriation made by Parliament by law in this behalf, pay such further sums as may be determined by it into the Pension Fund to 


Chap. III—Establishment to include all departments and Branches 645 
meet all the expenses in connection with the administration of the Pension Scheme other 
than the expenses towards the cost of any benefits provided by or under the Scheme. 
15. Employees’ Deposit-Linked Insurance Scheme (s. 6C) 
The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, frame a Scheme 
to be called the Employees’ Deposit Linked Insurance Scheme for the purpose of pro- 
viding life assurance benefits to such employees as are covered by any Scheme. [Sec. 
6C(1)] 
There shall be established, as soon as may be after the framing of the Insurance 
Scheme, a Deposit Linked Insurance Fund into which shall be paid by the employer from 
time to time in respect of every such employee in relation to whom he is the employer, 
such amount, not being more than one per cent, of the aggregate of the basic wages, 
dearness allowance (if any) for the time being payable in relation to such employee as the 
Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify. [Sec. 6C(2)] 
For the purposes of this sub-section, the expressions “Dearness allowance” and “Re- 
taining allowance” have the same meaning as in section 6. [Explanation]. 
The Central Government shall, after due appropriation made by Parliament by law, 
contribute to the Insurance Fund in relation to each employee covered by the Scheme an 
amount representing one-half of the contribution which an employer is required by sub- 
section (2), to make. 
Sub-s (4) is in two clauses: 
(a) The employer shall pay into the Insurance Fund such further sums of 
money, not exceeding one-fourth of the contribution which he is required to 
make under sub-section (2) as the Central Government may, from time to 
time, determine to meet all the expenses in connection with the administra- 
tion of the Insurance Scheme other than the expenses towards the cost of 
any benefits provided by or under that Scheme. 
(b) The Central Government shall, after due appropriation made by Parliament 
by law, pay into the Insurance Fund such further sums of money repre- 
senting one-half of the sums payable by the employer under clause (a) meet 
all the expenses in connection with the administration of the Insurance 
Scheme other than the expense towards the cost of any benefits provided by 
or under that Scheme. 
The Insurance Fund vests in the Board and is be administered by it in such manner as 
may be specified in the Insurance Scheme. [Sub-s (5)]. 
The Insurance Scheme may provide for all or any of the matters specified in Scheme 
IV. [Sub-s. (6)] 
The Insurance Scheme may provide that any of its provisions shall take effect either 
prospectively or retrospectively on such date as may be specified in this behalf in that 
Scheme. 
16. Laying of Scheme before Parliament (s. 6D) 
Every scheme framed under section 5, section 6A and section 6C has to be laid, as 
soon as may be after it is framed, before each House of Parliament, while it is in ses- 
sion, for a total period of thirty days which may be comprised in one session or in 
two or more successive sessions. If, before the expiry of the session immediately 
following the session or the successive sessions both Houses agree in making any 
modification in the scheme or both Houses agree that the scheme should not be 


646 Part X—The Employees Provident Funds and Miscellaneous, etc. 
made, the scheme will have effect only in such modified form or be of no effect, as 
the may be. Any such modification or annulment shall be without prejudice to the 
‘validity of anything previously done under that scheme. 
17. Modification of Scheme (s. 7) 
The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, add to, amend or 
vary the Scheme or the Family Pension Scheme, or the Insurance Scheme, as the case 
may be. [Sub-s. (1)] 
All notifications under sub-section (1) have to be laid before Parliament, as soon as 
may be, after they are issued. [Sub-s. (2)]. 
18. Determination of moneys due from employers (s. 7A) 
According to section.7A(1), the Central Provident Fund Commissioner, any Additional Central Provident Fund Commissioner, and any Deputy Provident Fund Commissioner, any Regional Provident Fund Commissioner, or any Assistant Provident Fund Commis- sioner may, by order decide a dispute regarding the applicability of the Act to any estab- lishment and determine the amount money due from an employer under the Act or under any of the schemes. 
He may conduct such inquiry as he may deem necessary for any of the above two pur- poses. 
The officer conducting the inquiry under sub-section (1) shall, for the purposes of such inquiry, have the same powers as are vested in a court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (5 of 1908), for trying a suit in respect of the following matters, namely: 
(a) enforcing the attendance of any person or examining him on oath; 
(b) requiring the discovery and production of documents: 
(c) receiving evidence on affidavit; 
(d) issuing commissions for the examination of witnesses; 
and any such inquiry shall be deemed to be a judicial proceeding within the meaning of sections 193 and 228, and for the purpose of section 196, of the Indian Penal Code. [Sub- Ss. (2)] 
No order shall be made under sub-section (1), unless the employer concerned is given a reasonable opportunity of representing his case. [Sub-s. (3)] 
Where the employer, employee or any other person required to attend the inquiry under sub-section (1) fails to attend such inquiry without assigning any valid reason or fails to produce any document or to file any report or return when called upon to do so, the offi- cer conducting the inquiry may decide the applicability of the Act or determine the amount due from any employer, as the case may be, on the basis of the evidence adduced during such inquiry and other documents available on record. [Sub-s. (3A)] 
Where an order under sub-section (1) is passed against an employer ex parte, he may, within three months from the date of communication of such order, apply to the officer for setting aside such order and if he satisfies the officer that the show cause notice was not duly served or that he was prevented by any sufficient cause from appearing when the

inquiry was held, the officer shall make an order setting aside his earlier order and shall

the service of the show cause notice if the officer is satisfied that the employer had notice 
of the date of hearing and had sufficient time of appear before the officer. 
Where an appeal has been preferred under the Act against an order passed ex parte and

No order passed under this section shall be set aside on any application under sub-

19. Review of orders passed under section 7A (s. 7B) 
Any person aggrieved by an order made under section 7A(1), but from which no ap- 
peal has been preferred under the Act, and who, from the discovery of new and important 
matter or evidence which, after the exercise of due diligence was not within his knowl- 
edge or could not be produced by him at the time when the order was made, or on ac- 
count of some mistake or error apparent on the face of record or for any other sufficient 
reason, desires to obtain a review of such order may apply for a review of that order to 
the Officer who passed the order. [Sub-s. (1)] 
Such officer may also on his own motion review his order if he is satisfied that it is 
necessary so to do on any such ground. [/bid, proviso] 
Every application for review under sub-section (1) shall be filed in such form and 
manner and within such time as may be specified in the Scheme. [Sub-s. (2)] 
Where it appears to the officer receiving an application for review that there is no suffi- 
cient ground for a review, he has to reject the application. [Sub-s. (3)]. 
Where the officer is of opinion that the application for review should be granted, he 
may grant the same. However, | 
(a) no such application shall be granted without previous notice to all the par- 
ties before him to enable them to appear and be heard in support of the or- 
der in respect of which a review is applied for, and 
(b) no such application shall be granted on the ground of discovery of new 
matter or evidence which the applicant alleges was not within his knowl- 
edge or could not be produced by him when the order was made, without 
proof of such allegation. [Sub-s. (4) and proviso] 
No appeal lies against the order of the officer rejecting an application for review, but an 
appeal under the Act lies against an order passed under review as if the order passed un- 
der review were the original order passed by him under section 7A. [Sub-s. (5)]

20. Determination of escaped amount (s. 7C) 
Where an order determining the amount due from an employer under section 7A or 
section 7B has been passed and if the officer who passed the order— 
(a) has reason to believe that by reason of the omission or failure on the part of 
the employer to make any document or report available, or to disclose, fully 
and truly, all material facts necessary for determining the correct amount 
‘due from the employer, any amount so due from such employer for any pe- 
riod has escaped his notice; 
(b) has, in consequence of information in his possession, reason to believe that any 
amount to be determined under section 7A or section 7B has escaped from his 
determination for any period notwithstanding that there has been no omission 
or failure as mentioned in clause (a) on the part of the employer. 
he may, within a period of five years from the date of communication of the order passed under section 7A or section 7B, re-open the case and pass appropriate orders re-determining 
the amount due from the employer in accordance with the provisions of this Act. 
21. Employers’ Provident Funds Appellate Tribunals (s. 7D) 
Section 7D says that the Central Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, constitute one or more Appellate Tribunals to be known as Employees 
Provident Funds Appellate Tribunal to exercise the powers and discharge the func- tion conferred on such Tribunal by the Act and every such Tribunal has jurisdiction in respect of establishments situated in such areas as may be specified in the notifi- cation constituting the Tribunals. 
A Tribunal consists of one person only to be appointed by the Central Government. A person is not be qualified for appointment as the Presiding Officer of a Tribunal, unless he is or has been, or is qualified to be, a Judge of a High Court. 
22. Term of Presiding Officer of Tribunal (s. TE) 
According to section 7E, the Presiding Officer of a Tribunal shall hold office for a term _ of five years from the date on which he enters upon his office or until he attains the age of sixty two years, whichever is earlier. 
23. Resignation (s. 7F) 
Section 7F provides that the Presiding Officer may, by notice in writing under his hand addressed to the Central Government, resign his office, provided that the Presiding Offi- cer, shall, unless he is permitted by the Central Government to relinquish his office sooner, continue to hold office until the expiry of three months from the date of receipt of such notice or until a person duly appointed as his successor enters upon his office or until the expiry of his term of office, whichever is the earliest. 
24. Salary and allowances and other terms and conditions of service of Presid- ing Officer (s. 7G) 
Section 7G provides that the salary and allowances payable to and the other terms and conditions of service including pension, gratuity and other retirement benefits of the Pre- siding Officer shall be such as may be prescribed, provided that neither the salary and allowance nor the other terms and conditions of service of the Presiding Officer shall be varied to his disadvantage after his appointment. 


Chap. I1I—Establishment to include all departments and Branches 649 
25. Staff of Tribunal (s. 7H) 
According to section 7H(1), the Central Government has to determine the nature and 
categories of the officers and other employees required to assist a Tribunal in the dis- 
charge of its functions and provide the Tribunal with such officers and other employees 
as it may think fit. 
The officers and other employees of a Tribunal have to discharge their functions under 
the general superintendence of the Presiding Officer. [Sub-s. (2)] 
The salaries and allowances and other conditions of service of the officers and other 
employees of a Tribunal are be such as may be prescribed. [Sub-s. (3)] 
26. Appeals to Tribunal (s. 71) 
Any person aggrieved by a notification issued by the Central Government, or an order 
passed by the Central Government or any authority, under the proviso to sub-section (3), 
or sub-section (4) of section 1, or section 3, or sub-section (1) of section 7A, or section 
7B except an order rejecting an application for review referred to in sub-section (5) 
thereof, or section 7C, or section 14B, may prefer an appeal to a Tribunal against such 
notification or order. [Sub-s. (1)] 
Every appeal under sub-section (1) shall be filed in such form and a manner, within 
such time and be accompanied by such fees, as may be prescribed. [Sub-s. (2)] 
27. Procedure of Tribunals (s. 7J) 
A Tribunal shall have power to regulate its own procedure in all matters arising out of 
the exercise of its powers or of the discharge of its functions including the places at which 
the Tribunal shall have its sittings. [Sub-s. (1)] 
A Tribunal shall, for the purpose of discharging its functions, have all the powers 
which are vested in the officers referred to in section 7A and any proceedings before the 
Tribunal shall be deemed to be a judicial proceedings within the meaning of sections 193 
and 228, and for the purpose of section 196, of the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860) and 
the Tribunal shall be deemed to be a civil court for all the purposes of section 195 and 
Chapter XXVI of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. [Sub-s. (2)] 
28. Right of appellant to take assistance of legal practitioner and of Govern- 
ment, etc. to appoint presiding officers (s. 7K) 
A person preferring an appeal to a Tribunal under this Act may either appear in per- 
son or take the assistance of a legal practitioner of his choice to present his case before 
the Tribunal. [Sub-s. (1)] 
The Central Government or a State Government or any other authority under this Act 
may authorise one or more legal Practitioners or any of its officers to act as presenting 
officers and every person so authorised may present the case with respect to any appeal 
before a Tribunal. [Sub-s. (2)] 
29. Orders of Tribunal (s. 7L) | 
A Tribunal may, after giving the parties to the appeal, an opportunity of being heard, 
pass such orders thereon as it thinks fit, confirming, modifying or annulling the order 
appealed against or may refer the case back to the authority which passed such order with 
such directions as the Tribunal may think fit, for a fresh adjudication or order, as the case 
may be, after taking additional evidence, if necessary. [Sub-s. (1)] 


650 Part X—The Employees Provident Funds and Miscellaneous, etc. 
A Tribunal may, at any time within five years from the date of its order, with a view to 
rectifying any mistake apparent from the record, amend any order passed by it under sub- 
section (1) and shall make such amendment in the order if the mistake is brought to its 
notice by the parties to the appeal. [Sub-s. (2)]. 
An amendment which has the effect of enhancing the amount due from, or otherwise 
increasing the liability of, the employer shall not be made under this sub-section, unless 
the Tribunal has given notice to him of its intention to do so and has allowed him a rea- 
sonable opportunity of being heard. [/bid, proviso] 
A Tribunal shall send a copy of every order passed under this section to the parties the 
appeal. [Sub-s. (3)]. 
Any order made by a Tribunal finally disposing of an appeal shall not be questioned in 
any court of law. [Sub-s. (4)]. 
30. Filling up of vacancies (s. 7M) 
If, for any reason, a vacancy occurs in the office of the Presiding Officer, the Central 
Government shall appoint another. person in accordance with the provisions of the Act, to fill the vacancy and the proceedings may be continued before a Tribunal from the stage at 
which the vacancy is filled. 
31. Finality of orders constituting a Tribunal (s. 7N) 
According to section 7-N, no order of the Central Government appointing any person as the Presiding Officer shall be called in question in any manner, and no act or proceed- ing before a Tribunal shall be called in question in any manner on the ground merely of any defect in the constitution of such Tribunal. 
32. Deposit of amount due, on filing appeal (s. 7-O) 
Section 7-O provides that no appeal by the employer shall be entertained by a Tribunal unless he has deposited with it seventy-five percent of the amount due from him as de- termined by an officer referred to in section 7A, provided that the Tribunal may, for rea- sons to be recorded in writing, waive or reduce the amount to be deposited under this section. 
33. Transfer of certain applications to Tribunal (s. 7P) 
According to s. 7P, all application which are pending before the Central Government under section 19A, before its repeal shall stand transferred to a Tribunal exercising juris- diction in respect of establishment in relation to which such applications had been made as if such application were appeals preferred to the Tribunal. 
34, Interest payable by the employer (s. 7Q) : 
According to s. 7Q, the employer shall be liable to pay the simple interest at the rate of 12% per annum or at such higher rate as may be specified in the scheme on any amount due from him under the Act from the date on which the amount has become so due til] the date of its actudl payment. Provided that higher rate of interest specified in the scheme shall not exceed the lending rate of interest charged by any scheduled bank.

36. Recovery of moneys by employers and contractors (s. 8A) 
This section provides for recovery of moneys by employers and contractors as fol- 
lows: 
(1) The amount of contribution (that is to say the employers’ contribution as well as 
employee’s contribution, in pursuance of any scheme and the employer’s contribution 
in pursuance of the insurance scheme), and any charges on the basis of such contribu- 
tion for meeting the cost of administering the Fund paid or payable by an employer in 
respect of an employee employed by or through a contractor may be recovered by such 
employer, from the contractor, either by deduction from any amount payable to the 
contractor under any contract or as a debt payable by the contractor. 
(2) A contractor from whom the amounts mentioned in sub-section (1) may be re- 
covered in respect of any ernployee employed by or through him, may recover from 
such employee the employee’s contribution by deduction from the basic wages, 
dearness allowance and retaining allowance (if any) payable to such employee. 
(3) Notwithstanding any contract to the contrary, no contractor shall be entitled to 
deduct the employer’s contribution or the charges referred to in sub-section (1) from 
the basic wages, dearness allowance, and retaining allowance (if any) payable to an 
employee employed by or through him or otherwise to recover such contribution or 
charges from such employee. 
Explanation.—In this section, the expressions, ‘““dearness allowance” and “retain- 
ing allowance” shall have the same meanings as in section 6. [Sec. 8A] 
The Schemes stated in Sec. 5 under the Act do not contemplate any obligation on 
the employer to remit Provident Fund contribution in respect of employees who are 
reappointed after their retirement from services.

40. Stay of proceedings under certificate and amendment or withdrawal (s. 8E) 
This section is as follows: 
(1) Notwithstanding that a certificate has been issued to the Recovery Officer for 
the recovery of any amount, the authorised officer may grant time for the payment of 
- the amount, and thereupon the Recovery Officer shall stay the proceedings until the 
expiry of the time so granted. 
(2) Where a certificate for the recovery of amount has been issued, the authorised 
officer shall keep the Recovery Officer informed of any amount paid or time granted 
for payment, subsequent to the issue of such certificate. 
(3) Where the order giving rise to a demand of amount for which a certificate of 
recovery has been issued has been modified in appeal or other proceeding under this 
Act, and as a consequence thereof, the demand is reduced but the order is the subject- 
matter of a further proceeding under this Act, the authorised officer shall stay the 
recovery of such part of the amount of the certificate as pertains to the said reduction 
for the period for which the appeal or other proceeding remains pending. 
(4) Where a certificate for the recovery of amount has been issued and subse- 
quently the amount of the outstanding demand is reduced as a result of an appeal or 
other proceedings under this Act, the authorised officer, shall, when the order which 
was the subject-matter or such appeal or other proceeding has become final and con- 
clusive, amend the certificate or withdraw it, as the case may be.

50. Offences by Companies (s. 14A) 
If the person committing an offence under the Act, the Scheme or the Pension 
Scheme or the Insurance Scheme is a company, every person who at the time of of- 
fence was committed was incharge of, and was responsible to the company for the 
conduct of the business of the company, as well as the company, shall be deemed to 
be guilty of the offence and shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished ac- 
cordingly. [Sec. 14A(1)] 
While considering offences of a company under Sec. 14A(1) of the Act, the direc- 
tor cannot be made vicariously liable for any and every contravention made by the 
company unless he is incharge of the day to day conduct of the affairs of the com- 
pany. Further, all the directors have overall responsibility in the conduct of the busi- 
ness of the company.” The court said that a director can be made vicariously liable

53. Cognizance and Trial of Offences (s. 14AC) 
The section runs as follows: 
(1) No court shall take cognizance of any offence punishable under this Act, the 
Scheme or the Pension Scheme or the Insurance Scheme, except on a report in writ- 
ing of the facts constituting such offence made with the previous sanction of the 
Central Provident Fund Commissioner or such other officer as may be authorised by 
the Central Government, by notification in the Official Gazette, in this behalf, by an 
Inspector appointed under section 13. 
(2) No court inferior to that of a Presidency Magistrate or a Magistrate of the first 
class shall try any offence under this Act or the Scheme or the Pension Scheme or the 
Insurance Scheme. 
54. Power to recover damages (s. 14B)

the Pension Fund or the Insurance Fund or in the transfer of accumulations required

Scheme or under any other conditions specified under section 17, the Central Provi- 
dent Fund Commissioner or such other officer as may be authorised by the Central 
Government, by notification in the Official Gazette, in this behalf may recover from 
the employer such damages, not exceeding the amount of arrears, as it may think fit 
to impose. 
Before levying and recovering such damages, the employer shall be given a rea-

of which a scheme for rehabilitation has been sanctioned by the Board for Industrial 
and Financial Reconstruction established under section 4 of the Sick Industrial Com- 
panies (Special Provision) Act. 1985, subject to such terms and conditions as may be 
specified in the Scheme.

55. Power of Court to make orders (s. 14C) 
The section is as follows: 
(1) Where an employer is convicted of an offence of making default in the pay- 
ment of any contribution to the Fund, the Pension Fund or the Insurance Fund or in 
the transfer of accumulations required to be transferred by him under sub-section 
(2) of section 15 or sub-section (5) of section 17, the court may, in addition to 
awarding any punishment, by order in writing require him within a period specified 
in the order (which the court may, if it thinks fit and on application in that behalf, - 
from time to time, extend), to pay the amount of contribution or transfer the accu- 
mulations, as the case may be, in respect of which the offence was committed. 
(2) Where an order is made under sub-section (1), the employer shall not be liable 
under this Act in respect of the continuation of the offence during the period or ex- 
tended period, if any, allowed by the court, but if, on the expiry of such period or 
extended period, as the case may be, the order of the court has not been fully com- 
plied with, the employer shall be deemed to have committed a further offence and 
shall be punished with imprisonment in respect thereof under section 14 and shall 
also be liable to pay fine which may extend to one hundred rupees for every day 
after such expiry on which the order has not been complied with.

instrument establishing the provident fund but subject to the provision, if any, con- 
tained in the Scheme, be transferred to the Fund established under the Scheme, and 
shall be credited to the accounts of the employees entitled thereto in the Fund.

57. Act not to apply to certain establishments (s. 16)

The main provision is as follows: 
This Act shall not apply— 
(a) to any establishment registered under the Co-operative Societies Act, 1912 
(2 of 1912), or under any other law for the time being in force in any State 
relating to co-operative societies, employing less than fifty persons and 
working without the aid of power: or

Government or a State Government and whose employees are entitled to 
the benefit of the contributory provident fund or old age pension in accor- 
dance with any scheme or rule framed by the Central Government or the 
state Government governing such benefits: or 
(c) to any other establishment set up under any central, provincial or state Act 
and whose employees are entitled to the benefit of contributory provident 
fund or old age pension in accordance with any Scheme or rule framed un- 
der that Act governing such benefits: or 
(d) to any other establishment newly set up, until the expiry of a period of three 
years form the date on which such establishment is, or has been set up.

exempt whether prospectively or retrospectively that class of establishment from the 
operation of this Act for such period as may be specified in the notification. 
The appellants enjoyed benefit of exemption under unamended provisions of sec- 
tion 16. After the amendment of 1998, they contended that they would continue to 
have the ‘infancy protection’ for period of 3 years starting from date of establishment 
of industry, even after amendment of S.16 and the amendment in no way alters any 
of rights accrued in favour of them. The High Court held that amendment was: in- 
tended to take away certain benefits by way of necessary amendments to section 16. 
The Supreme Court held that every statute would be prima facie prospective unless 
there are words sufficient to show the intention of legislature to affect existing rights. 
32. Regional Provident Fund Commr. v. Dev Kiran Paper Mills (P.) Ltd., (2000) 1 Lab LJ 514 (Kant), 
the paper mill was sold by the creditor (KSFC) to a purchaser. The sale was effected by the creditor 
after takeover from the mill owner. Hence there was no direct sale from the defaulting establishment 
to the purchaser. There was no continuity of establishment from the defaulting company to the pur- 
chaser. The purchaser was accordingly held to be entitled to infancy benefits. The court followed 
Provident Fund Inspector v. Secretary NSS Cooperative Society, (1969) 2 Lab LJ 693 (SC) where 
the facts were absolute similar to the present case, Union of India v. AS Amarnath, (1999) 1 Lab LJ 
1365 (SC), where the court considered whether the firms business was bona fide closed, a new firm 
of different partners utilising the licence and name of the closed firm, employing some of the same 
workmen and using the same machinery is deemed to be a new establishment or continuation of the 
old. The decision was that the firm was to be taken as a new establishment. In Satyajit Mills Ltd. v. 
Regional PF Commr., (1985) 1 Lab LJ 238 (SC), a factory which remained out of production for 3 
months was purchased and resumed with the same men and machinery, held continuation. 


664 Part X—The Employees Provident Funds and Miscellaneous, etc. 
As such, appellants are entitled to the protection, accrued to them prior to amend- 
ment for period of 3 years starting from the date on which establishment was set up, 
though the provisions of such infancy protection has been repealed by amendment. 
(a) Continuity in case of change of ownership 
An old factory was purchased by the petitioner. It was already in a state of a scrap. 
A new factory was erected in its place. There was a total discontinuity between the 
old and the new factory. The EPF Act does not apply where the old establishment 
came to an end and a new establishment came into being. The court accordingly held 
that the infancy protection under s. 16(1)(b) was available.’ The court said that its 
conclusions were supported by the following observations of the Full Bench of the 
Delhi High Court in Bajaj Food Products v. Central Board Trustees.” The court 
cited the following from the head note of the report: “The mere fact that the two of 
erstwhile partners of a dissolved firm have started a new business in the same prem- 
ises under a new name is not sufficient to conclude that the new establishment is a 
continuation of the old establishment. The Commissioner has accepted the findings 
of the Area PF Inspector that the old firm was dissolved, its machinery was disposed 
off, the employees were retrenched and the benefits admissible under the law were 
given to them. Sales Tax Regn. No. was surrendered. A new partnership firm had 
come into existence carrying on new business. There is no semblance of any connec- 
tion between the business carried on by the dissolved firm and the business carried 
on by the new firm. Partners of the new firm have raised their own capital from their 
own resources. Therefore, the new firm is entitled to infancy protection.” 
The Division Bench of the Karnataka High Court also considered the point of what 
is a new establishment in Regional Provident Fund Commissioner v. B Rukmini K, 
observed that where the firm owning a restaurant leased out the same and the lessee 
established a completely new establishment with everything new including labour, he 
was entitled to infancy protection. ’It was observed that the test to be applied by the 
Regional PF Commissioner is to see whether there is a genuine termination or end of 
the previous establishment and not a colourable attempt to clothe the old establish- 
ment as if it were a mere establishment. The claim for infancy should be rejected in 
that case because the changeover could only be a show for getting extended benefit. 
Similar statements are to be found in the judgment of the Madras High Court in 
Senthilnathans Pharmaceuticals v. RPF Commr.*® The Court found here that the es- 
tablishment was a new one started by the petitioner and it had nothing to do with the 
old establishment which was closed. In Lakshmi Rattan Engineering Works v. RPF 
Commr.,” the continuation of the working was emphasized. According to the ratio, 
the change in ownership or line of business makes no difference provided the estab- 
lishment has continued to work all along. In Sayaji Mills Ltd. v. RPF Commr.,”° Su- 
preme Court observed that a change in the ownership of a factory and the subsequent 
temporary interruption in the running of the factory did not have the effect of creat- 
ing a new establishment or the setting up of a new factory. The appellant purchaser 
had restarted the factory after investing some fresh capital for renovating the machin-

In Provident Fund Inspector v. NSS Cooperative Society,” the evidence showed 
that after the purchase of the printing press a new owner had come in the place of the 
former owner, the work of the press was stopped on the day of its sale and was 
started again after a break of three months. The machinery and men working before 
sale were replaced. On a fresh recruitment only six of the former workers were em- 
ployed again. It was held that a new establishment had come into existence. 
58. Authorising certain employees to maintain provident fund accounts (s.16A) 
Under section 16A, the Central Government may, on application made to it in this 
behalf by the employer and the majority of employees in relation to an establishment 
employing one hundred or more persons, authorise the employer by an order in 
writing to maintain a provident fund account in relation to the establishment subject 
to such terms and conditions as may be specified in the scheme. | 
No authorisation is to be made under this sub-section if the employer of such es- 
tablishment had committed any default in the payment of the provident fund contri- 
bution or had committed any other offence under the Act during the three years im- 
mediately preceding the date of such authorisation. 
Sub-section (2) says that where an establishment is authorised to make a provident 
fund account under sub-section (1) the employer in relation to such establishment 
shall maintain such account, submit such return, deposit the contribution in such 
manner, provide for such facilities for inspection, pay such administrative charges 
and abide by such other terms and conditions, as may be specified in the scheme. 
Sub-section (3) says that authorisation made under this section may be cancelled 
by the Central Government by order in writing if the employer fails to comply with 
any of the terms and conditions of the authorisation, or where he commits any of- 
fence under any provision of the Act. 
Before cancelling such authorisation the Central Government shall give the em- 
ployer a reasonable opportunity of being heard.

60. Transfer of accounts (s. 17A) 
(1) Where an employee employed in an establishment to which this Act applies 
leaves his employment and obtains re-employment in another establishment to which 
this Act does not apply, the amount of accumulations to the credit of such employee 
in the Fund, or as the case may be, in the provident fund of the establishment left by 
him shall be transferred, within such time as may be specified by the Central Goy- 
ernment in this behalf, to the credit of his account in the provident fund of the estab- lishment in which he is re-employed, if the employee so desires and the rules in rela- tion to that provident fund permit such transfer. 
(2) Where an employee employed in an establishment to which this Act does not apply leaves his employment and obtains re-employment in another establishment to which this Act applies, the amount of accumulations to the credit of such employee in the provident fund of the establishment left by him may, if the employee so desires and the rules in relation to such provident fund permit, be transferred to the credit of his account in the Fund or as the case may be, in the provident fund of the establish- ment in which he is re-employed.

Chap. III—Establishment to include all departments and Branches 669 
62. Liability in case of transfer of establishment (s. 17B) 
Where an employer, in relation to an establishment, transfers that establishment in 
whole or in part, by sale, gift, lease or licence or in any other manner whatsoever, the 
employer and the person to whom the establishment is so transferred shall jointly and 
severally be liable to pay the contribution and other sums due from the employer under 
any provision of this Act or the Scheme or the Pension Scheme or the Insurance 
Scheme, as the case may be, in respect of the period up to the date of such transfer. 
Provided that the liability of the transferee shall be limited to the value of the as- 
sets obtained by him by such transfer. 
63. Protection of action taken in good faith (s. 18) 
No suit prosecution or other legal proceeding shall lie against the Central Govern- 
ment, a State Government, the Presiding Officer of a Tribunal, any authority referred 
to in section 7A, an Inspector or any other person for anything which is in good faith 
done or intended to be done in pursuance of this Act, the Scheme, the Pension 
Scheme or the Insurance Scheme. 
64. Presiding officer and other officers deemed to be public servants (s. 18A) 
The Presiding Officer of a Tribunal, its officers and other employees, the authori- 
ties referred to in section 7A and every Inspector shall be deemed to be public ser- 
vants within the meaning of section 21 of the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860). 
65. Delegation of powers (s. 19) 
The appropriate Government may direct that any power or authority or jurisdiction 
exercisable by it under this Act the scheme, the Pension Scheme or the Insurance 
Scheme shall in relation to such matters and subject to such conditions, if any as may 
be specified in direction, shall be exercisable also— 
(a) where the appropriate Government is the Central Government, by such of- 
ficer or authority subordinate to the Central Government or by the State 
Government or by such Officer or authority subordinate to the State Gov- 
ernment, as may be specified in the notification, and 
(b) where the appropriate Government is State Government a by such Officer 
or authority subordinate to the State Government as may be specified in the 
notification. 
66. Power to issue directions (s. 20) 
The Central Government may, from time to time, issue such directions to state 
Governments, the Central Board, or any other authority under the Act or the Scheme 
as it may consider necessary— 
(i) for the proper implementation of the Scheme, or 
(ii) in order to remove any difficulty arising in the administration thereof, in- 
cluding difficulties in the matter of payment of accumulation in the Fund to 
the members after they cease to be such members. The authority to whom 
any such directions are issued shall comply with them. The State Govern- 
ment’s powers to issue directions have been omitted.

67. Power to make rules (s. 21) 
According to s.21, the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Ga- 
zette, make rules to carry out the provisions of this Act (1). 
According to sub-section (2) without prejudice to the generality of the forgoing 
power, such rules may provide for all or any of the following matters, namely:— 
(a) the salary and allowances and other terms and conditions of service of the 
Presiding Officer and the employees of a tribunal; 
(b) the form and the manner in which, and the time within which, an appeal shall 
be filed before a tribunal and the fees payable for filing such an appeal; 
(c) the manner of certifying the copy of the certificate to be forwarded to the 
Recovery Officer under sub-section (2) of section 8-C and, 
(d) any other matter which has to be or may be, prescribed by rules under this 
Act. 
According to sub-section (3), every rule made under this Act, shall be laid as soon 
as may be after it is made, before each house of Parliament, while it is in session, for 
a total period of thirty days which may be comprised in one session or in two or more 
successive sessions, and, if, before the expiry of the session immediately following 
the session or the successive sessions, aforesaid, both Houses agree in making any 
modification in the rule, or both Houses agree that the rule should not be made, the 
rule shall thereafter have effect only in such modified form or to be of no effect, as 
the case may be; so, however, any such modification or annulment shall be without 
prejudice to the validity of anything previously done under that rule.

73. The Assam Tea Plantation Provident Fund Act, 1955 
(a) Categories of Employees.—It covers now all categories of employees in the 
plantations in Assam excluding those whose total emoluments exceed Rs. 500 p.m. 
By an amendment of the Act in 1966, the rate of contribution was raised from 
614 per cent to 8 per cent of wages including all allowances. An employee may 
contribute voluntarily to the Fund any amount beyond the prescribed rate, but 
against this the employer is not required to pay his additional matching contribu- 
tion. 
(b) Group Insurance.—A Group Insurance Scheme was introduced for the 
provident fund members in 1963. Under the Scheme a blanket policy was taken 
by the Board for all provident fund members of the age group 18-40. Male mem- 
bers are covered for Rs. 500, women for Rs. 250, and staff for Rs. 1,000 each. 
Workers are required only to make a declaration of good health and no medical 
examination or proof of age is necessary. Premia payable to take the Life Insur- 
ance are deducted and paid annually from the Provident Fund accumulations of 
the members by the Board of Trustees. At the end of March 1966, 1,384,001 
members were covered by the blanket policy and the total value of the policy was 
about Rs. 8 crores. 
(c) Pension Fund.—The Scheme makes provision for the constitution of a Pension 
Fund from the accumulated undisbursed interest amount of the Provident Fund to en- 
able the plantation workers to enjoy pensionary benefits in addition to the Provident 
- Fund. The Pension Fund Scheme was introduced with effect from October 2, 1967. 
74, The Seamen’s Provident Fund Act, 1966 
(i) Scope and coverage.—As the problems of seamen working on board the ships 
for truncated periods are of a special nature, it was considered desirable to enact a 
separate provident fund legislation for them. Accordingly, the Seamen’s Provident 
Fund Act was passed in 1966. The Act generally follows the pattern of the Employ- 
ees’ Provident Funds Act, 1952. Every seaman engaged under the Merchant Ship- 
ping Act, 1958, excluding certain categories of officers and other employees, was 
covered by the Scheme under the Act. About 50,000 seamen are currently covered 
under the Scheme. 
(ii) Contributions —Every employer covered under the Act is required to contrib- 
ute to the Fund for the period from July, 1964 to July, 1968 at the rate of 8 per cent in 
respect of each seaman employed by him; every such seaman has also to contribute 
an equal amount to the Fund. The total contributions received towards the Provident 
Fund upto March 31, 1968 amounted to Rs. 3.04 crores. 
(iii) Administration.—The Fund is administered by a Board of Trustees consisting 
of representatives of Government, employers and employees. The Chief Executive of 
the Organisation is the Seamen’s Provident Fund Commissioner.

THE FATAL ACCIDENTS ACT, 1855 
(13 OF 1855) 
SYNOPSIS 
1. Suit for compensation to the family of 3. Plaintiff shall deliver particulars, etc, 
a person for loss occasioned to it by (COS) oo oer Sie rire Tc 
his death by actionable wrong (s. 1-A) 681 4, Interpretation Clause (S. 4).........:ee 682 
2. Not more than one suit to be brought 
Ete Delors ens wetter: ter eens eee 682 
The Fatal Accidents Act, 1855 is an Act to provide compensation to families for 
loss occasioned by the death of a person caused by actionable wrong. 
Preamble.—The Preamble to the Fatal Accidents Act, 1855 says that whereas no 
action or suit is now maintainable in any Court against a person who, by his wrongful 
act, neglect or default, may have caused death of another person, and it is often times 
right and expedient that the wrong-doer in such case should be answerable in dam- 
ages for the injury so caused by him. Thus, the Fatal Accidents Act has been enacted. 
The Act extends to the whole of India except the state of Jammu and Kashmir. 
1. Suit for compensation to the family of a person for loss occasioned to it by 
his death by actionable wrong (s. 1-A) | 
Section 1-A comes into play when the death of a person is caused by a wrongful 
act, neglect or default. The act, etc in question is such that if death had not ensued, 
the injured person would have been entitled to maintain an action and recover dam- 
ages from the wrong doer. The wrong doer who would have been liable if death had 
not ensued is to remain liable to an action or suits for damages. The death of the per- 
son injured would make no difference to such liability. This would be so even if the 
death has been caused under circumstances which constitute the death as a falonious 
act or other crime. 
Every such action or suit is for the benefit of the wife, husband, parent and child of 
the person whose death has been caused. The suit has to be brought in the name of 
the executor, administrator or representative of the deceased. The court can award 
such damages as it may think to be proportional to the loss resulting from the death 
to the respective parties on whose behalf the action has been brought. From the 
amount recovered costs and expenses have to be deducted including costs -which 
could not be recovered from the dependant. The balance amount is to be distributed 
amongst the parties specified above in such shares as the court may in its judgment 
or decree direct. 
As a general rule parents are entitled to recover the present cash value of the pro- 
spective service of a deceased minor child. In addition they may receive compensa- 
tion for loss of pecuniary benefits reasonably to be expected after the child attains 
majority. 
1. C.K. Subramonia lyer v. T. Kunhikuttan Nair, AIR 1970 SC 376 : (1969) 3 SCC 64 
681 


682 The Fatal Accidents Act, 1855 
In a case, a truck caught fire which was completely managed by its driver. It was 
not possible for the dependants of the deceased to adduce evidence as to the cause of 
the accident as to how the truck caught fire was within the exclusive knowledge of 
the opposite party. The Supreme Court applied the maxim res ispa loquitur and in 
the absence of any explanation from the defendant, he was held liable to pay com- 
pensation.” 
Brother of a person who dies in a motor vehicle accident is entitled to maintain a 
petition under section 11Q-A of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939, if he is a legal repre- 
sentative of the deceased. 
2. Not more than one suit to be brought (s. 2) 
In respect of the same subject-matter not more than one action or suit can be 
brought for. In any action or suit, the executor, administrator or representative of the 
deceased may insert a claim for and recover any pecuniary loss to the state of the 
deceased occasioned by such wrongful act, neglect or default. This sum, when recov- 
ered, will be deemed part of the assets of the estate of the deceased. 
3. Plaintiff shall deliver particulars, etc, (s. 3) 
The plaint in any such action or suit shall give— 
(a) a full particular of the person or persons for whom, or on whose behalf, 
such action or suit shall be brought, and ; 
(b) of the nature of the claim in respect of which damages will be sought to be 
recovered. 
4. Interpretation Clause (s. 4) 
The following words and expressions are intended to have the meanings hereby as- 
signed to them respectively, so far as such meanings are not excluded by the context 
or by the nature of the subject-matter, that is to say— 
(a) the word “person” shall apply to bodies politic and corporate; and 
(b) the word “parent” shall include father and mother and grand-father and 
grand-mother; and 
(c) the word “child” shall include son and daughter and grand-son and grand- 
daughter and step-son and step-daughter. > 
bs Shyam Sunder v. State of Rajasthan, AIR 1974 SC 890: (1974) 1 SCC 690. 3. Gujarat State Road Transport Corporation, Ahmedabad vy. Ramanbhai Prabhatbhai, AIR 1987 SC 1690 : (1987) 3 SCC 234. 


THE INDUSTRIAL EMPLOYMENT 
(STANDING ORDERS) ACT, 1946

Before the enactment of the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 
the bargain between the employer and workman was settled mutually by the eco- 
nomic law of demand and supply. The conditions of employment were governed by 
contracts between the employers and employees in different industrial establish- 
ments. It was taken for granted that the bargain would secure fair terms and condi- 
tions of employment to the workmen. But later on, the workers felt that they did not 
possess adequate bargaining strength to secure fair terms and conditions of service. 
So they started collecting themselves into trade unions. With the advent of trade un- 
ionism, the concept of collective bargaining came into being. These two collectively 
created new problems for maintaining industrial peace and production for the society. 
Only then it was thought that the society had a vital interest in the settlement of terms 
of employment of industrial labour and thus, the State, representing the society en- 
tered the scene and the settlement of labour problems became tripartite.’ The legis- 
lature made on attempt to inference between labour and employer by introducing the 
Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 so that the friction between em- 
ployer and workmen could be minimised. 
1. Statement of objects and reasons 
The Statement of objects and reasons of the Industrial Employment (Standing 
Orders) Bill recorded that the experience has shown that ‘Standing Orders’ defining 
the conditions of recruitment, discharge, disciplinary action, holidays, leave etc., go a 
long way towards minimizing friction between the management and workers in in- 
dustrial undertakings. Discussion on the subject at the tripartite Indian labour confer- 
ence revealed a consensus of opinion in favour of legislation. The Bill accordingly 
provided for the framing of ‘Standing Orders’ in all industrial establishments em- 
ploying one hundred or more workers. 
1. Western India Match Co. v. Workmen, AIR 1973 SC 2650 : (1973) 2 LLJ 403. 
683 


684 The Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 
2. Preamble of the Act 
The Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Bill, 1946 was passed by the legis- 
lature and it received the assent on 23rd April, 1946. It came on the statute book as 
the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 (20 of 1946). The Preamble 
of the Act says that “it is an Act to require employers in industrial establishments 
formally to define conditions of employment under them.” 
3, Amendments to the Act 
The Act has been amended by the following amendment Acts and* Adoptation 
Orders:— 
(i) The Indian Independence (Adaptation of Central Acts and Ordinances) 
Order, 1948. 
(ii) The Adaptation of Laws Order, 1950. 
(iii) The Part B States (Laws) Act, 1951 (3 of 1951). 
(iv) The Industrial Disputes (Amendment and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 
1956 (36 of 1956). 
(v) The Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Amendment Act, 1961 (16 
of 1961). 
(vi) The Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Amendment Act, 1963 (39 
of 1963). 
(vii) The Central Labour Laws (Extension to Jammu and Kashmir) Act, 1970 
(51 of 1970). 
(viii) The Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Amendment Act, 1982 (18 
of 1982) 
4. Object of the Act 
The object of the Act is to require employers in industrial establishments to define 
with sufficient precision the conditions of employment under them and to make the 
said conditions known to workmen employed by them.” In a case, it was observed by 
the Allahabad High Court that the contention that the purpose of the Act was to pro- 
vide for laying down of conditions of employment with sufficient precision and not 
to lay down the conditions themselves cannot be accepted. The High Court held that 
the expression ‘with sufficient precision’ between the words ‘define’ and ‘the condi- 
tions’ may lead to supposition that more emphasis was given to the precision than te 
the conditions. The main object of the Act was to define the conditions of employ- 
ment and to make them known to the workmen. 
The Supreme Court has laid down that the object of the Act is to require the em- 
ployer to make the conditions of employment precise and definite. The Act furthet 
intends to prescribe these conditions in the form of Standing Orders. 
The object of the Act is to have uniform Standing Orders in respect of the matters 
enumerated in the Schedule to the Act regardless of the time of appointment of

those who are appointed thereafter. 
Certified Standing Orders have statutory force and attract principles of natural jus- 
tice as also Articles 14 and 21 of the Constitution of India in case of termination of 
service under Standing Orders. 
If the certified Standing Orders are illegal, arbitrary and violative of principles of 
natural justice, they may questioned under Article 226 of the Constitution of India.® 
5. Short title, extent and application (s. 1) 
The Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 extends to the whole of 
India. It applies to every industrial establishment wherein one hundred or more 
workmen are employed presently or were employed on any day of the preceding 
twelve months. The onus to prove the number of workmen employed lies on the 
management. 
Once the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act becomes applicable to an 
establishment, it does not cease to apply on account of a subsequent fall in the num- 
ber of the workmen in the establishment. 
The appropriate Government may by notification in the Official Gazette apply the 
provisions of this Act to any industrial establishment where specified number of per- 
sons not less than hundred may be employed. The appropriate Government will have 
to give at least two months’ notice before applying this Act to any establishment. 
The provisions of this Act are not applicable to the following:— 
(1) any industry to which the provisions of Chapter VII of the Bombay Indus- 
trial Relations Act, 1946 (Bombay Act 11 of 1947) apply; or 
(11) any industrial establishment to which the provisions of the Madhya Pradesh 
Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1961 (Madhya Pradesh Act 
26 of 1961) apply. 
However, the provisions of this Act will be applicable to all industrial establish- 
ments under the control of the Central Government notwithstanding the provisions of 
Madhya Pradesh Act. 
In industrial establishments where Standing Orders are not applicable, law of 
master and servant governs the relationship between employees and employers. 
Any provision in the Standing Orders, for example, provision as to age of retire- 
ment, would apply to all the employees of the establishment irrespective of whether

INERPRETATION (s. 2) 
6. Appellate Authority [s. 2 (a)] 
The term ‘appellate authority’ means an authority appointed by the appropriate 
Government to exercise in the specified area the functions of an- appellate authority 
under this Act. Appointment of the authority is made by notification in the Official 
Gazette in which the specified area is also notified. 
In relation to an appeal pending before an Industrial Court or other authority im- 
mediately before the commencement of the Industrial Employment (Standing Or- 
ders) Amendment Act, 1963 (39 of 1963) that court or authority shall be deemed to 
be the appellate authority. 
7. Appropriate Government [s. 2(b)] 
The term ‘appropriate Government’ means the Central Government in respect of 
industrial establishments under the control of the Central Government or a Railway 
Administration or in a major-port, mine or oil field and the State Government, in all 
other cases. 
Where any question arises as to whether any industrial establishment is under the 
control of the Central Government, the Government may decide the question— 
(a) either on a reference made to it by the employer or the workman or a trade 
union, or other representative body of the workmen, or 
(b) on its own motion such question will be decided only after giving the par- 
ties an opportunity of being heard. The decision of the government will be 
final and binding on all the parties. 
It has been held that the workmen of an industrial establishment, where ‘appropri- 
ate Government’ is the Central Government will be governed by the Model Standing 
Orders of the Central Government till its own standing orders are certified and come 
into operation in accordance with the Act. © 
8. Certifying Officer [s. 2(c)] 
The term ‘certifying officer’ means a Labour Commissioner or a Regional Labour 
commissioner. It includes any other officer appointed by the appropriate Government 
to perform all or any of functions of a certifying officer under this Act. The appoint- 
ment must be made by the notification in the Official Gazette by the appropriate 
Government. 
9. Employer [s. 2(d)] 
The term ‘employer’ means the owner of an industrial establishment to which this 
Act for the time being applies and it includes the following: — 
(i) in a factory, any person named as manager of the factory under s.7(1)(f) of 
the Factories Act, 1948 (63 of 1948);

(iii) in any other industrial establishment, any person responsible to the owner 
for the supervision and control of the industrial establishment. 
10. Industrial Establishment [s. 2(e)] 
The term ‘industrial establishment’ means the following: — 
(i) an industrial establishment as defined in s. 2(ii) of the Payment of Wages 
Act, 1936 (4 of 1936), or 
(ii) a factory as defined in s. 2(m) of the Factories Act, 1948 (63 of 1948), or | 
(iii) a railway as defined in s. 2(4) of the Indian Railways Act, 1890 (9 of 1890), 
or 
(iv) the establishment of a person, who for the purpose of fulfilling a contract 
with the owner of any industrial establishment, employs workmen. 
The term ‘industrial establishment’ is to be given the meaning contained in the 
Payment of Wages Act, 1936 at the time of enactment of the Industrial Employment 
(Standing Orders) Act, 1946. Any subsequent amendment to the former Act would 
not affect the position vis-a-vis the latter Act. 
Where the Karnataka Agro-Industries Corporation had five workshops governed 
by the Factories Act in different parts of the State of Karnataka, service rules framed 
by the Board of Management were enforced without forming certified Standing Or- 
ders, a writ petition was filed for direction not to enforce the service rules introduced 
by it unilaterally, it was held that as the five workshops of the Corporation are regis- 
tered under the Factories Act and employ more than 100 workmen, they come under 
~the definition of industrial establishment of the Industrial Employment (Standing 
Orders) Act. Therefore, it is obligatory on the part of the Corporation to comply with 
sections 3, 4 and 5 of the Act. It cannot bind the workmen to the service rules unilat- 
erally. Only the Model Standing Orders will be. applicable to the workmen till the 
certified Standing Orders are brought into force. 
The question whether an establishment is an industrial establishment involves a 
factual aspect and unless raised before the trial court cannot be entertained in a writ 
petition after the arguments are over. 
The electricity department of a municipality is an industrial establishment and thus, 
this Act and the Model Standing Orders framed under it are applicable to every per- 
son who is an employee of the department. The Act is applicable to industrial es- 
tablishments of the State Electricity Board.’ 
A hospital providing medical treatment to people suffering from disease is neither 
an industrial establishment nor a workshop as contemplated in section 2(e) of the

11. Prescribed [s. 2(f)] 
The term ‘prescribed’ means prescribed by rules made by the appropriate Govern-

12. Standing Orders [s. 2(g)] 
The term ‘Standing Orders’ means rules relating to matters set out in the Schedule. 
The following matters are to be provided in the Standing Orders under this Act:— 
(1) Classification of workmen, for example, whether permanent, temporary, 
apprentices, probationers or badlis. 
(ii) Manner of intimating to workmen periods and hours of work, holidays, pay 
days and wage-rates. 
(ii) Shift working. 
(iv) Attendance and late-coming. 
(v) Conditions of , procedure in applying for, and the authority which may 
grant leave and holidays. 
(vi) Requirement to enter premises by certain gates, and liability to search. 
(vii) Closing and reopening of sections of the industrial establishment, and tem- 
porary stoppages of work and the rights and liabilities of the employer and 
workmen arising therefrom. 
(vill) Termination of employment, and the notice thereof to be given by em- 
ployer and workmen. 
(ix) Suspension or dismissal for misconduct, and acts or omissions which con- 
stitute misconduct. 
(x) Means of redress for workmen against unfair treatment or wrongful exac- 
tions by the employer or his agents or servants. | 
(x1) Any other matter which may be prescribed. 
The standing orders are rules relating to matters set out in the Schedule. In the ab- 
sence of statutory provision the mere fact that ownership of an industrial establish- 
ment has changed hands, the standing orders which were applicable to the industrial 
establishment of its previous owner would not automatically cease to apply merely 
because the industrial establishment has been purchased by someone else.” 
It has been held that the termination of employment and the notice thereof to be given by employer and workmen in clause (viii) of Standing Orders given in the 
Schedule are to be interpreted disjunctively. They comprise two distinct but con- nected matters. Termination of employment would be the primary subject whereas its notice would be the ancillary subject. To read the entry as one part qualifying the other would leave a sizeable gap in the area which the Schedule is apparently in- 
tended to cover.

Clause (xi) of the schedule provides for any other matter which may be prescribed. 
Any matter added by the appropriate Government shall be within its competence 
only if it relates to the conditions of employment.” The standing orders framed after 
coming into force of the Act bind even those employees who have entered into sery- 
ice before the framing of the standing orders inasmuch as such employees who are 
employed at the time when the standing orders are certified. 
Generally the conditions of service for industries laid down by standing orders are 
certified under the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946. However, 
the employee and employer may enter into special conditions of employment. How- 
ever, in case of conflict between them, the statutory conditions contained in standing 
orders prevail over the special conditions of employment between an employer and 25 : . 2 : ; ‘ 
employee.” Contractual stipulation in the letter of appointment cannot override the 
provisions of the statute. The latter shall have the overriding effect.” Such standing 
orders though binding between the employer and employees in the industry but not 
binding on industrial dispute. 
In acase of Steel Authority of India Ltd., the standing order 29 was called in ques- 
tion. Standing order 29 authorised the disciplinary authority to terminate the services 
of an employee without holding any enquiry in appropriate case after recording the 
reasons for it. It was held that such a provision is reminiscent of the days of hire and 
fire and it is unfortunate that a public sector undertaking is keeping such a provision 
in its standing orders. Therefore, the appeal was dismissed with the permission to 
initiate disciplinary proceedings. 
The certified Standing Orders have statutory force. The standing orders constitute a 
contract of conditions of service between the employer and the workman. Thus, the 
employer and workman cannot enter into a separate contract overriding the statutory 
contract embodied in the certified Standing Orders. 
The Supreme Court observed in a case, “the right to contract in industrial matters is 
no longer an absolute right and statutes dealing with industrial matters around with 
restrictions on the absolute right to contract. The doctrine of hire and fire is com- 
pletely abrogated both by statutes and by industrial adjudication, and even where the 
services of an employee are terminated by an order of discharge simpliciter, the le- 
gality and propriety of such an order can be challenged in Industrial Tribunals. These 
restrictions on the absolute right to contract are imposed because security of em- 
ployment is more and more regarded as one of the necessities for industrial peace and 
harmony and the contentment it brings about is a pre-requisite of social justice. If 
reasons for discharging an employee are furnished to the employee concerned, he not 
only has the satisfaction of knowing why his services are dispensed with but it be- 
comes easy for him in appropriate cases to challenge the order on the ground that it is

1. Submission of draft standing orders (s. 3) 
The employer of the establishment to which this Act becomes applicable has to 
submit the draft standing orders within six months from the date on which the Act 
becomes applicable to the establishment. The five copies of the proposed standing 
orders are to be submitted to the certifying officer by the employer for adoption in 
his establishment. | 
All the matters set out in the Schedule to the Act must be provided for in the draft 
standing order depending upon the industrial establishment. Where model standing 
orders have been prescribed, the draft standing orders should be in conformity with 
them to the extent it is possible. 
The draft standing orders shall be accompanied by a statement giving prescribed 
particulars of the workmen employed in the establishment including the name of the 
trade union to which they belong. 
A group of employers in similar industrial establishments may submit a joint draft 
of standing orders too. But this may be subject to certain prescribed conditions. 
The draft must conform to the model prescribed by the appropriate Government, in 
substance.’ But it need not copy model standing orders verbatim.” Section 3 does not 
require the workmen to ensure conformity of proposed modifications to standing or- 
ders with model standing orders.

There is no requirement in the standing orders schedule to frame it in respect of

3. Reasonableness of the Certifying Orders 
A duty is cast on the certifying officer to see that the draft standing orders or their 
modification not only should conform with the Model Standing Orders but also he 
has to see whether they are reasonable and fair or not.'* While adjudging the fairness 
or reasonable of any standing orders, the certifying officer should consider the social 
interest in the claims of employer and the social interest in the demands of the 
workmen. 
Certified standing orders which statutorily prescribe the conditions of service are 
deemed to be incorporated in the contract of employment of each employee with his 
employer. If any rule framed by a company read with standing orders confers abso- 
lute and unfettered discretion on the employer to allow or disallow rightful claim of 
employees, that would be unfair and unreasonable as also arbitrary subject to test of 
Article 14 of the Constitution.'° 
A mandatory duty has been cast upon the certifying officer by the Parliament under 
S. 4 which he must-discharge in a fair and quasi-judicial manner. If he finds that 
some provisions of the standing orders are unreasonable, he must refuse to certify the 
same. 
The findings of the certifying officer or appellate authority under this section are 
final but if the findings are recorded on extraneous considerations or under some 
misconception of law it is always open to the High Court under Article 226 to quash 
those findings. 
It has been held that in view of s. 4, the Supreme Court in appeal under Article 136 
shall have the power to adjudicate upon the fairness or reasonableness of the provi- 
sion of a standing order and declare it ineffective and unenforceable. 
Reduction of age of superannuation by certifying officer under the Act without 
hearing the workmen will be null and void. 
4. Matters which are not covered by the Schedule 
It has been held by the Supreme Court that the employer cannot insist upon adding 
a condition to the standing order which relates to the matter not included in the 
Schedule. The provision may be made in the standing order concerning the rights and 
liabilities of the employer and the employees as well as their enforcement by internal 
arrangement between them. 
If the certifying officer finds that some provisions of the standing orders relate to 
matters which are not included in the Schedule, he must refuse to certify the same.

5. Certification of Standing Orders (s. 5) 
On receipt of draft under s. 3, the certifying officer shall forward its copy to the 
trade union of the workmen, if it is present. Where no trade union is present, the copy 
will be forwarded to workmen in prescribed manner. Along with the copy a notice in 
the prescribed form is also sent to the workmen. The notice is to receive objections of 
the workmen which the workmen may desire to make to the draft standing orders. 
The workmen or the trade unions are required to submit objections to the certifying 
officer within fifteen days from the receipt of the notice. 
The certifying officer shall give an opportunity to the employer, trade union or 
other prescribed representatives of the workmen of being heard. After that, he will 
decide whether any modification or addition to the draft submitted by the employer is 
necessary to render the draft certifiable. He will make the order in writing accord- 
ingly. 
The certifying officer shall after making modifications, if required, certify the draft 
standing orders. After that within seven days he will send the copies of certified 
standing orders authenticated in the prescribed manner to the employer and to the 
trade union or other prescribed representatives of the workmen. Along with the certi- 
fied standing order, he will have to send copies of his order of modification or addi- 
tion to the draft standing orders. 
Certified standing orders contain statutory and non-contractual terms and condi- 
tions of service”’. These become part of the statutory condition of service and bind- 
ing on both the employer and the employees.” The certified standing orders have the 
overriding effect on other service or regulations. ”’ When the settlement arrived at 
between the workmen and the establishment is still in force, the parties are to remain 
bound by the terms of that settlement. Till the settlement is terminated, certified 
standing orders cannot be allowed to be amended.”* The certified standing orders are 
binding on the employers as well as all the workmen who were in employment at the 
time the standing orders came into force and those employed thereafter. 
After the amendment in 1957, the certifying officer and the appellate authority are 
duty bound to examine the question of fairness of the standing orders. There can be

matically. 
Termination of service in contravention of standing orders is bad." It has been 
held that provision for transfer of employees anywhere or detaining them for essen- 
tial services beyond duty hours in certified standing orders of a big organisation can- 
not be arbitrary. 
The topics which are neither included in the Schedule to the Industrial Employ- 
ment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 nor in the Model Standing Orders cannot be in- 
cluded in the standing orders. 
The provision for representation by an office bearer or a trade union in standing 
orders for certification is a mandatory provision. 
6. Appeals [s. 6] 
Any employer, workmen, trade union or other prescribed representatives of the 
workmen aggrieved by the order of the certifying officer may within thirty days from 
the date on which the copies of the draft standing orders are sent may appeal to the 
appellate authority. The decision of the appellate authority shall be final. The appel- 
late authority shall by order in writing confirm the standing orders either in the form 
certified by the certifying officer or after amending them by making certain modifi- 
cations or additions to it as it thinks necessary to make the standing orders certifiable. 
The appellate authority shall send copies of its order to the certifying officer, em- 
ployer and trade union or other prescribed representatives of the workmen within 7 
days of its order. The copy of the order must be accompanied by copies of the 
standing orders as certified by it and authenticated by it in the prescribed manner. 
Where no modification is made by it, it is not necessary to send the copies of stand- 
ing orders.
