The powers of the appellate authority are co-extensive with those of the certifying 
officer.® The certifying officer cannot dismiss the case for default.” The appellate 
authority has no power to set aside the order of the certifying officer. It can confirm 
or amend the standing orders. It can not remand the matter for fresh considera- 
tion. 
Mere non-participation in certification proceedings does not disentitle to prefer an 
appeal.” An order rejecting application for modification is not appealable under s. 6 
of the Act.” 
In Central Workshop Karamchari Sangh y. Industrial Tribunal it was held that the 
requirement that the memorandum of appeal must be signed by the authorised officer 
of the aggrieved party is directory in nature and its non-compliance cannot render an 
appeal non-maintanable. 
An appeal which is timely sent by registered post but reaches late does not become 
time-barred. 
In view of s. 9(1) of the General Clauses Act, 1897, the date on which the order 
under appeal was sent, should be excluded in computing the period of limitation. : 
Regarding the applicability of res judicata principle to the proceedings for modifi- 
cation of standing orders, it has been held by the Supreme Court that it is doubtful 
whether principles analogous to res judicata can be applied here. 
7. Date of Operation of Standing Orders (s. 7) 
Where no appeal is preferred, the standing orders come into operation on the ex- 
piry of thirty days from the date on which the authenticated copies of standing orders 
are sent. Where an appeal is preferred standing orders come into operation on the 
expiry of seven days from the date on which the copies of the order of appellate 
authority are sent. 
Section 7 is subject to no limitation. Thus, the standing orders after being certified 
must come into operation in accordance with it. 
8. Register of standing orders (s. 8) 
The certifying officer has to file a copy of all standing orders as finally certified in 
a register in the prescribed form maintained for the purpose. The certifying officer 
will provide a copy of it to any person applying for it on the payment of the pre- 
scribed fee. 
9. Posting of standing orders (s. 9) 
_ The text of the standing orders as finally certified are to be posted by the employer 
in English and in the language understood by majority of his workmen on special 
boards prominently. The special boards, are maintained for the purpose at or near the

10. Duration and modification of standing orders (s. 10) 
S. 10 provides that the finally certified standing orders shall not be liable to modi- 
fication until the expiry of six months from the date on which the standing orders or 
their last modifications came into operation except on agreement between the em- 
ployer and the workmen or a trade union or other representative body of the work- 
men. The standing orders are immutable only during the first six months from the 
date on which these came into operation. But after the said period there is no bar for 
applying for modifications to the certifying officer. 
The following persons can apply to the certifying officer for modification of the 
standing orders:— 
(i) an employer, or 
(ii) a workman, or 
(iii) a trade union, or 
(vi) other representative body of the workmen. 
The application for modification has to be accompanied by five copies of the modi- 
fications proposed to be made. Where such modifications are proposed to be made by 
agreement between the employer and the workmen or a trade union or other repre- 
sentative body of the workmen, a certified copy of that agreement shall be filed along 
with the application. In respect of such an application for modification all the fore- 
- going provisions of the Act are applicable in the same manner as they apply to the 
certification of the first standing orders. [sub-section (2)]. 
The above-stated provisions of sub-section (2) do not apply to an industrial estab- 
lishment in respect of which the appropriate Government is the Government of the 
State of Gujarat or the Government of the State of Maharashtra. 
S. 10 does not authorize the representative of an employer or a workman to make 
an application for modification of the certified standing orders because the right to 
apply for modification has been given personally to an employer or workman.” Ap- 
plication for modification of standing orders can be filed by workmen or trade union 
or other representative body of workmen. It is not necessary that such application 
must be filed by recognised or representative union with substantial majority of 
workmen. 
A provision in a standing order cannot be challenged by writ petition.” While the 
standing orders are in force, it is not permissible to seek statutory modification so 
that there may be one set_of standing orders for some employees and another set for 
the rest of the employees. 
This section [s. 10(2)] does not contain any time-limit for making modification ap- 
plication. It can be made at any time.

certified if it is found reasonable and fair. 
In Bharat Electronics Ltd vy. Bharat Electronics Ltd. Employees’ Union” it has 
been held that the provisions with regard to ‘abandonment of service’ in the standing 
order can be modified by the authority. In Barauni Refinery Pragatisheel Shramik 
Parishad y. Indian Oil Corporation Ltd.,” it has been held that during the operation 
of a settlement arrived at under sections 18(3) and 19(2) of the Industrial Disputes 
Act, 1947 postulating against any change in terms or conditions of service or raising 
of any demand involving additional financial burden, the workmen could not demand 
any modification of the standing orders for upward revision of the age of superannu- 
ation. 
It has been held by the Supreme Court that the modification relating to grant of 6 
days’ casual leave on a paid basis to workers, done by the certifying officer after 
considering certain relevant factors cannot be interfered by it under Article 136 of the 
Indian Constitution. 
Where the standing order relating to termination of service of a permanent work- 
man was modified requiring the employer to give reasons and communicating it to 
the workmen along with one month’s notice or one month’s pay in lieu of notice, the 
modification was held to be fair and reasonable. 
In a case involving take over of an electricity undertaking by the State, neither the 
Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act nor the Electricity Act provided for 
automatic continuance of the standing orders of the previous undertaking after its 
purchase, it was held that the purchaser must comply with s. 3 and without it there 
can be no certification under s. 5 which is a condition precedent to an application — 
under s. 6. 
In case a modification in the existing standing orders has been agreed upon be- 
tween the employer and the workman the certifying officer is not bound to accept the changes in case they are not in conformity with the prescribed model standing or- ders. | | 
In view of sections 4, 10 and 13(2), inconsistent part of the special agreement can- not prevail over the standing order.”

12. Powers of the Certifying Officers and Appellate Authority (s. 11) 
According to s. Il, every certifying officer and appellate authority shall have all 
the powers of a civil court for the following purposes:— 
(i) power for the purpose of receiving evidence, 
(ii) administering oaths, 
(iii) enforcing the attendance of witnesses, and 
(vi) compelling the discovery and production of documents. 
Every certifying officer and appellate authority shall be deemed to be a civil court 
within the meaning of section 345 and 346 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 
(2 of 1974). ! 
Clerical or arithmetical mistakes in any order passed by a Certifying Officer or ap- 
pellate authority or any error due to any accidental slip or omission may be corrected 
at any time by that officer or authority or the successor in office of such officer or 
authority. 
When the draft standing orders are submitted for certification, the certifying offi- 
cers should enquire whether the said orders are in conformity with the model stand- 
ing orders issued by the government and accordingly whether they are reasonable 
and fair.

13. Oral evidence in contradiction of standing orders not admissible (s. 12) 
According to this section, any oral evidence which has the effect of adding to or 
varying or, contradicting finally certified standing orders shail not be admitted in any 
court. 
14. Temporary application of model standing orders (s. 12A) 
S. 12A provides for temporary application of model standing orders to an industrial 
establishment. It says that notwithstanding anything contained in sections 3 to 12, for 
the period commencing on the date on which this Act becomes applicable to an in- 
dustrial establishment and ending with the date on which the certified standing orders come into operation in that establishment, the prescribed model standing orders shall be deemed to have been adopted in that establishment. The provisions of ss. 9, 13(2) 
and s. 13A apply to model standing orders as they apply to the certified standing or- ders. 
The abovestated provisions are not applicable to an industrial establishment in re- spect of which the appropriate Government is the government of the State of Gujarat or the Government of the State of Maharashtra. 
In a case, it has been held that every amendment to Model Standing Orders does not per se become applicable to an industrial establishment which has its own certi- fied standing orders. The only way in which a workman could get the benefit of the model standing orders would be to get their own standing order amended and certi- fied in accordance with the provisions of the Act. Until such modification and certifi- cation is made, the workers continue to be governed by their certified standing or- ders. 
Where an establishment had its certified standing orders and after addition of a new matter to the Schedule the model standing orders were modified, it was held that in the absence of compliance under s. 10, such amended model: standing orders would not become applicable to the establishment. 
It has been held in a case that where there are two categories of workmen, one in respect of the daily rated workmen and the other in respect of the monthly rated workmen, if there are certified Standing orders in respect of the daily rated workers only, the prescribed model standing orders should be deemed to have been adopted for those who are employed on the monthly basis until such categories have their own standing orders.” 
The Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 is a special law vis-a vis regulations framed under the general law. Hence the provisions of the former prevail over the latter.”’ Where the petitioner impugned his transfer from one place to an- other on the ground that though there is a provision of transfer in the appointment order, the standing orders subsequently certified did not contain any provision for transfer and as such his transfer was illegal, it was held that the certified standing orders prevail over terms and conditions contained in the appointment order and thus, the transfer order will have no effect.°® Similarly, in another case it was held that the regulations made under s. 79(c) of the Electricity Supply Act, 1946 is respect of con- ee ee ee ee

15. Penalties and Procedure (s. 13) 
Certain penalties and procedures have been provided in s. 13 by the Act. An em- 
ployer who fails to submit draft standing orders (under s. 3) or who modifies his 
standing orders but not in accordance with s. 10, is punishable with fine. The fine 
may extend to Rs. 5000. If the offence is a continuing offence a further fine is im- 
posed which may extend to Rs. 200 for every day after the first day during which the 
offence continues. 
An employer who does any act in contravention of the certified standing orders or 
his industrial establishment shall be punishable with fine which may extend to Rs. 
100. In the case of a continuing offence, a further fine is imposed which may extend 
to Rs. 25 for every day after the first during which the offence continues. 
The prosecution for an offence punishable here will be instituted only after the 
previous sanction of the appropriate Government. Any court inferior to that of a Met- 
ropolitan Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate of the second class will not try any of- 
fence under this section. 
It has been held in a case that if the management has no objection to certain matters 
being included in the standing orders and if its inclusion is accepted by the workman 
as well as the certifying officer, that clause in the standing orders cannot be struck 
off. Since the management did not apply for modification of that clause under s. 10, 
after the prosecution under s. 13, it was held not open to the management to contend 
that the inclusion of that clause was ultra vires the Act. 
16. Interpretation of standing orders (s. 13A) | 
If any question arises as to the application or interpretation of a certified standing 
order, it may be referred to any one of the Labour Courts constituted under the In- 
dustrial Disputes Act, 1947 (14 of 1947). Such Labour Court must have been speci- 
fied by the appropriate Government by notification in the Official Gazette for the 
disposal of such proceedings. The following persons may refer the question to the 
Labour Court:— 
(i) any employer, or 
(ii) workman, or 
(iii) a trade union or other representative body of the workmen. 
The Labour Court after giving an opportunity of being heard to the parties decides 
the question. The decision taken by the Labour Court remains final and binding on 
the parties. 
Although the ordinary rules of interpretation of statutes would be applicable to in- 
terpretation of standing orders as well, the limited purpose of s. 13-A is to provide a

A workman cannot go to a civil court for the enforcement of his right which ema-

A Labour Commissioner is required to interpret any question raised as to the appli-

certified under the Act. 
While considering the question of interpretation of a standing order, the Labour 
Court cannot accord an interim relief.

Under this section, a rule or regulation, notified by the appropriate Government, 
will exclude the applicability of the Act to the extent that the rule or regulation COV-

in which the workmen employed could properly be described as Government ser-

over of management by Electricity Board is binding on workmen who opted for 
Board’s service agreeing to their service conditions and to be governed by the regu- 
lations. 
18. Power to exempt [S. 14] , 
The appropriate Government may by notification in the Official Gazette exempt 
any industrial establishment or class of them either conditionally or unconditionally. 
The exemption may be either from all the provisions of the Act or any of them. 
19. Delegation of Powers (s. 14A) 
The appropriate Government may delegate some of its power under s. 14A by noti- 
fication in the Official Gazette. The delegated powers may be exercisable by the ap- 
propriate Government either under this Act or any rules made under it. The delega- 
tion of power may be in relation to matters which may be given in the direction and 
will be subject to such conditions which may be similarly given in the direction. 
Such delegated powers will be exercisable also— 
(a) Where the appropriate Government is the Central Government, by such 
officer or authority subordinate to the Central Government or by the State 
Government or by such officer or authority subordinate to the State Gov- 
ernment as may be specified in the notification.

20. Power to make rules (s. 15) 
The appropriate Government may make rules for carrying out the purposes of this 
Act under s. 15. Rules may be made after previous publication by notification in the 
Official Gazette. This is the general power of making rules. In particular, such rules 
may— 
(a) prescribe additional matters to be included in the Schedule and the proce- 
dure to be followed in modifying Certified Standing Orders in accordance 
with any such addition; Before making any rules, representatives of both 
employers and workmen are consulted by the appropriate Government. 
(b) set out model standing orders for the purposes of this Act; 
(c) prescribe the procedure of certifying officers and appellate authorities; 
(d) provide for any other matter which is to be or may be prescribed. 
Every rule made by the Central Government is laid before each House of Parlia- 
ment as soon as it is made. For laying down the rules the Parliament must be in ses- 
sion for a total period of thirty days which may be comprised in one session or in two 
or more successive sessions. If before the expiry of the session immediately follow- 
ing the session or successive sessions both Houses agree in making any modification 
in the rule shall have effect only in the modified form. But where both Houses agree 
that the rule should not be made the rule shall have no effect. However, any such 
modification or annulment shall be without prejudice to the validity of anything pre- 
viously done under that rule i.e., it will not effect the previous state of things done 
under the rule.

The Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 is an act to regulate the employment of women in 
certain establishments for certain period before and after child-birth and to provide 
for maternity benefit and certain other benefits. 
With the advent of modern age, as the number of women employees is growing, 
the maternity leave and other maternity benefits are becoming increasingly common. 
But till 1961, there was no beneficial piece of legislation intending to achieve the 
object of doing social justice to women workers employed in factories, mines and 
plantation. For this purpose, the Maternity Benefit Bill was passed by both the 
Houses of Parliament and received the assent of the President on 12th December’ 
1961 and became an act named “The Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 (53 of 1961).” 
The object of maternity leave and benefit is to protect the dignity of motherhood 
by providing for the full and healthy maintenance of women and her child when she 
is not working. 
Till now, six amendments have been made to the original Act. The list of amend- 
ing acts is given below:— 
(1) The Central Labour laws (Extension to Jammu and Kashmir) Act, 1970 (51 
of 1970). 
(2) The Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 1972 (21 of 1972). 
(3) The Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 1973 (52 of 1973). 
(4) The Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 1976 (53 of 1976).

706 Chap. I—Introduction 
(5) The Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 1988 (61 of 1988). 
(6) The Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 1995 (29 of 1995). 
1. Short Title, Extent and Commencement (s. 1) 
(1) This Act may be called the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961. 
(2) It extends to the whole of India.” 
(3) It shall come into force on such date® as may be notified in this behalf in 
the Official Gazette— 
(a) in relation to mines and other establishment wherein parsons are em- 
ployed for the exhibition of equestrian, acrobatic and other perform- 
ances, by the Central Government; and 
(b) in relation to other establishments in a State, by the State Government. 
2. Application of the Act (s. 2) 
In the first instance, the Act applies— 
(1) (a) to every establishment being a factory, mine or plantation including any 
such establishment belonging to Government, and 
(b) to every establishment wherein persons are employed for the exhibition of 
equestrian, acrobatic and other performances; 
(2) to every shop and establishment in which ten or more persons are employed, or 
were employed, on any day of the preceeding twelve months. Such shops or estab- 
lishments must be within the meaning of any law for the time being in force in rela- 
tion to shops and establishments in a State. 
The State Government may declare that all or any of the provisions of the Act shall 
also apply to any other establishment, or class of establishments, industrial, commer- 
cial, agricultural or otherwise. The State Government has to take prior approval of 
the Central Government for this purpose. The declaration is made by notification in 
the Official Gazette and two months’ notice is given to the establishments of the in- tention of the State government regarding applicability of the Act. 
Same as otherwise provided in sections 5A and 5B nothing contained in this Act shall be applicable to any factory or other establishment to which the provisions of the Employees’ State Insurance Act, 1948 is applicable. 
It has been held that the word ‘establishment’ has a wide meaning. It generally denotes a shop, commercial organisation or a public institution, provided they are not specifically exempted by the appropriate Government from the applicability of the Act.°

3. Appropriate Government [s. 3(a)] 
In relation to an establishment being a mine or an establishment wherein persons are employed for the exhibition of equestrian, acrobatic and other performances, the

appropriate Government is the Central Government. In relation to any other estab- 
lishment, the State Government is the appropriate Government. 
4. Child [s. 3(b)] 
The definition of ‘child’ only provides that ‘child’ includes a still-born child. 
5. Delivery [s. 3(c)] | 
The definition says that the term’ delivery’ means the birth of a child. 
6. Employer [s. 3(d)] 
An ‘employer’ means— 
(i) in relation to an establishment under the control of the Government, any 
person or authority appointed by the Government for the supervision and 
control of employees. Where any such person or authority is not appointed, 
then the head of the department is the employer; 
(ii) in relation to an establishment under any local authority, the person ap- 
pointed by such authority for the supervision and control of employees. 
Where no person is so appointed, the chief executive officer of the local 
authority is the employer; 
(iii) in any other case, the person or authority having the ultimate control over 
the affairs of the establishment. Where affairs are entrusted to any other 
parson called either a manager, managing director, managing agent, or by 
any other name, such person will be the employer. 
7. Establishment [s. 3(e)] 
According to section 3(e), an ‘establishment’ means:— 
(i) a factory, 
(ii) a mine; 
(iii) a plantation; 
(iv) an establishment wherein persons are employed for the exhibition of 
equestrian, acrobatic and other performances; 
(v) ashop or establishment; or 
(vi) an establishment to which the provisions of this Act are applicable under s. 
21). 
8. Factory [s. 3(f)] : 
‘Factory’ means a factory as defined in s. 2(m) of the Factories Act, 1948 (63 of 
1948). 
9, Inspector [s. 3(g)] 
_ The term ‘inspector’ means an Inspector appointed under s. 14 of the Maternity 
Benefit Act, 1961. 
10. Maternity Benefit [s. 3(h)] 
The term ‘maternity benefit’ means the payment referred in s. 5(1) of the Act. 


708 Chap. I—Introduction 
11. Medical termination of pregnancy [s. 3(ha)] 
The term ‘medical termination of pregnancy’ means the termination of pregnancy 
permissible under the provisions of Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act, 1971. 
12. Mine [s. 3(i)] 
The term ‘mine’ means a mine as defined in s. 2 of the Mines Act, 1952 (32 of 
L952). 
13. Miscarriage [s. 3(j)] 
‘Miscarriage’ means expulsion of the contents of a pregnant uterus during the 
twenty-sixth week of pregnancy or at any period prior to that. It does not include any 
miscarriage, the causing of which is punishable under the Indian Penal Code (45 of 
1860). 
14. Plantation [s. 3(k)] 
The term ‘plantation’ means a plantation as defined in s. 2(f) of the Plantations La- 
bour Act, 1951 (69 of 1951). 
15. Prescribed [s. 3(])] 
The term ‘prescribed’ means prescribed by rules made under this Act. 
16. State Government [s. 3(m)] 
In relation to a Union Territory, the term ‘State Government’ means its Adminis- 
trator. 
17. Wages [s. 3(n)] 
The term ‘wages’ means all remuneration paid or payable in cash to a woman, if 
the terms of the contract of employment, (express or implied) were fulfilled. It in- 
cludes:— . 
(1) Such cash allowances (including dearness allowance and house rent allow- 
ance) as a woman is for the time being entitled to, 
(2) incentive bonus, and - 
(3) the money value of the concessional supply of food grains and other articles, 
but does not include— 
(a) any bonus other than incentive bonus, 
(b) over time earnings and any deductions or payment made on account of 
fines, 
(c) any contribution paid or payable by the employer to any pension fund or provident fund or for the benefit of the woman under any law for the 
time being in force. 
18. Woman [s. 3(0)] 
The term ‘woman’ means a woman employed, whether directly or through any agency, for wage in any establishment.

1. Work by women prohibited during certain periods [s. 4] 
Under this section, work by any woman is prohibited during the period of six 
weeks immediately following the day of her delivery, miscarriage or medical termi- 
nation of pregnancy. During this time period, any employer cannot employ a woman 
if he knows of her condition. ; 
Besides restricting employers from giving employment to women during this cer- 
tain period, the Act has imposed restriction on the women too, It says that no women 
shall work in any establishment during the six weeks immediately following the day 
of her delivery, miscarriage or medical termination of pregnancy. 
After making request in this behalf, any woman shall not be required by her em- 
ployer to do during this time period any work which: 
— is of an arduous nature; or 
which involves long hours of standing; or 
— which in any way is likely to interfere with her pregnancy or with the normal 
development of the foetus, or 
is likely to cause her miscarriage; or 
709 


710 The Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 
— otherwise is likely to affect her health adversely. 
These provisions have no effect on provisions of section 6. Here the pregnant 
woman has been given protection so that no adverse affect is made on the develop- 
ment of foetus or her health. 
The protection from such type of work is available during the following time- 
period: — 
(a) the period of one month immediately preceding the period of six weeks, be- 
fore the date of her expected delivery. 
(b) any period during the period of six weeks for which the pregnant woman 
does not avail of leave of absence under s. 6. 
2. Right of payment of maternity benefits [s. 5] 
According to s. 5, every woman is entitled to the payment of maternity benefit at 
the rate of the average daily wage for the period of her actual absence, i.e., the period 
immediately preceding the day of her delivery, the actual day of her delivery and any 
period immediately following that day. 
The employer has also been made liable to pay maternity benefits under the sec- 
tion. | 
Now the question arises, what is average daily wage? The average daily wage 
means the average of the women’s wages payable to her for the days on which she 
has worked during the period of three calendar months immediately preceding the 
date from which she absents herself on account of maternity, the minimum rate of 
wage fixed or revised under the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 (11 of 1948) or ten ru- 
pees, whichever is the highest. 
However, a condition is attached to the payment of maternity benefits. The condi- 
tion says that no woman shall be entitled to maternity benefits unless she has actually 
worked in an establishment of the employer (from whom she is claiming maternity 
benefit) for a period of not less than 80 days in the twelve months immediately pre- 
ceding the date of her expected delivery. But the qualifying period of eighty days is 
not applicable to a woman who has immigrated in to the State of Assam and was 
pregnant at the time of the immigration. 
_ For the calculation of days on which a woman has actually worked in the estab- 
lishment during the period of twelve months immediately preceding the date of her 
expected delivery the following days are taken into account— 
(a) the days for which she has been laid off, or 
(b) was on holidays declared under any law for the time being in force to be 
holidays with wages. 
_The maximum period of maternity benefit is twelve weeks of which not more than six weeks will precede the date of expected delivery of a woman i.e., pre-natal. 
In case a woman dies during this period, the maternity benefit will be payable only for the days upto and including the day of her death. 
_ Where a woman, after delivering a child, dies during her delivery or during the pe- riod immediately following the date of her delivery for which she is entitled for the maternity benefit, leaving behind in either case the child, the employer shall be liable for the maternity benefit for that entire period. If the child also dies during that period 


Chap. II—Main Provisions 711 
the employer will be liable for the maternity benefit for the days upto and including 
the date of the death of the child. 
In a case, the question was whether sunday is to be counted in calculating the 
amount of maternity benefit. It was held that the term week signifies a cycle of seven 
days including sundays. The legislature intended that computation of maternity bene- 
fit is to be made for the entire period of the woman worker’s actual absence i.e., for 
all the days including sundays, which may be wageless holidays falling within that 
period and not only intermittent periods of six days thereby excluding sundays falling 
within that period. | 
3. Continuance of payment of maternity benefit [s. 5A] 
Section 5A continues payment of maternity benefit in certain cases. The maternity 
benefit is provided under two labour legislations, namely, the Maternity Benefit Act, 
1961 and the Employees’ State Insurance Act, 1948. This section continues the pay- 
ment of maternity benefit under this Act to women employed in factories or other 
establishments where Employees State Insurance Act, 1948 is applicable. It says that 
every woman entitled to the payment of maternity benefit under this Act shall con- 
tinue to be so entitled until she becomes qualified to claim maternity benefit under s. 
50 the Employees’ State Insurance Act if that Act is applicable to the establishment 
in which she is working. 
4. Payment of maternity benefit in certain cases [s. 5B] 
S. 5B provides that every woman is entitled to the payment of maternity benefit 
under this section in the following cases:— 
(a) who is employed in a factory or other establishment to which the provisions 
of the Employees’ State Insurance Act, 1948 (34 of 1948) apply ; 
(b) whose wages (excluding remuneration for overtime work) for a month ex- 
ceed the amount specified in s. 2(9)(b) of that Act ; and 
(c) who fulfills the conditions specified in s. 5 (2). 
5. Notice of claim for maternity benefit and its payment [s. 6] 
Any woman employed in an establishment and entitled to maternity benefit may 
give notice in writing in the prescribed form, to her employer regarding her maternity 
benefit and any other amount to which she is entitled. She may state in the notice that 
amount and maternity benefit will be paid either to her or her nominated person in 
the notice. She will also notify to her employer that she will not work in any estab- 
lishment during the period for which she receives maternity benefit. 
In case of a pregnant woman, notice will also state the date from which she will be 
absent from work. This date shall not be earlier than 6 weeks from the date of her 
expected delivery. 
On receipt of the notice, the employer will permit such woman to absent herself from 
the establishment during the period for which she receives the maternity benefit. 
The amount of maternity benefit is payable in two installment /.e., one installment 
for the pre-natal (before birth of the child) and another for the post-natal period (after 
the birth of the child). The amount of maternity benefit for the period preceding the 
date of woman’s expected delivery is paid in advance by the employer on production 
1. B.B. Shah y. Presiding Office, Labour Court, Coimbatore, AIR 1978 SC 12: (1978) 1 LLJ 29. 


712 The Maternity Benefit Act, 196] 
of prescribed proof of her pregnancy. The amount-due for the subsequent period will 
be paid by the employer to the woman within forty-eight hours of production of re- 
quired proof that the woman has delivered a child. 
In case a woman who is otherwise entitled to maternity benefit or any other 
amount under this Act fails to give notice to her employer, even then she will be en- 
titled to the maternity benefit and due amount. In any such case, an Inspector may 
either on his own motion or on the application made by the woman to him, order the 
payment of such benefit or amount within the specified time-period in his order. 
The two grounds which are available to an Inspector to take action for payment of 
maternity benefit are:— 
(i) on his own motion i.e., suo motu, and 
(ii) on application of the woman to him claiming the maternity benefit and 
amount which is due to her. 
6. Payment of maternity benefit in case of death of a woman [s. 7] — 
If a woman entitled to maternity or any other amount under this Act, dies before 
receiving them, the employer will pay such benefit or amount to the person nomi- 
nated by that woman in the notice (under s. 6). In case, there is no such nomination 
he will pay benefit or the amount to her legal representative. Where a woman after 
delivering the child dies during her delivery or during the period immediately fol- 
lowing the date of her delivery, leaving behind her child, the employer is under duty 
to pay such benefit or amount to the person. nominated in the notice or to her legal 
representative in case no nomination is made. Even where the child also dies during 
the said period, he will pay the maternity benefit or amount for the days up-to and 
including the date of the death of the child, to the person nominated in the notice or 
to her legal representative in case no nomination is made. 
7. Payment of medical bonus [s. 8] 
Where no pre-natal confinement and post-natal care is provided by the employer 
free of charge to a woman employee, he will have to pay medical bonus. S. 8 says 
that in such a case every woman entitled to maternity benefit is also entitled to re- 
ceive from her employer a medical bonus of two hundred and fifty rupees. 
8. Leave for miscarriage, etc. [s. 9] 
In case of miscarriage or medical termination of pregnancy, a woman is entitled to 
leave with wages at the rate of maternity benefit, for a period of six weeks immedi- ately following the day of her miscarriage or medical termination of pregnancy. However, she will have to give the prescribed proof of the same. 
9. Leave with wages for tubectomy operation [s. 9A] 
In case of tubectomy operation, a woman is entitled to leave with wages at the rate of maternity benefit for a period of two weeks immediately following the day of her tubectomy operation. Here again she will have to give the prescribed proof that she has undergone that operation 
10. Leave for illness arising out of pregnancy, delivery, premature birth of a AGH T mero medical termination of pregnancy or tubectomy opera- ion [s.

entitled to leave with wages at the rate of maternity benefit for a maximum period of 
one month. This leave with wages is in addition to leaves under s. 6 when a woman 
due to pregnancy goes on maternity leave after giving notice to her employer and 
under s. 9 where leave for miscarriage or medical termination of pregnancy is given. 
Under this section, the leave is given for a maximum period of one month. Here 
again the woman who wants to avail the leave has to give the necessary proof. 
11. Nursing Breaks [s. 11] 
Every woman who returns to duty after delivering a child is entitled to two breaks 
of the prescribed duration for nursing her child until the child attains the age of fif- 
teen months. These breaks are in addition to the rest interval allowed to her. 
12. Dismissal during absence of pregnancy [s. 12] 
S. 12 gives some protections to a woman employee who absents herself under the 
Act. Section 12 says that when a woman absents herself from work according to the 
Act, it will be unlawful for her employer to— 
(i) discharge or dismiss her during such absence or on account of such ab- 
sence, Or 
(ii) give notice of discharge or dismissal on such a day that the notice will ex- 
pire during such absence, or 
(iii) vary to her disadvantage any of the conditions of her service. [Sub-section 
(1)] 
In case of discharge or dismissal of a woman during her pregnancy if she is entitled 
to medical bonus or maternity benefit, such discharge or dismissal will not effect her 
maternity benefit or medical bonus. Where she would have been entitled to them if 
she was not discharged or dismissal, she will remain entitled to them. 
In case the woman is dismissed for any prescribed misconduct, the employer may 
deprive her of the maternity benefit or medical bonus or both by order in writing 
communicated to the woman. 
Any woman deprived of maternity benefit or medical bonus or both or discharged 
or dismissed during or on account or her absence, may appeal to the prescribed 
authority within sixty days from the date on which order of discharge, dismissal or 
deprivation 1s communicated to her. [Sub-section (2)}]. 
The provisions of sub-section (2) does not affect the provisions of sub-section (1). 
13. No deduction in wages in certain cases [s. 13] 
Any deduction from the usual and normal daily wages of a woman entitled to ma- 
ternity benefit is not made by reason only of — 
(a) the nature of work assigned to her by virtue of the provisions of s. 4(3). 
(Where no pregnant women shall be required to do work during the pre- 
scribed period of pregnancy any work which 1s of arduous nature, or in- 
volves long hours of standing, or ts likely to interfere with her pregnancy or 
development of foetus or is likely to cause miscarriage or otherwise ad- 
versely affect her health). 
(b) breaks for nursing the child allowed to her under s. 11. (Where two breaks 
for nursing the child allowed to a woman after returning to her work after 
her delivery besides the interval of rest allowed to her). 


714 The Maternity Benefit Act, 196] 
14. Appointment of Inspectors [s. 14] 
The appropriate Government may appoint same officers to be Inspectors by notifi- 
cation in the Official Gazette. The appropriate Government may define the local lim- 
its of the jurisdiction within which the Inspectors will exercise their powers under 
this Act. 
15. Powers and duties of Inspectors [s. 15] 
S. 15 has conferred powers and duties to the Inspectors. Such powers have been 
made subject to some prescribed restrictions or conditions. An Inspector may exer- 
cise all or any of the powers given below:— 
(a) He may enter at all reasonable times any premises or places where women 
are employed or work is given to them in an establishment for the purposes 
of examining any registers and notices required to be kept or exhibited un- 
der this Act. He may require their production for inspection. He may take 
for his assistance any persons in the service of the Government or any local 
or other public authority. 
(b) He may examine any person whom he finds in any premises or place and 
has reason to believe that he is employed in the establishment. However, 
the inspector cannot compel any person to answer any question or give any 
evidence tending to incriminate himself. The proviso says that no person 
shall be compelled under this section to any question or give any evidence 
tending to incriminate himself. 
(c) He may require the employer to give information regarding the follow- 
ing:— 
(i) names and addresses of women employed, 
(il) payments made to them, 
(11) applications or notices received from them under this Act, 
(d) He can take copies of any registers and records or notices or any portions of them. 
16. Inspectors to be public servants [s. 16] 
S. 16 says that every inspector appointed under this Act shall be deemed to be a athe servant within the meaning of s. 21 of the Indian Penal Code, 1960 (45 of 
17. Power of inspector to direct payments to be made [s. 17] 
Certain powers have been given to the Inspectors regarding payments to be made to woman under this Act. Any woman may make a complaint to the Inspector on the following grounds:— 
(1) where a woman Claims that maternity benefit or any other amount to which she is entitled and any person claiming that payment due (where the woman has died under s. 7) has been improperly withheld. 
(ii) where she claims that her employer has discharged or dismissed her during on it a of her absence from work in accordance with the provisions of this Act. 


Chap. !I—Main Provisions | IS 
_ On receiving such a complaint or on his own motion the Inspector may make an Inquiry or Cause an enquiry to be made. If after the inquiry he is satisfied that— 
(a) the payment has been wrongfully withheld, he may direct the payment to be made in accordance with his orders. 
(b) she has been discharged or dismissed during or on account of her absence from work according to the provisions of this Act, he may pass such orders as are just and proper according to the circumstances of the case. 
Any person aggrieved by the decision (abovestated) of the Inspector may appeal to the prescribed authority within 30 days from the date on which the decision of the Inspector was communicated to him. 
In case no appeal is made against the decision of the Inspector, his decision will be final. But where appeal is made, the decision of the prescribed authority is consid- ered final. In a case, it has been held that availability of the remedy to appeal to pre- scribed authority will not bar the aggrieved person to file a suit against the decision 
of the Inspector in any court of competent jurisdiction. 
Any amount payable under this section is recoverable as an arrear of land revenue 
by the collector. The amount is recovered only after the Inspector issues a certificate 
for that amount. 
18. Forfeiture of maternity benefit [s. 18] 
S. 18 provides for the forfeiture of maternity benefit. It says that if a woman works in 
any establishment after she has been permitted by her employer to absent herself for ma- 
ternity leave, she will have to forfeit her claim to the maternity benefit for such period. 
19. Abstract of Act and rules thereunder to be exhibited [s. 19] 
It has been made mandatory for the employers to display in a conspicuous place in 
every part of the establishment in which women are employed, an abstract of the 
provisions of this Act and all the rules made thereunder. The abstract and the rules 
must be in the language or languages of the locality. 
20. Registers, etc. (s. 20) 
Every employer has to prepare and maintain prescribed registers, records and 
muster-rolls in the prescribed manner. 
21. Penalty for contravention of Act by employer [s. 21] 
Some penalty provisions have been given in the Act where the employer contra- 
venes provisions of the Act. An employer will be punishable with fine and impris- 
onment in the following cases: — 
(1) where he fails to pay any amount of maternity benefit to a woman entitled 
to it, or 
(ii) discharges or dismisses such woman during her maternity leave, or on ac- 
count of her absence from work in accordance with the provisions of this 
Act. 
Imprisonment given shall not be less than three months but may extend to one 
year. Fine will not be less than two thousand rupees but may extend to five thousand 
rupees. 
2. Thomas Eapen y. Assistant Labour Officer, 1993 LLR 800 (Ker). 


716 The Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 
However, the court may impose a sentence of imprisonment for a lesser term or 
fine only in lieu of imprisonment on the ground of sufficient reasons which are to be 
recorded in writing. 
If any employer contravenes provisions of this Act or rules made under it and in 
case no other penalty is provided under the Act for such contravention, he shall be 
punishable with imprisonment or fine. Imprisonment in such a case may extend to 
one year. Fine may extend to five thousand rupees. He shall be given penalty with 
imprisonment, or with fine or with both. 
Where the maternity benefit or amount has not already been recovered from the 
employer, the court shall recover such maternity benefit or amount (in addition to the 
fine imposed) as if it were a fine and pay the same to the entitled person. 
22. Penalty for obstructing Inspector [s. 22] 
Separate penalties for obstructing Inspector appointed under the Act are given in 
section 22. Any person who obstructs an Inspector shall be punishable with impris- 
onment which may extend to one year or with fine which may extend to five thou- 
sand rupees or with both. Penalty may be given on the following grounds:— 
(1) when a person fails to produce on demand by the Inspector any register or 
document in his custody kept according to the Act, or rules under it, or 
(2) conceals or prevents any person from appearing before or being examined 
by an Inspector. 
23. Cognizance of offences (s. 23) 
Any one of the following persons may file a complaint regarding the commission 
of an offence under this Act in any court of competent jurisdiction:— 
(1) Any aggrieved woman, an office-bearer of a trade union registered under 
the Trade Unions Act, 1926 (16 of 1926) of which such a woman is a 
member, or : 
(2) a voluntary organisation registered under the Societies Registration Act, 
1860 (21 of 1860), or 
(3) an Inspector appointed under the Act. 
The complaint has to be filed within one year from the date on which the offence is 
alleged to have been committed. No complaint can be filed after the expiry of one 
year from the date on which the offence was committed: 
If any woman of a registered trade union or of a registered voluntary organisation has 
been denied any of the benefits of the Act, then she has the right to file a complaint in 
any court of competent jurisdiction. But this right is subject to the condition that 
whether the Maternity Benefit Act is applicable to the establishment where she works. 
Any court inferior to that of Metropolitan Magistrate or a Magistrate of a first class 
cannot try any offence under this Act. 
24. Protection of action taken in good faith [s, 24] 
Any suit, prosecution or other legal proceeding shall not lie against any person for 
anything which is done in good faith or intended to be done in pursuance of the Act 
or rules or any order made under the Act. 
3. Thomas Eapen y. Assistant Labour Officer, 1993 LLR 800 (Ker). 


Chap. II—Main Provisions gA7 
25. Power of Central Government to give directions [s. 25] 
The Central Government may give such directions as it may deem necessary to a 
State Government for carrying into execution the provisions of this Act. The State 
Government will comply with such directions. 
26. Power to exempt establishments [s. 26] 
The appropriate Government has been given the power to exempt certain estab- 
lishments from the applicability of provisions of this Act where the benefits granted 
by the establishment are not less favourable than those provided by this Act. The ex- 
emption may be done by notification in the Official Gazette. It may be subject to 
such conditions and restrictions as may be specified in the notification. The exemp- 
tion may be from all the provisions of the Act or any of the provisions or of any rule 
made under it. 
The appropriate Government on being satisfied with regard to grant of benefits, has 
the power to exempt an establishment or a class of establishments, i.e., hospitals, 
nursing homes and dispensaries, from the operation of all or any of the provisions of 
the Act. This exemption remains in force as long as it has not been cancelled by fur- 
ther notification. 
27. Effect of laws and agreements inconsistent with this Act [s. 27] 
S. 27 provides that the provisions of this Act shall have effect notwithstanding 
anything inconsistent therewith contained in any other law or in the terms of any 
award, agreement or contract of service, whether made before or after coming into 
force of this Act. This means that provisions of this Act have overriding effect over 
anything inconsistent with it contained in any law or any agreement etc. 
But where under any such award, agreement, contract of service or otherwise, a 
woman is entitled to more favourable benefit in respect of any matter than this Act, 
she will remain entitled to more favourable benefits in respect of that matter. How- 
ever, in respect of other matters she will remain entitled under this Act. 
This Act does not prohibit a woman from entering into an agreement with her em- 
ployer from granting her rights or privileges in respect of any matter which are more 
favourable to her than those to which she would be entitled under this Act. 
28. Power to make rules [s. 28] 
S. 28 provides that the appropriate Government may make rules for carrying out 
the purposes of this Act by notification in the Official Gazette. This power is subject 
to the condition of previous publication. In particular, and without prejudice to the 
generality of the foregoing power, such rules may provide for the following:— 
(a) the preparation and maintenance of registers, records and muster-rolls, 
(b) the exercise of powers (including the inspection of establishments) and the 
performance of duties by Inspectors for the purposes of this Act, 
(c) the method of payment of maternity benefit and other benefits under this 
Act in so far as provision has not been made therefor in this Act, 
(d) the form of notices under s. 6, 
(e) the nature of proof required under the provisions of this Act, 
4. Thomas Eapen y. Assistant Labour Officer, 1993 LLR 800 (Ker). 


718 The Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 
(f) the duration of nursing-breaks under ie iL 
(g) acts which may constitute gross misconduct for purposes of s. 12, 
(h) the authority to which an appeal under s. 12(2) (b) shall lie. The form and 
manner in which such appeal shall be made and the procedure to be fol- 
lowed in respect of its disposal, 
(i) the authority to which an appeal shall lie against the decision of the In-

(j) the form and manner in which complaints may be made to Inspectors under

(k) any other matter which is to be, or may be prescribed. 
Every rule made by the Central Government under this section is to be laid before 
each House of Parliament as soon as may be after it is made. It is laid when each 
House of Parliament is in session for a total period of thirty days which may be com- 
prised in one session or in two or more successive sessions. If before the expiry of 
the session immediately following the session or the successive sessions, both 
Houses agree in making any modification in the rule or both Houses agree that the 
rule should not be made, the rule shall have effect in modified form or shall have no 
effect. Any such modification or annulment shall not effect the validity of anything 
previously done under that rule. 


THE APPRENTICES ACT, 1961 
SYNOPSIS 
1, Statement of Objects and Reasons ...... 719 2. Amendment Act 41 of 1986 
The Apprentices Act, 1961 is an Act to provide for the regulation and control of 
training of apprentices and for matters connected therewith. 
1. Statement of Objects and Reasons 
The Statement of Objects and Reasons of the Act states that the question of under- 
taking legislation for regulating the training of apprentices in industry has been under 
the consideration of the Government for a long time. Expert committees which went 
into the consideration have recommended such legislation. It was found that certain 
establishments in the public and private sectors have been carrying out programmes 
of training of skilled workers on a systematic basis, the industry in general has not as 
yet fully organised such programmes. 
In the context of the five year plan and the large scale industrial development of 
the country, there was increasing demand for skilled craftsmen. Therefore, the Gov- 
ernment considered it necessary fully to utilise the facilities available for the training 
of apprentices and to ensure their training in accordance with the programmes, stan- 
dards and syllabi, drawn up expert bodies. Thus, the Apprentices Act, 1961 was en- 
acted by Parliament in the twelfth year of the Republic of India. 
2. Amendment Act 41 of 1986 
The Apprentices Act, 1961 provides for the regulation and control of training of 
apprentices. The Statement of Objects and Reasons of the Amending Act 41 of 1986 
states that the vocationalisation of higher secondary education has been attempted in 
Our country as part of the efforts to provide meaningful education leading to suitable 
employment opportunities at the appropriate levels. It is also hoped that this would 
relieve the pressure on our higher education system. Vocationalisation implies edu- 
cation through work experience and hence adequate facilities are to be provided for 
the vocational stream to learn the practical aspects of the subject through field studies 
and to supplement the institutional learning. Providing apprenticeship facilities to the 
products of vocational stream assumes relevance in this context. 
A pilot scheme called Special Vocational Education Training Scheme was laun- 
ched in 1983-84 under the supervision of the Regional Boards of Apprenticeship 
Training. The Scheme provided “on the job training” to the product of the vocational 
stream and also provided for training of weaker sections, specially to the Scheduled 
Castes and the Scheduled Tribes, minorities, physically handicapped and women. 
In the light of the experience gained during the two years which indicated that the 
scheme was welcomed by the states, training agencies and the products of the voca- 
tional stream, it is proposed to amend the Apprentices Act, 1961 to provide training 
for the products of vocational stream by creating a separate category of apprentices 
called “the technician (vocational) apprentices” and administer the scheme through 
719 


720 The Apprentices Act, 1961 
the Regional Boards of Apprenticeship Training who are implementing the appren- 
ticeship training scheme for graduates and technician apprentices. 
Therefore, the object of the Amending Act 41 of 1986 is to provide “‘on the job 
training” to the products of the vocational stream so that adequate competence and 
skill required for various occupations are acquired which would lead to suitable em- 
ployment or self-employment opportunity in organised industries, agriculture and 
other service sectors of economic activity including agro and rural based industries. 
Section 3-A of the Apprentices Act, 1961 was also amended so as to remove diffi- 
culties that were faced in the working of the scheme of reservations of training places 
for the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.

1. Extent, Commencement and Application [s. 1} 
The Apprentices Act, 1961 extends to the whole of India. It came into force on Ist 
March’ 1962. This provisions of the Act do not apply to— 
(a) any area or to any industry in any area unless the Central government speci- 
fies that area or industry as an area or industry to which the said provisions 
will apply with effect from the given date. The specification will be by no- 
tification in the Official Gazette. 
(b) any such special apprenticeship scheme for imparting training to appren- 
tices as may be notified by the Central Government in the Official Gazette. 
DEFINITIONS [S. 2] 
2. All India Council [s. 2(a)] 
‘All India Council” means the All India Council of Technical Education estab- 
lished by the resolution of Government of India in the former Ministry of Education 
No. F. 16-10 / 44-E, III, dated the 30th November, 1945. 
3. Apprentice [s. 2(aa)] 
“Apprentice” means a person who is undergoing apprenticeship training in pursu- 
ance of a contract of apprenticeship. 
According to Black’s Law Dictionary, an apprentice is a person usually a minor, 
bound in due form of law to a master, to learn from his art, trade, or business and to 
serve him during the time of his apprenticeship. Under this Act, The term ‘appren- 
tice’ means a person who is undergoing apprenticeship training in the designated 
721 


722 The Apprentices Act, 1961 
trade in pursuance of a contract of apprenticeship. Therefore, “it is inherent in the 
word apprentice that there is no element of employment as such in a trade or industry 
but only an adequate well-guarded provision for training to enable the trainee after 
completion of his course to be suitably absorbed in earning employment as a regular 
worker. The fact that a career may have been absorbed in the company where he is 
undergoing the training, is not relevant for the purpose of comprehending the content 
of the time.” 
“Where under the terms and conditions of agreement under which apprentices are 
engaged by a company they are mere trainees for a particular period for a distinct 
purpose and the company is not bound to employ them in their work after their 
training period is over, such apprentices cannot be said to be employed in the work of 
the company or in connection with the work of the company more so when they are 
not given wages defined in section 2 (22). Thus an apprentice is not an employee 
within section 2(9) of the Act.” 
The period of training / apprenticeship cannot be treated as an employment.” 
4. Apprenticeship Training [s. 2(aaa)] 
“Apprenticeship training” means a course of training in any industry or establish- 
ment undergone in pursuance of a contract of apprenticeship and under prescribed 
terms and conditions which may be different for different categories of apprentices. 
5. Apprenticeship Adviser [s. 2(b)] 
‘Apprenticeship adviser” means the Central Apprenticeship Adviser appointed un- 
der section 26(1) or the State Apprenticeship Adviser appointed under section 26 (2). 
6. Apprenticeship Council [s. 2(c)]

Apprenticeship Council established under section 24(1). 
7. Appropriate Government [s. 2(d)]

(a) the Central Apprenticeship Council, or

nician (vocational) apprentices, or 
(d) any establishment of any railway, major port, mine or oil field, or 
(€) any establishment owned, controlled or managed by— 
(i) the Central Government or a department of the Central Govern- 
ment, . 
(ii) a company in which not less than fifty-one percent of the share 
capital is held by the Central Government or partly by Central 
Government and partly by one or more state Governments.
