1. Qualifications for being engaged as an apprentice [s. 3] - 
A person shall not be qualified for being engaged as an apprentice to undergo ap- 
prenticeship training in any designated trade, unless he— 
(a) is not less than fourteen years of age; and 
(b) satisfies such standards of education and physical fitness as may be pre- 
scribed. 
The person must have completed fourteen years of age and he must satisfy pre- 
scribed standards of education and physical fitness. In relation to apprenticeship 
training in different designated trades and for different categories of apprentices dif- 
ferent standards may be prescribed. 
2. Reservation of training places for the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled 
Tribes in designated trades [s. 3-A] 
In every designated trade the employer has to reserve training places for the 
Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the prescribed number. Where there is 
more than one designated trade in an establishment, such training places will also be 
reserved on the basis of the total number of apprentices in all designated trades in the 
such establishment. 
The number of training places will be prescribed on the basis of the population of 
the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes in the State concerned. 
The Explanation attached to the section provides that the expressions” Scheduled 
Castes’ and “Scheduled Tribes” will have the meanings as in clauses (24) and (25) of 
Article 366 of the Constitution. 
wy 


728 The Apprentices Act, 1961 
3. Contract of Apprenticeship [s. 4] 
To undergo apprenticeship training, it is necessary to have a contract of apprentice- 
ship with the employer. A person who wants to be engaged as an apprentice to un- 
dergo apprenticeship training in a designated trade has to enter into a contract of ap- 
prenticeship with the employer. In case he is a minor, his guardian may enter into a 
contract of apprenticeship with his employers. 
The apprenticeship training shall be deemed to have commenced on the date on 
which the contract of apprenticeship was entered into. Every contract of apprentice- 
ship may contain such terms and conditions as may be agreed to by the parties to the 
contract. Such terms and conditions will have to be consistent with the provisions of 
the Act or any rule made thereunder. 
Every contract of apprenticeship will be send for registration by the employer to 
the Apprenticeship Adviser within the prescribed period. If the Apprenticeship Ad- 
viser is satisfied that the person described as an apprentice in the contract is qualified 
under this Act for being engaged as an apprentice to undergo apprenticeship training 
in the designated trade specified in the contract, he. will register the contract of ap- 
prenticeship. 
The Central Government may, after consulting the Central Apprenticeship Council 
make any rule varying the terms and conditions of apprenticeship training of any 
‘category of apprentices undergoing such training. In case the Central Government 
makes any such rule varying the terms and conditions of apprenticeship training, 
then, the terms and conditions of every contract of apprenticeship relating to that 
category of apprentices and subsisting immediately before the making of such rule 
shall be deemed to have been modified accordingly. 
The respondent was appointed as an apprentice trainee and on completion of his 
training of 3 years was relieved as per terms of his appointment as an apprentice. He 
was held entitled to benefit of S. 25-F of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 relating to 
retrenchment by both the Labour Court as well as the High Court. It was held by the 
Supreme Court that section 4(4) of the Apprentices Act, 1961 relating to period 
within which the employer has to send every contract of apprenticeship to the Ap- 
prenticeship Adviser for registration is only directory and not mandatory. Thus, non- 
registration of apprenticeship contract will not change the character of apprentice or 
confer status of workmen to him. It was further held that the Labour Court or Indus- 
trial Tribunal will not have a jurisdiction to entertain disputes arising from termina- 
tion of service of apprenticeship. The respondent could not be declared to be a 
workman and claim the benefit of section 25-F of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. 
4. Novation of Contract of Apprenticeship [s. 5] 
_ Where an employer with whom a contract of apprenticeship has been entered into 
is unable to fulfill his obligations under the contract for any reason, novation of con- 
tract of apprenticeship is permitted under this section with the approval of the Ap- 
prenticeship Adviser. With the approval of the Apprenticeship Adviser if it is agreed 
between the employer, the apprentice or his guardian and any other employer that the 
apprentice shall be engaged as an apprentice under the other employer for the unex- 
pired portion of the apprenticeship training, the agreement, on registration with the 
Apprenticeship Adviser, shall be deemed to be the contract of apprenticeship be- 
tween the apprentice or his guardian and the other employer. The contract of appren- 
ticeship with the first employer will terminate or end from the date of such registra- 
1. UPSEB v. Shiv Mohan Singh, (2005) 1 LLJ 117 : (2004) 8 SCC 402. 


Chap. II—Apprentices and their Training 729 
tion. With the termination, no obligation under that contract will be enforceable at 
the instance of any party to the contract against the other party to the contract. 
5. Period of apprenticeship training [s. 6] 
The period of apprenticeship training, which shall be specified in the contract of 
apprenticeship, shall be as follows:— 
(a) in case of trade apprentices, who, having undergone institutional training in 
a school or other institution recognised by the National Council, have 
passed the trade tests or examinations conducted by that Council or by an 
institution recognised by that Council, the period of apprenticeship training 
will be such as may be determined by that Council. 
(b) in the case of trade apprentices who, having undergone institutional training 
in a school or other institution affiliated to or recognised by a Board or 
State Council of Technical Education or any other authority specified by 
the Central Government in this behalf, have passed the trade tests or ex- 
aminations conducted by that Board or State Council or authority, the pe- 
riod of apprenticeship training will be such as may be prescribed. The 
authority will be specified by the Central Government by notification in the 
Official Gazette. 
(c) in the case of other trade apprentices, the period of apprenticeship training 
will be such as may be prescribed. 
(d) in the case of graduate or technician apprentices, technician (vocational) 
apprentices, the period of apprenticeship training will be such as may be 
prescribed. 
6. Termination of Apprenticeship Contract [s. 7] _ 
The contract of apprenticeship terminates on the expiry of the period of apprentice- 
ship training. 
Either party to a contract of apprenticeship may make an application to the Ap- 
prenticeship Adviser for the termination of the contract. When such an application is 
made, a copy of it has to be sent to the other party to the contract by post.. 
After considering the contents of the application and the objections, if any, filed by 
the other party, the Apprenticeship Adviser, may terminate the contract by order in 
writing if he is satisfied, 
(i) that the parties to the contract have or any of them has failed to carry out 
the terms and conditions of the contract, and 
(ii) that it is desirable in the interests of the parties or any of them to terminate 
the same. 
Where a contract is terminated— 
(a) for failure on the part of the employer to carry out the terms and conditions 
of the contract, the employer will pay to the apprentice the prescribed com- 
pensation; 
(b) for such failure on the part of the apprentice, the apprentice or his euardian 
will refund to the employer as cost of training such amount as may be de- 
termined by the Apprenticeship Adviser. 


730 The Apprentices Act, 196] 
Notwithstanding anything contained in any other provision of this Act, where a 
contract of apprenticeship has been terminated by the Apprenticeship Adviser before 
the expiry of period of apprenticeship training and a new contract of apprenticeship 
is being entered into with a new employer, the Apprenticeship Adviser may, if he is 
satisfied that the contract of apprenticeship with the previous employer could not be 
completed because of any lapse on the part of the previous employer, permit the pe- 
riod of apprenticeship training already undergone by the apprentice with his previous 
employer to be included in the period of apprenticeship training to be undertaken 
with the new employer. 3 
7. Number of apprentices for a designated trade [s. 8] 
The Central Government after consulting the Central Apprenticeship Council will 
determine for each designated trade the ratio of trade apprentices to workers other 
than the unskilled workers in that trade by order notified in the Official Gazette. 
However, any employer may engage a number of trade apprentices in excess of the 
ratio determined by the Central Government. 
In determining the ratio, the Central Government shall have regard to facilities— 
(i) available for apprenticeship training under this Act in the designated trade 
concerned, as well as 
(ii) that may have to be made available by an employer for the training of 
graduate or technician apprentices, technician (vocational) apprentices, if 
any in pursuance of any notice issued to him under sub-section (3-A) by the 
Central Apprenticeship Adviser or such other referred person in that sub- 
section. 
The Apprenticeship Adviser, by notice in writing, may require an employer to en- 
gage such number of trade apprentices within the ratio determined by the Central 
Government for any designated trade in his establishment, to undergo apprenticeship 
training in that trade and the employer will comply with such requisition. But in 
making any such requisition, the Apprenticeship Adviser will have regard to the fa- 
cilities actually available in the establishment concerned. 
It is further provided that the Apprenticeship Adviser, on a representation made to 
him by an employer and keeping in view the more realistic employment potential, 
training facilities and other relevant factors, may permit him to engage such number 
of apprentices for a designated trade as is lesser than the number arrived at by the 
ratio for that trade, not being lesser than 20% of the number so arrived at. But this is 
subject to the condition that the employer shall engage apprentices in other trades in 
excess in number equal to such shortfall. 
The Central Apprenticeship Adviser or any other person not below the rank of an 
Assistant Apprenticeship Adviser authorised by the Central Apprenticeship Adviser 
in this behalf by writing shall, having regard to— 
(1) the number of managerial persons (including technical and supervisory per- 
sons) employed in a designated trade; 
(11) the number of management trainees engaged in the establishment; 
(ii1) the totality of the training facilities available in a designated trade; and 
(iv) such other factors as he may consider fit in the circumstances of the case. 


Chap. II—Apprentices and their Training 731 
by notice In writing, require an employer to impart training to such number of gradu- 
ate or technician apprentices, technician (vocational) apprentices in such trade in his 
establishment as may be specified in such notice and the employer will comply with 
such requisition. (Sub-Section 3-A),. 
The expression ‘management trainee’ here means a person who is engaged by an 
employer for undergoing a course of training in the establishment of the employer 
(not being apprenticeship training under this Act) subject to the condition that on 
successful completion of such training, such person shall be employed by the em- 
ployer on a regular basis. 
_ Several employers may join together for the purpose of providing practical training 
to the apprentices under them by moving them between their respective establish- 
ments. . 
Where having regard to the public interest, a number of apprentices in excess of 
the ratio determined by the Central Government or in excess of the number specified 
in a notice issued under sub-section (3-A) should in the opinion of the appropriate 
Government be trained, the appropriate Government may require employers to train 
the additional number of apprentices. Every employer to whom such requisition is 
made, shall comply with it if the Government concerned makes available such addi- 
tional facilities and such additional financial assistance as are considered necessary 
by the Apprenticeship Adviser for the training of the additional number of appren- 
tices. In case any employer is not satisfied with the decision of the Apprenticeship 
Adviser he may make a reference to the Central Apprenticeship Council. Such refer- 
ence will be decided by a Committee of the Central Apprenticeship Council ap- 
pointed by that Council for the purpose and the decision of that Committee shall be 
final. 
8. Practical and basic training of apprentices [s. 9] 
Every employer will make suitable arrangements in his workshop for imparting a 
course of practical training to every apprentice engaged by him in accordance with 
the programme approved by the Apprenticeship Adviser. 
The Central Apprenticeship Adviser or any other person not below the rank of an 
Assistant Apprenticeship Adviser authorised by the Central Apprenticeship Adviser 
in this behalf in writing shall be given all reasonable facilities to each such apprentice 
with a view to test his work and to ensure that the practical training is being imparted 
in accordance with the approved programme. 
The proviso says that the State Apprenticeship Adviser or any other person not 
below the rank of an Assistant Apprenticeship Adviser authorised by the State Ap- 
prenticeship Adviser in writing in this behalf shall also be given such facilities in 
respect of apprentices undergoing training in establishments in relation to which the 
appropriate Government is the State Government. 
Those trade apprentices who have not undergone institutional training in a school 
or other institution recognised by the National Council or any other institution affili- 
ated to or recognised by a Board or State Council of Technical Education or any 
other authority which the Central Government may specify in this behalf by notifica- 
tion in the Official Gazette, shall before admission in the workshop for practical 
training, undergo a course of basic training. 
Where an employer employs in his establishment five hundred or more workers, 
the basic training to the trade apprentices will be imparted either in separate parts of 
the workshop building or in a separate building which shall be set up by the em- 


78Z The Apprentices Act, 1961 
ployer himself. The appropriate Government may grant loans to employer on easy 
terms and repayable by easy installments to meet the cost of the land, construction 
and equipment for such separate building. 
Notwithstanding the abovestated provision, if the number of apprentices to be 
trained at any time in any establishment in which five hundred or more workers are 
employed, is less than twelve, the employer in relation to such establishment may 
depute all or any of such apprentices to any Basic Training Center or Industrial 
Training Institute for basic training in any designated trade, in either case, run by the 
Government. In case an employer deputes any such apprentice, the employer will pay 
to the Government the expenses incurred by the Government on such training, at the 
rates specified by the Central Government. 
Where an employer employs in his establishment less than five hundred workers, 
the basic training shall be imparted to the trade apprentices, in training institutes set 
up by the Government. 
In any such training institute, which shall be located within the premises of the 
most suitable establishment in the locality or at any other convenient place the trade 
apprentices engaged by two or more employers may be imparted basic training. 
In the case of an apprentice other than a graduate or a technician apprentice, tech- 
nician (vocational) apprentice, the syllabus of and the equipment to be utilised for, 
practical training including basic training shall be such as may be approved by the 
Central Government in consultation with the Central Apprenticeship Council. 
In the case of graduate or technician apprentices, technician (vocational) appren- 
tices the programme of apprenticeship training and the facilities required for such 
training, in any subject field in engineering or technology or vocational course shall 
be such as may be approved by the Central Government in consultation with the 
Central Apprenticeship Council. 
Recurring costs (including the costs of stipends) incurred by an employer in con- 
nection with basic training, imparted to trade apprentices shall be borne— 
(i) by the employer if such employer employs two hundred and fifty workers 
or more, 
(ii) by the employer and the Government in equal shares up to the limit laid 
down by the Central Government and beyond that limit, by the employer 
alone if such employer employs less than two hundred and fifty workers. 
This cost is not applicable to those trade apprentices— 
(a) who have undergone institutional training in a school or other institution 
recognised by the National Council, have passed by the trade tests or ex- 
aminations conducted by that council or by an institution recognised by that 
Council, and 
(b) who, having undergone institutional training in a school or other institution 
affiliated to or recognised by a Board or State Council of Technical Educa- 
tion or any other authority specified by the Central Government in this be- half by notification in Official Gazette, have passed by the trade tests or ex- aminations conducted by that Board or State Council or authority. 
In connection with practical training, including basic training imparted to above- stated two categories [(a) and (b)] of trade apprentices, the recurring costs (including 


Chap. [I—Apprentices and their Training 733 
the cost of stipends), if any, incurred by an employer, shall be borne by the employer 
in every case. 
Recurring costs (excluding the cost of stipends) incurred by an employer in con- 
nection with the practical training imparted to graduate or technician apprentices, 
technician (vocational) apprentices shall be borne by the employer and the cost of 
stipends shall be borne by the Central Government and the employer in equal shares 
upto the limits laid down by the Central Government and beyond that limit, by the 
employer alone. 
9, Related Instruction of apprentices [s. 10] 
A trade apprentice wks is undergoing practical training in an establishment shall 
be given a course of related instruction appropriate to the trade during the period of 
practical training. The instruction should be approved by the Central Government in 
consultation with the Central Apprenticeship Council. The instruction is given with a 
view to give the trade apprentice such theoretical knowledge as he needs in order to 
become fully qualified as a skilled craftsman. 
Related instruction shall be imparted at the cost of the appropriate Government but 
when so required, the employer will afford all facilities for imparting such instruc- 
tion. 
The time spent by a trade apprentice in attending classes on related instruction 
shall be treated as part of his paid period of work. 
In the case of trade apprentices who, after having undérgone a course of institu- 
tional training, have passed the trade tests conducted by the National Council or have 
passed the trade tests and examinations conducted by a Board or State Council of 
Technical Education or any other authority specified by the Central Government in 
this behalf, the related instruction may be given on such reduced or modified scale as 
may be prescribed. The authority will be specified by the Central Government by 
notification in the Official Gazette. 
Where any person during his course in a technical institution has become a gradu- 
ate or technician apprentice, technician (vocational) apprentice and during his ap- 
prenticeship training he has to receive related instruction, then, the employer shall 
release such person from practical training to receive the related instruction in such 
institution for such period as may be specified by the Central Apprenticeship Adviser 
or by any other person not below the rank of an Assistant Apprenticeship Adviser 
authorised by the Central Apprenticeship Adviser in writing in this behalf. 
10. Obligations of employers [s. 11] | 
Every employer has the following obligations in relation to an apprentice: — 
(a) to provide the apprentice with the training in his trade in accordance with 
the provisions of this Act and the rules made under it; 
(b) if the employer himself is not qualified in the trade, to ensure that a person 
who possesses the prescribed qualifications is placed in charge of the 
training of the apprentice; 
(c) to provide adequate instructional staff, possessing prescribed qualifications 
for imparting practical and theoretical training and facilities for trade test of 
apprentices; 
(d) to carry out his obligations under the contract of apprenticeship. 


734 The Apprentices Act, 196] 
These obligations of the employers are imposed without affecting the other provi- 
sions of this Act. 
“The entire Act is designed to advance industrial progress by providing properly 
trained apprentices. It is in the interests of the general public that the declaration of a 
particular trade has been made as a designated trade and in-fixing the ratio sufficient 
care has been taken in the Act to see that the public as well as representatives of 
trades and officers of the Government are all associated and sufficient guidelines 
have been provided for the selection of the trade as well as the ratio to be fixed. Sec- 
tion 11 makes it obligatory on the employer to provide training for the apprentice and 
section 13 provides for their remuneration. Section 12 provides for the relationship 
between the employer and the apprentice under a contract of apprenticeship. Though 
the restriction, to some extent, may interfere with the freedom of trade or business 
guaranteed under Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, they are reasonable as they are 
in the interests of trade and business and as such the interests of the general public 
are protected by the terms of Clause (6) of Article 19. The fact that an individual em- 
ployer finds it difficult to employ additional labour as an apprentice cannot be a rea- 
son for striking down the law as unreasonable.” 
11. Obligations of apprentices [s. 12] 
(1) Every trade apprentice undergoing apprenticeship training has the follow- 
ing obligations:— 
(a) to learn his trade conscientiously and diligently and endeavour to 
qualify himself as a skilled craftsman before the expiry of period of 
training, 
(b) to attend practical and instructional classes regularly; 
(c) to carry out all lawful orders of his employer and superiors in the es- 
tablishment; and 
(d) to carry out his obligations under the contract of apprenticeship. 
(2) Every graduate or technician apprentice, technician (vocational) apprentice 
undergoing apprenticeship training has the following obligations:— 
(a) to learn his subject field in engineering or technology or vocational 
course conscientiously and diligently at his place of training; 
(b) to attend the practical and instructional classes regularly; 
(c) to carry out all lawful orders of his employer and superiors in the es- 
tablishment; 
(d) to carry out his obligations under the contract of apprenticeship which shall include the maintenance of prescribed records of his work. 
12. Payment to apprentices [s. 13] 
The employer shall pay to every apprentice during the period of apprenticeship training stipend— 
(a) at a rate not less than the prescribed minimum rate, or 
(b) the rate which was being paid by the employer on 1“ January, 1970 to the category of apprentices under which such apprentice falls, whichever is

higher, as may be specified in the contract of apprenticeship. The stipend so 
an EUS Shall be paid subject to prescribed conditions and at prescribed 
intervals. : | 
An apprentice shall not be paid by his employer on the basis of piece work. He will 
also be not required to take part in any output bonus or other incentive scheme. 
13. Health, safety and welfare of apprentices [s. 14] 
Where any apprentices are undergoing training in a factory, the provisions of 
Chapters III, IV and V of the Factories Act, 1948 will apply in relation to health, 
Sate and welfare of the apprentices as if they were workers within the meaning of 
that Act. 
Where any apprentices are undergoing training in a mine, the provisions of Chapter 
V of the Mines Act, 1952 will apply in relation to health and safety of apprentices as 
if they were persons employed in the mine. 
14. Hours of work, overtime, leave and holidays [s. 15] 
The weekly and daily hours of work of an apprentice while undergoing practical 
training in a workshop will be such as may be prescribed. 
An apprentice will not be required or allowed to work overtime except with the ap- 
proval of the Apprenticeship Adviser who shall not grant such approval unless he is 
satisfied that such overtime is in the interest of training of the apprentice or in public 
interest. 3 
An apprentice will be entitled to prescribed leaves and to such holidays as are ob- 
served in the establishment in which he is undergoing training. 
15. Employer’s liability for compensation for injury [s. 16] 
If personal injury is caused to an apprentice, by accident arising out of and in the 
course of his training as an apprentice, his employer will be liable to pay him com- 
pensation. The compensation will be determined and paid in accordance with the 
provisions of the Workmen’s Compensation Act, 1923 and is subject to the modifi- 
cations specified in the Schedule. 
16. Conduct and discipline [s. 17] 
In all matters of conduct and discipline, the apprentice will be governed by the 
rules and regulations applicable to the employees of the corresponding category in 
the establishment in which the apprentice is undergoing training. 
17. Apprentices are trainees and not workers [s. 18] 
Save as otherwise provided in this Act,— 
(a) every apprentice undergoing apprenticeship training in a designated trade in 
an establishment shall be a trainee and not a worker, and 
(b) the provisions of any law with respect to labour shall not apply to or in re- 
lation to such apprentice. 
18. Records and Returns [s. 19] 
Every employer shall maintain records of the progress of training of each appren- 
tice undergoing apprenticeship training in his establishment in the prescribed from. 


736 The Apprentices Act, 1961 
Every such employer shall also furnish such information and return in prescribed 
form to prescribed authorities at prescribed intervals. 
19. Settlement of disputes [s. 20] 
Any disagreement or dispute between an employer and an apprentice arising out of 
the contract of apprenticeship shall be referred for decision to Apprenticeship Ad- 
viser. Any person aggrieved by the decision of Apprenticeship Adviser may, within 
30 days from the date of communication to him of such decision, prefer an appeal 
against the decision to the Apprenticeship Council. Such appeal shall be heard and 
determined by a Committee of that Council appointed for the purpose. The decision 
of the Committee shall be final and subject only to such decision, the decision of the 
Apprenticeship Adviser shall be final. 
20. Holding of test and grant of certificate and conclusion of training [s. 21] 
Every trade apprentice who has completed the period of training shall appear for a 
test to be conducted by the National Council to determine his proficiency in the des- 
ignated trade in which he has undergone his apprenticeship training. When the trade 
apprentice passes this test he is given a certificate of proficiency in the trade by the 
National Council. | 
The progress in apprenticeship training of every graduate or technician apprentice, 
technician (vocational) apprentice shall be assessed by the employer from time to 
time. 
Every graduate or technician apprentice, technician (vocational) apprentice, who 
completes his apprenticeship training to the satisfaction of the concerned Regional 
Board, is granted a certificate of proficiency by that Board. 
21. Offer and acceptance of employment [s. 22] 
It will not be obligatory on the part of the employer to offer any employment to 
any apprentice who has completed the period of his apprenticeship training in his 
establishment. It will also not be obligatory on the part of the apprentice to accept an 
employment under the employer. But where there is a condition in a contract of ap- 
prenticeship that the apprentice, after the successful completion of the apprenticeship 
training, will serve the employer, the employer shall be bound to offer suitable em- 
ployment to the apprentice on such completion of training. 
In such a case the apprentice shall be bound to serve the employer in that capacity 
for such period and on such remuneration as may be specified in the contract. 
Where in the opinion of the Apprenticeship Adviser such period or remuneration is 
not reasonable, he may revise such period or remuneration so as to make it reason- 
able. Such revised period or remuneration shall be deemed to be the period of remu- 
neration agreed to between the apprentice and the employer. 
In dealing with the claim of trainees to get employment after successful completion 
of their training the following points should be considered:— 
(1) Other things being equal, a trained apprentice should be given preference 
over direct recruits. 
_ (il) For this, a trainee would not be required to get his name sponsored by any 
employment exchange. 
(ii) If age bar would come in the way of the trainee, the same would be relaxed

concerned. If the service rule is silent on this aspect, relaxation to the extent

given. 
(iv) The training institute concerned would maintain a list of the persons trained

The persons trained earlier would be treated as senior to the persons trained later.

Certain diploma holders in Electrical Engineering Course were appointed as ap- 
prentices in the Technical Training Institute, Punjab State Electricity Board. This 
contract of apprenticeship provided that on successful completion of training the ap- 
prentice would be absorbed in the Department if there are vacancies. The Govern- 
ment of India issued instructions requesting inter alia the Punjab Electricity Board 
that trained apprentices be absorbed in industries upto a minimum of 50% of the di- 
rect requirement vacancies. A writ petition was filed by an apprentice challenging the 
advertisements issued by the Board on the ground that they are entitled to appointed 
upto 50% of the posts which are advertised. The Supreme Court held that in spite of 
the provisions contained in sub-section (1) of section 22 the employer is obliged to 
offer suitable employment to an apprentice if the contract of apprenticeship contains 
a provision that the apprentice shall serve the employer after successful completion 
of the training. When such an offer is made the apprentice is bound to serve the em- 
ployer. When the contract of apprenticeship is not happily worded in regard to ab- 
sorption after successful completion of training, it is not proper to indulge in hair- 
splitting approach and try to affect the right of employees, when the contract says 
that “ the apprentice shall be absorbed”’. It creates reciprocal rights and obligations on 
the employee and the employer.’ In such a case, offering employment to the appren- 
tice to the extent of 50% of the posts will not violate the law regarding reservation of 
posts because the entitlement to appointment is due to sub-section (2) of section 22 
and the contractual obligation arising out of the contracts of apprentices. 
The following principles have been laid down about claim of apprentices to get 
employment after successful completion of their training: — 
(1) Other things being equal, a trained apprentice should be given preference 
over direct recruits. 
(2) For this purpose, a trainee would not be required to get his name sponsored 
by any employment exchange. 
(3) If age bar comes in the way of the trainee, the same would be relaxed in 
accordance with the provisions in service rules. If the service rules are si- 
lent on this aspect, relaxation to the extent of the period for which the ap- 
prentice had undergone training would be given. 
(4) The training institute concerned would maintain a list of the person trained 
yearwise. The person trained earlier would be treated as senior to the per- 
sons trained later. In between the trained apprentices, preference shall be 
given to those who are senior.

The respondent completed one year training in the welders trade with Ma- 
hanadi Coal Fields Ltd. Some appointments were to be made in that organi- 
sation and the respondent was also called for the purpose. He was inter- 
viewed but no appointment letter was issued to him. He filed a writ petition 
praying for a mandamus to be issued asking the appellant to give him ap- 
pointment on the post of welder. The Supreme Court held that the Appren- 
tices Act, 1961 and the rules made thereunder showed that in the absence of 
any conditions in the contract of apprenticeship to the effect that the ap- 
prentice should serve the employer, an apprentice such as the respondent 
here could not claim any right to get employment on completion of his 
training. No writ of mandamus could be issued to the appellants to give ap- 
pointment to the respondent.

1. Authorities [s. 23] 
In addition to the Government, there are following authorities under the Act:— 
(a) The National Council; 
(b) The Central Apprenticeship Council; 
(c) The State Council; 
(d) The State Apprenticeship Council; 
(e) The All India Council; 
(f) The Regional Boards; 
(g) The Board or State Councils of Technical Education; 
(h) The Central Apprenticeship Adviser; 
(i) The State Apprenticeship Adviser. 
Every State Council will be affiliated to the National Council and every State Ap- 
prenticeship Council will be affiliated to the Central Apprenticeship Council. Every 
Board or State Council of Technical Education and every Regional Board will be 
affiliated to the Central Apprenticeship Council. 
Every authority in relation to apprentice ship training under this Act, performs such 
functions as are assigned to it by or under this Act or by the Government. However, a 
State Council will also perform such functions as are assigned to it by the National 
Council and the State Apprenticeship Council and the Board or State Council of 
Technical Education will also perform such functions as are assigned to it by the 
Central Apprenticeship Council, 
2. Constitution of Councils [s.24] — . 
The Central Apprenticeship Council: 
The Central Government establishes the Central Apprenticeship Council by notifi- 
cation in the Official Gazette. The Council consists of a Chairman and a Vice- 
739 


740 The Apprentices Act, 1961 
Chairman and such number of other members as the Central Government may think 
expedient. These members are appointed by the Central Government by notification 
in the Official Gazette from among the following categories of persons:— 
(a) representatives of employers in establishments in private and public sec- 
tors, 
(b) representatives of the Central Government and of the State Governments, 
(c) persons having special knowledge and experience on matters relating to 
industry, labour and technical education, 
(d) representatives of the All India Council and of the Regional Boards. 
The prescribed number of persons will be appointed as members from each of the 
abovestated categories. The term of office of members, the procedure to be followed 
in the discharge of their functions by, and the manner of filling vacancies among, the 
members of the Council shall be such as may be prescribed. 
_ The fees and allowances, if any, to be paid to the Chairman and the Vice-Chairman 
and the other members of the Council shall be such as may be determined by the 
Central Government. 
The State Apprenticeship Council: 
The State Government establishes the State Apprenticeship Council by notification 
in the Official Gazette. The Council consists of a Chairman and a Vice-Chairman and 
such number of other members as the State Government may think expedient. The 
members will be appointed by the State Government by notification in the Official 
Gazette from among the following categories of persons:— 
(a) representatives of employers in establishments in the public and private 
sectors, 
(b) representatives of the Central Government and of the State Governments, 
(c) persons having special knowledge and experience of matters relating to 
industry, labour and technical education, and . 
(d) representatives of the Board or of the State Council of Technical Education. 
The numbers of persons to be appointed as members of the State Apprenticeship 
Council from the above-stated categories, the term of office of, the procedure to be 
followed in the discharge of their functions by, and the manner of filling vacancies 
among, the members of the Council shall be such as the State Government may de- 
termine by notification in the Official Gazette. 
The fees and allowances, if any, to be paid to the Chairman and the Vice-Chairman 
and the other members of the Council shall be such as may be determined by the 
State Government. 
3. Vacancies not to invalidate acts and proceedings [s. 25] 
Any act done or proceeding taken by the National Council, the Central Apprentice- ship Council, the State Council or the State Apprenticeship Council under this Act will be questioned on the ground merely of the existence of any vacancy in, or defect in the Constitution of, such Council. 
4. Apprenticeship Advisers [s. 26] 
The Central Government appoints a suitable person as the Central Apprenticeship Adviser by notification in the Official Gazette. The State Government appoints a 


Chap. IlI—Authorities 741 
ais person as the State Apprenticeship Adviser by notification in the Official 
azette. 
The Central Apprenticeship Adviser shall be the secretary to the Central Appren- 
ticeship Council and the Apprenticeship Adviser shall be secretary to the State Ap- 
prenticeship Council. 
The Government may appoint suitable persons as Additional, Joint, Regional, 
Deputy and Assistance Apprenticeship Advisers to assist the Apprenticeship Adviser 
in the performance of his functions. All such advisers will be subject to control of the 
Apprenticeship Adviser and perform such functions as may be assigned to them by 
the Apprenticeship Adviser (s. 27). Every Apprenticeship Adviser and every Addi- 
tional, Joint, Regional, Deputy or Assistant Apprenticeship Adviser appointed under 
this Act, will be deemed to be a public servant within the meaning of section 21 of 
the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860) (s. 28). 
5. Power of entry, inspection, etc. [s. 29] 
Subject to any rules made in this behalf, the Central Apprenticeship Adviser, or 
such other person, not below the rank of an Assistant Apprenticeship Adviser, as 
may be authorised by the Central Apprenticeship Adviser in writing in this behalf, 
may— 
(a) enter, inspect and examine any establishment or its part at any reasonable 
time. He may take with him such assistants as he thinks fit; 
(b) examine any apprentice employed therein or require the production of any 
register record or other documents maintained in pursuance of this Act. He 
may take statements of any person on the spot or otherwise which he may 
consider necessary for carrying out the purposes of this Act. 
(c) make such examination and enquiry as he thinks fit in order to ascertain 
whether the provisions of this Act and the rules made under it are being ob- 
served in the establishment; 
(d) exercise such other powers as may be prescribed. 
Any of the above-stated powers may be exercised by a State Apprenticeship Ad- 
viser or such other person not below the rank of an Assistant Apprenticeship Adviser, 
as may be authorised by the State Apprenticeship Adviser in writing in this behalf. 
However, this power may be exercised only in relation to establishments for which 
the appropriate Government is the State Government. 
However, no person shall be compelled under this section to answer any question 
or make any statement which may tend to directly or indirectly incriminate him. 
6. Offences and Penalties [s. 30] 
(A) If any employer— 
(a) engages as an apprentice a person who is not so qualified for being so 
engaged, or 
(b) fails to carry out the terms and conditions of a contract of apprentice- 
ship, or 
(c) contravenes the provisions of this Act relating to the number of ap- 
prentices which he is required to engage under those provisions, 


742 The Apprentices Act, 1961 
He shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to six 
months or with fine or with both. 
(B) If any employer or other person— 
(a) required to furnish any information or return— 
(i) refuses or neglects to furnish such information or return, or 
(ii) furnishes or causes to be furnished any information or return 
which is false and which he either knows or believes to be false or 
does not believe to be true, or 
(iii) refuses to answer, or gives a false answer to any question neces- 
sary for obtaining any information required to be furnished by 
him, or 
(b) refuses or willfully neglects to afford, any reasonable facility for mak- 
ing any entry, inspection, examination or inquiry authorised by or un- 
der this Act, to the Central or the State Apprenticeship Adviser, or 
such other person not below the rank of an Assistant Apprenticeship 
Adviser, as may be authorised by the Central or the State Apprentice- 
ship Adviser in writing in this behalf. 
(c) requires an apprentice to work overtime without the approval of the 
Apprenticeship Adviser, or 
(d) employs an apprentice on any work which is not connected with his 
training, or 
(e) makes payment to an apprentice on the basis of piece-work, or 
(f) requires an apprentice to take part in any out-put bonus or incentive 
scheme, he shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which 
may extend to six months or with fine or with both. 
If any employer or any other person contravenes any provision of this Act for 
which no punishment is provided under section 30, he shall be punishable with fine 
which shall not be less than one thousand rupees, but may extend to three thousand 
rupees. (section 31) | 
7. Offences by companies [s. 32] 
If the person committing an offence under this Act is a company, every person, 
who at the time the offence was committed was in charge of, and was responsible to, 
the company for the conduct of business of the company, as well as the company, 
shall be deemed to be guilty of offence and shall be liable to be proceeded against 
and punished accordingly. 
But if he proves that the offence was committed without his knowledge or that he exercised all due diligence to prevent the commission of such offence, he will not be liable to punishment. 
In spite of the above provisions, where an offence has been committed by a com- pany under this Act and it is proved that the offence has been committed with the consent or connivance of, or is attributable to any negligence on the part of any di- rector, manager, secretary or other officer of the company, such director, manager, secretary or other officer of the company shall also be deemed to be guilty of that offence and shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly. 


Chap. III—Authorities 743 
For the purposes of this section— 
(a) “company” means body corporate and includes a firm or other association 
of individuals; and 
(b) “director’ in relation to a firm means a partner in the firm. 
8. Cognizance of offences [s. 33] 
The cognizance of any offence under this Act or any rules made under it will be 
taken by the Court only on a written complaint about it by the Apprenticeship Ad- 
viser or the officer of the rank of Deputy Apprenticeship Adviser and above. The 
complaint has to be made within six months from the date on which the offence is 
alleged to have been committed. 
9. Delegation of powers [s. 34] 
The appropriate Government may delegate any power exercisable by it under this 
Act or rules made under it by notification in the Official Gazette. The appropriate 
Government may direct that any power exercisable by it, in relation to such matters 
and subject to such conditions, if any, as may be specified in the direction be exercis- 
able also— 
(a) Where the appropriate Government is the Central Government, by such 
officer or authority subordinate to the Central Government, or by the State 
Government or by such officer or authority subordinate to the State Gov- 
ernment, as may be specified in the notification; and 
(b) Where the appropriate Government is the State Government, by such offi- 
cer or authority subordinate to the State Government, as may be specified 
in the notification. 
10. Construction of References [s. 35] 
(A) Unless the context otherwise requires, any reference in this Act or in the 
rules made under it to the Apprenticeship Council shall mean to apprentice- 
ship Training in a designated trade in an establishment in relation to which 
the Central Government is the appropriate Government, the Central Ap- 
prenticeship Council and in relation to apprenticeship training in a desig- 
nated trade in an establishment in relation to which the State Government is 
the appropriate Government, the State Apprenticeship Council. 
(B) Unless the context otherwise requires, any reference in this Act or in the 
rules made under it to the Apprenticeship Adviser shall— 
(a) mean in relation to apprenticeship training in a designated in an estab- 
lishment in relation to which the Central Government is the appropri- 
ate Government, the Central Apprenticeship Adviser and in relation to 
apprenticeship training in a designated trade in an establishment in re- 
lation to which the State Government is the appropriate Government, 
the State Apprenticeship Adviser. 
(b) be deemed to include an additional, Joint, a Regional, a Deputy or on 
Assistant Apprenticeship Adviser performing the functions of the Ap-- 
prenticeship Adviser as assigned to him by the Apprenticeship Adviser. 
11. Protection of action taken in good faith [s. 36] 
Any suit, prosecution, or other legal proceeding shall not lie against any person for 
anything which is in good faith done or intended to be done under this Act. 


744 The Apprentices Act, 1961 
12. Power to make rules [s. 37] 
The Central Government may make rules for carrying out the purposes of this Act 
after consultation with the Central Apprenticeship Council. The rules will be made 
by notification in the Official Gazette. 
Rules made under this Act may provide that a contravention of any such rule will 
be punishable with fine which may extend to fifty rupees. 
Every rule made under this section shall be laid as soon as may be after it is made 
before each House of Parliament while it is in session for a total period of thirty days 
which may be comprised in one session or more successive sessions. If, before the 
expiry of the session immediately following the session or the successive sessions 
aforesaid, both Houses agree in making any modification in the rule or both Houses 
agree that the rule should not be made, the rule shall thereafter have effect only in 
such modified form or be of no effect, as the case may be. However, any such modi- 
fication or annulment shall be without prejudice to the validity of anything previ- 
ously done under that rule i.e.,.it will not effect validity of any thing done before 
modification or annulment.

The Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 is an Act to provide for the payment of equal 
remuneration to men and women workers and for the prevention of discrimination on 
the ground of sex against women in the matter of employment and for other con- 
nected and incidental matters. 
1. Statement of Objects and Reasons 
Article 39 of the Indian Constitution envisages that the State shall direct its policy, 
among other things, towards securing that there is equal pay for equal work for both 
men and women. To give effect to this constitutional provision, the President prom- 
ulgated on the 26th September, 1975, the Equal Remuneration Ordinance, 1975 so 
that the provisions of article 39 of the Constitution may be implemented in the year 
which is being celebrated as the International Women’s Year. The ordinance pro- 
vides for payment of equal remuneration to men and women workers for the same 
work of a similar nature and for the prevention of discrimination on grounds of sex. 
The Ordinance also ensures that there will be no discrimination against recruitment 
of women and provides for the setting up of Advisory Committees to promote em- 
ployment opportunities for women. Later on the Ordinance was converted into the 
Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 (25 of 1976). 
2. Amendment Act 49 of 1987-Statement of Objects and Reasons 
The Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 while requiring equal payment to be made to 
men and women doing the same or similar work and stipulating that no discrimina- 
tion should be made between men and women workers in recruitment does not spe- 
cifically state that discrimination should not be made between men and women while 
in employment. This is a lacuna which can enable an employer to discriminate 
against women in matters like promotions, training, transfers, etc., It is, therefore, 
proposed to modify section 5 of the Act to prohibit discrimination against women not 
only in recruitment but also in relation to conditions of service subsequent to em- 
ployment such as promotions, training, transfers etc. 
Inspite of the Equal Remuneration Act having been passed more than 10 years ago 
there are several employers who continue to pay lower wages to women. One of the 
745 


746 The Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 
reasons for this is that the penalty laid down is not sufficiently stringent. The penal- 
ties fixed under section 10 are therefore being enhanced. 
Inspite of the known prevalence of disparity in wages between men and women, 
there have not been many reports of violations of the Act. It is, therefore, proposed to 
permit voluntary organisations, in addition to the inspecting staff to file complaints 
regarding violations of the Act. 
Section 15 of the Equal Remuneration Act is also being amended to specifically 
provide that it cannot be used to justify discriminatory practices against women 
workers. 
(I) Short title, extent and commencement [s. I] 
The Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 received the assent of the President on 11-2- 
1976 and extends to the whole of India. 
(IT) Definitions [s. 2] 
(1) Appropriate Government [s. 2(a)] 
‘“Appropriate Government” means— 
(1) in relation to any employment carried on by or under the authority of the 
Central Government or a railway administration, or in relation to a 
banking company, a mine, oilfield or major port or any corporation es- 
tablished by or under a Central Act, the Central Government, and 
(ii) in relation to any other employment, the State Government. 
(2) “Commencement of this Act” [s. 2(b)] 
“Commencement of this Act” means, in relation to an establishment or 
employment, the date on which this Act comes into force in respect of 
that establishment or employment. 
(3) Employer [s. 2(c)] 
“Employer” has the same meaning assigned to it in clause (f) of section 2 
of the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972. 
According to s. 2(f) of the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, “employer” 
means, in relation to any establishment, factory, mine, oilfield, plantation, 
port, railway company or shop— 
(i) belonging to, or under the control of, the Central Government or a 
State Government, a person or authority appointed by the appropriate 
Government for the supervision and control of employees, or where no person or authority has been so appointed, the head of ministry or the Department concerned, 
(ii) belonging to, or under the control of, any local authority, the person appointed by such authority for the supervision and control of employ- ees or where no person has been so appointed, the chief executive offi- cer of the local authority, 
(iil) in any other case, the person, who, or the authority which, has the ul- timate control over the affairs of the establishment, factory, mine, oil- field, plantation, port, railway company, or shop, and where the said 


The Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 747 
affairs are entrusted to any other person, whether called a manager, 
managing director or by any other name, such person. 
(4) “Man” and “woman” [s. 2(d)] 
“Man” and “woman” means male and female human beings, respectively, 
of any age. 
(5) Notification [s. 2(a)] 
“Notification” means a notification published in the Official Gazette. 
(6) “Prescribed” [s. 2(f)] 
“Prescribed” means prescribed by the rules made under this Act. 
(7) Remuneration [s. 2(g)] 
“Remuneration” means the basic wage or salary, and any additional 
emoluments whatsoever payable, either in cash or in kind, to a person em- 
ployed in respect of employment or work done in such employment, if the 
terms of the contract, express or implied, were fulfilled. 
(8) Same work or work of a similar nature [s. 2(h)] 
‘Same work or work of a similar nature’ means work in respect of which 
the skill, effort and responsibility required are the same, when performed 
under similar working conditions, by a man or a woman and the differ- 
ences, if any, between the skill, effort and responsibility required of a man 
and those required of a woman are not of practical importance in relation to 
the terms and conditions of employment. _ 
Whether a particular work is same or similar in nature to another work can 
be determined on three considerations: 
(i) the Authority should take a broad view of similarity; 
(ii) it should also take an equally broad view to decide whether the dif- 
ferences are of practical importance as the very concept of similar 
work implies differences in detail; the claim for equality should not 
be denied on trivial grounds; 
(111) duties actually performed and not those theoretically possible should 
be looked at.’ 
Where the question was whether “Agragamies” of West Bengal Civil Emergency 
Force were entitled to be placed in the scale on par with Firemen in the West Bengal 
Fire Service, it was held by the Supreme Court that the firemen and leaders are a 
specialised fire fighting personnel while agragamies are given elementary training in 
various fields. When called upon to assist, the agragamies assist fire fighting person- 
nel including firemen and leaders just as they assist personnel of other departments. 
It is idle to contend that they perform the same duties and functions as firemen and 
leaders. They assist not only the Fire Service Department but also Police, Municipal, 
Medical, Health, Social service Department etc. Merely because academic qualifica- 
tions and physical requirements of both are similar, it cannot be said that they per- 
1. Mackinnon Mackenzie & Co. Ltd. v. Audrey D’ Costa, (1987) 1 LLJ 536: AIR 1987 SC 1281. 


748 The Equal Remuneration Act, 1 976 
form similar duties, functions and responsibilities as leaders and firemen and there- 
fore, the same scale cannot be granted to them. 
Whenever sex discrimination is alleged, there should be a proper job evaluation be- 
fore proceeding any further. If two jobs are accorded an equal value on the basis of 
non-discriminatory criteria (by looking directly at the nature and extent of the job’s 
demand) as distinct from other criteria setting out different values for man and 
women on the same demand and the two employed on the job are paid differently, it 
was held that it clearly amounts to sex discrimination, 
In a case, the responds are working in Higher Secondary Schools in M.P. and con- 
ditions of their service are governed by Madhya Pradesh Non-Gazetted Class III 
Educational Service (Non-Collegiate Branch Service) Recruitment and Promotion 
Rules, 1973. In other Higher Secondary Schools in M. P, the lecturers are categorised 
as technical and non-technical lecturers. The conditions of service of lecturers in 
these schools are governed by M. P. Education Department (Technical) Class III 
Non-Ministerial Recruitment Rules, 1980. It was held that it is not sufficient to say 
that their qualifications are the same, the schools are of the same status or that the 
service conditions are similar. But whether they discharge similar duties, functions 
and responsibilities. There is no material to show that the duties, functions and func- 
tions of both the categories of lecturers are identical or similar. Though Equal Remu- 
neration Act, 1976 is mainly directed against discrimination against workmen and is 
not applicable to respondents or applicants to which they belong, yet relevance of the 
definition cannot be denied. The Equal Remuneration Act lays stress upon the simi- 
larity of the skill, effort and responsibility when performed under similar conditions. 
Therefore, the Equal Remuneration Act would not apply to the respondents. 
The principle of equal pay for equal work would not apply where educational 
qualifications and other considerations such as source of recruitment and nature of 
work done vary between two classes of employees, although the nature of work done 
is the same. 
(9) Worker [s. 2(i)] 
“Worker” means a worker in any establishment or employment in respect 
of which this Act has come into force. 
(10) Words and Expressions [s. 2(j)] 
Words and expressions used in this Act and not defined but defined in the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 shall have the same meanings respectively 
assigned to them in that Act. 
(III) Act to have Overriding Effect [s. 3] 
The provisions of this Act have effect notwithstanding anything inconsis- 
tent therewith contained in any other law or in the terms of any award, 
agreement or contract of service, whether made before or after the com- 
mencement of this Act, or in any instrument having effect under any law 
for the time being in force.

1. Duty of Employer to pay equal remuneration to men and women workers 
for same work or work of a similar nature [Section 4] | 
No employer shall pay remuneration to any worker employed by him in an estab- 
lishment or employment at rates less favourable than those at which remuneration is 
paid by him to the workers of the opposite sex in such establishment or employment 
for performing the same work or work of a similar nature. The remuneration may be 
payable in cash or in kind, for complying with this provision, no employer shail re- 
duce the rate of remuneration of any worker. 
Where, in an establishment or employment, the rates of remuneration payable be- 
fore the commencement of this Act for men and women workers for the same work 
or work of a similar nature are different only on the ground of sex, then 
higher/highest of such rates shall be rate at which remuneration shall be payable to 
such men and women workers, on and from such commencement. Higher rate will be 
applicable where only two rates are present. 
In case more than two rates are prevailing, then the highest of them will become 
the rate payable. 
However, the above-stated will not be deemed to entitle a worker to the revision of 
the rate of remuneration payable to him or her with reference to the service rendered 
by him or her before the commencement of this Act. 
Where the confidential lady stenographers were doing the same work or work of a 
similar nature which the male stenographers were doing, they were held entitled to 
equal remuneration in spite of an agreement between the management and employ- 
ees’ union providing difference between the remuneration of the male and the lady 
749 


750 Chap. 11—Payment Of Remuneration At Equal Rates 
stenographers, respectively. It was held that the settlement has to yield to the provi- 
sions of the Act. 
2. No Discrimination in Recruitment [s. 5] 
Section 5 prohibits employers from discriminating women in recruitment on and 
from the commencement of this Act. No employer shall make any discrimination 
against women while making recruitment for the same work or work of a similar na- 
ture or in any condition of service subsequent to recruitment such as promotions, 
training or transfer except where the employment of women in such work is prohib- 
ited or restricted by or under any law for the time being in force. Thus, only in those 
works where employment of women is prohibited or restricted by or under any law 
for the time being in force, the women can be denied work by the employer. 
The provisions of this section do not affect any priority or reservation for sched- 
uled castes or scheduled tribes, ex-servicemen, retrenched employees or any other 
class or category of persons in the matter of recruitment to the posts in an establish- 
ment or employment. 
3. Advisory Committee [s. 6] 
The appropriate Government will constitute one or more Advisory Committees for 
the purpose of providing increasing employment opportunities for women. The Ad- 
visory Committee advises the appropriate Government with regard to the extent to 
which women may be employed in such establishments or employments as the Cen- 
tral Government may notify in this behalf. 
Every Advisory Committee consists of not less than ten persons, to be nominated 
by the appropriate Government, of which one-half shall be women. The Advisory 
Committee regulates its own procedure. 
In tendering its advice, the Advisory Committee takes into consideration the fol- 
lowing: — 
(i) the number of women employed in the concerned establishment or em- 
ployment, 
(11) the nature of work, 
(ii1) hours of work, 
(iv) suitability of women for employment 
(v) the need for providing increasing employment opportunities for women, 
including part-time employment, and 
(vi) such other relevant factors as the Committee may think fit. 
The appropriate Government may, after considering the advice tendered to it by the 
Advisory Committee and after giving to the persons concerned in the establishment or 
employments an opportunity to make representations, issue such directions in respect 
of employment of women workers, as the appropriate Government may think fit. 
4. Authorities for hearing and deciding complaints and claims [s. 7] 
The appropriate Government may appoint such officers, not below the rank of a 
ae Officer, as it thinks fit to be the authorities for the purpose of hearing and 
eciding— j 
1. Mackinnon Mackenzie & Co. Ltd. v. Avdrey D’ Costa, (1987) 1 LLJ 536 : AIR 1987 SC 1281. 


Part X—The Employees Provident Funds and Miscellaneous etc., Tol 
(a) Complaints with regard to the contravention of any provision of this Act; 
(b) Claims arising out of non-payment of wages at equal rates to men and 
women workers for the same work or work of a similar nature. 
The authorities are appointed by the appropriate Government by notification and 
by the same or subsequent notification, it may define the local limits within which 
each such authority shall exercise its jurisdiction. 
Every claim or complaint shall be made in the prescribed manner. If any question 
arises as to whether two or more works are of the same nature or of a similar nature, 
the appointed authority will decide the question. Where a complaint or claim is made 
to the authority it may, after giving the applicant and the employer an opportunity of 
being heard, and after such inquiry it may consider necessary, direct— 
(i) in the case of a claim arising out of non-payment of wages at equal rates to 
men and women workers for the same work or work of a similar nature, 
that payment be made to the worker of the amount by which the wages 
payable to him exceed the amount actually paid; 
(1i) in the case of complaint, that adequate steps be taken by the employer so as 
to ensure that there is no contravention of any provision of this Act. 
Every authority appointed under the section shall have all the power of a Civil 
Court under the Civil Procedure Code, 1908, for the purpose of taking evidence and 
of enforcing the attendance of witnesses and compelling the production of docu- 
ments. Every such authority shall be deemed to be a Civil Court for all the purposes 
of section 195 and Chapter XXVI of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. 
Any worker or employer aggrieved by any order made by the authority may prefer 
an appeal against his order. The appellate authority will be specified by the appropri- 
ate Government by notification. The appellate authority may after hearing the appeal 
confirm, modify or reverse the order appealed against. No further appeal shall lie 
against the order made by the appellate authority. 
An appeal may be preferred within thirty days from the date of the order of the 
authority. If the authority is satisfied that the appellant was prevented by sufficient 
cause from preferring the appeal within the specified period of thirty days, it may 
allow the appeal to be preferred within a further period of thirty days but not there- 
after. 
The provisions of section 33-C(1) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 apply for 
the recovery of money due from an employer arising out of decision of an authority 
appointed under this section.

CHAPTER III 
5. Duty of Employers to maintain registers [s. 8] 
On and from the commencement of Equal Remuneration Act, 1976, a duty has 
been imposed on every employer to maintain prescribed registers and other docu- 
ments in relation to the workers employed by him. 
6. Inspectors [s. 9] 
The appropriate Government may appoint such persons as it thinks fit to be In- 
spector by notification. The Inspectors are appointed for the purpose of making an 


752 Chap. III— Miscellaneous 
investigation as to whether the provisions of this Act, or the rules made under it are 
being complied with by employers. The appropriate Government may define the lo- 
cal limits within which an Inspector may make such investigation. 
Every Inspector shall be deemed to be a public servant within the meaning of sec- 
tion 21 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. 
An Inspector may, at any place within the local limits of his jurisdiction— 
(a) enter, at any reasonable time, any building, factory, premises or vessel. He 
may take such assistance as he thinks fit; 
(b) require any employer to produce any register, muster roll or other docu- 
ments relating to the employment of workers, and examine such docu- 
ments; 
(c) take on the spot or otherwise, the evidence of any person for the purpose of 
ascertaining whether the provisions of this Act have been complied with or 
are being complied with. 
(d) examine the employer, his agent or servant or any other person found in 
charge of the establishment or any premises connected therewith or any 
person whom the Inspector has reasonable cause to believe to be, or to have 
been a worker in the establishment; 
(e) make copies or take extracts from, any register or other document main- 
tained in relation to the establishment under this Act. 
Any person required by an Inspector to produce any register or other document or 
to give any information shall comply with such requisition. 
7. Penalties [s. 10] 
(1) If after the commencement of this Act, any employer, being required by or un- 
der the Act, so to do— 
(a) omits or fails to maintain any register or other document in relation to 
workers employed by him, or 
(b) omits or fails to produce any register, muster-roll or other document 
relating to the employment of workers, or 
(c) omits or refuses to give any evidence or prevents his agent, servant, or 
any other person in charge of the establishment, or any worker, from 
giving evidence, or 
(d) omits or refuses to give any information, 
he shall be punishable with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to one 
month or with fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees or with both. 
(2) If, after the commencement of this Act, any employer— 
(a) makes any recruitment in contravention of the provisions of this Act, or 
(b) makes any payment of remuneration at unequal rates to men and women 
workers, for the same work or work of a similar nature, or 
(c) makes any discrimination between men and women workers in contra- 
vention of the provisions of this Act, or 


Part X—The Employees Provident Funds and Miscellaneous etc., 753 
(d) omits or fails to carry out any direction made by the appropriate Gov- ernment section 6. (sub-sec. (5)) 
he shall be punishable with fine which shall not be less than ten thousand rupees but which may extend to twenty thousand rupees or with imprisonment for a term which shall be not less than three months but which may extend to one year or with both for the first offence, and with imprisonment which may extend to two years for the sec- ond and subsequent offences. 
(3) If any person being required so to do, omits or refuses to produce to an Inspec- tor any register or other document or to give any information, he shall be punishable with fine which may extend to five hundred rupees. 
8. Offences by companies [s. 11] 
Where an offence under this Act has been committed by a company, every person who, at the time the offence was committed, was in charge of, and was responsible to, the company, for the conduct of the business of the company, as well as the com- pany, shall be deemed to be guilty of the offence and shall be liable to be proceeded 
against and punished accordingly: 
Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section shall render any such person li- 
able to any punishment, if he proves that the offence was committed without his 
knowledge or that he had exercised all due diligence to prevent the commission of 
such offence (sub-section (1)). 
Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), where any offence under 
this Act has been committed by a company and it is proved that-the offence has been 
committed with the consent or connivance of, or is attributable to, any neglect on the 
part of any director, manager, secretary or other officer of the company, such direc- 
tor, manager, secretary or other officer shall be deemed to be guilty of that offence 
and shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly (sub-section 
(2)). 
Explanation.—For the purposes of this section.— 
(a) “company” means any body corporate and includes a firm or other associa- 
tion of individuals; and 
(b) “director’’, in relation to a firm, means a partner in the firm. 
9. Cognizance and trial of offences [s. 12] 
No Court inferior to that of a Metropolitan Magistrate or a Judicial Magistrate of 
the first class shall try any offence punishable under this Act (sub-section (1)) 
No Court shall take cognizance of an offence punishable under this Act except 
upon— 
(a) its own knowledge or upon a complaint made by the appropriate Govern- 
ment or an officer authorised by it in this behalf, or 
(b) a complaint made by the person aggrieved by the offence or by any recog- 
nised welfare institution or organisation. (sub-section (2)) 
Explanation.—For the purposes of this sub-section “recognised welfare institution 
or organisation” means a social welfare organisation or institution recognised in this 
behalf by the Central or State Government. : 


754 Chap. III— Miscellaneous 
10. Power to make rules [s. 13] 
The Central Government may, by notification, make rules for carrying out the pro- 
visions of this Act. 
Such rules may provide for all or any of the following matters, namely:— 
(a) the manner in which complaint or claim referred to in sub-section (1) of 
section 7 shall be made; 
(b) registers and other documents which an employer is required under section 
8 to maintain in relation to the workers employed by him; 
(c) any other matter which is required to be, or may be, prescribed. 
Every rule made by the Central Government under this Act shall be laid, as soon as 
may be after it is made, before each House of Parliament, while it is in session, for a 
total period of thirty days which may be comprised in one session or in two or more 
successive sessions, and if, before the expiry of the session immediately following 
the session or the successive sessions aforesaid, both Houses agree in making any 
modification in the rule or both Houses agree that the rule should not be made, the 
rule shall thereafter have effect only in such modified form or be of no effect, as the 
case may be; so, however, that any such modification or annulment shall be without 
prejudice to the validity of anything previously done under that rule. 
11. Power of Central Government to give directions [s. 14] 
The Central Government may give directions to a State Government as to the car- 
rying into execution of this Act in the State. (sub-section (7)) 
12. Act not to apply in certain special cases [s. 15] 
Nothing in this Act shall apply— 
(a) to cases affecting the terms and conditions of a woman’s employment in 
complying with the requirements of any law giving special treatment to 
women, or 
(b) to any special treatment accorded to women in connection with— 
(i) the birth or expected birth of a child, or 
(ii) the terms and conditions relating to retirement, marriage or death or to 
any provision made in connection with the retirement, marriage or 
death. 
13. Power to make declaration [s. 16] 
Where the appropriate Government is, on a consideration of all the circumstances 
of the case, Satisfied that the differences in regard to the remuneration, or a particular 
species of remuneration, of men and women workers in any establishment, or em- ployment is based on a factor other than sex, it may, by notification, make a declara- 
tion to that effect, and any act of the employer attributable to such a difference shall not be deemed to be a contravention of any provision of this Act. 
14. Power to remove difficulties [s. 17] 
If any difficulty arises in giving effect to the provisions of this Act, the Central Government may, by notification, make any order, not inconsistent with the provi- aN this Act, which appears to it to be necessary for the purpose of removing the ifficulty: E 


Part X—The Employees Provident Funds and Miscellaneous etc., ToS 
Provided that every such order shall, as soon as may be after it is made, be laid be- fore each House of Parliament. 
15. Repeal and saving [s. 18] 
The Equal Remuneration Ordinance, 1975 (12 of 1975), is hereby repealed. 
Notwithstanding such repeal, anything done or any action taken under the Ordi- nance, so repealed (including any notification, nomination, appointment, order or direction made thereunder) shall be deemed to have been done or taken under the corresponding provisions of this Act, as if this Act were in force when such thing 
was done or action was taken.
